News.title: Oasis 2027 tour live: How to register for tickets as full tour dates and prices revealed
News.content:
Oasis have finally confirmed their upcoming Live '27 tour, with a string of dates across the UK and Ireland next year and shared details on how to get hold of tickets

The news you've all been waiting for – the 'period of reflection' is over and Oasis are back. Following months of speculation, the Manchester legends have confirmed they're hitting the road again.

And fans don't have to wait long. They'll kick off with their first show on May 21 at Glasgow's Celtic Park, before concluding their five Scotland shows on May 29. After a few days off, they'll be returning to their hometown for 11 dates at the Etihad Stadium, with their first show taking place on June 4, before wrapping up on June 26.

After touring around Europe and America, they'll be back to perform four shows at Knebworth on September 11, 12, 18 and 19. Noel has also confirmed that this tour announcement has been a year in the making. But fans hoping to get their hands on tickets need to be quick. A registration system has been implemented to reduce wait times in virtual queues and prevent ticket touting.

Fans must register by 4pm BST on September 17. Those who are successful will receive a non-transferable code to access their allocated on-sale window. Ticket sales will take place in the UK on September 25, 26 and 27, with three windows each day.

Speaking on TalkSport tonight, he said the decision to tour again was made after their second Wembley show last year. He said: "Nobody knew what was going to happen and how it was going to go. We did Cardiff and Manchester, and by the time we got to Wembley, someone said 'Well y'know...' And yeah, it was decided we were gonna do it. And it was all set in motion then."

But, unfortunately, there won't be any new music from the band. "There won't be any new music, no," he revealed. And could the band continue after 2027? "I dunno," Noel said.

Like this story? For more of the latest showbiz news and gossip, follow Mirror Celebs on TikTok, Snapchat, Instagram, Twitter, Facebook, YouTube and Threads.

News.title: UK weather maps show 16 areas forecast to hit 27C in September heatwave - full list
News.content:
UK weather maps show 16 areas forecast to hit 27C in September heatwave - full list

The UK is set to warm up once again within just 10 days as temperatures could reach 27C in multiple parts of the nation, according to weather maps by forecaster WXCharts

View 3 Images The orange hues denote the warmer areas on September 24 (Image: WXCharts)

This striking weather map shows large swathes of the UK will experience one last heatwave this year.

‌



Conditions are poised to get warmer once more in just 10 days, with temperatures potentially hitting 27C across several regions. This is significantly greater than the average temperature for September.

‌



Although the hottest weather is anticipated on September 24, it should be warm enough for several days to meet the official heatwave criteria in multiple areas. This would then become the sixth heatwave the UK will have experienced this year.

‌



The map above is taken using the forecast for September 24 when the mercury across southern and central England could rise to 27C.

Parents warned Halloween pumpkins could be too small to carve this year after drought wreaks havoc READ MORE :

View 3 Images People enjoy the warm weather on Porthminster Beach in St Ives, Cornwal (Image: Joe Sene/PA Wire)

Along the south coast, temperatures could surge to 26C from Brighton through to Portsmouth, while Cornwall will remain cooler at approximately 21C. Temperatures are forecast to reach around 21C as far north as Cumbria.

‌



Wales may enjoy some relief with temperatures hovering around 22-23C, while Scotland and Northern Ireland are likely to see highs in the late teens.

However, the Met Office's long-range forecast for September 19-28 presents a different picture to WXCharts. It indicated conditions are set to stay unsettled, with intermittent rain or showers pushing in from the North Atlantic, occurring most frequently across northern and western regions of the UK, with strong winds expected at times, reports the Express.

It continued: "There will also be some reasonably dry and more settled periods in between these systems, especially across southern areas.

Article continues below

"There is a chance settled weather may expand further northwards during the final week of September. Temperatures for the period as a whole will probably be close to average overall, but there is scope for some rather warm days at times, as well as relatively cool nights which may bring the occasional grass frost."

View 3 Images Due to the heatwaves, grasslands like this on Wimbledon Common have become dry and parched (Image: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock)

Full list of counties with 27C anticipated in September

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle switch Archie and Lilibet's school following security concerns
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle switch Archie and Lilibet's school following security concerns

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s children spent two days settling into their new school last week and meting classmates - but now Harry and Meghan have made a switch

View 3 Images Meghan Markle and Prince Harry have changed their kids' school (Image: Getty Images)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have moved their children to a new school just two days after they started — following security concerns over the school run.

‌



Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, had only spent two days at their original school last week, meeting classmates and settling in, before the Duke and Duchess of Sussex reluctantly decided to withdraw them.

‌



Sources close to the couple stressed that there was no problem with the school itself, with concerns instead focused on the practicalities and security of getting the children there and back each day.

‌



Heavy traffic in the area and the distance between the school and the family’s current home are understood to have put pressure on their small private security team.

Prince Harry step closer to taxpayer funded security after Home Office green lights new review READ MORE :

View 3 Images Meghan recently shared a candid video of her time back in the UK (Image: INSTAGRAM)

One incident reportedly made it difficult for their vehicles to remain together in convoy, prompting further concerns about whether the school run could be carried out safely.

‌



Harry and Meghan’s security team had carried out checks on the school during the summer, after the couple decided to return to the UK, but were unable to properly assess the school run until the new term began.

A friend of the couple told HELLO!: “It’s a real shame, because they absolutely adored the school, the kids and their parents.

“It was perfect for them in every way and the children really enjoyed their time there. They really wanted to make it work, but they had to make a difficult decision based on the fact that the team couldn’t make the school run operationally secure.”

‌



View 3 Images Sources close to Meghan and her husband say the decision has been a difficult one (Image: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP)

The children will now attend another school in the area after visiting for a taster session on Monday, it is believed.

Harry was reportedly spotted settling Lilibet into reception, while the couple have also been added to parents’ WhatsApp groups.

‌



A spokesman for Harry and Meghan said: “The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements.

“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

“This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”

‌



The abrupt move comes as Harry continues to push for greater security protection for his family while they are in the UK.

Meghan has also been granted her first government-backed security review since the couple stepped down as working royals in 2020.

The Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec) has asked Harry and Meghan to provide details of their daily routines, including the school run, as part of an assessment of any changes to the threat they face.

‌



Harry has been fighting to have his VIP police protection reinstated since September 2021 and pursued a legal challenge through the courts until May 2025, when he lost his Court of Appeal case.

At the time, he told the BBC: “I can’t see a world in which I would bring my wife and children back to the UK at this point.”

‌



But last December, it emerged that Ravec’s Risk Management Board would review his case, with the process beginning in July this year.

Security concerns were also raised during the family’s visit to the UK in June, when Meghan pulled out of planned public appearances alongside Harry, with their team citing concerns about security in central London.

In August, Harry and Meghan announced they would be moving back to the UK with their children for an extended period, with Archie and Lilibet subsequently enrolled at a school close to their new home.

Article continues below

The Duke is due to make a number of public appearances in the coming days, although it has not yet been confirmed whether Meghan will join him.

News.title: UK weather maps show 28C heat surge with 37 counties reaching 25C or more – full list
News.content:
UK weather maps show 28C heat surge with 37 counties reaching 25C or more – full list

A late-month warm spell could see temperatures climb to 25C or higher in parts of England and Wales, according to new weather maps

View 2 Images Large parts of England could see a spell of warm weather in 10 days (Image: Maureen McLean/Shutterstock)

Britain could see a spell of much warmer weather later this month, with temperatures potentially reaching 25C or more in 37 counties.

‌



Forecasts indicate that areas of high pressure could have a greater influence on the weather during the last week of September, bringing a return to above-average daytime temperatures and some drier spells.

‌



The warmer conditions would come after an unsettled week. The Met Office is forecasting changeable weather over the next seven days, with bands of rain, blustery winds and heavy showers moving in from the Atlantic, interspersed with some drier and brighter interludes.

‌



But on September 24 (Thursday), maximum temperature maps from WXCharts, using ECMWF's high-resolution weather model, suggest the mercury could climb to a very warm 28C in parts of southern England, particularly London and the Home Counties.

Large parts of southern England and the Midlands, as well as parts of northern England and eastern Wales, could also see highs of 25C or more, according to the maps.

View 2 Images Long-range forecasts suggest areas of high pressure could have a greater influence on the weather towards the end of September (Image: WXCharts)

Scientists note that long-range forecasts are useful for giving a broad indication of temperature trends but cannot reliably predict conditions on a specific day several weeks in advance. The Met Office says that beyond a week, day-to-day weather becomes increasingly difficult to forecast.

‌



Earlier this month, the national weather service announced that the summer of 2026 - which had an average mean temperature of 16.5C - was provisionally the hottest on record in the UK.

The summer was also among the sunniest on record in some parts of the country and was notably dry for many areas, although late-season rainfall prevented several places from breaking low-rainfall records.

Dr Amy Doherty, who leads the National Climate Information Centre at the Met Office, said: "The conditions we’ve seen this summer have broken UK climate records once again. These records are now breaking with increasing frequency, reflecting the influence of human-induced climate change on the temperatures we’re experiencing in the UK.

Article continues below

"Particularly notable is how much we’ve exceeded the previous summer mean temperature record, set just last year. The figures also knock the infamous summer of 1976 down to seventh for average summer mean temperature, with the top five warmest summers all occurring since 2003."

A recent rapid climate attribution study conducted by Met Office scientists revealed that the record-breaking summer was made around 130 times more likely because of human-induced climate change.

This warming trend is expected to continue as the global average temperature increases in response to greenhouse gas emissions.

News.title: Deadly danger from toxic Nazi U-boat sank by Britain 80 years ago remains today
News.content:
Deadly danger from toxic Nazi U-boat sank by Britain 80 years ago remains today

The Nazi U-864 submarine was torpedoed by the HMS Venturer near the island of Fedje, Norway towards the end of the Second World War - and is still leaking toxic mercury into the environment

View 2 Images The Nazi U-boat is still toxic over 80 years on (artist's impression) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Norwegian authorities face a difficult decision over a toxic Nazi U-boat buried on the seabed after it was found to be leaking 67 tonnes of liquid mercury.

‌



The U-864, a German Type IXD2 submarine, was torpedoed by the HMS Venturer near the island of Fedje on February 9, 1945, just three months before the end of Second World War in Europe.

‌



It has sat 492ft beneath the surface on the seabed ever since, where it has slowly leaked liquid mercury from its rusting steel containers.

‌



Amid calls for the U-boat to be recovered to protect sea life and the local fishing industry, Norway's coastal administration sent a robot vehicle down to the scene of the wreck in June to investigate.

View 2 Images It was sunk just three months before the end of World War II after a Nazi plan was rumbled (Image: Mirrorpix)

Iconic Spitfires honoured at Duxford Battle of Britain airshow to mark 90-year milestone READ MORE :

The voyage revealed the alarming scale of the toxic risk of the U-boat - finding that 80% of the 22 containers recovered for analysis had actively leaked mercury into the seabed.

‌



Earlier this month, they concluded in a report that the wreck and the area around it should be entombed in a protective covering that would prevent any further leakage.

Officials said that that lifting the U-boat would be too risky, as moving it in its rusted, degraded condition risked the containers falling and spreading the mercury further, in a higher concentration.

The Norwegian government, which has already spent over 400 million NOK (£31.8million) on various studies regarding the U-864, said they were currently considering the report's findings.

Article continues below

Local campaigners have argued for years that the U-boat wreck should be removed entirely, as they fear covering the wreck could inadvertently cause the German torpedoes still stowed on the vessel the boat to detonate, or crush the remaining containers filled with mercury.

But the plan - which could have seen Japan build advanced jet fighters and missiles to defend its occupied territory in Asia - was rumbled by the British intelligence services, who had cracked the German navy's Enigma code.

The HMS Venturer fired four torpedoes at the ship, the final of which struck its target, killing all 73 personnel on board.. It was the only time a submerged submarine sank another throughout all of World War II, with all other fatal hits coming when one of the subs was on the surface.

News.title: Husband admits drugging his wife to sexually abuse and rape her over 20-year period
News.content:
Husband admits drugging his wife to sexually abuse and rape her over 20-year period

The man in his 60s, who is from the Stockport area, choked back tears after he pleaded guilty to 60 charges at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court on Monday

View Image Man in his 60s has admitted drugging and raping his wife over a 20 year period (Image: MEN Media)

A man in his 60s has admitted drugging and raping his wife over a 20-year period.

The husband, from the Stockport area, pleaded guilty to 60 charges at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

The man, who cannot be named as it would identify his wife, choked back tears as he entered his pleas.

His wife sat in the public gallery being comforted by family members as her husband entered guilty pleas over 18 minutes.

She wiped her eyes, while her husband, wearing a dark grey suit, blue shirt and dark tie, stood in the dock with his hands clasped in front of him.

Judge Maurice Greene told him he could sit as he broke down in tears while entering his guilty pleas.

He admitted 60 charges, including for rape, assault by penetration, administering a substance with intent, sexual assault, attempted rape and sharing intimate photographs or film.

Twelve other men, aged between 28 and 74, who are also accused of sexual offences relating to the same victim deny all of the charges against them

The 12 other men, who deny all of the charges against them, are; Karl Lindsay, 56,.Daniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable, Kent; David Graves, 59, from Derbyshire; Jonathan Kirk, 43, from the Stockport area; Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich, Cheshire; Philip Wild, 58, from the Stockport area; Mohammed Sabir, 28, from the Stockport area; Sean Peers, 38, from the Stockport area; Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester; Alan Keelan, 42, from Greater Manchester; Richard Townsend, 37, from Greater Manchester; Robert Stewart, 70, from the Stockport area.

A jury has already been sworn in to try the case, which was originally due to last up to 15 weeks.

News.title: Boy, 7, in critical condition after crash with car while his riding bike in Coleraine
News.content:
Boy, 7, in critical condition after crash with car while his riding bike in Coleraine

The youngster was riding a bike in Coleraine, Co Derry, when he was involved in a collision with a car and taken to hospital, where he remains in a critical condition

View Image The PSNI is investigating the crash (stock) (Image: Jonathan Porter/PressEye)

A seven-year-old boy is in a critical condition in hospital after a crash with a car while riding his bike in Northern Ireland.

‌



The youngster was cycling in Coleraine, Co Derry, at around 6.40pm on September 13, when he was involved in a collision with a black Volkswagen Scirocco, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said.

‌



Emergency services rushed to Warnocks Lane, where the boy was given medical treatment before being taken to hospital.

‌



He remains in a critical but stable condition, reports Belfast Live.

Police have launched an appeal for witnesses and are urging anyone who was travelling in the area to check dashcam or other footage as officers work to establish what happened.

Article continues below

A PSNI spokesperson said: “Warnocks Lane which was closed in both directions for a time has now fully reopened to road users. Our enquiries are ongoing today to determine what happened.

“We would ask anyone who was travelling in the area to review dash-cam or other footage they may have captured of the collision and call us on 101 with any information. The reference number is 1271 13/09/26.”

A report can also be made using the PSNI’s online reporting form.

News.title: Prince Harry step closer to taxpayer funded security after Home Office green lights new review
News.content:
Prince Harry step closer to taxpayer funded security after Home Office green lights new review

The Duke of Sussex has been writing "incessantly" to the Home Office to grant him taxpayer funded security and now has won a new review after moving his famly back to the UK

View 4 Images Prince Harry has beeb buoyed by the Home Office granting him a new security review (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Prince Harry has succeeded in forcing the Home Office to open a new review into his right to taxpayer funded security.

‌



As The Mirror revealed last month, the government department will now carry out a new Risk Management Board hearing at his request, after months of appeals from the Duke of Sussex. It is understood the new review will look at the risks and threats to both the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

‌



Harry has previously lost a case at the High Court and a subsequent hearing at the Court of Appeal, before he wrote directly to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood asking for a renewed assessment of his security situation.

‌



Home Office sources say Harry has been in constant contact with the department in recent months, describing his correspondence as "incessant".

View 4 Images Prince Harry has beeb buoyed by the Home Office granting him a new security review (Image: Getty Images)

The prince and his wife Meghan arrived back in the UK last month for what sources close to the couple have described as an “extended stay”.

‌



They have enrolled their two children, Archie, seven and Lilibet, five at a British school and are said by friends to be settling into their new life in the country.

On August 28, The Mirror exclusively reported how the Home Office was on the verge of issuing a new review of the Sussexes’ security situation due to the family relocating to the UK.

One government source suggested “the goalposts have moved”.

‌



One government insider said: “Officials have been asked to make a new assessment now that the family in question have chosen to reside in the UK.

“Any recommendations will be made in due course.”

View 4 Images The Duchess of Sussex has shared a glimpse of family life in footage posted to Instagram following their return to the UK. (Image: @meghan/Instagram)

‌



Harry, 42 on Tuesday, was stripped of his right to security while in the UK when he and Meghan in 2020 decided to quit their royal roles and set up home in the United States.

Since then the duke has appealed to the British government to change its position, claiming he is still a target for terrorists and fixated persons when in the UK.

His privately funded security team compiled a report which was sent to the Home Office, claiming he is the focus of six terrorist plots, five of which originated in the UK.

‌



Harry has appealed for a new risk assessment to be carried out by the Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), the body that was integral in stripping away his security detail.

The last review into the prince's security risk took place at the end of July, before the duke informed the Home Office of his plans to relocate his family back to the UK from the US.

Harry is understood to have given the security committee less than two weeks’ notice that he was moving his family back, amid fears the news would leak.

‌



The duke had previously been told that he may be eligible for protection if he gave Ravec at least 28 days’ notice of his plans to visit the UK.

Harry’s team reportedly chose to inform the committee that he would be travelling to the UK for an extended period of engagements in September - and not permanently relocating his family.

Harry later informed the Home Office of the family’s intention to have an extended stay.

‌



The duke told his father - the King - officially on Sunday, August 16 - just three days before the news of the family’s relocation was leaked to a number of media outlets known for favourable coverage of the Sussexes in the past.

The family landed in the UK on Thursday, August 26.

View 4 Images Harry only told King Charles of his planned return to the UK three days before the global news broke (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



On Sunday afternoon, Meghan, 45, shared a glimpse of family life in the UK in new footage of the family posted to her personal Instagram.

The 34-second clip, which features Wham!'s Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go, begins with Meghan and Harry, walking along a country path as she turns and says "come on, you".

UK flag and heart emojis are shown throughout the video, which also shows Archie running towards deer as Lilibet rides her bike.

‌



Following the Mirror’s exclusive story, a spokesperson for the Sussexes told The Telegraph: that the committee had been “kicking the can down the road for the last seven years”.

They added: “We have always adhered to the rules they set, even as the goalposts have moved along the way,” they said. “Playing by those rules has never made any difference.

“Despite the facade of a proper process, they have never shown any real intention of doing anything other than maintaining the status quo.

Article continues below

“Geography was the backbone of Ravec’s argument for withdrawing enhanced protective security in 2020.

“The couple’s decision not to live in the UK was treated as a significant factor in that decision.

“That barrier has now been removed, and an obvious off-ramp exists for the committee to do the sensible thing: protect the King’s son and grandchildren.”

News.title: AI 'kill switch' may need to be mandatory, Anthropic co-founder says
News.content:
An artificial intelligence "kill switch" which can be checked by a third-party may need to be mandatory for companies, a co-founder of one of the world's largest AI firms has said.

Jack Clark, one of seven founders of Anthropic, said a way of shutting off AI software completely if it gets too dangerous was something society "might want to eventually pass rules around".

Clark said "most labs have different ways of being able to pull the plug", including Anthropic, but said lawmakers may need to enforce having one.

AI's rapid developement and fears over the risks it poses to humanity have been thrust into the spotlight by a series of warnings from executives and staff at AI firms.

Some have said publicly there is a chance the technology could, if unchecked, kill all humans.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei over the weekend called for the pace of AI development to slow and be more closely monitored, as the company has done before, though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

Amodei added that any action to reign in AI development should be done "without sacrificing commercial advantage".

Clark told the BBC that specifics around "kill switch" requirements and verification should be part of "the larger policy conversation" taking place around AI.

"Should you mandate for companies to definitely have a kill switch? Is that kill switch verifiable by a third party?" he asked.

"I think that's the kind of thing society is going to want to know and might want to eventually pass rules around."

Anthropic, which was formed in 2021 by a group of former employees of its rival OpenAI, is currently at the centre of a debate around AI safety.

Last week, a post from an artificial intelligence researcher who quit Anthropic over concerns AI could wipe out humanity went viral.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger said he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was ">10% within the next decade".

Computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC on Friday that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans was "not unreasonable", external.

He and others with similar concerns have suggested AI could do so by taking control of important systems connected to the internet and turning them on humans.

However, some in the AI industry have suggested the fears around it destroying humanity are overstated or may be designed to generate hype.

Clement Delangue, leader of the developer platform Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI bots, said last week: "Sorry, but asking Jacob [Coxon] about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change."

"Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

George Arison, the leader of Grindr, said the fears going around AI tools were being used by the companies to support their business plans.

"The only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work,'" Arison said.

Asked what percentage he would put on all humans being killed by AI, Clark said: "I don't think these statistics are that useful", but added that allowing AI to continue as a "totally unregulated industry" was a bad idea.

"We are rolling dice with immense risks," Clark said. "And the point is, we have to change the course of this industry."

News.title: Burnham cancels engagements after death of his father
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cancelled official engagements on Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's.

He had been due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street on Monday, and was expected to speak at the annual trade union TUC Congress in Brighton on Tuesday.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

He had also said his father's illness was so advanced that he did not know his son had become prime minister.

Burnham told the BBC that while his father could not be there when he entered No 10 to take up the role, he and his mother had "exchanged a few words about my dad and how proud he would be".

"That's a little hard, but then again I've said, it's their achievement", he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg in July.

"The emotion of that moment was, well, bittersweet - it was painful in one way but beautiful in another."

The prime minister later said care home staff had shown his father footage of him entering Downing Street, calling it a "wonderful" thing.

Burnham said he wanted to help "my dad and the millions like him" when setting out plans to reform adult social care.

He said he had been "overwhelmed" by the skills and professionalism of care workers supporting his father.

Burnham has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In his 2024 book Look North, he wrote that neither of his parents had attended university, but could have done had they "grown up in a different time and different place".

"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go."

Opposition politicians have offered their condolences to Burnham and his family.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

"A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won't ever be the same again."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "My heart goes out to the prime minister on the loss of his dad.

"From our conversations he sounded like a wonderful man."

Green party leader Zack Polanski said: "There are moments in life such as this sad time that transcend politics and I join the whole country in sending condolences."

News.title: Farage says £72m donations are compliant 'with the law today'
News.content:
On Monday the House of Lords debated the government's Representation of the People Bill which caps the amount British people living overseas can donate to political parties at Â£100,000.

The bill also states that those who moved back to the UK would have to wait for at least a year before donating more than Â£100,000.

The legislation states that donors must have been registered as in the UK by 25 March 2026 in order to avoid the cap.

It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK.

Education Minister Georgia Gould told the BBC's Today programme the government was "really worried about the big money that is coming into politics... and sometimes money from overseas that is shaping politics rather than the ordinary voters".

She said the new rule changes had been added to the bill, following a report by former senior civil servant Sir Philip Rycroft into foreign interference in British politics, published on 25 March.

The two Â£36m donations to Reform have reignited questions about political funding.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on Radio 5 Live, Sir Philip said examining domestic donations had not been within the remit of his review but that there was a case for capping all donations, whether they came from British citizens living in the UK or overseas.

"I don't see any reason why we should have these mega sums of money coming into British politics," he said.

He added that the government's decision to retrospectively ban certain donations was "going to be controversial" but said: "If you say, you're going to change the rules to cap donations at some point in the future, then clearly the risk is that you get a lot of those donations coming through the door before you're able to do that."

Farage said the donations would allow his party to "catch up with the other big parties" and enable them to "professionalise".

He argued that trade unions gave money to Labour so that it would enact their policies and that donors gave money to the Conservative Party in order to get "knighthoods and peerages".

By contrast he said neither Harborne or Delo would get peerages or government contracts, if Reform won the next general election.

Asked if the two men had influence over Reform's policy on cryptocurrency, Farage said he had shown them his party's paper on the subject and they both "thought it made sense".

He added that the two men "will not benefit" from Reform's policies, which he said aimed to properly regulate cryptocurrency.

Farage was speaking on the same day as the Trade Unions Congress, the federation of trade unions, held its annual conference.

TUC general secretary Nowak said Reform were a "party for sale" and their donations were "a crisis for democracy".

Sharon Graham, leader of the Unite union, said the government should go further and put a cap between Â£500,000 and Â£1m on individual donations made by UK residents

Speaking on Sunday, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. Similarly, the Green Party urged the Labour Party to "find its spine and support a tight cap".

News.title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour after 'Free Palestine' speech
News.content:
Rapper Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour after making pro-Palestinian comments on stage earlier this month.

The artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - had been the opening act for Sheeran's Loop tour, but was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "Free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches.

Macklemore stood by his comments on Monday, confirming that he had been cut from the tour and writing in a statement that the real victims are the Palestinian people in Gaza.

Ed Sheeran has not yet commented, and who will replace Macklemore for the rest of the tour is unknown.

The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore, a long-time pro-Palestine activist, performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.

After that performance, the campaign group StopAntisemitism criticised the rapper, saying "Jewish fans bought tickets to see Ed Sheeran sing... not to be ambushed by Macklemore's anti-Israel propaganda."

The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.

"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.

Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

News.title: Staff slept while patient killed at NHS mental health unit
News.content:
Hugo's father, William Flint Cahan, who has attended each day of the inquest with other family members, says there was "complacency" by staff, as well as a lack of care.

He maintains his son's death was "preventable had the level of care been as it should have been."

Hugo's brother, Jolyon, who is an NHS doctor, says the "litany of failures, both incompetence and dishonesty, that pervaded the care of both patients was harrowing."

Over the past 12 years, local coroners have sent at least 29 Prevention of Future Deaths (PFD) notices to the Trust. These are sent to an organisation when a coroner identifies problems which, if not dealt with, could lead to further deaths.

The BBC has analysed the reports which cover both in patient and community services. In more than half of cases there had been a failure to properly assess the risk the patient posed to themself or to others. Poor communications between staff, other agencies and families were also repeatedly highlightedy.

The strongest warnings were about poorly carried out observations and falsified records â basic care needed to keep patients safe.

A report in 2021 by the coroner that carried out the Flint Cahan inquest warned that "a culture of impunity existed" at the Trust where "inaccurate and misleading recording of clinical records was tolerated."

In 2024, two further reports highlighted observations being missed then records falsified to suggest patients had been checked.

In response to one of the PFD's, the Trust said extensive training programmes and quality checks were introduced.

In 2025, a fourth report, into the death of a young woman, again highlighted falsified observation records. The coroner said, "despite assurances" from the Trust in numerous action plans", the inquest had "revealed widespread concerns" about how observations were carried out across two wards."

Other serious concerns raised in the reports include, how staff have responded to emergencies, with delays in resuscitation and - on one occasion - nursing staff giving chest compressions to a patient's stomach rather than their chest.

Brian Dow of the mental health charity, Rethink, is calling for a national register of patient safety to keep tabs on the type of care mental health units across the country are providing.

"We have been here before" with poor observations, records being falsified and unacceptable care, he says.

"We have got to have a better approach to patient safety in what are the most difficult and most vulnerable wards with the people who are the most unwell."

In a statement, Dr David Bridle, Chief Medical Officer at ELFT, said the Trust is deeply sorry to Hugo's family for the failings in his care.

He said the actions of the staff identified by the coroner were "wholly unacceptable and do not reflect the standards, values or behaviours we expect".

Dr Bridle says the Trust has worked to improve its services and "will ensure the learning from the coroner's findings informs our continuing work to strengthen patient safety and care."

News.title: Harry and Meghan to have security review and children change school
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are going to be given a review of their publicly-funded security after their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

It has also emerged that the Sussexes have changed their children's school, only days after they first started, over security concerns about the school run.

The prince previously mounted an unsuccessful legal challenge over his police security when he was visiting from the US.

But the family's return to the UK has meant a different set of circumstances for their taxpayer-funded security, and last week Ravec - which stands for the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures - met to discuss their case.

This committee, which includes representatives of the Home Office, the police and the Royal Household, seems ready to review potential dangers.

This means a so-called Risk Management Board will consider the threats against them and the level of police protection they might need - although no final decision on the outcome has been reached.

The review will include security for their children Archie, aged seven, and Lilibet, aged five - and as first reported by HELLO! magazine, the children have switched schools from where they started earlier this month because of a security issue.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

A source close to the couple said: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It is understood that Prince Harry had a review of his potential risks earlier in the summer, but before it was known that he would be returning to live in the UK.

This will be the first such security review for Meghan since she and Prince Harry ceased being working royals when they moved to the US in 2020.

Meghan posted footage on social media of the family at the weekend, showing a family outing in the countryside.

Separately on Monday, Prince Harry was told that Uganda would now take part in the Invictus Games next year.

It had appeared that Uganda was going to withdraw from the games for injured servicemen and women, in the fallout from a letter sent on behalf of King Charles emphasising that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.

The King's private secretary had spoken on the phone to Uganda's military chief, reassuring him that he approved of Uganda's participation in the games.

News.title: Member of UK armed forces dies in road traffic incident in Ukraine
News.content:
A member of the UK armed forces has died in a road traffic incident in Ukraine, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) has announced.

The individual's family has been informed and has "requested a period of grace before further details are released", the MoD's statement said.

The incident on Saturday was not the result of hostile action, the BBC understands.

The British government has previously acknowledged a small number of personnel in Ukraine to support Kyiv's armed forces and provide security to diplomatic staff.

It is not known which service the individual was in or what their role was.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting shared his "deepest condolences" with their loved ones, writing on social media: "This is very sad news for the family and for those grieving with them in our armed forces."

A 28-year-old paratrooper, who died while watching the testing of a new defensive capability away from the front lines in December, was the first member of the armed forces killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

On Sunday, a Russian drone hit and damaged a train in Yahodyn, near the Ukraine-Poland border - shortly after former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through on a different train on the same line.

The UK's national security adviser Jonathan Powell was among those on board.

No casualties were reported. Russia's defence ministry said it had struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but Ukraine's state railway company said the drone's intended target "could have been the diplomatic train".

The UK has been one of Ukraine's closest allies during the war.

Ukraine was the location of Andy Burnham's first overseas trip as prime minister in August, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats".

Chairing his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, Burnham also agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for Scalp missiles.

News.title: Westminster's time is coming to an end, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish leaders say
News.content:
The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end".

The nationalist leaders from Plaid Cymru, Sinn FÃ©in and the SNP - who want their countries to leave the United Kingdom - signed an agreement on Monday which said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".

But while Scotland's John Swinney and Northern Ireland's Michelle O'Neill called for referendums at a joint press conference, Wales' Rhun ap Iorwerth declined to give a timetable for one in his country.

Labour and Reform accused Plaid of wanting to break up the UK.

Swinney and ap Iorwerth's governments later backed a separate agreement agreed to work together on pressing UK government on "fairness" in funding and powers.

For the first time since devolution began, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all have first ministers who want to leave the United Kingdom.

All three met on Monday as representatives of their parties. Sinn FÃ©in president Mary Lou McDonald also attended.

The memorandum of understanding said: "For people watching across these islands - for people watching around the world - there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end.

"No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.

"We recognise that our parties have different constitutional positions and that each nation will determine its own future in its own way and in its own time."

News.title: Speedboat killer jailed for attack on girlfriend
News.content:
Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd has been jailed for 20 months with a further four years on extended licence for violently assaulting his girlfriend, including hitting her chest with a set of hot barbecue tongs.

The 38-year-old had pleaded guilty to two counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and damaging property at Isleworth Crown Court in July.

The attacks happened in February and June last year and sparked Shepherd's recall to prison.

He was originally jailed in 2018 for six years and six months for manslaughter over the death of 24-year-old Charlotte Brown when his speedboat crashed during a first date.

Shepherd was jailed for a further four years at Exeter Crown Court in 2019 for a drink-fuelled attack on a barman in March 2018 at a Devon hotel.

He was released on licence in January 2024, but faced recall to prison in September last year after he was accused of violence towards the woman.

According to a prosecution summary of the case, Shepherd started dating his former partner in August 2024, but towards the end of the year she accused him of being abusive and threatening.

In February 2025, he admitted pinning down the woman and "punching her several times, causing bruising to her arm and top of leg" during an argument.

In the second incident, in June 2025, Shepherd got angry with her after she said that he had burned a pizza on the barbecue, and "proceeded to hit her with the barbecue tongs on her left breast which caused a permanent scar".

News.title: No police collusion in sectarian murder but multiple RUC failings included tip-off to suspect
News.content:
An inquiry into the sectarian murder of Robert Hamill has found police officers who were in a vehicle near the attack did not condone or collude with the attackers.

However, the inquiry said there were multiple police failings in the investigation, including a tip-off to a suspect to destroy the clothing he wore that night.

The report, published on Monday, external, highlighted multiple wrongful omissions in the subsequent murder investigation including a failure to properly search the home of a key suspect.

Robert Hamill was 25 when he died after he was beaten by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh, in 1997.

The inquiry concluded in 2009 and its report was completed in 2011 but the findings could not be published until three prosecutions in connection with the case concluded.

The inquiry concluded: "We find that Robert Hamill had been assaulted before the Land Rover officers got out of their vehicle.

"However, they were not aware of the assault and after they had got out of their vehicle, they attempted to restore order.

"They did not in any way condone or collude with attackers."

Although the inquiry found that the four officers in the police Land Rover could not have prevented the murder, the police investigation was flawed â both at the scene and in the days that followed.

"The inquiry found that serving RUC [Royal Ulster Constabulary] officers were guilty of wrongful omissions and that those omissions arose both at the scene and during the initial investigation," it said.

The inquiry concluded that some of the mistakes in the investigation were negligent, while others were deliberate.

The 290-page report followed an inquiry which cost approximately Â£33m.

The actions of the officers in the Land Rover have been the subject of many claims and counter-claims in the past three decades.

Given how close they were to the scene, questions have been asked about why they did not intervene sooner.

The inquiry found that they were "distracted talking to two members of the public".

On whether they could have done more, the three-person inquiry panel did not have a unanimous view.

Two members concluded that the officers in the police vehicle were not guilty "of any wrongful act or omission in relation to the death of Robert Hamill".

However, on this issue the chairperson Sir Edwin Jowitt "expressed a dissenting view".

News.title: Police officer who put suspect in headlock and punched him 9 times faces misconduct hearing
News.content:
A police officer who punched a suspect nine times in the head used unreasonable force on multiple occasions, a police misconduct hearing has been told.

PC Richard Williams faces eight allegations relating to the arrest of Steven Clark, including using a headlock or "choker", unreasonable use of incapacitant spray, and throwing or dropping Clark into the back of a police van.

A misconduct hearing at North Wales Police headquarters in Colwyn Bay heard Williams denies wrongdoing.

He was cleared of assault and intentional strangulation following a seven-day trial in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, in 2025.

In May 2023, police were called to Porthmadog in Gwynedd, following a report of a domestic argument.

A woman told officers, Clark, then 34, was "off his head on wacky backy" and possibly other drugs.

The misconduct hearing was played several clips of police body-worn camera footage, as well as mobile phone video recorded by onlookers.

When police tried to arrest Clark, the misconduct hearing was told things "take a turn", and the suspect ended up on the ground.

It is alleged Williams used handcuffs to "cause pain to Clark's wrist", who "winced and reacted".

News.title: This is what women in sport look like - female athletes hit back
News.content:
Female athletes have spoken out against a controversial sports gambling advert starring actress Sydney Sweeney.

The advert has gone viral online and features American Sweeney naked but covering parts of her body with various pieces of sporting equipment.

It has sparked a strong reaction, with many female athletes criticising its sexualisation of women in sport, and how they are being defined by their appearance rather than their achievements as sportswomen.

Amy Hunt, who became a four-time European champion earlier this summer, referenced the advert after she ran a season's best 22.10 seconds to finish fourth in the 200m final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Sunday.

"Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Hunt said in her post-race interview with BBC Sport.

Referring to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth fastest ever over the distance, she added: "21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening."

American actress Sweeney, 29, starred in the television series Euphoria and her films include Anyone But You and The Housemaid.

The backlash has included many other athletes from a range of sports posting videos of themselves competing or training, and describing the frustrations and struggles they have faced throughout their careers.

The trend was started by American gymnast Gracie Kramer, who posted a montage of herself training with the caption, "I don't know what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what women in sport look like."

Kramer told BBC World Service's Newshour show she "did not expect" the reaction to her post and "just wanted to uplift women and remind them that you may see these types of ads but remember that this is not the only thing that matters".

She said it was "so cool" to see "all the incredible athletes hopping on this trend, uplifting themselves, uplifting each other", adding she was used to getting "very demeaning and objectifying" messages from men because of competing in a leotard as a gymnast.

Kramer added: "Unfortunately being objectified pretty much my entire career, it made me feel strong enough to post about this and to stand up for the women that don't want to be objectified and don't want to be looped into this unfortunate narrative that's been pushed for a long time."

News.title: Key convicted Palestine Action member on the run
News.content:
A key member of Palestine Action, who is currently on the run, has been convicted in his absence over a break-in that caused damage put at Â£1.2m to an arms firm.

Sean Middlebrough, 33, originally from Liverpool, absconded in October last year after being granted bail for his brother's wedding. The self-proclaimed revolutionary communist has since sent messages to supporters describing himself as a "prisoner of war".

His trial began this summer in his absence and last month the jury convicted him of criminal damage by a majority of nine-to-one.

Prosecutors told the court Middlebrough had helped to plan and organise the August 2024 break-in at Elbit Systems in Bristol, a British defence firm with an Israeli parent company. The break-in happened 10 months before the government banned the group under counter-terrorism powers.

News.title: Uganda will now take part in Harry's Invictus Games after King's reassurance
News.content:
Uganda's military leaders have confirmed their country will take part in Prince Harry's Invictus Games for wounded veterans, after saying last week they were going to pull out of the event.

The change of heart follows a phone call with the King's principal private secretary, Sir Clive Alderton, who told them the King had "no problem" with Uganda's participation in the games.

This support from Buckingham Palace is likely to be seen as an olive branch, helping Prince Harry with his sports events for injured service men and women.

It had seemed that Uganda's involvement would be a victim of the fall-out over a letter sent on behalf of the King clarifying that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.

Uganda's military chief, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said the withdrawal had been made so as "not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III".

But it seems that a private conversation between Sir Clive Alderton and General Kainerugaba has resolved any worries about the King not being supportive of Uganda taking part in the games, which are being held in Birmingham next year.

According to a spokesman for Uganda's military, Sir Clive had "encouraged the CDF [Chief of Defence Forces] to proceed with preparations" to take part in the games.

"In the telephone conversation, General Kainerugaba appreciated the King's message and clarity provided by Buckingham Palace on the subject, promising that the UPDF [Ugandan People's Defence Force] would resume preparations to participate in the upcoming games," said the Ugandan military spokesman.

It is not clear whether the Palace initiated the change of plan by calling the Ugandans, or whether it was the Ugandans who first contacted the Palace for their views.

General Kainerugaba, son of Uganda's president, had announced last Wednesday the withdrawal from the games in a social media post on X.

"We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval," said the general's announcement.

That approval now seems to have been provided, opening the way for Uganda to take part. The country had only been announced as a participant in July.

Rob Owen, CEO of the Invictus Games Foundation, welcomed the news that "Uganda has confirmed it will continue to be part of the Invictus community".

"Uganda became our 26th nation earlier this year, joining a growing movement that provides year-round recovery opportunities for wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans across the world," said Owen.

This change of minds ends a row which had been linked with the letter sent by the Palace about the status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, which had made clear that they were private citizens and could not carry out official royal engagements.

It had given an impression of tensions as Prince Harry and Meghan settled into life in the UK.

A royal source said there was now a "positive outcome" for all sides and thanked the Ugandans for their understanding.

Where there is any uncertainty about the role of the Sussexes, organisations are welcome to seek guidance from the Palace, said a royal source.

News.title: Chief coroner calls for inquiry into Manchester synagogue attack
News.content:
The chief coroner overseeing inquests into the deaths of two men killed in the attack on a Manchester synagogue is to ask the government to hold a public inquiry instead.

Judge Alexia Durran, chief coroner of England and Wales, said she would write to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to recommend the inquests be converted into a public inquiry after being told some MI5 material could not be heard in open court because of national security concerns.

Inquests were planned into the deaths of Adrian Daulby, 53, and Melvin Cravitz, 66, following the attack by Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, a Syrian-born British citizen, on Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue in Manchester last October.

Inquests have no mechanism to hold secret or private hearings, excluding press and public.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have moved their children to a new school just two days into the new school term.

The children of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle – seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet – started at their new school just last week after the family relocated back to the UK.

The location of their new home and details of the children's school ​have been kept private. But the distance between their home and the original school, with heavy traffic in ​the area, had caused concern for their security team.

open image in gallery Prince Harry and Meghan remain private citizens, the King clarified ( PA Wire )

A spokesperson for the duke and duchess said: "The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family's security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements.

"The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

The school move comes after a reported meeting last week of the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures (Ravec), which is responsible for making decisions about royal security.

open image in gallery The footage posted on Instagram features Meghan with the Duke of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet on outdoor adventures ( Instagram )

The couple controversially returned to the UK in August after they stepped down as working royals in 2020 amid the Megxit crisis and moved to the United States for six years.

Buckingham Palace released a letter on behalf of King Charles last month reiterating the King’s stance after Harry and Meghan announced their return, confirming there would be no alteration to their role and status as private individuals and non-working royals.

Prince Harry is waiting to hear the conclusion of the Risk Management Board’s threat assessment as Ravec is expected to decide at the meeting as to whether the Sussex family should be entitled to taxpayer-funded security now they live in the UK.

open image in gallery ( Matt Porteous/Kensington Palace )

The Telegraph reported that the committee chairman wrote to the duke last week confirming that in light of their changed circumstances, it had commissioned a new risk assessment for him and a separate one for Meghan.

The Wales children, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis, attend Lambrook School in Berkshire, and Prince George has started boarding at Eton College.

Pictures were released of the prince’s first day at Eton, where his father and uncle Harry both attended as children, as the duke and duchess of Wales both walked him onto the premises.

Meghan meanwhile shared a first glimpse of family life in the UK on social media this week.

Meghan and Harry were seen walking hand in hand in the first shot, with the duchess turning around to whoever is holding the camera and saying: “Come on, you, come on.”

The footage posted on Instagram features Meghan with the Duke of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet on outdoor adventures to the tune of Wham!’s ‘Wake Me Up Before You Go Go’.

The video also shows one of the children sitting by a roaring fireplace, Lili wearing wellies while riding a bicycle with training wheels and a doll on the back, and Archie running past his sister in his wellies.

Jason Eaton insisted he was acting on orders from the CIA and Mossad when he shot three Palestinian college students who were walking past his home a few days after Thanksgiving. He said the U.S. and Israeli intelligence agencies transmitted the messages to him via FM radio and that God was commanding him to protect his Jewish neighbors.

Eaton’s claims were at the heart of his insanity defens e as he went on trial Monday on attempted murder charges in a case that shook Burlington, Vermont, and reverberated in the West Bank, where the three wounded men grew up and became friends as schoolmates in Ramallah before moving to the U.S. for college.

The November 2023 shooting, weeks after the start of the Israel-Hamas war, spawned calls for a hate crime investigation. But no hate crime charges were filed as questions persisted about whether anti-Palestinian animus, an altered mental state or something else had compelled Eaton to open fire on Hisham Awartani, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid, who were all 20 at the time.

The men testified one after another as Eaton, now 51, watched stoically from the defense table in a Burlington courtroom. He has pleaded not guilty but doesn't dispute that he was the shooter. If convicted, he faces up to life in prison. If found not guilty by reason of insanity, he could be ordered to undergo mental health treatment.

Defense lawyer Joshua O’Hara, previewing testimony from a defense psychiatrist, told jurors in an opening statement that Eaton was suffering from a delusional, psychotic disorder after losing his job at a credit union two weeks before the shooting.

While listening to a local NPR affiliate, Eaton believed he was hearing messages that he attributed to the CIA, O’Hara said. At first, the messages were encouraging and validating, the lawyer said, but subsequent messages turned dark, insisting that Eaton “has to go out and shoot somebody.”

Prosecutor Sally Adams told jurors that a state psychiatrist who is slated to testify concluded that Eaton did not have a mental disease or defect. Evidence will show he intended to kill the men, was not legally justified in shooting them, and does not meet the test of legal insanity, Adams said.

Authorities found three shotguns in Eaton's apartment and a Ruger .380-caliber handgun that crime lab testing concluded was the gun used in the shooting, Adams said. Eaton had purchased the gun seven months earlier from a Vermont gun store.

“If the defense tries to focus on the story that Mr. Eaton tells about why he intended to kill these three young men, that story is only part of the whole picture,” said Adams, the chief administrative deputy at the Chittenden County State’s Attorney's Office.

Awartani, Aliahmad and Abdalhamid, all of whom are now 23, told jurors of their holiday weekend visit to Awartani’s grandmother's house, a trip to a bowling alley to celebrate his twin cousins' birthday, and the walk they took near the University of Vermont campus after dusk that ended in bloodshed.

Awartani, who was studying at Brown University in Rhode Island at the time, said they were smoking cigarettes and speaking a mix of English and Arabic. Two of them said they were wearing traditional Palestinian scarves known as keffiyehs. Awartani said he first noticed Eaton standing on a porch as they approached the apartment house where he lived.

Within seconds, Awartani said, Eaton was off the porch and walking toward them. His face was expressionless and he didn't say anything. As Eaton got to about five to 10 feet (1.5 to 3 meters) away, “he pulled out a handgun and started shooting at us,” said Awartani, who was paralyzed from the waist down in the shooting and now uses a wheelchair.

Jacob Pyne, who lived in a different apartment in the same house as Eaton, testified that he heard four to six gunshots, followed by footsteps going up the stairs of the apartment house. He said he ran outside and heard two men speaking, one of whom was more vocal and yelling, “I’ve been shot, help me." He then brought the men blankets and called 911.

Abdalhamid, a student at Haverford College near Philadelphia, said he fled and hid behind another home after seeing Aliahmad fall to the ground. He said he only realized later when he sat down that he had also been wounded. Awartani was shot in the chest and the bullet ricocheted off his scapula, causing paraplegia in his spinal cord. Aliahmad, who was a student at Trinity College in Connecticut, was struck in the collarbone, and Abdalhamid was shot in the right buttock.

O’Hara, the supervising attorney at the Chittenden County Public Defender Office, told jurors that Eaton was confused by the messages he said he was receiving, and became convinced that the CIA and Mossad were enlisting him into “overwatch duty” to protect a Jewish family living across the street.

“These were delusions,” O’Hara said. “He believed in the moment that he was doing something that was right. He had been commanded to do this. And that he did not have the ability to appreciate the wrongfulness of his conduct in the moment because he believed he’d been instructed to do this by a government agency or God.”

Congress is back — at least for a little bit.

The House of Representatives and the Senate returned on Monday after the Labor Day weekend, the Republican midterm convention and the Jewish High Holy Day of Rosh Hashanah.

But the House will only be in session for a week, since House Speaker Mike Johnson canceled the final two weeks of the session before the midterms. This means there will be scant time for legislating.

Yet, this is all happening — or not happening — at a moment when many feel that Congress must act with haste. Last week, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, resigned and posted a thread on X warning, “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” This came after rogue OpenAI agents hacked AI firm Hugging Face.

Do not expect the Republican-controlled Congress to act. Why? Because President Donald Trump does not want any action.

open image in gallery Speaker of the House Mike Johnson has adopted President Donald Trump’s line to basically have no guardrails around AI at the moment. ( AFP/Getty )

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” Trump posted on Truth Social Monday. The president also continued his support for AI data centers despite pushback even from members of his own party.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” he said.

Rather, Washington is set to try and vote on the Protect College Sports Act — which is why Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) appeared on ESPN’s College Gameday to be roundly booed — and potentially to vote on legislation on cryptocurrency known as the CLARITY Act.

And Johnson seems to be falling into line. Over the weekend, he told CBS’ Face the Nation that “some guardrails, some safety measures” might be needed, the United States should not “lose our edge in the global competition on this with China because that would be a national security threat.”

Democrats are not as optimistic as Johnson. Many have found some stray Republicans who want to see some safeguards around AI.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has dismissed any need for legislative action on AI ( Getty Images )

“The models keep getting more powerful, and nothing but the honor system is holding AI companies accountable,” Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) said. “Congress can fix that. The question is whether we will before more damage is done.”

Trahan is the co-author, alongside Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.), of the FRONTIER Act, which would create a tiered system of regulations, have ongoing assessments and independent audits of AI developers.

Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) has a separate piece of legislation with Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) called the AI Kill Switch Act, which would mandate that AI firms have the ability to throttle, suspend or shut down AI systems.

“Dear Speaker Johnson: Your party controls subpoena power. You can do the “big meeting” right now by issuing subpoenas to AI industry leaders and summoning them to testify before the American people,” he said in response to Johnson’s words. “Instead, you changed the House schedule to give us two more weeks of vacation.”

The Senate for it’s part seems to be at least willing to hear about AI. Axios reported that Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) will convene an event with former Trump adviser Steve Bannon focused on “pro-human” AI.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) was more blunt in his assessment of the risks AI poses, saying it posed a bigger risk than nuclear weapons or the internet.

“This is more akin to Doctor Frankenstein telling us ‘the monster is loose, help me stop the monster,’” he told CNN’s Jake Tapper.

But with members already gearing up to go home by the time they arrive on the House floor, they likely will not carve out time to act as quick as AI’s own executives and cofounders are warning. And given the election is mostly about the cost of living, it might be some time before AI becomes a pressing political issue.

News.title: One of Charles Manson’s cult followers has died in prison
News.content:

Bruce Davis, a former follower of cult leader Charles Manson who was convicted of two murders more than half a century ago, has died while serving a life sentence, according to officials.

Davis died on Friday at the California Medical Facility in Vacaville, as reported by the Solano County coroner’s office to ABC News.

Born Bruce McGregor Davis in Monroe, Louisiana, he was 83 years old. After spending more than a year in hiding, he had voluntarily surrendered to Los Angeles police on December 2, 1970.

Davis had been denied parole numerous times over the decades, according to state officials. State parole boards had recommended him for release seven different times, though Governors Gavin Newsom, Arnold Schwarzenegger and Jerry Brown consistently rejected those recommendations. While incarcerated, Davis earned a college degree and became an ordained prison minister with a clean disciplinary record.

Davis was convicted in 1972 on two counts of first-degree murder, conspiracy and robbery for his role in the 1969 killings of musician Gary Hinman and stuntman Donald “Shorty” Shea. During a 2014 parole hearing, Davis admitted to holding a firearm while Manson attacked Hinman with a sword and cutting Shea with a knife.

Bruce Davis, who was serving a life sentence for two murders committed more than 50 years ago as a member of Charles Manson’s group, has died ( California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation )

"I wanted to be Charlie's favorite guy,” Davis said during a 2014 parole hearing.

Following the Hinman homicide, other group members used the victim’s blood to write “political piggy” on a wall.

Davis was not involved in the separate 1969 murders of actress Sharon Tate and six others carried out by different members of the Manson group, according to police records.

Other members of the Manson group remain behind bars or have died in custody over the decades. Charles Manson died in prison in 2017 at the age of 83.

Other high-profile figures from the commune — including Charles "Tex" Watson, Patricia Krenwinkel and Bobby Beausoleil — continue to serve life sentences in California prisons. Other members, such as Leslie Van Houten and Steve “Clem” Grogan, were eventually freed through parole or court rulings in recent years.

News.content:
