Sports.title: McGregor criticises 'team of individuals' after Celtic's Old Firm collapse
Sports.content:
"You saw a team and a team of individuals."

Captain Callum McGregor was scathing in his assessment of Celtic's League Cup defeat to Rangers.

The Hoops travelled to Ibrox for a quarter-final tie against their Old Firm rivals unbeaten in seven domestic games this season.

And McGregor offered no excuses for the 3-0 defeat: "It wasn't us. The difference between the two sides was you saw a team and then you saw a team of individuals as well.

"Rangers were a team and you could see that.

"We looked like a team of individuals who like to do our own thing and play when we got the ball, not necessarily run when you don't have the ball when that's the thing you can't do when you come here.

"You can't defend with six players, it's impossible."

The cup exit comes after Celtic's Champions League qualifying defeat by Austrian side LASK, where they surrendered a 4-0 aggregate lead to be beaten 5-4.

Image: Celtic collapsed in the second leg of their Champions League qualifier against LASK

They host Hungarian side Ferencvaros in the Europa League on Thursday before Rangers travel to Celtic Park in the Scottish Premiership on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

"We've put ourselves under pressure, we need to respond on Thursday and then we need to respond on Sunday but we very quickly need to get to the level," McGregor added.

"But trying to get the message to everyone that we have to be the team that we want to be.

"We need to find a way to do that quickly because we lost a big game against LASK and we lost another big game on Sunday and it's not acceptable.

"There'll be other big games throughout the season and eventually you have to win one if you want to be considered a good team.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Celtic manager Martin O'Neill reacts to their 3-0 defeat to Rangers in the League Cup quarter-finals

"If we want to be a good Celtic team then we'll have to win the big games. One thing we've always done is win big games and turned up when it mattered.

"So far this season we've been bitty in games and we need to fix it."

Image: Rangers beat Celtic in the first Old Firm of the season

With the memories of Austria still fresh in his mind, McGregor feared the defeat could have been even more damaging.

He said: "Yeah, you don't want fours and fives for sure.

"As soon as the goals go in, then I'm saying to Cameron Carter-Vickers and Liam Scales, no more goals.

"We need to just tighten this up. Of course we always want to get back in the game, we always want to be a team that, even at 3-0 down you still want to have a chance.

"But you have to understand the circumstances as well, well beaten at 3-0 with good goals against you, but if it starts to run at fours and fives then you're talking about a different ball game."

Sports.title: Brundle: Debating the rule that cost Norris and why Madring needs changes
Sports.content:
The inaugural Madring grand prix was ok, the new venue offering some interesting aspects such as the long and banked turn 12 and testing high-speed sections between continuous and unrelenting walls and barriers.

It all had a feeling of work in progress. We know they lost a lot of time in the build process with particularly bad weather, and as a temporary race track adjacent to the international airport, and effectively racing around the Madrid equivalent of the Birmingham NEC, it had its challenges.

The pitlane and paddock were simply vast, creating some logistical challenges for all and, much more importantly, the track layout was not conducive to overtaking, to say the least.

As the cars swung at high speed from side to side through some of the more tortuous sections, and with a reasonably fast corner onto the not especially long pit straight, along with an energy dense layout meaning hybrid batteries would be replenished far more easily than on the four high speed and long straights just a week earlier in Monza, the only way to overtake was a highly risky lunge, or wait for rivals to make a mistake.

It's not as challenging to overtake as Monaco, but not that far short either. Given the extremely long pit lane which feeds back onto the inside of turn three, it took a lengthy 25 seconds to pit under green-flag conditions.

However, under a virtual or actual safety car, due to the speeds and geography of the layout, there was a chunky 12-second advantage in pitting under the safety car while rivals are travelling much more slowly. And that decided who would win the race.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix.

The first-lap Madring melee

With so little circuit knowledge, especially for Lando Norris who had missed virtually a full practice session with car gremlins, and for others who had had sizeable shunts along the way, this meant that all three available tyre compounds were represented on the grid.

On the front row, pole sitter Norris, after a sensational qualifying lap, and fellow front-row sitter Kimi Antonelli had medium compounds. Max Verstappen was on soft compound tyres, like Lewis Hamilton. Others like Charles Leclerc's Ferrari and George Russell's Mercedes were on the hard compound tyres.

And that's how they set off. Norris got away reasonably well and aggressively covered off Antonelli. The young Italian would fail to slow enough, and bypass both of the two early chicanes, hitting the throttle hard through the run-off areas.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli found himself going wide twice on the opening lap of the Spanish Grand Prix.

This meant he would clearly have to give back to Norris the lead he now had, but Verstappen read this very well, and using his speed, guile, and soft compound tyres, he would not let Antonelli simply hand the place back to Norris without helping himself to second place.

However, in the melee early after the start, Verstappen too had a straight run through a chicane, in his view to avoid a shunt with Hamilton.

In the view of the stewards however he had gained an unfair advantage and, much to Max's chagrin, his team told him, before the stewards did, to hand the place to Lewis which by now necessarily included Antonelli too.

It probably cost Max a victory in the end.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Verstappen FUMES over Red Bull team radio after being told to give position back to Lewis Hamilton after running off track in an incident at the first corner.

How the Virtual Safety Car turned the race Antonelli's way

Antonelli is definitely getting the rub of the green in this phase of the season, although it must be said that his speed and consistency have enabled him to make sure he doesn't waste these golden opportunities, and on lap 14 he would be handed another.

Norris had been flying out front, looking very assured. But when Lance Stroll lost his Aston Martin under braking and became marooned down one of the few and short run-off areas, it looked reasonably certain that there would be a virtual safety car to recover that.

Norris was fast approaching the pit-lane entry, the team didn't want to pit him on simply the chance of a safety car rather than the certainty, given how hard it was to overtake even significantly slower traffic if they didn't pit.

Just as the race director gave the VSC order, Norris had passed the pit entry. But his lead was over four seconds and, critically, Mercedes did have time to pit Antonelli. If only Lando hadn't been in such great form…

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lando Norris admits team 'were too quick' after missing a crucial VSC pit stop that cost him race lead.

Ferrari kept Leclerc out on his hard tyres, the relatively early safety car hurting his strategy. But clearing away stricken cars had been rather slow all event and might, just might, Norris be able to complete another lap at safety car speed and still get a cheap pit stop in?

Not at all. It went green and full racing speed when he was two corners from the pit-lane entry, and he then had to navigate the whole pit lane whist his main rivals were flat out. And to cap it all, McLaren delivered him a seven-second pit stop rather than the usual two seconds.

Undeterred, Lando set about catching up to Verstappen and Antonelli in fine fashion.

Leclerc would impressively lead until he pitted on lap 48 to park his tired hard tyres. If that sounds long, a very unimpressed Pierre Gasly was left out on track by his Alpine team for 55 of the 57 laps.

This all left Antonelli in the lead, but with Verstappen pushing hard as Norris was catching him, the three leaders were close together in the final stages.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Craig Slater reflects on all the big talking points after a chaotic Spanish Grand Prix.

But there was no way past, and having led his 13th straight F1 race, Antonelli would now lead the championship by 81 points from his team-mate Russell. It's the fifth consecutive race where the 20-year-old Italian has extended his points lead.

Mercedes power units also won their 251st race in F1 history, tieing with Ferrari. Impressive numbers all round.

Russell in the other Merc was mighty fast too and would catch Leclerc but had to be content with following him home in fifth place, being a relative outlier on a two-stop strategy by pitting on laps 14 and 28.

It simply won't fall into place for George, he's not catching any breaks this season so far.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton was forced to retire early at the Spanish Grand Prix.

Sadly, Hamilton's Ferrari had brake issues in the opening laps and he would retire for the first time since Brazil last season. This meant Liam Lawson, standing in for the injured Isack Hadjar, grabbed eight more points in sixth place for Red Bull to go with Verstappen's excellent 18 for second place, in a car which wasn't second fastest.

The VSC rule debate and expectations of 2027 Madring change

Antonelli and Verstappen were both immediately magnanimous post-race when declaring it Norris' victory without the unfortunate virtual safety car timing. Should a driver lose a race because another driver has made a mistake or had a car failure?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli admitted it wasn't the way he wanted to win and that Lando Norris deserved the Spanish GP victory.

What goes around comes around in the course of a season and even a career, but it felt rather like a robbery on Sunday.

Some racing categories temporarily close the pit lane except for emergency repairs (or emergency refuelling if they have that), but that can all get a bit confusing and congested too in the pit lane and is still not equal for everyone.

One solution might be to ensure that if a virtual safety is deployed, then it must stay in place for at least a full lap of all the runners to keep it fairer. Although, of course, that costs green flag full-speed racing time, which is what people want to see in the grandstands and on their devices.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jude Bellingham talks Real Madrid's start of the season and F1 on Martin Brundle's Grid Walk.

By next year I hope and expect that the Madring will have some track layout changes to improve overtaking, a more condensed and practical set up behind the scenes, and better signage for all. It has all the ingredients to make a credible contribution to the F1 season.

Sports.title: Carra: Arteta becoming like Sir Alex after ref criticism
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher says Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta is "becoming the Sir Alex Ferguson of the Premier League" after strongly criticising the penalty awarded against his side in Saturday's 2-0 win at Sunderland.

A furious Arteta described the saved second-half penalty as "unacceptable" after referee John Brooks pointed to the spot when Arsenal defender Ezri Konsa brought down Dan Ballard.

The Gunners have subsequently sought an explanation from refereeing body Pro Ref over the penalty award.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Was Ezri Konsa’s challenge on Dan Ballard enough for Sunderland to be awarded a penalty?

Arteta's anger has led Carragher to draw a comparison with ex-Manchester United boss Ferguson, who was famously unafraid to publicly criticise match officials, even while his side were the dominant domestic force.

Arsenal did not concede a penalty in last season's title-winning campaign and Carragher believes "don" Arteta is using his Premier League-champion status to influence referees' decision-making.

He told Monday Night Football: "This was Mikel Arteta becoming the Sir Alex Ferguson of the Premier League right now.

"He's the don at the moment; he's the Premier League champion.

"A lot of new managers about... he's been in his role for six or seven years, and he feels he's in a position of power to say, 'Yeah, it wasn't a penalty'. And I don't think it was a penalty.

"But it'd be interesting to see how long it takes for another referee to give a penalty against Arsenal in a similar situation.

"I thought it was very interesting in the press conference; one of the journalists made a point about, no matter what question you asked him, he kept going back to the penalty, so he was determined to get the narrative out that this won't happen again to his club.

"But that's a manager - we've seen it with Sir Alex Ferguson, we've seen it with Jose Mourinho."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from the Premier League clash between Sunderland and Arsenal

Former Luton, Middlesbrough and Wolves boss Rob Edwards was the special guest on MNF and concurred with Carragher's view on Arteta.

He said: "I think Jamie's right. He's put himself into a position now where he's looking after his team and his football club, and people will listen to the Premier League-winning manager, won't they?

"They will listen to him; he's a powerful voice there now."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Was Ezri Konsa’s challenge on Dan Ballard enough for Sunderland to be awarded a penalty?

Latest from Sky Sports' Sam Blitz:

Arsenal are set to hold talks with Pro Ref over the penalty Sunderland were awarded on Saturday.

The Gunners want an explanation for why the penalty was given on the field and then approved by VAR.

Arsenal have regularly asked Pro Ref for consistency in refereeing decisions.

Image: Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta (left) was shown a yellow card in their win at Sunderland

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta said at his post-match press conference at the Stadium of Light:

"The first question we have to discuss is this. This is not acceptable at this level.

"It was a beautiful game of football with two teams, with an atmosphere in the stadium that was unbelievable.

"Sunderland are so well organised, they are so good in so many phases, they have great players and they create a lot of issues. We have to cope with all of that in a really difficult week.

"And on top of that, we have to go through what we have done today, that, in my opinion, is not acceptable.

"I watched it 20 times and I cannot find a way to understand how they think to give a penalty in that situation, or the way the VAR has to intervene.

"So I don't know what to think.

"I'm sad that we have to discuss this after such a beautiful game, that at this level, has the gravity of that. Because that changes the course of the season and it can cost you the championship.

"At this level, with all the work we put in, this cannot happen."

Sports.title: BMW PGA Championship: Field, format and prize money as McIlroy returns
Sports.content:
Which players could impress at the BMW PGA Championship? Will LIV Golf players feature? Who is playing in the Celebrity Pro-Am? We get you up to speed ahead of this week's DP World Tour event at Wentworth, live on Sky Sports.

What is the BMW PGA Championship?

The BMW PGA Championship is one of the flagship events on the DP World Tour calendar, with the tournament first being held in 1955.

It should not be confused with the BMW Championship, the second of the PGA Tour's two FedExCup Playoffs, with the BMW PGA Championship hosted annually in Surrey, England, each September.

Alex Noren returns as the defending champion after he defeated Adrien Saddier in a play-off at last year's tournament.

Where is the BMW PGA Championship played?

The tournament is hosted annually at Wentworth Club, one of England's most prestigious golf courses.

Wentworth was first opened as a golf club in 1922 and has since hosted some prestigious events, including the 1953 Ryder Cup and the AIG Women's Open in 1980.

Who can impress?

Some big names are set to tee up at Wentworth including two-time Masters champion Rory McIlroy.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rory McIlroy wowed fans by chipping in for birdie on the opening hole of the 2025 BMW PGA Championship

The world No 2 won the BMW PGA Championship in 2014 and returns to Wentworth hoping to improve on a tied-41st place finish at the Amgen Irish Open. Despite dropping down the leaderboard, McIlroy said he was "encouraged" by certain aspects of his game coming into this week.

Patrick Reed has enjoyed a fine season on the DP World Tour since he left LIV Golf at the beginning of the year. The 2018 Masters champion currently leads the Race to Dubai Rankings and comes into the week off the back of an impressive tied-second finish at the Amgen Irish Open.

Prior to last weekend, Shane Lowry's last victory on the DP World Tour came at the BMW PGA Championship in 2022. But on Sunday, he carded a seven-under 63 to secure a staggering 11-shot victory at the Amgen Irish Open.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Matt Fitzpatrick has enjoyed his most successful season on the PGA Tour in 2026, winning three events

Englishmen Tommy Fleetwood and Justin Rose are two other players who can impress this week. Fleetwood has four top-five finishes on the PGA Tour this season, notably placing tied-fourth at The Open at Royal Birkdale.

Rose has also enjoyed a great season on the PGA Tour, which included a victory at the Farmers Insurance Open and a tied-third finish at The Masters.

What LIV Golf players will feature at the BMW PGA Championship?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jon Rahm is one of multiple LIV Golf players in the field at Wentworth

Jon Rahm is one of multiple LIV Golf players in the field this week. This year the Spaniard clinched his third successive LIV Golf Individual Championship in August, and also finished tied for second at the PGA Championship in May.

His Legion XIII team-mate Tyrrell Hatton is also in the field this week. Hatton has enjoyed a great year at the majors, placing tied-third at The Masters and tied for seventh at the US Open, but arrives at Wentworth after missing the cut at the Amgen Irish Open.

What's at stake?

A £6.6m ($9m) prize purse is up for grabs this week at Wentworth. Last year's winner, Noren, took home a cash prize of £1.13m ($1.53m).

With this being a Rolex Series Event, a total of 8,000 Race to Dubai Rankings points are also up for grabs.

What is the Celebrity Pro-Am at the BMW PGA Championship?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gareth Bale, Tom Holland and Sir James Anderson have all played in the Celebrity Pro-Am in the past

Each year, Wentworth hosts a celebrity Pro-Am event featuring star-studded fields packed with big names from the sporting world and the entertainment industry.

This year is no different, with the DP World Tour having already announced that former Chelsea stars John Terry and Eden Hazard will both play in the event, alongside ex-Liverpool striker Robbie Fowler.

The BMW PGA Championship Celebrity Pro-Am is set to take place on Wednesday, the day before the tournament, with one professional player leading a team of amateurs in the competition.

Sports.title: Australia's Smith 'doesn't know' if he will play in 2027 Ashes
Sports.content:
Australia's Steve Smith says he "does not know" if he will play in next summer's Ashes in England.

Smith will turn 38 a couple of weeks before the first Test at Trent Bridge next June.

The batter has never won an Ashes series away from home and the 2027 contest would surely represent his last chance to do so.

Image: Smith averages 54.27 in Test matches in England

Speaking to The Telegraph, Smith said: "I don't even know if I'll be there yet. I'm kind of a series-by-series proposition, as I've been for a while. That's still a fair way away for me right now.

"I'd love to win [an Ashes in England] but you wait and see if that comes to fruition."

Smith's Test record in England is stellar - an average of 54.27 across 23 matches with his haul of 2,334 runs including eight hundreds and 10 half-centuries.

The right-hander averaged a shade over 50 across his nine Test outings in 2025, while in three games this year - one against England and two versus Bangladesh - he is averaging 61.40.

Image: Smith made scores of 71, 44 and 42 in the recent 1-1 home draw with Bangladesh

He said: "I feel I'm batting really nicely. I've found different ways to go about things on these tricky surfaces and still be able to score runs.

"So trying to contribute as well as I can for the team, score runs, take catches, help out in leadership areas where I need to - it's been a good, fun couple of years."

'Some balls now are just unplayable'

Smith - who is eager to prolong his T20 career and play for Australia in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics - also had his say on how bowlers perfecting the wobble-seam delivery in Test cricket is making life incredibly difficult for batters.

Image: Smith wants to represent Australia in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics

He said: "There are some balls now that are just unplayable. Some of these balls have your name on it and you can't do anything about it.

"If it's seaming two degrees, you're not hitting that ball, or you shouldn't be hitting that ball. If you're hitting it, you're probably not a very good batter, to be honest. You're playing down the wrong line.

"And if it's coming into you, and it's hitting the top of the stumps and you're getting trapped in front, you can't do anything about it."

England did not play a frontline spinner during their recent 3-0 home sweep of Pakistan with part-time tweaker Dan Lawrence supporting the four-pronged pace attack of Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue, Jofra Archer and Gus Atkinson.

For Australia, Nathan Lyon is not always a certain pick now due to seam-friendly conditions.

Image: Ollie Robinson flourished for England during a seam-dominated 2026 home summer

Smith added: "When the ball's moving as much as it is, and you can create relentless pressure by bowlers just continually hitting the spot, spin's by far the easiest thing to face and the thing that you can score freely off.

"It's a shame that we've had such spicy wickets that it's got to that point, because I love playing a spinner. I love watching spin bowlers bowl. I was a spin bowler myself back in the day.

"I'd love to see spin play much more of a part in Test cricket again."

Australia's next red-ball assignment is a three-match series in South Africa from October 9 - the first time they have tackled the Proteas away from home since the ball-tampering scandal in 2018 which led to bans for Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

Sports.title: Pollock open to exploring opportunities
Sports.content:
England star Henry Pollock would consider playing abroad or changing sports altogether and has an open-minded approach to his career as talks with Northampton Saints continue.

Pollock's focus remains on rugby and he is at the advanced stage of negotiations for a new contract with Gallagher Prem champions Northampton.

However, the 21-year-old is also looking to eventually broaden his horizons having signed for Eddie Hearn's Matchroom Talent Agency.

"I definitely want to go and live in different countries, explore new sports, explore new avenues," Pollock said.

"Eddie and the Matchroom team are constantly messaging me, calling me about different avenues and they've been great with that kind of stuff. I'm not going to say no to any opportunity.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' James Cole explains why a £1m contract at Northampton is unlikely but why it could be the shape of things to come in rugby union

"At the minute rugby is my main priority so I'm focusing on that in the near future, but as I said, you never know what's happening around the corner."

Hearn told Northampton in August that Pollock is "certainly a seven-figure player" because of the commercial clout he brings and the Lions flanker has taken the £1m-plus valuation in his stride.

"I don't see it as pressure," he said. "I see it as him doing his job. He's the best sports promoter in the world. The reason he's the best is because he gets his client what he deserves.

"Eddie's been great for me and he's given me so many avenues to get into. The way that he can give me access to loads of different stuff has been amazing.

"I have no bad words about him. The sport of rugby needs to change and hopefully this is a change."

Stay at Northampton on the horizon?

While Pollock's options for his future remain vast, it is understood that he is close to remaining at Northampton.

While Pollock wants to remain at a club that has been "special" to him, he understands that, during his career, he may need to make "selfish" decisions for his trajectory.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rugby star Henry Pollock tries sharing his golf tips using a simulator with Sky Sports reporter Mantej Mann as the Northampton Saints player likes to play the sport in his spare time.

"Northampton's been so great to me, I've been here my whole career and they've made me who I am. For me to stay here would be so special," said Pollock.

"Obviously, I know it's not as easy as that and I know there's lots of moving parts that come into play. I'm very open to new opportunities and I'm very open to exploring that.

"I'm so young so I think it's only right that I assess those options and find the best decision for myself.

"Your career is so short that you look back on yourself and you almost regret not exploring new avenues, exploring different things," he later added.

"I think for me, you almost have to be quite selfish in that aspect, think what's right for you. If that is staying here, then that's great, I'll be here for however long. If it's not, then I'll be open to new opportunities."

Sports.title: VARs who wrongly confirmed Haaland’s goal at Manchester United are stood down
Sports.content:
The video assistant referee officials who allowed Erling Haaland’s winning goal in the Manchester derby on Sunday have been stood down. Matt Donohue and his assistant, Blake Antrobus, have been told by Pro Ref they have not received appointments for this weekend’s round of Premier League fixtures.

Howard Webb, the chief ­refereeing officer, took the decision with his management team after a review of the weekend’s action. Their availa­bility will be reconsidered after the international break.

Donohue was called on to check Michael Oliver’s decision to ­disallow Haaland’s 60th-minute goal for offside. Using semi-automated ­offside technology, Donohue was able to establish that the Manchester City striker was onside and he overturned ­Oliver’s call. But he failed to spot Enzo Fernández had ­influenced play from an offside position, an ­infringement which Pro Ref said should have led him to recommend an on-field review.

This is the first time officials have been made to stand down this season owing to an error. Donohue, an EFL referee since 2018, has taken charge of three Championship matches this season as well as his VAR work. His EFL profile says he has completed Pro Ref’s “Enhanced VAR ­Training Programme”. ­Antrobus is also an assistant referee in the ­Premier League and ran the line in the first three matchdays.

Quick Guide How do I 

Pro Ref acknowledged an “error of ­judgment” in the Haaland incident in a statement on Sunday night and is understood to have contacted ­Manchester United to explain the mistake.

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola tells Liverpool forwards they must do more to make his system work
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola has shifted the focus on to Liverpool’s forwards for the team’s uninspiring display against Fulham, insisting they need to give more to make his system work.

The head coach admitted his team took “a step backwards” with their goalless draw on Saturday. His central midfield pairing of Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai struggled to contain their Fulham counterparts, winning two of five duels and one of nine duels respectively. But Iraola believes the problems started further forward with the pressing of Liverpool’s expensively assembled attack.

“It’s not a matter of just the midfielders,” he said. “When we have been good collectively the mid­fielders have looked a lot better and recovered more balls. It’s not because they are winning duels that they play better, it’s because we are helping them more to win the duels.

“If the ones up front do their job very well then the defenders and midfielders look good. If we are allowing them to defend one v one all the time and we are not aggressive, then our defenders will also struggle. If the players ahead of you are doing their job then you look a better midfielder or defender because you win more easier duels, you have more chance of winning one. It is more collective.

“It isn’t about changing this player for that player. That’s the help we have to give to our defenders and midfielders so everyone looks better, looks smarter and are in better positions.”

Iraola is unlikely to field the same frontline of Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Víctor Muñoz when Tottenham visit Anfield in the Carabao Cup third round on Tuesday. Trey Nyoni is pressing for a start in midfield and Iraola confirmed that Giorgi Mamardashvili, whom he tried to sign for Bournemouth, would replace ­Alisson in goal.

View image in fullscreen The Liverpool goalkeeper Giorgi Mamardashvili will make his first appearance of the season in the Carabao Cup tie against Tottenham. Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty Images

On the issues of Saturday, which contributed to a third draw in four Premier League games, he also said: “Compared to previous games, we won the ball a lot lower in the pitch. We don’t concede a lot, and the only big chance we conceded was our goal‑kick that we messed up. But we were recovering the ball always very low and when that happens you have to attack against 11 players and that makes it more difficult to make the difference.

“In previous games we could win it a lot higher and use our quick transitions to attack against less players and use the space better. That is key to our system. We need to recover the ball as high as possible because it makes the offensive side a lot easier, and we have more situations to attack in one v one.”

Sports.title: ‘Very weak. Very bad’: how Rodri’s verdict exposed woeful Valencia’s crisis | Sid Lowe
Sports.content:
Kiat Lim wanted to see Valencia play so badly, so that is what he did. It was week four in La Liga, 6 September, and for the first time since he was given the presidency 18 months earlier, the owner’s 33-year-old son was going to watch his team play a competitive game. He was going to do it from the inside, too, so he took a flight to Spain, landing at Manises in a black mask and cap, a van to the hotel, then the team bus to Mestalla. He looked through the window as they rolled along Avenida Suecia, a huge, noisy crowd waiting, but when he got off and headed through the iron gate with its ornate club badge, he saw that this was no welcome.

Above him as he went in were giant portraits of Mario Kempes, Antonio Puchades, Juan Sol, Gaizka Mendieta, David Villa and Santiago Cañizares, footballers from a better time; around him were yellow banners and whistles for the footballers there now. Inside, Lim saw the game start with the lower south stand empty as fans stayed away until the 19th minute, the sound of another protest drifting in from the street. They were out there still when, sitting alongside Joan Laporta, he saw Lamine Yamal score the sixth-minute opener then get a second. And although that, also from Lamine Yamal, was ruled out, he eventually saw Barcelona get four more, presiding over a 5-0 debut defeat.

He had seen supporters leave early, seen those that stayed turn towards him, chanting for him and his family to leave for good. He had seen the hankies come out and his players head into the tunnel heads bowed. He heard his manager insist that they were hurt but not sunk. What he did not see – what no one had seen yet but everyone would see soon enough – was the verdict from the bench.

Withdrawn after an hour to a standing ovation, the World Cup winner Rodri took a towel and turned to Pau Cubarsí. “This lot are very weak, eh?” Spain’s captain said. “Very weak, mate. Very bad.” He asked where they finished last season, pulled a face that said seriously?! when he was told just outside Europe, and noted that they had not left their own half. Valencia, he said, were malísimo. Awful.

View image in fullscreen Rodri was caught on camera calling his former club ‘very weak’. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

The sequence was caught on camera by El Día Después, and soon it was everywhere. Rodri called Valencia’s captain José Luis Gayà, saying sorry. After Barcelona’s Champions League win against Feyenoord three days later, he offered a public apology. It was, the Valencia coach, Carlos Corberán, said, a touch of self-preservation about his reaction, the least Rodri could do: apology accepted but his “unfortunate” words had “not been born of respect”. Yet there was no taunt, no mocking, no derision, no sign of a smile; instead there was a kind of shocked sadness. His words had not been thrown in anyone’s faces and were not for sharing. They were also true.

And if Corberán noted that “Mestalla had applauded him too”, an aggravating factor, some of them would do it again: it had needed saying. Within a few days someone had designed T-shirts declaring: “They’re very bad.” Underneath it read: “We’re all Rodri.” They had barely started printing off before Corberán was gone. Shoot the manager, not the messenger.

Barcelona’s victory over Valencia last Sunday was the third time in four games that they had scored five. Three days later they did it again. But those were not really the same – at Mestalla it was hard to avoid the feeling that Hansi Flick’s side could have scored 10 if they wanted to – and this was not just about Barcelona, this was about them. Valencia really are malísimo. Four games into season, they had conceded nine and scored one – and that was a gift, scored by a man who is now seriously injured. They had a solitary point, were bottom, and things were not about to get any better. This Friday, they lost the Used To Be Big Derby, 1-0 to Sevilla at the Sanchez Pizjuan, Juan Iglesias’s header condemning Valencia to the worst start in their history and Corberán to the sack.

There is something about these two; the last two times Sevilla fired their manager (García Pimienta and Matías Almeyda), it was after defeat to Valencia, while this is the third time Valencia fired a coach having lost at the Sánchez-Pizjuán: Quique Sánchez Flores in 2007, Nuno Espírito Santo in 2015 and now Corberán. Sánchez Flores got sacked at 4am. This time the wait was a little longer, if not much. When Valencia’s players and staff got back to Paterna to collect their cars in the small hours of Saturday, 100 fans waited to shout abuse and by the time training had finished there on Sunday morning the decision was made. Corberán was told during a video call from Singapore, Lim 10,000km away again.

The coach who arrived in December 2024 with Valencia in the relegation zone and pulled them up to 12th; the manager who saw them slip into the relegation zone again at the halfway stage last season only to pull clear all the way to the edge of Europe, would not get the chance to try again. Just five weeks into the season, two months after his contract was extended for another year, and 10 days after the CEO, Ron Gourlay, insisted that stability meant standing by a coach he believed in even if fans, some players and an increasingly belligerent media might not, he was gone.

Mind you, Gourlay has gone too. At that defiant two-hour, via-translator press conference Gourlay insisted that if his critics were going to wait for him to go, their coffee would get cold, but he has been sacked along with all his staff. Braulio Vázquez, has joined from Osasuna – even though Braulio recently said Osasuna are the “only real club left” – given the task of finding a new coach, with the B team manager taking over for the time being. His arrival ushers in a restructuring and a “new era” at Valencia, the statement said.

Quick Guide La Liga results Show Sevilla 1-0 Valencia Racing Santander 2-1 Alavés Osasuna 0-2 Espanyol Athletic Bilbao 1-1 Elche Real Madrid 4-1 Rayo Vallecano Celta Vigo 1-1 Málaga Levante 2-4 Barcelona Getafe1-1 Deportivo A Coruña Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Braulio knows the club – he was sporting director there between 2011 and 2013 and his son is the left-back – and has been successful at Osasuna, widely considered a more convincing candidate than the man who was there until Sunday afternoon. Few fans are sorry to see Corberán go: in fact they have been chanting for just that, the social fracture another factor. A change of coach can change things, a change of CEO or sporting director too. Look at Valencia’s squad and they should and probably will be better than this, the academy keeps producing talent, and Mestalla still fills weekly. There are coaches out there that would convince, with Ernesto Valverde and Jagoba Arrasate’s names the first to be floated. They certainly couldn’t be much worse than they have been so far. But patience is thin and faith thinner, a pessimism long since having crept in, and not unjustifiably so.

The only thing most fans want of the owners now is for them to leave which plays a part too, everyone caught in the never-ending tension. It is less than two years since Gourley took over, a year since Lim said that they have a “proper sporting plan now ... which is not to say we did not in the past but now we have professionals in place.” He was already the sixth man to supposedly have responsibility for signings since Peter Lim bought the club in 2014. Óscar Sánchez will be Valencia’s fifteenth coach since then – and even Voro, the eternal caretaker who has had the job six times does not want it any more. Only Nuno and Marcelino have better win percentages than Corberán. This summer, they spent €9m (£7.7m); 13 clubs spent more. More than 20 players have come in and gone out in the last two years. Over the last seven seasons they have spent short of €70m; they have sold for more than €230m.

View image in fullscreen Carlos Corberán was sacked by Valencia after their worst start to a season in their history. Photograph: Fran Santiago/Getty Images

There was a line in Rodri’s apology that talked about context and context is everything: Valencia being bad was not one Sunday; the fear is that it’s any given Sunday, that the days when they were good may be gone. He said that his comments were born of surprise, sadness, but the saddest thing is many weren’t surprised at all. This is what it is, they thought, grateful that someone else said it; forgive them if they do not foresee a way out. Yet if ambition must be adjusted it is hard not to hold on to what you were, your identity still, and maybe that’s a problem too. The Valencia Rodri returned to is not the Valencia he left behind. The year he went to England, they were a Champions League team; they have not made Europe since. And on Sunday he was right, Corberán taking the fall within a week.

“We all want Valencia to get back to where they should be, one of the best clubs in our league,” Rodri said three days later, but he had already said enough, a truth told. Sitting in the stands, Lim had just about seen enough too.

Sports.title: Ludek Miklosko, former West Ham and QPR goalkeeper, dies aged 64
Sports.content:
The former West Ham and QPR goalkeeper Ludek Miklosko has died at the age of 64. Miklosko, who won caps for Czechoslovakia and Czechia, had cancer.

Miklosko joined West Ham from Baník Ostrava in 1990 for £300,000 after a trial and helped the club win promotion to the top division in his first season. He left in 1998 having made 373 appearances, joining QPR, initially on loan. Miklosko ended his career there in 2001 and returned to West Ham, where he worked as a goalkeeping coach until 2010.

He later worked for a sports agency before taking roles at Baník Ostrava as a board member and sporting director.

View image in fullscreen Ludek Miklosko made 373 appearances for West Ham. Photograph: Tony Marshall/Empics Sport/PA Images/Alamy

West Ham said Miklosko would “for ever hold a special place in the hearts of the West Ham family”. The club described him as a “beloved, inspirational goalkeeper and gentle giant of a man”.

Miklosko played 40 times for Czechoslovakia and twice for Czechia in an international career that began in 1982. He said in 2024 that he was withdrawing from cancer treatment.

His son Martin Miklosko said in a statement shared by West Ham: “We are heartbroken at his loss, but take huge comfort from the immense support he received from all of you, along with the knowledge that he is now at peace and no longer suffering.

“Dad simply loved West Ham United, and especially hearing his name sung loud and proud at every game. The club, and its fans, were and always will be a part of our family, so thank you all from the bottom of our hearts.”

Sports.title: Top of the table, empty in the stands: inside the revolt against Lazio’s owner | Nicky Bandini
Sports.content:
Gennaro Gattuso has given some memorable post‑game interviews down the years. Who could forget his “sometimes maybe good, sometimes maybe shit” rant at OFI Crete or the face of the beleaguered interpreter tasked with translating it?

Last year, not long before taking charge of the Italian national team, Gattuso got into a finger‑jabbing, language‑swapping, almost‑nose‑to‑nose shouting match with Josko Jelicic on Croatian television.

There was something more affecting about the soft way he spoke in his Calabrian accent on Saturday. Without anger, but with an air of melancholy. “Football without fans is shit,” he said. “What do you think? I’d say it’s better to stay home. Better to go for a walk with the dogs.”

He had just seen his Lazio side let a two-goal lead slip at home against Milan, but that was hardly a disaster. The Biancocelesti are still top of the table, at least until Roma and Inter play on Monday. For a team who lost several starters in the summer, who began his tenure with a cup defeat by a Serie B club in August and whose fans refuse to enter their own stadium, this season has already exceeded expectations.

It may represent the beginnings of a redemption arc for Gattuso, who stood down from managing Italy in April after failing to qualify for the World Cup. He was not a popular choice to succeed Maurizio Sarri in Rome.

He is not the reason why supporters are boycotting Lazio’s home games in huge numbers. Season ticket sales have fallen from close to 30,000 last year to less than 4,500, according to the football finances website Calcio e Finanza. Last season’s home game against Milan drew 50,000 spectators, but the same fixture on Saturday had less than half that number, with a noisy majority cheering for the visitors.

Lazio’s fans have not stopped caring. Hundreds gathered outside the team’s training ground before the game, forming a convoy of mopeds to escort the players’ bus to Ponte Milvio – a bridge that crosses the Tiber River close to the Stadio Olimpico. A statement released by supporters’ groups beforehand had announced their intention to go from there “to watch the game in a pub or at home”.

View image in fullscreen Gennaro Gattuso said that football means very little without fans. Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/AP

It is an act of protest specifically against the club’s owner, Claudio Lotito. Fans have travelled in their thousands to away games, even for unglamorous pre-season friendlies, reinforcing the message that they still care about their club, but do not want to endorse the man who controls it.

The feud with Lotito is not new. In January, an open letter was posted on Change.org accusing him of denying fans the right to dream throughout his more than two decades as owner. “It has been years, almost seven, since we lifted a trophy,” reads the petition, signed by more than 45,000. “These are years in which we have not signed a footballer to stir the heart of fans young and old.”

Quick Guide Serie A results Show Venezia 2-4 Fiorentina Genoa 1-1 Frosinone Lazio 2-2 Milan Atalanta 1-2 Cagliari Lecce 3-2 Monza Napoli 1-0 Bologna Sassuolo 3-2 Juventus Monday's fixtures: Como v Parma Torino v Roma Internazionale v Udinese Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

There are layers to these grievances. The letter references the club’s handling of a memorial for Vincenzo Paparelli, a Lazio supporter killed by a flare fired from the Roma end during a derby in 1979. Lotito was accused of denying Paparelli’s niece a chance to walk on to the pitch during an event last November.

He denied that version of events, saying “the real problem was that four representatives of the organised support wanted to go with her”.

Lotito has been accused of simply not paying attention to Lazio with his focus elsewhere. He is active in politics, having been elected to the Italian senate in 2022.

He bought another football club, Salernitana, in 2011, and over the next 10 years helped them to get promoted from Serie D to the top flight, at which point he was forced to sell up due to the conflict of interest. Rules have since been modified to prevent simultaneous ownership of two teams in the top three divisions, but that did not deter Lotito from completing the takeover of another fourth-tier club, Reggina, this summer.

Have such investments kept him from pursuing the big‑name signings Lazio fans crave? It is not exactly clearcut. Lazio could not have bought anyone last summer anyway, as they were placed under a transfer embargo for failing to meet liquidity requirements introduced by the Italian Football Federation. These, too, were the subject of debate as Lotito argued they failed to weigh the club’s successes in operating without major outstanding debts.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Diego Moreira scored the equaliser for the visitors in a stadium that felt like a Milan home game. Photograph: Giuseppe Cottini/AC Milan/Getty Images

Navigating those rules required selling a string of important players – Taty Castellanos and Mattéo Guendouzi in January, Mario Gila, Alessio Romagnoli and Ivan Provedel in the summer. But after the embargo was lifted, Lazio made some canny signings. The centre-back Danilho Doekhi arrived from Union Berlin on a free transfer, the striker Albert Gudmundsson came in on loan from Fiorentina, as did the midfielder Davide Frattesi from Inter.

The last of those looks like a steal, secured for a €5m (£4.28m) loan fee last month, with a right to buy for €10m next year. Frattesi cost Inter more than twice that much when they signed him off the back of a break-out season at Sassuolo in 2023, only to keep him for the next three years as understudy to Nicolò Barella, Hakan Calhanoglu and others in a stacked midfield.

After joining Lazio this summer, Frattesi – still just 26 – said he had deliberately chosen a club that would put the weight on his shoulders. He scored in his first three games: winners against Bologna and Genoa, then the opener in a 2-1 victory away against Udinese.

He did not find the net this weekend. Lazio’s best attacking work originated from Mattia Zaccagni on the left wing. He had a cross converted at the back post by Matteo Cancellieri in the 10th minute, then another forced home at the second attempt by Tijjani Noslin after a defender knocked it on to the crossbar. Zaccagni had a close-range attempt of his own well saved by Mike Maignan in-between. It could have been a rout. Instead, Milan made three half-time substitutions and one of them, the €50m signing Diego Moreira, scored a pair of fine goals to ensure the game finished 2-2.

Might things have gone differently in a stadium packed with Lazio supporters, instead of one that felt like Milan’s home away from home? “Maybe with our fans here we would have managed to hold out,” Zaccagni said. “But the draw is a fair result in the end.”

Gattuso thanked the fans who had come to show their support beforehand. “I don’t think anyone is happy with this situation,” he said. “Everyone wants to come to the stadium, to have 50,000 people, 55,000 people.

“I think those fans came [to the training ground] because they recognise what the players are giving them. The fact of not giving up. The fact they are wearing the shirt with pride. That’s my reading. And that made me emotional today, seeing the people who came. It’s not football without the fans.”

Sports.title: Polanski the first managerial victim of Bundesliga season as Gladbach fail again | Andy Brassell
Sports.content:
It could not go on. Even at this early stage the sinking feeling was familiar and impossible to shake, and something had to give at Borussia Mönchengladbach. The first Bundesliga coaching change of the season is upon us just three games in, and it is not a major surprise that it is Eugen Polanski departing. Neither is it a shock that Gladbach are involved; after all, it was at exactly this point last season – three games in – that they parted ways with Gerardo Seoane.

A club with more prospects and direction would have chosen to move on from Polanski in the summer, but the reality is that Gladbach have few of either. Saturday afternoon’s humiliation at Freiburg – a club enjoying a 100% record, guided by poise and purpose, having spent the Johan Manzambi money wisely – was no bad day at the office but a season in microcosm. The home side cruised into a 2-0 lead inside the first half-hour before the Gladbach captain, Tim Kleindienst, was sent off for a second yellow card (after an utterly avoidable first one). One former Gladbach player, Yannik Engelhardt, scored twice while another, Matthias Ginter, made two assists. It finished 5-0 and could have been way worse.

Polanski fell on his sword on Sunday morning and there is no doubt how painful it is. Polanski first arrived at Gladbach when he was eight years old, came through the academy, made his professional debut for the club in 2004 and was head coach of the under-23s for three years before being parachuted into the first-team role to mop up the mess just under a year ago, after Seoane was sacked.

“Borussia Mönchengladbach was and always will be my club,” he reflected on Sunday. “That’s why it hurts so much that things have turned out like this. After successfully avoiding relegation, we made a number of changes for this season. We had high hopes, but we didn’t manage to achieve them. I’m sorry about that. I sincerely hope that Borussia gets back on track very quickly.”

View image in fullscreen Freiburg fans watched their side put five goals past Borussia Mönchengladbach. Photograph: SPP Sport Press Photo./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

Polanski’s sincerity is not in doubt but he must know that his words carry more hope than expectation. He never really stood a chance, an inexperienced coach inheriting a bad situation and a squad of limited means. The last time they were in Europe, five-and-a-half years ago, Gladbach reached the Champions League last 16, before being bounced out by eventual finalists Manchester City. Marco Rose’s team was equipped with talent including Yann Sommer, Ginter, Denis Zakaria, Ramy Bensebaini, Jonas Hofmann and Marcus Thuram.

Today’s vintage is just not of the same quality. The intervening years have not been kind and losing Thuram and Bensebaini, for example, after their contracts expired underlines how poorly succession has been managed. Roland Virkus, who stepped down as sporting director last September but is still involved in the scouting department, copped a lot of the blame for the talent drain, but many of the contractual issues were inherited rather than caused by him. The incumbent, Rouven Schröder, is now coming under the microscope – for sticking with Polanski in hope more than anything else, and for a wide-ranging recruitment campaign that hasn’t worked at all so far.

Kleindienst captured the current direction of travel. Having launched into some of his teammates after last week’s home defeat by Elversberg (in which they let a 3-1 lead slip before losing the game in stoppage time), suggesting in an interview afterwards with ZDF that some of them “should watch less TikTok, or whatever,” he left his side high and dry in Freiburg. The 2.Bundesliga is full enough of fallen giants. At this rate, another could be joining them soon enough.

Thank you for your feedback.

Talking points

After the week in which the Ballon d’Or nominees were announced Harry Kane belatedly made his contribution to the Bayern-driven campaign in his favour, scoring an artful second-half winner for a first Bundesliga goal of the season which prised a tough win for his team at Elversberg. The home side lost their 100% record but gained plenty of credit, and Maurice Krattenmacher – bought from Bayern – scored a spectacular equaliser to offer the possibility a point against the champions. “We played bravely from the back,” said their goalkeeper Nicolas Kristof. “We can be proud of how we performed today.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Nicolas Kristof makes himself big for Elversberg to deny Harry Kane. Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters

Borussia Dortmund are the only other team apart from Freiburg on maximum points three games in after they swept aside Paderborn on Saturday afternoon. Though much has been made of Fábio Silva aiming to challenge Serhou Guirassy for his place they played well together here, with the latter setting up the former for the opener and both being at pains to demonstrate just how well they get along. Substitute Felix Nmecha sealed the deal with a late double (the second of which was a spectacular overhead kick) but the best news for Niko Kovac was fitness related, with Nico Schlotterbeck making a surprise first appearance of the season after injury and Konstantinos Karetsas judged well enough to travel back to his hometown of Genk and perform the ceremonial kick-off before the game with Gent after his worrying collapse in the Champions League against Villarreal; it is hoped he will resume training this week.

Leipzig and Martin Demichelis, on the other hand, desperately needed a result after Thursday night’s comprehensive Champions League defeat at Como followed a shock defeat at Werder Bremen domestically and, happily for them, Hamburg were very obliging visitors. It was a Sunday afternoon breeze capped by a first goal back for the returning Christopher Nkunku. HSV could be in for a long season, though the pending contract extension for coach Merlin Polzin is not expected to be threatened by this reverse.

Talking of early pressure Leverkusen avoided a second straight away defeat, this time at high-flying Augsburg, where the king of the rabona finish, Patrik Schick, applied one such touch in the penultimate minute of normal time to rescue a point for Carles Martínez. Sporting director Simon Rolfes firmly but fairly reminded it was “absolutely the coach’s job” to ensure the “concentration and fighting spirit in every situation” that had eluded Die Werkself at the beginning of the second half as they let an interval lead slip, with Michael Gregoritsch’s brace making him Augsburg’s all-time top scorer in the Bundesliga.

After last week’s heroic rearguard action against Bayern, Schalke were able to spread their wings and get a first Bundesliga win in nearly three-and-a-half years at Union. Robin Gosens’ superb volley to open the scoring in the first half was their first goal in the top flight in 1,203 days. Miron Muslic had not been joking when he said pre-match that this would be “no beauty contest,” but a determined defensive effort (and more Loris Karius excellence) secured the points and left the Union manager,Mauro Lustrinelli, with much to ponder.

The Niclas Füllkrug revival continues, with the on-loan West Ham striker scoring his second in two games to salvage a point for Bremen after they had trailed at Köln. “You can see that he leads by example as a player,” enthused his head coach, Daniel Thioune. “That’s what we’ve been missing. His connection with the club is very strong.”

Sports.title: PSG have finally won a game in Ligue 1 – but they were far from convincing
Sports.content:
It was just a flicker. Ferran Torres picks the ball up and passes it to João Neves. The Portugal midfielder plays it into Ousmane Dembélé, who has lured in Raphaël Le Guen and eliminates him with a mesmeric first-time back-heel into the path of Torres.

The Brest defence are just cones in a training drill, mere extras in this work of art as the Spaniard glides back into the scene to pass the ball into Egil Selvik’s bottom-left corner from 25 yards; it happened in slow motion, but was too quick for the Norwegian goalkeeper to react.

It is a move that had the slick and elegant fluidity of what we have come to expect from Paris Saint-Germain. Just four minutes in, the champions were ahead and the Stade Francis Le-Blé anticipated a show of force, a statement from their visitors.

Luis Enrique had described PSG’s start to the Ligue 1 season as catastrophic. A comfortable 6-1 win against Slovan Bratislava in the Champions League last Wednesday signalled a welcome return to form. The Sopposition manager, none other than Yaya Touré, described his opponents on the night as a machine – we have heard that before.

But once again, PSG were defective in Brittany on Sunday night, even if they did leave with all three points. Torres’s sublime finish was the only goal of the game. It was the Spaniard’s sixth since joining from Barcelona in the summer. All of his six efforts on target this season have found the net. He is clearly still riding the crest of a wave of confidence, having scored the winner in the World Cup final.

Torres’s supreme confidence is not shared by his teammates. Vitinha in particular has yet to resurface since the summer break and PSG are suffering from the lack of incision he usually provides. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is not quite back to his usual levels either and going into this game, there were creeping doubts about Matvey Safonov in goal. The Russian was at fault last weekend when Stanis Idumbo finished at his near post to secure a win for Monaco. It was at his near post he conceded to Kai Havertz in the Champions League final in May; if there is a weakness in PSG, Safonov was the most likely candidate.

But it is only thanks to him that PSG ended a run of five games without a win against French opponents. He was not forced into action when Nuno Mendes played Kamory Doumbia in one-on-one in the second half, the Mali international striking the outside of the PSG post.

Safonov did get a strong hand down low to his left when Doumbia rose highest to thunder a header towards goal and in the dying stages Pathé Mboup’s curled effort to the far post was tipped around the corner.

View image in fullscreen Goalkeeper Matvey Safonov kept PSG in the game with a number of saves. Photograph: Xavier Laine/Getty Images

Brest finished with a higher xG than the European champions, but had no points to show for it. Moments of brilliance in both areas were the difference. But that is what PSG are confined to at the minute: moments, flickers of brilliance.

“It was the worst of our four Ligue 1 matches, even if we won,” said Luis Enrique. “In the other three matches, we showed a high level at the back, but our opponents scored every chance. This time, it was the opposite.”

Alarm bells are not ringing. PSG often start slowly and it is only the quality of opposition faced at the start of the last campaign that ensured there was not such a significant deficit to the leaders. They are five points behind Lille, Monaco and Rennes, all of whom are on 10 points.

Last week, Marquinhos said that it was “a matter of ambition and motivation” as PSG hoped to replicate the success of the past two seasons. Just like Torres’s passed finish, PSG are all about timing and they have a knack for peaking at the right moment.

There were no doubts Brest were up to the occasion. The Stade Francis Le-Blé was a cauldron of emotion as Eric Roy was commemorated. The Brest manager, who guided the club into European competition for the first time, in 2024, died in June due to pancreatic cancer that began when he was appointed as the club’s manager in January 2023. His diagnosis was never made public.

Roy’s daughter, Victoria-Rose, spoke on the pitch before the match, “King Eric” shirts were worn on the sidelines and there were further moments of commemoration in the stands throughout the game. Hugo Magnetti said they had played for Roy. “He would have been proud of us, but he would have also ticked us off for missing some big chances.”

The game, at times, felt like a subplot, but what happened in it was not inconsequential. Some of those fears about waning “ambition and motivation” were deepened, as was a crisis of confidence among some of PSG’s key players, despite victory. But there were also flickers of brilliance Luis Enrique must hope will become more enduring as the season progresses.

Talking points

Will Still and Auxerre have their first points on the board thanks to their young English forward Cameron Archer. The Southampton loanee made his debut last weekend and scored a stunner in a 3-1 defeat to Lyon. This weekend he scored the only goal of the game against Nice. The win drags Auxerre off the bottom of the table – a place now occupied by their opponents on the day. Nice, without a win, have scored once in their first four matches. Their coach, Olivier Pantaloni, says there are traces of last season’s difficult campaign lingering in the minds of his players. They must quickly dispel them in order to avoid a repeat.

Four games in and the temperature is already rising in Marseille. The season started well, with a 4-0 home win to Strasbourg on opening day, but they have since lost to Monaco, Paris FC and Rennes. There is no real shame in any of those defeats; the matches were close and the opponents are expected to be in the race for Europe. “We can rival these teams but not yet beat them,” said Bruno Génésio after the 1-0 defeat at Rennes on Friday. Génésio added it was not up to him to state the club’s objectives this season – a clear message to his superiors. “We may need to explain things more clearly Maybe we have to say it so that people can understand.” The lack of quality and depth in the squad says enough; Marseille are outsiders in the race for European football.
