Sports.title: 'I wasn't welcome here, it was a s***storm... but it's great to be back': Sheffield Wednesday legend DAVID HIRST is back where he belongs - enjoying pints and pies with fans in his brand new bar at Hillsborough
Sports.content:
First there was an invitation to dinner, a handshake and a discussion about the protocol of nicknames when David Hirst met David Storch.

'Is it David or Dave or is it Hirsty?' the American millionaire plotting to buy Sheffield Wednesday wanted to know. 'Hirsty's good enough for me, and then we'll know who you're talking to,' replied the local hero, scorer of 149 goals across 11 years at Hillsborough from 1986.

'Well, that's great, because my name's Storchy.'

This was March, soon after Storch's Arise consortium became the preferred bidder to buy the Owls out of administration after a ruinous decade under the ownership of Dejphon Chansiri.

When they met again, it was at the West Bromwich Albion game in May.

'A fantastic carnival atmosphere, exactly how it should be every game at Hillsborough,' says Hirst. 'He came into the guest lounge, and everybody is Mr Chairman this and that, and I'm like, "Hey, Storchy, over here, mate".

Sheffield Wednesday legend David Hirst is back at the club and in a bar bearing his name

Hirst was invited back from exile under the new ownership of American David Storch

Storch is helping to rebuild Wednesday in League One after a ruinous decade under the ownership of Dejphon Chansiri, pictured

'Even to me it felt a bit wrong, but he did give me permission to use it.'

Wednesday are reborn under Storch. Not only on the pitch, where Henrik Pedersen's team sit top of League One after six games, but more importantly off it, where the new owners have embraced the club's history and the city's heritage to re-energise one of the great clubs of northern football.

'We met just before the takeover in a little restaurant in Sheffield,' recalls Hirst. 'We had a great chat about plans they had if the takeover came to fruition. I was sold from the start.

'It was all about reconnecting and finding out who and what they needed to know to get our club back where it belongs.

'They've come with such a positive attitude into what was to be honest an absolute s***storm.'

Besides installing a serious executive team and recruiting 18 new players, including the return of Barry Bannan, the new owners restored the 1970s owl as the club crest and struck a kit deal with Umbro to produce a classic home kit with blue-and-white stripes and black shorts.

Another popular move involved luring Hirst out of exile and back to Hillsborough as club ambassador.

What better way to tempt a Yorkshireman who likes a pint than to give him his own bar in the heart of the South Stand.

Sheffield Wednesday are top of League One after recruiting 18 new players, including bringing back Barry Bannan to the club

A bar has been named in honour of Hirst, scorer of 149 goals across 11 years at Hillsborough from 1986

'I don't know how the other lads felt but I wasn't welcome after my previous adventures with Mr Chansiri,' says Hirst, alluding to the row surrounding his son George, now at Stoke, in 2018 after an unseemly contract dispute.

'Things were well documented from one side and that was Mr Chansiri's side. He embellished and elaborated on things that weren't true and it wasn't something I was prepared to slug out in public, so I walked away.

'We weren't the bitter ones. We understood George had to leave through situations beyond our control. I was still a Wednesday fan. I still watched from afar. I'm a blue, George is a blue.

'Thankfully it worked out well for both of us and now it's great to be back.

'It was a no-brainer for me. I'd been away for 10 years and to come back and the welcome I received… the only thing missing was the fatted calf.'

Hirst is in his natural habitat. Hirsty's Social opened at the start of this season. It is a casual corporate vibe with the focus on pies and ale rather than prawn sandwiches, and with fans mingling, chatting, keeping an eye on the live sport rather than wedding reception table service, all of which goes down well with the man with his name above the door.

'Come on, get the tellies on,' shouts Hirst as he strolls into his bar three hours before kick-off on Saturday against Wigan with news from Edgbaston that Joe Root has played on only to be reprieved by a no-ball call in the Test against Pakistan and keen to catch up on the Solheim Cup latest.

He is engulfed by requests for selfies and autographs, resisting offers to buy him another pint. Well, some of them. He greets those he knows with a bear hug.

'Anyone who was here against Bromley, yes I am wearing the same clothes,' admits Hirst as he addresses his audience. 'Yes, I have washed them before you ask, but we all liked the 7-2 win, so I thought I'd give it another go.'

Hirst had walked away from the club after a row surrounding his son George, now at Stoke, in 2018 after an unseemly contract dispute with Chansiri

Hirst, 40 years on from joining the Owls, believes the club is more Sheffield centric than it has been in years under its American owners

Last month marked 40 years since he joined the Owls from Barnsley for £250,000. 'Thanks for the reminder,' the 58-year-old rolls his eyes. 'I've been here so long I know virtually everybody in the stadium.

'It's nice to come and have a drink with some of them and chat about yesteryear or what's happening going forward.

'We've had a good start. If we'd got beat every game it might be different but everybody coming in here has a smile on their face.'

The room is dominated by an enormous 'WEDNESDAY' sign which once adorned the back of the West Stand. It was found unused and unloved beneath the stand and has been repurposed to hang over the bar.

There are plans to decorate the walls with Hirst's old shirts and photographs and other memorabilia, including his original contract, also unearthed among the piles of old documents.

Brecht Vierstraete, an artist and a Wednesday fan from Belgium, appears with a gift, a framed portrait of Hirst who promises it will go on display.

Among his guests are former players Mel Sterland and Rodger Wylde. Somehow Wylde topples from a small stage during a brief Q&A session on the microphone and returns smiling and thankfully unhurt and tells the American owners they're going to be need a bigger stage, only to be admonished by Hirst for bringing the x-rated language of the dressing room into his bar.

The soundtrack is peppered with Sheffield music. There's beer from the nearby Thornbridge brewery and fine pies by local bakers Jackson's. The logos and emblems stitched into the carpets have all been designed by creative agency Peter & Paul in Kelham Island, a mile or so from Hillsborough.

Last month marked 40 years since Hirst (pictured battling Denis Irwin in 1997) joined the Owls from Barnsley for £250,000

Sheffield pop artist Pete McKee presented Storch with an original painting at the first home game of the season against Bradford. 'This place has had three licks of paint since 1966, and now we're getting murals and paintings on the wall,' says Hirst.

The McKee painting, which now hangs in the boardroom, is of Storch in his Wednesday stripes, meta shades and a garland around his neck, an image taken from the West Brom game when the new owner walked out to tell a full house he had completed the takeover and convinced the EFL to waive the 15-point penalty they expected this season.

As far as first impressions go, it was emphatic. Hillsborough erupted and the aviation tycoon had lift off although Wednesday's identity under its new American owners is more Sheffield centric than it has been for years.

It is one of the vital differences. When Chansiri bought the club in 2015, he spent heavily on players and reached the play-off final, one win from returning to the Premier League, but they lost the game, broke the EFL's financial rules, suffered points deductions and descended into crisis.

By the time the administrators moved in, it was an empty shell of a club.

'I've seen Storchy and other members of his staff in and around the city,' says Hirst. 'They've been at Sunday League football, non-league football, in the city shaking hands and speaking to people. That never happened before.

'With Mr Chansiri, it was his box and that was that. There was no input or output. He ran things the way he saw fit and the guy spent a hell of a lot of money, but you can't buy dreams like that.

Hirst is in his natural habitat in the new bar, which has a casual corporate vibe with the focus on chatting with fans

'He thought you could come from nowhere and run a football club his way. It turned out spending a vast amount of money wasn't the right way. The right way is to get the knowledge around you and listen to the right people.'

Hirst's attire fails to inspire another win so the Owls settle for a goalless draw against Wigan, enough to keep them top and remind everyone about the dangers of getting carried away.

Wednesday are building from scratch under strict EFL spending restrictions.

'Let's not kid ourselves,' says Hirst. 'We were weeks if not days from going under. We've an old ground that needs some care. They're working on it.

'Things are not going to be perfect this season on or off the field. Hopefully, it's good but I come from the real world, and I've been around football for long enough to know there's no magic wand in this game.'

Sports.title: Why US Open champion Alexander Zverev still has plenty to prove if he truly wants to join Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner at the top, writes TAMARA PRENN
Sports.content:
Why US Open champion Alexander Zverev still has plenty to prove if he truly wants to join Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner at the top, writes TAMARA PRENN

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Unexpectedly, ESPN’s coverage of the US Open men’s final between Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton ended with a plea.

‘Get healthy, Carlos and Jannik,’ American tennis icon John McEnroe said as his parting shot, responding to whether the new champion would take his dominance into next year’s Australian Open.

For all of the German’s mammoth achievements this season, Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner remain the ghosts at the feast. Last year, the two men split the Grand Slams, most often in finals against one another.

Their dominant 2025 suggested their young rivalry would take the baton from the previous generation, Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer, with the Spaniard and the Italian shutting out all but the very best opponents at the very top of the sport. But who would be their Novak Djokovic?

Despite being an ever-present in the top 10, a majors finalist and Olympic gold medallist in 2021, Zverev was largely shut out of conversations over who would make the duo a trio.

He is older than both stars, part of a generation including Daniil Medvedev and Stefanos Tsitsipas once tipped to take the reins from the Big Three, only to be shut out by Djokovic’s longevity and Sinner and Alcaraz’s precocity. And when he did make it to Grand Slam finals, it wasn’t pretty.

Alexander Zverev won the second Grand Slam of his career at the US Open on Sunday night

Zverev overcame Ben Shelton in the final, but can he challenge a fully fit Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner?

The strongest evidence for why Zverev had long held a reputation for stuttering at the very biggest moments came in his first US Open final, six years ago. The then-23-year-old scythed through his draw at a 2020 Covid-19 tournament defined by its absences: Nadal, Federer, and Djokovic, defaulted after striking a line judge in the throat with a ball accidentally. He held a two-set lead against Dominic Thiem, lost it, served for the championship in the fifth set, and lost that too. The Austrian player left with the trophy, and Zverev started growing scar tissue.

Then came Paris, four years later, against Alcaraz. Having lost the opening set, Zverev clawed back the next two, only to lose in five. His next Grand Slam final, against Sinner in Melbourne in 2025, was a rout.

This season, with Alcaraz recovering from a wrist injury between April and late August and Sinner struck down by the sweltering heat at the French Open, and kept out by knee inflammation in New York, Zverev has undergone valuable healing.

‘I think God has seen how hard we worked, how much we suffered, how much pain we went through,’ he said before lifting yesterday’s trophy. ‘I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before.’

What winning two Grand Slams has not done however, is prove he is capable of going toe-to-toe with either Sinner or Alcaraz.

The Italian is a particular problem for Zverev, who has not been able to beat the 25-year-old in their last 10 meetings. After winning Roland-Garros in June, Zverev arrived at Wimbledon playing with lightness and explosivity - neither of which are qualities which normally define his game. This allowed him one set against Sinner when they met in the final, and then it was business as usual.

When asked on Sunday if he considered himself the best player in the world, he paused. ‘If we say right now with Jannik being injured and Carlos coming back from injury, maybe.

‘Four, five months ago when both of them were healthy, I wasn't. I was losing to Jannik all the time. If everyone is healthy, I think Jannik is still ahead.’

Sinner and Alcaraz dominated in 2025 but both have struggled with injuries and fitness setbacks this year

Zverev is yet to quite prove himself against the duo (pictured after losing the Wimbledon final to Sinner back in July)

Baked into that response then, is the idea that Alcaraz might occupy a similar plane to Zverev. But Zverev’s recent record against Alcaraz is only slightly more intricate than his head-to-head against Sinner. The Spaniard is the only other player to shut him out at the Slams this year.

When they met at the Australian Open, the clash went to five testing sets across a mind-bending five hours and 27 minutes. But Alcaraz was significantly impaired by persistent cramp, and an injury to his right leg deep in the third set. Zverev, one of the fittest athletes on the tour, could not kill him off, and Alcaraz went on to win his career Grand Slam.

With Sinner’s return to the tour this season still unconfirmed, Zverev could yet end the year as world No1. But the real test comes against Sinner and Alcaraz when fit in 2027.

The player who will take the mantle as disruptor must have Grand Slam form against the greatest - and of the two finalists, it was Shelton who put himself in that conversation after his quarter-final classic against Alcaraz last week. Without beating tennis’ two biggest stars, Zverev is only picking up their scraps.

Sports.title: Blundering Manchester derby VAR officials set to be BLOCKED from working  on Man United matches after being stood down for 'error of judgement' in allowing Erling Haaland's offside winner to stand
Sports.content:
Blundering Manchester derby VAR officials set to be BLOCKED from working on Man United matches after being stood down for 'error of judgement' in allowing Erling Haaland's offside winner to stand

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The bungling VAR duo at the centre of the Manchester derby fiasco are set to be blocked from officiating on United matches for the foreseeable future, Daily Mail Sport understands.

Matt Donohue and assistant Blake Antrobus were stood down for this weekend's fixtures after refs' chief Howard Webb admitted 'an error of judgement' was made over the staggering decision to allow Erling Haaland's winner for City at a stunned Old Trafford.

And it can also be disclosed that the pair are now highly unlikely to work on future United games for some time, according to those with knowledge of the situation.

Donohue and Antrobus will not officiate on any matches until 'at least after the international break' according to ref's body Pro Ref who, once again, find themselves in damage limitation mode.

Haaland's 60th minute strike was initially ruled out on the field for offside, with the Norwegian deemed to have strayed beyond United's last man.

However, VAR intervened and deemed that the City striker was actually being played onside by the outstretched boot of United defender Patrick Dorgu.

The VAR who made an 'error of judgement' in awarding a goal to Manchester City in Sunday's derby at Old Trafford has not been appointed to a Premier League game this weekend

Haaland's goal was given after a VAR review, with it having originally been ruled offside

However, Enzo Fernandez was in an offside position and attempted to go for the ball, meaning it should have been disallowed, with Pro Ref later apologising to Man United for the error

Referee Michael Oliver was subsequently ordered to overturn his decision. However, the officials appeared to miss the fact that Haaland's team-mate Enzo Fernandez, who was in an offside position, had clearly interfered with play given his proximity to United defender Lisandro Martinez and keeper Senne Lammens.

On Sunday night former World Cup Final referee Webb, who is said to be 'devastated' at the fiasco, explained that the VAR pair established that because Fernandez did not play the ball any offside offence was 'subjective' - but admitted they had not 'recognised the likely impact of his position and should have recommended an on-field review'.

He also apologised to United for the 'error of judgement' and promised a review would take place following their 1-0 loss.

Baffled United boss Michael Carrick, whose side have now won just one of their opening four fixtures, said he was at a loss, when interviewed post-match. 'The explanation I got was he (Fernandez) wasn't interfering with play,' he said. 'So I just don't get it. I really don't get it.

'I can't understand how they're trying to help referees and putting so many layers behind them with so many people, screens, and so many whatever offices to try and come up with the right decisions.

'If that's how the rules are interpreted, that you're not interfering with play because you've thrown yourself at the ball six yards from goal and pretty much nearly touched it, which then Lisandro has to react from – it's worrying if that's really how the game's seen by those who are officiating it.'

Carrick added: 'I think we all understand what that rule means and it's pretty obvious. It's as obvious as it gets.'

On Monday, Pro Ref announced that Donohue and Antrobus had been stood down, but the move has done little to quieten noise across fans, ex-players and media.

The highly avoidable mistake has put refereeing chief Howard Webb under scrutiny

Matt Donohue (left) was on VAR for the game alongside his assistant Blake Antrobus (right)

Some have called for the Premier League to ditch VAR entirely, making the point that a system operated by humans is, perhaps, unlikely to effectively eradicate human error.

Such a scenario is deemed a long shot, given that clubs voted 19-1 to keep the system at the last poll in 2024 and that the one dissenting voice, Wolverhampton Wanderers, are no longer in the Premier League.

The mess came on a problematic weekend for the refs' body which also saw it come under fire from Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta. The Spaniard hit out after Sunderland were awarded a penalty after Ezri Konsa was adjudged to have dragged Dan Ballard to the ground from a long throw – a decision upheld following a VAR review.

'I am so upset,' said Arteta, who claimed Ballard had initiated the contact. 'It is unacceptable at this level, unacceptable. It can change the course of the season. I've seen it 10 times to make sure and I said "it is not possible it is penalty".

'It is a judo roll. That's what it is. This cannot happen.' The Gunners have also reached out to Pro Ref for an explanation.

With the season just four matches old, there have been a number of other contentious decisions. The Premier League Key Match Incidents panel ruled Arsenal should have had a penalty at Aston Villa for Ian Maatsen's challenge on Bruno Guimaraes and also that the Villa man should have received a second yellow.

The same panel ruled Nottingham Forest should not have been awarded a penalty at Liverpool for Alisson's challenge on Nico Williams, while still-goalless Tottenham Hotspur were left stunned when Omar Marmoush failed to win a penalty having gone down under contact from Newcastle United's Malick Thiaw, although the panel ruled 4-1 that the penalty threshold was not met.

Meanwhile, at City, there is a privately-held view that justice has eventually been served. In January 2023's derby, they were on the receiving end of a similar call when Marcus Rashford was deemed to not be interfering for Bruno Fernandes' equaliser in an Old Trafford tussle their hosts would go on to win 2-1.

Following the match then City manager Pep Guardiola disclosed that the club would not be making an official complaint. 'Sometimes it happens in our favour, sometimes it's like that,' he said.

Sports.title: Kimi Antonelli profits from a Lando Norris mess to win a race he never should have done. The Italian looks unbeatable this season and the chances of a world championship fight look finished
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli profits from a Lando Norris mess to win a race he never should have done. The Italian looks unbeatable this season and the chances of a world championship fight look finished

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Change the 'stupid' rules, cried Lando Norris, after this mugging in Madrid. And this is why.

First, every time there is a glimmer of a world championship fight breaking out, a ray of light behind the curtain, Kimi Antonelli closes the shutters.

His latest example of this knack came here, when he won a race he never should have done.

And the clear victim of ill-fortune was Norris, who finished third, a place back from Max Verstappen. For the Briton was in command of the Spanish Grand Prix at its shiny new venue, on the outskirts of the capital as he transformed a fabulous pole position into a lead over the 20-year-old Antonelli of more than six seconds in 15 laps.

Norris's McLaren is now seriously fast. And Norris was, therefore, on the scent of his third win in four races, driving more assuredly than Antonelli, who at least twice ran off the track but was holding on in second place. And, then, a huge stroke of fortune fell Antonelli's way.

This occurred as Lance Stroll's Aston Martin went into the wall, his brakes apparently cooked. A virtual safety car (VSC) was deployed. By this stage Norris was beyond the pit-lane entrance. Antonelli was not, and was called in. He was afforded the cheap stop as the action was slowed and Stroll's machine was cleared.

Kimi Antonelli celebrates on the podium after winning a race he never should have done

A stroke of fortune fell the Italian's way as he strengthened his grip on the championship

Norris had to wait a lap later, the decisive fact, for his change of rubber. Adding salt to the wound, the stop lasted a yawning 7.0sec. Not the best.

The world champion came out in fifth place and 13sec back from Antonelli. How fortunes change. Norris's chances were extinguished immediately, and it is the Italian who is edging towards the world title at the youngest age ever.

'We didn't do anything that made us lose it and I am not complaining,' said Norris, trying manfully to be as sanguine as he could in the circumstances. 'We were just insanely unlucky. I was the only one of the whole grid who didn't get a chance to do a pit stop.

'I felt like I deserved more.

Asked about the VSC variants, he said: 'It is a stupid rule and the issue has been brought up many times over the years by different drivers. Perhaps you shouldn't be able to pit for a lap or you block the pit entry. There are things that can be done or make it more simple and fairer, but it is part of a wider discussion.

'It is something all drivers would want. It is complicated, but I hope it doesn't happen to anyone again. It is not the way a race should be lost.'

Whatever happens to the rules, or doesn't, Antonelli is rewriting some of Formula One's accepted truths, as he is well on his way to eclipsing the then 23-year-old Sebastian Vettel, the most youthful of title-holders. And this is in only his second season.

The old verity that experience counts super highly and you must bide your time is being ripped up as never before.

Antonelli has won eight times this campaign, including at Monza a week ago in front of his home crowd. He was cheered and rhapsodised, though his success was in a way only compensation for the partisans after Ferrari performed disappointingly.

David Beckham was among the superstar guests at the race in Madrid over the weekend

Jude Bellingham was joined by a host of fellow football stars on the grid for the Spanish GP

Beckham takes selfies with fans after attending Visit Qatar's 'La Parada' in Madrid on Saturday

He has also gained from the affection and favours of his Mercedes team, from boss Toto Wolff down (my assertion, which they deny). Poor George Russell is hardly the chosen one there. But, it has to be admitted, that in all racing teams love is lavished on the faster of every given pair, and that character is the man-child called Kimi. Russell has won just twice in 2026.

Mercedes believe they have found their star, their future, and who can say they are wrong? Antonelli certainly looks unbeatable this season. The arithmetic supports the assertion. His lead over Russell, who finished fifth, is 81 points with nine rounds remaining.

As for Norris? He is 106 points adrift, which leaves him with an uphill task almost as steep as the North Ridge of Everest.

And Lewis Hamilton, who retired six laps in with brake problems, is barely better placed, 101 off the summit. Ferrari are too error-prone and Hamilton is not quite as good as he once was – though he is admittedly rejuvenated this season compared to last – and it will be tough for him to scale the eighth world title he wants to leave as his lifetime's mark.

He clashed with Verstappen on the opening lap. Verstappen passed Hamilton and clawed his way into second place. 'He has to give the place back,' implored the Briton.

Verstappen countered: 'He was out of control.'

Red Bull told Verstappen to yield. He has never rushed to pull out of an arm wrestle, and he gave his race engineer and pal Gianpiero Lambiase a blast of industrial language. 'Mate, what the f*** are you guys going on about?'

After the tough talk, he yielded. But, in a boring race, pretty much devoid of overtaking, Verstappen did hand the place back. But Hamilton was soon plummeting down the field with his technical problems.

Lando Norris had been leading the way before making a mess of a change of rubber

'I hit the brake, the car started stopping and then the pedal took a step and, all of a sudden, the car didn't decelerate as fast as it would normally,' he explained.

Charles Leclerc got the other Ferrari home in fourth place, having led for a long period prior to his late stop. Antonelli resumed the lead, coming home 4.3sec ahead of runner-up Verstappen. Norris harried his pal to the line, just 0.7sec back, to clinch the final podium place.

The last words here centre on Antonelli. 'Beautiful work, an absolute masterclass,' eulogised Peter Bonnington, his race engineer.

'Bono', once the voice in Hamilton's ear during his glory days at Mercedes, is chivvying his new student all the way to what now seems to be an inevitable title a few months out of his teens.

Sports.title: Alexander Zverev slammed for 'ultimate disrespect' after calling out Ben Shelton's girlfriend Trinity Rodman in US Open victory speech
Sports.content:
US Open fans have ripped into 'disrespectful' Alexander Zverev after he called out Ben Shelton's girlfriend, Trinity Rodman, during his US Open victory speech.

The 29-year-old finally banished his Flushing Meadows demons, subduing a New York crowd to win 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 on Sunday afternoon.

Shortly after the match had ended, Zverev jumped on the microphone to deliver his victory speech and made sure to address Shelton's doting partner during it.

On Sunday, Rodman, who played for the NWSL's Washington Spirit earlier in the day, had made a late dash to be in New York for the end of Shelton's US Open final.

'Hey Trinity, I thought you have a game today, no? Well done to you as well. You're the lucky charm, so. Not today, but usually,' Zverev joked.

Rodman appeared to take the address in her stride, laughing along to the German's comments while being shown on the big screen inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Fans have called out Alexander Zverev after he addressed Ben Shelton's girlfriend, Trinity Rodman, during his US Open victory speech after defeating his American rival on Sunday

Soccer star Rodman was left in tears as she watched her boyfriend fall to defeat in the final

"You're the lucky charm … not today but usually.” 😅



Alexander Zverev to Trinity Rodman after he beat her boyfriend Ben Shelton in the US Open Final 🎾 pic.twitter.com/W9q60Yuwor — ESPN (@espn) September 13, 2026

Though neither Rodman nor Shelton took the comments as a slight, fans on social media lamented Zverev for his remarks.

'Bro beat him and took a shot at his girl. Pure humiliation,' one fan wrote on X. 'Alexander Zverev is a menace,' another account added.

'Didnt care much for this mocking of Trin. She has been all class in the support of her BF,' another fan wrote on social media.

One fan wrote: 'Beats him for the title, now trying to steal his gal. Cold,' while another simply called it: 'The ultimate disrespect by Zverev.'

Meanwhile, Shelton has called on tennis bosses to impose a shot clock on second serves in the wake of his US Open final defeat by Zverev – after the No 1 seed routinely bouncing the ball more than a dozen times before hitting his serve.

As it stands, players have 25 seconds to start their first service motion after the end of the previous point. There is no strict time limit on second serves, with the rules stating only that it must be hit 'without delay,' and no maximum number of ball bounces.

Zverev’s habit has sparked calls for change from tennis legends such as Andy Roddick and John McEnroe. And, in the wake of Sunday’s final, Shelton echoed those frustrations.

The German star finally redeemed his heartbreak in Flushing Meadows back in 2020

‘I definitely think for a first serve, you should be able to do whatever you want - you can use the full 25 seconds every time,’ the American said.

‘I think that there should be some sort of rule… limiting time on second serve. You shouldn't have unlimited time. For our sport, for the fans, I think it's tough to be sitting there that long for the next play, the next action to happen.'

Shelton added: ‘I'm sure at some point it will be something that these tournaments look at just because there is such a delay in play in some matches.’

According to reports, Zverev had bounced the ball more than 12,000 times over his first five matches at this US Open. Following his semifinal loss to the German, Karen Khachanov claimed: 'The way he bounces the ball, it annoys not only me, of course, [but] a lot of players.'

Sports.title: Travis Kelce's final season plans: Insiders spill on Taylor marriage pressures, new career decided during 'retirement conversation'... and why he's desperate to avoid same fate as Tom Brady
Sports.content:
When Travis Kelce strolled down the tunnel and into Arrowhead Stadium for the first preseason game of his 14th NFL season last month, the world's attention homed in on one specific aspect of his appearance.

It wasn't his physique. Nor his fitness levels. It wasn't even his signature outlandish fashion sense or his customary preseason 'El Travador' moustache.

No. It was his left ring finger that commanded attention and the glinting gold wedding band now wrapped around it. It was the latest addition to his jewelry collection, a new ring to join the three he has claimed from the Kansas City Chiefs' Super Bowl triumphs.

Yet, when he steps onto the Arrowhead field for the Chiefs' 2026 season opener against the Denver Broncos on Monday night, all talk of star-studded nuptials to the biggest pop star on the planet will fade into the background.

Instead, the question on everyone's lips will be whether he will be walking away from this NFL season with a fifth - and final - ring in his collection.

This offseason has been Kelce's most significant. Six weeks before wandering down Arrowhead's tunnel, the tight end was making his way down the aisle, marrying Taylor Swift in a blockbuster celebration at Madison Square Garden in New York City on July 3.

Chiefs star Travis Kelce is entering his 14th - and perhaps final - season in the NFL

The tight end flashed his gold wedding ring as he entered Arrowhead Stadium in preseason

Kelce, 36, is coming off a milestone offseason having married pop star Taylor Swift in July

Three months earlier, he entered into another contract. The three-time Super Bowl winner announced that NFL retirement would wait, returning for a 14th season.

Yet, while this season may be his first as a married man, it may also be his last ever. If it is, he is making it count.

2025 was a punishing season for Kelce and the Chiefs. Kansas City missed the playoffs for the first time since 2014 - Kelce's second season in the league - their fate sealed by a loss to divisional rivals the Los Angeles Chargers in December, a game which saw Patrick Mahomes fall to an ACL injury.

Kelce, an elder statesman in the Chiefs locker room, was guilty of a number of game-altering errors. He dropped a pass near the goal line in a Week 2 game against the Philadelphia Eagles. Another came against the Texans in the game that all but sealed Kansas City's playoff fate.

'Travis is leaning into this year with so much more of an open mind and perspective because the rest of his life is set in stone,' an insider told the Daily Mail.

'Football has been a part of his life forever, but the loss of Patrick last year and his performance on the field really upset him. He didn't want to end things that way.

'Although this season will likely be his last, he wanted to make sure he was in the best shape of his life no matter what.'

The source added: 'All bets are off. He is anticipating it to be the best season ever. That's easier said than done, but that is the goal, and the mentality he is in right now.

Kelce has won three Super Bowls during a remarkable career with the Kansas City Chiefs

But the 2025 season ended in disaster with Kansas City finishing 6-11 and missing the playoffs

'He had his dream wedding, his social life is stuff of legend, he's seen the promised land in his professional life, and he wants to secure at least one more of those moments this year.'

Kelce, it appears, is determined to right his wrongs. If he's going out, he's going out on top. But Kelce may find that harder than expected.

Over the past decade, Kelce has developed a reputation as one of the greatest in his position. Dodging and weaving past opposition defenses, his route-running rivals legendary tight ends.

But now, three weeks shy of turning 37, Kelce is learning that there is no defender harder to shake than Father Time.

Kelce's new wedding ring wasn't the only aspect of his appearance that raised eyebrows during training season. Fans pounced on the veteran, claiming he had finally succumbed to a 'dad bod,' many joking that his new wife was 'feeding him well.'

He was also shrouded in whispered claims from around the league that he is 'done' and his career 'over.'

But when Kelce's career is officially 'over' is a decision only he can make and one that reportedly hinges on the Chiefs' start to the season.

'Several weeks from now, how he is doing, how the team is doing and hopefully being injury free will solidify [his decision on] next year,' our insider said.

Swift and Kelce tied the knot in a star-studded ceremony at Madison Square Garden

Fans mocked Kelce for appearing to have a 'dad bod' during the Chiefs' training camp

'Either way, going into this season as a married man, in the best shape of his life and with Patrick (Mahomes) back, he is like a kid in a candy store.'

Kelce himself has not stated that this will be his last dance. He's also not said anything to the contrary either.

There have, however, been multiple clues fueling the narrative. The most telling came in the form of a photo shared to Instagram by former NFL star and training associate Cris Carter in July.

The image showed Kelce and his long-time trainers. The caption that accompanied it said that the tight end was preparing for 'THE LAST DANCE' alongside 'Next stop Canton/HOF.'

Then, there was the emergence of the $5million new addition to Kelce and Swift's property portfolio. It was revealed this month Kelce has purchased a 131-year-old, recently renovated mansion on the Lake Erie shore near Cleveland, Ohio.

The ultra-private, millionaire enclave perhaps provides a forever home for the A-list couple. Another sign that Kelce is preparing to ride off into the sunset with his new bride, bidding farewell to the NFL once and for all.

For her part, Swift is ready for the happily ever after. Kelce's return to football - beginning with training camp on July 28 - brought a premature end to the couple's honeymoon era.

'Taylor is eager to start a family. As much as one would think that Travis would have to be home for that - and yes, he would - she never wants to pressure him to retire,' the source close to the couple revealed.

The three-time Super Bowl winner purchased a $5million lakefront Ohio mansion in March

Photos obtained by the Daily Mail show inside the sprawling property next to Lake Erie

'Have they talked about him being done? Absolutely. But when he is done, he is still going to be a commentator, do movies and be active. So, if he still wants to play after this year, she would be OK with it. She gets to live her dreams, so he should be able to do the same.

'She would never want him to ever say to her to stop making music and performing, so she is there for him, instead of pressuring him to retire.'

Being forced to spend time apart is nothing uncommon for the newlyweds, whose hectic schedules have provided a challenge ever since they first started dating back in 2023. Swift was on the road with her mammoth world tour while Kelce was hopping from state to state for games.

When he was afforded the time, he joined Swift on the road, jumping onstage for a show in London and even traveling to Buenos Aires, Argentina. They also enjoyed a holiday in Australia.

Swift has spent the past few years juggling work commitments alongside embracing her newfound 'WAG' status. She has been crowned the Queen of Chiefs Kingdom, presiding over the NFL dynasty from her beau's luxury Arrowhead suite with his family and friends. And this season will be no different.

'She will be at all his games, but she will also be busy herself,' the insider shared. 'They have gone through this schedule before, so it is nothing that Taylor is concerned about.

'She's looking forward to enjoying everything this year brings. They are newly married; they are doing everything that they love in their professional life. To enjoy these moments is what it is all about.

'They both know they are very lucky to be in the situation they are in, and they are going to enjoy it all until the wheels fall off. And she loves that they will enjoy it together.'

The Shake It Off hitmaker has supported Kelce at games throughout the past three seasons

Cris Carter has claimed on social media that 2026 will be Kelce's last season in the NFL

Swift is savoring every last moment she can with her NFL beau before the season kicks off. Exclusive photos obtained by the Daily Mail captured the couple emerging from dinner at the Ambassadors Clubhouse in New York on Sunday evening, dressed to the hilt - just over a week before the Chiefs returned to action.

It was one of many pap walks the love birds have taken over the course of their three-year relationship - many of which have fueled accusations of off-field distractions.

Since going public in September 2023, it's been no secret that the pair's high-profile romance has made waves of equal proportion in both Hollywood and the sporting world - with every morsel of their cozy date nights and lavish vacations picked over by music and NFL fans alike.

The couple's jetsetting adventures and lavish nights on the town have coincided with Kelce's dip in form over the two previous seasons. And NFL analysts pointed the finger at Swift.

For a time, it appeared that the grind of more than a decade in the NFL had begun to take its toll. The ritz and razz of his Hollywood lifestyle too tempting. Had Kelce's head been turned by the prospect of celebrity?

Kelce has already dipped his toe into TV and film. He took jobs on the big and small screen - presenting 'Are You Smarter Than a Celebrity,' appearing in 'Grotesquerie' and shooting his cameo in 'Happy Gilmore 2.'

And even he admitted that his focus had wavered as he juggled his relationship with Swift and took his first steps into TV and film.

But now, his dalliances with the silver screen are on pause. For one more season at least, the spotlight is back on the football field.

Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes is set to return in Week 1 after an ACL injury last year

Three-time Super Bowl-winner Kelce will turn 37 during the upcoming NFL campaign

Kelce clearly believes he has something left to achieve. A shot at redemption for the Chiefs after a season of misery. He wouldn't have returned if he thought otherwise. The question is: Is it one roll of the dice too many?

Those athletes who go out on top - including NFL greats Peyton Manning and John Elway, who retired after winning the Super Bowl - are far outweighed by heroes who keep coming back for more.

Even Tom Brady is familiar with that fate, performing a retirement U-turn only for his final season to end in sideline tantrums and divorce.

Kelce will be hoping his final chapter follows a different script.

It is perhaps fitting that this season's Super Bowl falls on Valentine's Day. One final win on the NFL's greatest stage would, as Daily Mail's source says, 'be the storybook ending of his career to lead into his forever life with Taylor.'

Sports.title: Brendon McCullum reveals Kevin Pietersen was 'shocked' when he was offered England coaching gig - and wants the outspoken legend to 'challenge' his methods after previous criticism
Sports.content:
Brendon McCullum reveals Kevin Pietersen was 'shocked' when he was offered England coaching gig - and wants the outspoken legend to 'challenge' his methods after previous criticism

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Brendon McCullum has admitted Kevin Pietersen was 'shocked' when he first asked him to join England's white-ball set-up as a batting mentor.

Pietersen joined up with the squad in Southampton on Sunday ahead of Tuesday's first T20 against Sri Lanka at the Utilita Bowl – the first of six limited-overs games in 13 days – and has been encouraged by McCullum to 'challenge' any aspect of the dressing-room's culture.

His appointment comes less than two years after Pietersen criticised England's training schedule during a white-ball tour of India, saying he was 'absolutely gobsmacked' that nets had been cancelled before the last two ODIs. He later described the situation as 'absolutely disgraceful'.

Those comments cropped up when McCullum first contacted Pietersen, who averaged 40 during his 136 ODIs for England and helped them win the T20 World Cup in 2010.

'That was one of the first things we talked about,' said McCullum. 'He said: 'Gee, I was just criticising you not long ago.' I said: 'I don't care about that. Some of it's fair and some of it would need some explanation, but I have no problem with that.'

'It's healthy when you create an environment where you're able to challenge. That's one thing I want him to do. It's not just bury himself in the batting per se, but look across the entire environment, and if there's anything you pick up then just come and challenge me on it.'

Kevin Pietersen (left) was 'shocked' to be offered a coaching role with England, Brendon McCullum (right) has said

Meanwhile, McCullum has urged fast bowler Brydon Carse to 'get his house in order' following his arrest outside a Derby nightclub last month – and reminded other players of the price they may pay if they make headlines for the wrong reasons.

'I hope it's crystal clear what is expected, not just of this group, but of those who have got aspirations to play for us,' he said. 'There is a lot of talent around, if you're not prepared to do that, there are other guys who will be given those opportunities.

'I've spoken to Carsey a lot and it's the same message. You need to make good decisions off the field that allow you to be able to be the best version of yourself. As far as Carsey is concerned, it's a good chance for him now to get his house in order and then push for selection for the next opportunity that arises.'

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
