World.title: Why the Lagos-Calabar coastal highway, By Eric Teniola
World.content:
I guess it is not by accident that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu (GCFR) is constructing a highway between Calabar and Lagos. The construction is political, historical and economical. I will dwell on the historical aspect. It is an acknowledgement of the peaceful Calabar city and what that ancient city still means to the rest of us.

There is an old adage that says “GOD LOVES CALABAR, A LAND OF BEAUTY”. Truly the serenity of Calabar will impress anyone. The soul of a city is in its people. The people of Calabar are not lacking at all. Valued historic buildings scatter Calabar. A drive around Calabar city is a wonderful experience.

Maybe, the construction of the highways is a compensation for Calabar for not having a rail system that was first constructed in 1891 between Lagos and Ibadan under the British rule. Even when the eastern line was constructed between Port Harcourt and Maiduguri by the British later, Calabar was left out. During that colonial era, Minna, Zaria, Kaura Namoda, Jos, Kuru, Kano and many cities enjoyed rail facilities but not Calabar.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It was not until the Lagos/Calabar railway line project was conceived by the regime of president Goodluck Jonathan in 2014 with approval from the Federal Executive Council. However, the project has not seen the light of the day.

The British colonial administration moved the country’s administrative headquarters from Calabar after the Chiefs of old Calabar signed the 1884 Treaty of Protection.

The territory of old Calabar served as the first colonial government centre for the Southern Protectorate and the oil Rivers Protectorate. However, this changed in the fourteenth year of the 20th century when the administrative centre was changed to Lagos.

Lagos was the first capital of Nigeria and became the country’s first administrative centre in 1914.

Calabar is a living museum of Nigeria history.

Lagos is the first national administrative centre for the West African nation. It was declared as such during the Amalgamation Proclamation of 1914 by Sir Lord Frederick Lugard, the Governor General, after the unification of the Northern and the Southern Protectorates. The nation has had two official capitals since 1914.

On 1 January 1914, the newly appointed Governor General of Nigeria, Sir Lord Frederick Lugard, announced Lagos as the first capital city. In his speech during the Amalgamation Proclamation of 1914, Lugard declared that: “For the present, the Central Headquarters will remain at Lagos, and the Governor-General will divide his time between the Headquarters Stations of the Northern and Southern Provinces”. The evolution of the nation’s capital cities began with Nigeria’s colonisation by the British Empire. This journey started with the unification of the Southern and Northern Protectorates in 1914 under Governor-General Sir Frederick Lugard.

Prior to the unification of the British Protectorate, Calabar now CROSS RIVERS STATE CAPITAL served as the central administrative centre for the Southern Protectorate. Before 1914, Kaduna City in Kaduna was the political capital of the Northern Protectorate.

After coming under English rule on 10 September 1884, Old Calabar was designated as the first principal city for the Southern Protectorate, the Oil River Protectorate, and the Niger Coast Protectorate.

Calabar, known initially as Akwa Akpa in the Efik language, is located in the Southeastern region of the country. It served as a significant precolonial trading port for the West African region.

In 1900, Sir Lord Frederick Lugard settled in Lokoja, making it the regional seat of government before moving the administration centre further up the Niger River to Jebba in 1902. In the same year, he moved the regional capital to Zungeru in Niger. In 1912, Lord Lugard’s quest for a more accessible and centrally located administrative centre led him to Kaduna. Although he declared Lagos as the seat of the government in 1914, he did not hide his preference for Kaduna.

When Portuguese explorers in the 15th century reached this part of the Guinea coast, they called the tribes of the area “Calabar”. These historic inhabitants were Quas, Efuts, and Efiks. Efik people migrated from the area of the Niger River to the shores of Calabar. They were fleeing civil war with their kindred and the Ibibio people.

Since the 16th century, Calabar has served as an international seaport, exporting such goods as palm oil. During the centuries of the Atlantic slave trade, it became a major port for shipment of African slaves to the Americas. The Spanish maintain the Calabar designation.

Tribes around that region were taken in as slaves for slave trade. Those minority tribes were subject to slave raids by more powerful tribes or ethnic groups in the region.

From 1725 until 1750, roughly 17,000 enslaved Africans were sold from Calabar to European slave traders; from 1772 to 1775, the number soared to more than 62,000. Old Calabar (Duke Town) and Creek Town, 16 kilometres (10 mi) northeast, were crucial towns in the trade of slaves in that era.

The first Army Barracks in Nigeria was built in Calabar in 1903. The first national newspaper in English published in Eastern Nigeria was called The Nigeria Eastern Mail, and it was first published in Calabar. On security, the first maximum security prison was built in Calabar in 1890.

Calabar holds a foundational place in Nigeria football history as the location of the country’s first recorded organised football match on 15 June, 1904 at the Hope Waddell Training Institution in Calabar. Students from the Hope Waddell Training Institution played against sailors from a visiting British naval ship (frequently cited as the HMS Thistle or HMS Dwarf).

Mary Mitchelle Slessor arrived Nigeria in 1878 under the auspices of United Free Church of Scotland, now the Presbyterian Church Mission. She resided in Odukpani Local Government Area, where she vehemently fought for the abolition of the ancient custom of killing twin children and their mothers. She built herself a two-bedroom mud house with a veranda, a store and a palour. She called it a Caravan while the villagers called it “Fine Pass All”.

In 1889, a missionary carpenter, Mr Owens, was made to put up a more permanent structure for her. The walls were made of iron sheets while the doors and windows were made of wood. The staircase leading to the first floor had 21 steps and was supported by two pillars and wooden railings. Cross River State continued with marking of the birthday of Mma Mary Slessor about a hundred years after her birth.

There are so many things to say about Calabar. No doubt the construction of the coastal highway between Lagos and Calabar serves to remind us about the importance of Calabar.

In the late nineteenth century, as European powers scrambled to consolidate territorial control in Africa, the British formalized their influence along the Niger Delta coast. In 1884, Queen Victoria signed a treaty of protection with the chiefs of Akwa Akpa (Old Calabar), enabling Britain to exercise control over the surrounding territory. Soon after, the Oil Rivers Protectorate was established in 1885 to manage trade and suppress inter-tribal conflicts in the coastal region. In 1893, this territory was renamed the Niger Coast Protectorate. Calabar was designated as the official capital of these protectorates.

Calabar’s location and commercial history underpinned its selection as headquarters. It had long been a thriving port for palm oil and other exports that were critical to British industrial needs. The transition from the slave trade to palm oil shifted economic power to local merchant houses, which then negotiated with European firms. British protection treaties signed with Efik chiefs in the 1880s facilitated smoother trade and strengthened British influence in the region. This commercial reach also fed into colonial objectives, enabling the British to tighten control over indigenous socio-economic networks.

Beyond administration, Calabar became a centre for early educational and religious developments in Nigeria. Scottish missionaries established schools and churches in the mid-19th century, influencing local institutions and social reforms. For example, the Hope Waddell Training Institution, founded in 1846, became one of the earliest secondary schools in the region. Such institutions shaped local elites and contributed to the cultural synthesis that characterised colonial Calabar.

In addition to education, Calabar was the site of early colonial legislative engagement. In 1922, the British established the Legislative Council with elected members from Calabar and Lagos, marking one of the first forms of representative governance in British West Africa. This council approved budgets and enacted laws, laying important groundwork for the later political evolution of Nigeria.

Calabar’s role as the headquarters of the Oil Rivers Protectorate, the Niger Coast Protectorate, and the Southern Nigeria Protectorate positioned it as a birthplace of modern nation.

On a personal note, I feel excited any time I visit Calabar. The serenity of the ancient city excites me.

It should be noted that nationalism and the struggle for Nigeria’s independence more or less started in Calabar when Professor Eyo Ita declared in the early struggle “This is the day of Nigeria youth. It must build a new social order, for whereas yesterday belonged to our fathers and their distant future belongs to posterity today and the immediate tomorrow are ours. We can and must shape them according to our needs and desires. The time has come when the young people of Calabar must live creatively, must build new and better homes, must bring new forms to birth in literature language, arts, music, methods and tools of industry, when they must dream of purer and juster laws and promote better health.

We must secure bare living first before we can think of luxuries of life. Calabar is a land of beauty. Nigeria is a land of beauty. Our sons and daughters must reveal its concealed beauties through the use of pencil and colour. Calabarian youth, like the knights of old, and like the militants’ youths of modern Russia, who volunteer to save their society at all cost, must pledge themselves completely to the cause of emancipating Calabar. The love of Calabar must consume us. The zeal for her emancipation must be our food and drink. We are either Calabarians or nothing. To the degree in which Calabar is saved to that degree shall we be saved.

Our God is He who cares for our homes, our womanhood, our childhood, the moral manhood of our race, our economic welfare, our health, and our political freedom. Who respects the beauty of the black man no less than he is interested in other races of mankind. This God speaks to us through the fruits of our land, through the animals that inhabit it, through the love and fellowship of our darling mothers and friends. He is the God of Nigeria, her abiding genius, her sustaining power. The youth must realise that it is serving His cause through the activities of its movement. It must realise that the whole of Nigeria is of supreme value before God, and that its creative work is part of the vast plan of the Divine Converser of our values”.

By building this highway, I am sure President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is appreciating the people of the South South and their leaders. The emergency of President Goodluck Jonathan GCFR on 6 May 2010, the establishment of NDDC, the Ministry of Niger Delta and the Amnesty Programme is not enough compensation for the people of South South region.

No doubt that region has contributed a lot to the modern-day Nigeria. Their leaders too, some of who are alive while some deceased, have served to make this country a great one. I think we owe them a debt of gratitude. I don’t think we can compensate them enough for their services. I will name a few at the risk of offending many.

We have Professor Eyo Ita (1903–1972), Ernest Sesei Ikoli (1893-1960), Kenule Beeson Saro-Wiwa (10 October 1941 – 10 November 1995), Major Isaac Jasper Adaka Boro (10 September, 1938- 9 May 1968), Chief Edwin Clarke (25 May, 1927 – 17 February, 2025), Chief Eyo Ita Esua (1901-1973), Dr Clement Isong (20 April, 1920- 29 May 2000), Dr Joseph Wayas GCON (21 May 1941 – 30 November 2021), Chief Anthony Eromosele Enahoro (22 July, 1923 – 15 December, 2010), Chief Godswill Akpabio (63) GCON, Chief Artur Edwin Prest (1906-1976) and Sir Festus Okotie-Eboh (18 July 1912 – 15 January 1966).

Others are Former President Goodluck Jonathan (68) GCFR, Chief Ufot Ekaette (17 April 1939 – 25 September 2019), Chief Allison Akene Ayida (16 June, 1930 – 12 October, 2018), King Jaja of Opobo (1821-1891), Chief Douglas, Amanyanabo of Opobo (1915-1980), Professor Horatio Oritsejolomi Thomas (1917-1979), Dr Udo Udoma (21 June 1917 – 2 February 1998), Chief Humphrey Omo-Osagie (1896-1977), Chief Michael Ani (30 November, 1917 – 18 December, 1985), Sir Dennis Osadebay (29 June, 1911 — 26 December, 1994), Dr Okoi Arikpo (20 September 1916- 26 October 1995), Chief Wenike Opurum Briggs (10 March 1918 – 21 April 1987), Chief Harold Dappa-Biriye (26 September 1920-2005), Chief Louis Orok Edet (1914–1979), Chief Margaret Ekpo and many others.

Let us take a look at some of them.

Professor Eyo Ita ((1903–1972) was the founder of the Nigeria Youth League Movement. He was born in Calabar. He had his education at Duke Town School and then to Calabar’s famous Hope Waddell Training Institute. After teaching at the Baptist Academy, Obanikoro, Lagos (1926-1928), he went to the USA where he studied at the Teacher’s College of Columbia University, majoring in religions and education. He later read for BA in Canada. On his return in 1933, he became active as an educationist, a pamphleteer, and a nationalist who believed strongly in a role for Nigeria’s youth.

He formed the Nigeria Youth League Movement, which had little effective existence at first. After spending some time at Ogbomoso, where he taught but also wrote pamphlets and press articles, he returned in 1938 to Calabar, where a National Institute had been founded by local educated people, and he became its head. Then he started his own West AFRICAN People’s Institute, an educational institution for which he became famous. It had a press which published his works: The Assurance of Freedom (1949), Crusade for Freedom (1949), The Revolt of the Liberal Spirit in Nigeria (1949), Sterile Truths and Fertile Lies (1949), Two Vital Fronts in Nigeria’s Advancement (1949), National Youth Renaissance (undated), Theory of Social Symbiosis (1951), etc.

Chief Eyo Ita was a leading member of the National Council for Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC) after its foundation in 1944, and was elected to the Eastern Nigeria House of Assembly in 1951on the party’s ticket. In 1948 he became the first National Vice-President of the NCNC. After elections in 1951, which the NCNC won in the Eastern Region, he became Minister for Natural Resources and Leader of Government Business for the Region. A year later there was a crisis within the NCNC, in January 1953, the nine NCNC ministers in the East resigned, but Chief Ita and five others withdrew their resignations, and stayed as ministers despite a hostile House of Assembly, until new elections in the same year installed a government under the NCNC leader, Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe.

Before that, Chief Eyo Ita had formed a National Independence Party (NIP) with Dr. E.U. Udoma and Jaja Wachukwu. Later in 1953 the Calabar-Ogoja-Rivers (COR) movement was founded to call for separation of the non-Ibo minorities from the Eastern Region, and Chief Ita was one of the leading figures for some years. Later his NIP joined the United National Party (UNP) of Alvan Ikoku to form the National Independence Party.

In 1959 he announced he was leaving the COR movement, and returned to the NCNC. The “professor” as he was called, was not prominent in politics thereafter. After independence he devoted his time to developing and improving his school.

Chief Ernest Sesei Ikoli (1893-1960) was born on 25 March 1893 in Rivers State. He was the son of an illustrious merchant who traded on the coast of south-east Nigeria. His mother was among the first women from the Niger Delta to receive Western education. He had his education at the Bonny Primary School and then Kings College in Lagos, where he was one of the foundation students on its opening in 1909; later he taught there, becoming assistant Mathematics master in 1913.

After resigning from Kings’ College in 1919, he went to journalism as editorial assistant at the Lagos Weekly Record under the editorship of Thomas Horatio Jackson, who had taken over from his father John Payne Jackson who founded the paper in 1889. After two years with the Record, Ikoli founded his own newspaper, the African Messenger, in 1921. He remained its editor and proprietor until 1926 when he was appointed the first editor of the newly founded Daily Times, whose first editorial he wrote on 1 June 1926.

The previous year the Daily Times had taken over Ikoli’s African Messenger. In 1928 he left the Daily Times to found The Nigerian Daily until 1931 when it ceased publication.

Chief Ernest Ikoli also took part in politics in Lagos, starting as secretary of the local branch of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) of Marcus Garvey. In 1934, he, Vaughn, H.O. Davies and others became the leaders of the new Lagos Youth Movement (NYM), which in 1938 was renamed the Nigerian Youth Movement and came under the leadership of Dr DK Abayomi. Three years later he was elected to the Legislative Council in Lagos, in a bitterly contested election in which he was opposed by Samuel Akinsanya (who later became the Odemo of Ishara). He was elected President of the NMY in 1943.

Meanwhile from 1938 to 1944 he edited another newspaper, The Daily Service, the NYM organ, with Chief Samuel Ladoke Akintola. Chief Ikoli was re-elected to the Legislative Council as an Independent in 1946, because of the disqualification of his opponent; in 1947 he decided not to seek re-election again.

While Chief Ikoli’s active political life was short-lived, he is remembered by his former political colleagues as a former political colleague as a foremost politician with a determined mind. One of these, a former political opponent who became a prominent traditional ruler, Oba Samuel Akinsanya, Odemo of Ishara, said of him in the first yearly Ernest Ikoli Memorial Lecture inaugurated by the Sunday Times of Nigeria in 1979: “I worked together with Ernest Ikoli for many years. We did many things together. We fought many things together. And I cannot remember any political agitation or representation to the colonial government in those days with which Chief Ikoli was not associated. In fact, he would one of the foremost leaders.”

On 21 October 1960, three weeks after Nigeria became independent, Chief Ernest Ikoli died and was widely mourned.

Dr Clement Isong (20 April, 1920 – 29 May 2000) was the second Nigerian to be Governor of Central Bank of Nigeria. Dr. Isong was brilliant, industrious and highly talented who excelled in various fields. He was a teacher, banker, economist, administrator and politician.

He was born on 20th April, 1920 in Eket, Akwa Ibom State to Mr and Mrs Nathaniel Isonguyo.

He attended University College, Ibadan, Iowa Wesleyan College, Mount Pleasant, Iowa, USA and Harvard Graduate School of Arts and Science where he obtained PhD in Economics.

Dr Isong taught Economics in University of Ibadan. He joined Central Bank of Nigeria as Secretary and later became Director of Research. He was seconded to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as an adviser in the African department.

Dr Isong served as the Governor of the CBN from 1967 to 1975 at a critical time in the history of Nigeria. After retirement, he joined politics. He was elected the first civilian Governor of Cross River State from 1979 to 1983. Having contributed to the growth of Nigeria, Dr. Isong was honoured with Commander of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (CFR) in 1982. He died on 29th May, 2000.

Dr Clement Isong’s portrait appears on the N1000 Note.

Sir Dennis Chukude Osadebay (29 June 1911 — 26 December 1994) was a former premier of the now defunct Mid-Western Region of Nigeria, which now comprises Edo State and Delta State. He was one of the pioneering Nigerian poets who wrote in English.

As a politician, he was said to have detest for party politics and tried to form unbiased opinions on important matters of the period. He was also a leader of the movement to create a Mid-Western region during the Nigerian First Republic.

Chief Osadebay was born in Asaba, Delta State, to parents of mixed cultural backgrounds. He attended Asaba Government School at Asaba, the Sacred Heart School in Calabar and Hope Waddell Training Institute. He joined the labour force in 1930 as a customs officer working in Lagos, Port Harcourt and Calabar. He subsequently went to England to study Law during the 1940s. It was while studying that he started publishing poetic verses. He was then known as a newspaper poet, as most of his writings were published in the West African Pilot and a few other newspapers.

In his writings, Chief Osadebay used both his personal life and public events as inspiration. In Africa Sings, a collection of poems, he delved into themes from a personal point of view, such as a sullen poem written about his 25th birthday and the coming of middle age. However, his best work in the volume were poems written from an impersonal viewpoint. In his adventurous poem “black man troubles”, he used pidgin English to lament the status of black Africans in colonial Africa and injustice in the society. His poems were also notable for faithfully representing modern poetic rhythm.

Chief Osadebay was one of the founding members of the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC) in 1944. He left the country to read law a few years later. After, completing his studies, he returned to Nigeria and established a law practice in Aba and was also made the legal adviser of the NCNC. In 1951, he contested and won a seat on the Western Region House of Assembly, which was dominated by the rival Action Group (AG). He soon became the leader of opposition in the region from 1954 to 1956 but gave the mantle to Adegoke Adelabu in 1956. After the death of Adegoke Adelabu, he took on his familiar oppositional role in 1958. In 1960, he became the Speaker in the Western Region and upon the creation of the Mid-Western Region in 1963, became the pioneer premier of the newly created region.

Chief Festus Okotie-Eboh (18 July 1912 – 15 January 1966) was the finance minister of Nigeria from 1957 to 1966 during the administration of Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa.

He was born on 18 July 1912 in a town along the Benin River in Niger Delta. He was educated at the Sapele Baptist School, and after a year as a municipal clerk taught for several years. He joined the Bata Shoe Company in 1935 as a clerk. Through private study and determination, he qualified in 1942 as an accountant and was later appointed Chief Clerk in Lagos. He went on to become a deputy manager of the Sapele branch of the Bata Shoe Company which then sent him to Czechoslovakia, where he studied for and obtained diplomas in business administration and chiropody. He was in that country at the time of the communist coup d’etat of 1948.

On his return to Nigeria, he resolved to go into business on his own. He became a timber and rubber merchant and opened a chain of schools and enterprises with which he laid the foundations for his own personal fortune. He entered politics in 1951 when he was elected to the Western Region House of Assembly. He had already been chosen the first secretary of the Warri National Union and was secretary-general of the Itsekiri National Society. He moved to the Federal House of Representatives in 1954 as the member for the Warri division and in the same year became the national treasure of the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC; the party later changed its name to the National Council of Nigerian Citizens).

He was appointed Federal Minister of Labour in 1955. He became Finance Minister in 1957 combining with his duty as leader of the NCNC parliamentary party in the Federal House.

Chief Festus Okotie-Eboh was a man of influence and power, with considerable financial strength and know-how. He retained the important Finance portfolio until the fall of Nigeria’s first civilian administration.

Professor Horatio Oritshejolomi Thomas (1917-1979), was an eminent surgeon, university teacher and administrator He combined a brilliant medical career with headship of Nigeria’s two major universities. He specialised in facial reconstructive and plastic surgery. He trained as an assistant to the renowned Sir Archibald MacIndoe in this discipline.

Professor Oritshejolomi Thomas was born in 1917 in Sapele, where his family-owned rubber plantations. He was educated at Methodist Boys’ High School in Lagos and Birmingham University in England, where he read medicine. He was the pioneer provost of the College of Medicine at the University of Lagos, as well as the first Nigerian to be admitted to the Royal College of Surgeons of England. For a while, from the time he completed his studies until 1948, he worked as a lecturer in Anatomy at Birmingham University as well as a surgeon in various British hospitals.

Professor Oritshejolomi Thomas returned to Nigeria in 1949, to become a member of the pioneering staff of University College, Ibadan, that was just beginning to function under a special relationship with the University of London. At that time there was a growing in Nigeria to create institutions of higher learning, both to meet individual aspirations and national manpower needs and to enable university degrees to be granted in the country. The new University of Ibadan, though short of adequate facilities, provided the basis for that development. Professor Oritshejolomi Thomas, who taught surgery at the university, was one of the intakes of its fifteen staff members.

In 1953, he returned to Britain for specialist course in plastic surgery at East Grinstead, Sussex. He returned home in the mid-1950s before the new teaching hospital of the University moved to its permanent site at Agodi in Ibadan. He worked there until the University became an autonomous institution in 1962, rising to become one of its leading heads of department and respected academic staff.

In 1962, when the Lagos University Teaching Hospital and the College of Medicine was established by the Federal Government, Professor Oritshejolomi Thomas was made head of its department of Surgery. Soon he became head of the College of Medicine, first as Dean of the Medical School and Chairman of Lagos University Teaching Hospital (LUTH) Board of Management and later Provost of the College of Medicine.

During his seven years’ headship of the College, he served for a while as acting Vice-Chancellor of the University of Lagos. He remained head of the College of Medicine for seven years, reverting to his earlier position of head of department in 1969.

In 1972, Professor Oritshejolomi Thomas was appointed Vice Chancellor of the country’s premier university, Ibadan, whose development owes much to the contributions of the generation of distinguished scholars like himself. Professor Oritshejolomi Thomas held that office until he retired in 1975.

Chief Edwin Clarke (May 25, 1927 – February 17, 2025) attended primary and secondary schools at Effurun, Okrika and Afugbene before completing further studies at the Government Teacher Training College, which later became Delta State University, Abraka. Thereafter, Clark worked briefly as a schoolteacher before travelling to the United Kingdom to earn a law degree.

He worked with the administrations of the military governor Samuel Ogbemudia and head of state, General Yakubu Gowon GCFR between 1966 and 1975. In 1966, he was a member of an advisory committee to the military governor of the Mid-Western Region, David Ejoor and was appointed Federal Commissioner of Information in 1975.

Chief Clark’s involvement in the political process began during the pre-independence period when he was elected as Councillor for Bomadi in 1953. Clark later joined National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC).

He was later appointed Midwestern Commissioner of Education and later, Finance from 1966 to 1975. During the second republic, he was a member of the national executive committee of the National Party of Nigeria (NPN) and the treasurer of the party in Bendel State (now, in part, Delta State and previously the Mid-Western Region province). In 1983, he was an elected senator for three months at the twilight of the Shagari administration.

Beginning in 1996, Chief Clark was a self-described leader of the Ijaw nation. He supported the Ijaw ethnic group in Delta State during an ethnic crisis in Warri and led Ijaw leadership delegations to meet political leaders. Chief Edwin Clark was the founder of Edwin Clark University which was established in 2015.

In 2016, Chief Clark founded the Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF) along with other leaders. The organization’s stated objective is “to dialogue with stakeholders and lobby for increased attention and implementation of restructuring, development and security policies by the Government of Nigeria.

Eric Teniola, a former director at the Presidency, wrote from Lagos.

World.title: Strike: Resumption halted in federal unity colleges in Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu
World.content:
Students and workers of federal unity colleges in Anambra, Ebonyi and Enugu States on Monday stayed away from school as education unions’ strike delayed the commencement of the 2026/2027 academic session.

A check by the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) across the three states showed that students had yet to resume at the federal government colleges.

The situation in Anambra

In Anambra, Federal Government Girls’ College, Onitsha; Federal Government College, Nise and Federal Science and Technical College (FSTC), Awka, were closed to academic activities.

The schools were largely quiet, with no noticeable movement of students or commencement of academic activities as of the time of NAN’s visit.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

A teacher at FSTC, Awka, who pleaded anonymity, confirmed that the school was affected by the strike.

She said the teachers were awaiting clear directives from the school authorities and relevant education unions before resuming.

Similarly, a parent, Georgina Alaneme, said she did not take her child to school due to uncertainty about the resumption.

“The management of the Federal Government College, Nise, sent us a message telling us they are on strike. So, we did not bother taking my child to school on Sunday,” she said.

Complete shutdown in Enugu

It was a similar situation in Enugu State as education unions in the state grounded academic activities at the Federal Government College, Enugu, over the alleged planned sale of federal unity colleges.

A NAN correspondent who visited the school at the Independence Layout, Enugu, on Monday, reports that the school was completely shut down.

NAN also recalls that the federal government had directed students of the unity colleges nationwide to resume on Monday, 14 September.

However, education unions opposed the resumption amid controversy surrounding the concession of King’s College, Lagos.

A teacher at the school, who pleaded anonymity, told NAN that both teachers and students were chased away from the school.

“We resumed school as usual, but suddenly, union members arrived and chased us away and locked the entrance gate, preventing people from entering the school.

“We heard that the federal government is planning to sell unity schools, as they started with King’s College, Lagos,” she said.

Another parent, Victoria Omenazu, whose child is a boarding student in the school, said they were turned back on Sunday when they came to the school ahead of the Monday resumption.

Mrs Omenazu said they were told that a new resumption date would be announced to them later.

“I wonder why the government wants to concession the unity schools which unite the country.

Federal Government Colleges remain the best and most affordable option compared to private schools. This is unfair,” she said.

She appealed to the government to rescind the decision on the concession.

Staff members prevented from accessing the school premises

In Ebonyi, the Academic Staff Union of Secondary Schools directed its members at Federal Government Girls’ College, Ezzamgbo, to disregard the federal government’s directive on the resumption of unity schools.

The union also urged the federal government to reverse its planned move to sell King’s College, Lagos and other unity schools.

NAN reports that the unity schools in Ebonyi remained shut on Monday despite the federal government’s directive for students and staff to resume on 14 September.

NAN’s checks at some of the schools showed that many staff members were not allowed into the premises as the gates remained locked on the orders of the union leaders.

Other federal unity schools in the state include Federal Government College, Okposi, and Federal Science and Technical College, Amuzu.

The development followed controversy surrounding the federal government’s reported plan to sell, concession or privatise some federal unity colleges, including King’s College, Lagos.

The proposed policy has generated opposition from parents, education unions and other stakeholders, who have expressed concerns about its potential implications for access to quality, affordable secondary education.

Union leaders adamant

The Unit Chairman of the Academic Staff Union of Secondary Schools at Federal Government Girls’ College, Ezzamgbo, Rachael Benson-Ogbu, said in a notice issued on Monday that the directive of “no resumption” remained in force.

Mrs Benson-Ogbu said the decision followed consultations with the union’s national headquarters in Abuja on Sunday night.

According to the notice, the status quo remains pending further deliberations between the union and officials of the Federal Ministry of Education.

“The union will meet with ministry officials on Monday to deliberate on the situation and determine the next line of action.

“So, no staff or student should be allowed into the school premises from Monday, 14 September, except resident staff.

“The school gate shall remain firmly closed until further directive,” the notice stated.

She therefore directed members of the union to converge at the school gate to ensure compliance with the directive and to demonstrate what she described as their collective resolve.

Jacob Nwankwo, a parent at Federal Government College, Okposi, expressed concern about the federal government’s reported plan to sell King’s College and other unity schools nationwide.

Mr Nwankwo, however, urged the federal government to reconsider and cancel any such plan.

“The institutions represent an important part of Nigeria’s educational heritage and should continue to be managed as public schools for the benefit of future generations,” he said.

READ ALSO: FCT doctors insist on signed commitment to suspend strike

Another Academic Staff Union of Secondary Schools leader at Federal Government College, Okposi, who declined to give his name, urged members to remain united, disciplined and committed to the struggle.

“Our collective strength lies in our unity and unwavering commitment to the cause,” the union leader said.

Ijeoma Michael, an SS2 student of the college in Okposi, said she was unhappy that her school had not resumed after the long vacation.

Miss Michael urged the union and the federal government to reach an agreement to ensure that the schools were reopened for academic activities.

“Well, I don’t really know why our school did not open, but I overheard my mum saying that it was due to a disagreement between the federal government and the union leaders,” she said.

World.title: Journalist jailed two yrs for security comment in Mali
World.content:
A Malian journalist was sentenced on Monday to two years in prison following remarks during a TV programme about his west African nation’s security situation.

Abderhamane Keita, an editor at the daily Le Temoin paper, was taken into custody in early June for “undermining national unity and the credibility of the state” and “publishing and disseminating false or misleading information”.

He was prosecuted after asserting on a TV programme focused on the security situation in Mali that the northern city of Kidal was being run by the leader of the jihadist group JNIM.

Since late April, the Al-Qaeda-linked Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM) and its Tuareg separatist allies have waged a series of attacks aimed at weakening the country’s junta rulers.

This has included taking Kidal and assassinating the minister of defence in April.

Keita appeared before the country’s national cybercrime unit last week, with his verdict announced Monday.

His lawyer told AFP that they would appeal the decision.

The media watchdog Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called Keita’s conviction “unjust” and a “new way of criminalising journalism”.

The head of the group’s sub-Saharan Africa bureau, Sadibou Marong, said it “sends out a particularly troubling signal to media professionals in Mali and the region”.

Mali’s authorities, RSF added, should “put an end to the use of the justice system against journalists”.

Mali has been wracked since 2012 by a serious security crisis, notably fuelled by violence from jihadists allied to Al-Qaeda or the Islamic State group, along with criminal gangs and armed separatists.

In recent years Mali’s junta, which came to power in two successive coups in 2020 and 2021, has taken numerous measures against the press and critical voices.

Authorities have also dissolved political parties and banned associations’ political activities.

AFP

World.title: FG raises N1.23trn to tackle N4trn GenCos’ legacy debt
World.content:
The Federal Government has raised about N1.23 trillion through two bond issuances to tackle N4 trillion legacy debt owed to electricity Generation Companies (GenCos).

Mr Akin Odeyemi, Chief Executive Officer, Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc (NBET), disclosed this during the ceremony in Abuja on Monday.

Odeyemi said the latest Series 2 issuance raised N728.9 billion, following N501 billion secured through Series 1 in January.

He said Series 2, launched in August, involved 11 GenCos, compared with eight companies that participated in the first issuance.

According to him, the increased participation reflects growing stakeholder confidence in the debt reduction programme.

“The increased participation is a positive development and reflects the growing confidence of stakeholders in the programme,” Odeyemi said.

He said the participation also demonstrated the programme’s ability to provide a credible framework for addressing verified outstanding obligations.

Odeyemi said the N728.9 billion Series 2 bond would be implemented in two tranches, identified as Tranches A and B.

He said accumulated outstanding obligations had affected the ability of electricity market participants to meet their financial commitments.

The NBET chief executive said the debt burden had also constrained GenCos’ capacity to invest further in electricity generation.

“It is therefore important that the Debt Reduction Programme is viewed not simply as an initiative for settling historical debt,” he said.

Odeyemi said the programme should instead be viewed as part of broader efforts to restore financial confidence, liquidity and sustainability.

“It should also be viewed as part of a broader effort to restore financial confidence, liquidity and sustainability to the Nigerian Electricity Supply Industry,” he said.

Mr Taiwo Oyedele, Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, said Series 2 comprised N402 billion in cash bonds.

Oyedele said another N326.9 billion was allotted as non-cash bonds to participating GenCos under the Presidential Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme.

He said the transaction addressed accumulated legacy obligations that had weakened liquidity and constrained investment across the electricity market.

“This transaction addresses an important challenge in Nigeria’s electricity market, which is accumulated legacy obligations,” Oyedele said.

According to him, the obligations had also affected confidence across the electricity value chain.

Oyedele said the Federal Government’s objective was to resolve legitimate legacy obligations through a structured and transparent process.

He stressed that the bond programme must be accompanied by reforms capable of preventing the recurrence of similar debts.

“This means that the bond programme cannot stand alone,” Oyedele said.

He called for stronger market discipline, improved revenue assurance and reductions in technical and commercial losses across the electricity sector.

Oyedele also advocated greater efficiency and accountability throughout the electricity ecosystem to strengthen the sustainability of the market.

“It is also important that we are leveraging Nigeria’s domestic capital markets,” he said.

The Minister of Power, Mr Joseph Tegbe, said the bond issuance demonstrated the Federal Government’s commitment to addressing structural challenges confronting the electricity industry.

Tegbe, represented by the ministry’s Permanent Secretary, Mr Mahmuda Mamman, said the initiative formed part of efforts to create stable electricity supply.

He said the programme would also lay the foundation for sustainable development by strengthening the financial position of the electricity sector.

Mrs Olu Verheijen, Special Adviser to President Bola Tinubu on Oil and Gas, said Series 1 produced settlement agreements with 11 GenCos.

Verheijen said the agreements represented 21 power plants, adding that Series 2 would deepen implementation of the debt reduction programme.

“Now we are moving deeper into implementation with Series 2,” she said.

She said Series 1 had demonstrated the viability of the model, while Series 2 was intended to scale its implementation.

“As I said at the investor forum in July, Series 1 proved the model and Series 2 is scaling it,” Verheijen said.

Verheijen stressed that expanding the programme was crucial to delivering meaningful impact across Nigeria’s electricity industry.

“As important as it is, you would agree that scaling is what truly makes the difference,” she said.

(NAN)

World.title: Oyo govt confirms arrest of 5 terrorists after Igbeti attack
World.content:
Oyo State Government has confirmed the arrest of five suspected terrorists involved in the attack on a military camp on the outskirts of Igbeti in the Olorunsogo Local Government Council on Sunday.

The State Deputy Governor, Mr Bayo Lawal, made this known in Igbeti on Monday shortly after he was conducted around the scene of the attack by the Commanding Officer, 81 Battalion, Lt Col. Innocent Asogwa.

According to a statement issued by the state Commissioner for Information and Civic Orientation, Prince Dotun Oyelade, Lawal said the five arrested terrorists were in military uniforms, while more arrests were expected to be made.

He said that the military had sent at least 120 soldiers into the bush on the trail of the other terrorists.

He explained that the fire that burnt the Operation Burst vehicle and the camp structure was caused by grenade launchers used by the terrorists, which ignited the cooking cylinders on the premises.

The deputy governor further said that the state’s newly procured surveillance aircraft engaged constantly in random exercises and cannot be permanently in the sky, but will remain handy for all operations and reconnaissance.

He said that an emergency committee of the five adjoining local government councils of Olorunsogo, Oriire, Saki East, Orelope, and Irepo had been set up to immediately provide all the needs of the security men in the areas and liaise with the state government for prompt assistance.

He equally assured residents of Igbeti and the entire people of Oke-Ogun that the state government was committed to the security of lives and property.

(NAN)

World.title: King’s College: FG moves to defuse crisis, assures workers of ‘no sack’
World.content:
•Dr Tunji Alausa, Minister of Education

By Joseph Erunke, Abuja

The Federal Government has moved to defuse the escalating crisis over the controversial management arrangement for King’s College, Lagos, assuring workers that none of them would be sacked, victimised or punished as a result of the dispute.

The Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, gave the assurance on Monday after a high-level meeting with the Trade Union Congress, TUC, and other stakeholders, even as he announced that the implementation of the arrangement for the King’s College Old Boys Association to continue managing the institution would proceed.

The development came as the TUC announced the suspension of the industrial action earlier directed against its affiliates, following the government’s assurances and the constitution of a seven-member committee to further examine areas of concern raised by the unions.

Alausa said the committee would review the agreement already signed and consider additional recommendations that could be incorporated into the document.

The committee, which is expected to complete its assignment within one to two weeks, will comprise two representatives of the Federal Ministry of Education, including the Minister of State for Education and the Acting Permanent Secretary; one representative of the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment; two senior representatives of the TUC; and two representatives of the King’s College Old Boys Association.

According to the minister, the government’s decision followed extensive deliberations conducted in the spirit of mutual respect and national interest.

He acknowledged that stakeholders might not secure everything they demanded but maintained that dialogue remained the best avenue for resolving the contentious issues surrounding the institution.

Alausa was, however, categorical that the controversy would not be allowed to result in job losses or victimisation.

He said all academic and non-academic workers at the college would continue to be treated in accordance with the Public Service Rules, particularly in matters concerning their deployment.

“No staff will be dismissed,” the minister assured, adding that there would also be “no demonisation or punishment” of any member of staff because of the issues under consideration.

The assurance appeared to provide a major relief for the unions, which had mounted pressure against the proposed arrangement and accused the authorities of failing to adequately address workers’ concerns.

Speaking on the outcome of the meeting, TUC General Secretary, Comrade Nuhu Toro, described the engagement as “fruitful and robust,” saying the concerns of the unions were presented and considered in good faith.

Toro subsequently announced the suspension of the industrial action directed against the unions’ affiliates to enable the newly constituted committee to carry out its assignment.

He, however, warned that the unions could resume the suspended action if necessary after the committee’s work.

The TUC scribe said the committee would provide the unions an opportunity to scrutinise the relevant policy document, articulate their concerns and make contributions before the parties reconvene within the stipulated one-to-two-week period.

Beyond the immediate labour dispute, Toro stressed the urgent need to rescue King’s College from its deteriorating physical condition, warning that the status quo could no longer be allowed to continue.

He said the dilapidated state of the iconic institution required urgent intervention, even as he described the outcome of the meeting as a “win-win” for the parties.

While the unions secured assurances on the protection of their members, he said, the government had demonstrated willingness to revisit areas requiring further consideration.

King’s College, Lagos, one of Nigeria’s historic secondary schools, had recently become the centre of a dispute following the arrangement allowing its Old Boys Association to continue managing aspects of the institution.

The controversy had triggered strong opposition from organised labour and culminated in industrial action and protests, with workers demanding greater clarity and protection of their interests.

With Monday’s resolution, however, the Federal Government is proceeding with the management arrangement while creating a fresh window for the unions and other stakeholders to influence possible amendments to the existing agreement.

Alausa reaffirmed the government’s commitment to continued dialogue with organised labour and other stakeholders, stressing that the process would be guided by the law, mutual respect and the national interest.

He also pledged that the government would work with stakeholders to strengthen King’s College, preserve its heritage and improve its learning environment while protecting the interests of students and staff.

The minister said the intervention was part of the Federal Government’s broader effort to improve the management and physical condition of public educational institutions and raise the quality of learning under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda.

World.title: Houthis say Saudi Arabia hits Yemen with 54 strikes after attack on bases
World.content:
Yemen’s Houthi armed forces patrol as Yemeni prisoners loyal to the Houthi authorities arrive in the capital Sanaa on September 12, 2026, after being released on the west coast where he and others were being held by Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces. Some 210 prisoners were released following a week-long offensive, in which the Iran-backed Houthis on September 11, 2026, captured Yemen’s Red Sea coast from the internationally recognised government, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed amid the US-Iran war. (Photo by Mohammed HUWAIS / AFP)

Yemen’s Houthis said on Monday Saudi Arabia launched airstrikes across the west of the country after the Iran-backed group earlier announced it targeted military bases in the kingdom.

The group, fighting the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, last week seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which has become vital as the wider US-Iran war chokes the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis said Riyadh targeted Yemen with 54 strikes over 24 hours, after the group fired dozens of drones and missiles at Saudi military facilities, prompting the Saudi civil defence to issue alerts in the southern cities of Khamis Mushait and Abha.

The civil defence later issued a brief alert for Najran in southwestern Saudi Arabia without elaborating on the cause for the warning.

A Khamis Mushait resident told AFP he heard “intense blasts” which left fires burning for a “long time”.

“Honestly, we couldn’t sleep at all.”

Houthi missile attacks in western Yemen killed eight troops from Yemeni government forces, two military sources with the Aden-based administration told AFP.

The Iran-backed group’s Al-Masirah TV channel said two civilians were killed in Saudi strikes that destroyed a bridge in Taiz province, which has seen some of Yemen’s fiercest clashes in recent days.

The renewed fighting in Yemen comes as the wider regional war remains at a stalemate. But US President Donald Trump on Monday said he was open to holding talks with Iran.

“The failing Nation of Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly. I will determine whether or not the U.S.A. will choose to engage — The concept of which we are open to,” Trump said on his Truth Social network.

– Wider regional war –

On Monday, a proposed meeting between Gulf states and Iran over the future of Hormuz was postponed, with Tehran accusing Riyadh of using Yemen as a “pretext” to delay the talks.

Tehran has long supported the Houthis, a member of its anti-Israel “axis of resistance”, including with weapons and technology, but analysts dispute the extent to which Iran is behind the renewed fighting.

“Iran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs,” foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters on Monday, saying the Houthis are “entirely independent actors who make their decisions based on their own interests”.

Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was expected to hold talks with Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Tuesday, Cairo announced.

Mirette Mabrouk, an expert with the Washington-based Middle East Institute, said Prince Mohammed would seek “assurances that if necessary, Egypt will step up to protect Bab al-Mandab”.

She said Egypt, whose vital Suez Canal route has also been threatened by the Houthi blockade, “will fight if necessary, but that is not the default position”.

“The default position is to exercise every other option before that,” she added.

Last week, US media reported Trump had rejected a personal request from the Saudi crown prince to intervene in the war.

Yemen’s prolonged civil war had been dormant for four years before reigniting in July over an Iranian flight to the capital Sanaa, becoming the latest conflict drawn into the wider regional war.

The Houthis’ military spokesman Yahya Saree on Monday said Saudi Arabia “conducted 54 airstrikes over the past 24 hours using F15 and Typhoon aircraft”.

He said the areas of Taiz, Lahj, Al-Jawf, Marib, and Hodeida were targeted.

– Forced to flee –

Yemeni government forces on Sunday said they had recaptured positions in the southwestern province of Taiz from Houthi fighters and carried out airstrikes, telling the official Saba news agency they killed at least 10 gunmen.

The Saudi crown prince received US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Jeddah on Monday to discuss “the latest developments in the region”, according to Saudi news agency SPA.

The US admiral travelled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for urgent coordination meetings, according to US news site Axios.

The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital Sanaa in 2014 at the outset of the civil war, driving the government to Aden in the south.

The following year, Saudi Arabia led a coalition to intervene on the side of the government, launching wave after wave of airstrikes as the conflict escalated into one of the worst humanitarian disasters in the world.

On Monday, the UN’s migration agency said the renewed fighting in the Arab world’s poorest country had forced 93,864 people to flee their homes.

AFP
