“I believe in the first 100 days after we kick this government out, we should be able to cut out the fat that is being utilised at State House so that we can pay our teachers and fund our hospitals,” he said.

Sifuna’s remarks came a day after Ruto accused opposition leaders of using ethnic profiling and intimidation to influence voters in areas perceived to be opposition strongholds.

Speaking in Ngong and Ongata Rongai in Kajiado County, Ruto defended the broad-based UDA-ODM political arrangement, saying the pact was aimed at promoting national unity and ensuring equitable distribution of national resources.

“They are intimidating people along ethnic lines, telling them they must vote a certain way. Do not allow yourselves to be divided through tribalism and hatred. Their agenda is to spread tribalism and hatred,” Ruto said.

The exchange comes as political parties and leaders intensify preparations for the 2027 General Election, with the opposition seeking to consolidate its support base while the Kenya Kwanza administration defends its record and broad-based political arrangement.

World.title: Why Trump’s effort to build more refineries won’t lower gas prices
World.content:
President Donald Trump wants to reverse the decades-long decline in the number of US refineries in operation, which he believes is key to lowering gas prices, and he recently called oil executives to the White House to make that push.

“President Trump and his entire energy team will continue supporting reopening shuttered refineries, expanding the capacity of existing refineries, and constructing new refineries to lower prices and strengthen our national security,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told CNN.

But more US refineries won’t bring down prices in the near term and aren’t likely to take place in the long term either.

A new oil refinery with significant unit capacity hasn’t been built in America since 1977, and there were about twice as many oil refineries operating in 1982 as there are today. And even if a building boom were to start tomorrow, it would take years to produce the gasoline and diesel needed to alleviate current prices.

American oil companies, meanwhile, aren’t exactly rushing to build refineries. While the industry is wildly profitable, it’s also aware that the current energy market disruptions are temporary.

The spike in gas prices, triggered by wars in Iran and Ukraine, won’t last long enough to warrant the years of construction and multi-billion-dollar investment needed to build new refineries.

“What’s the Strait of Hormuz going to look like in four to five years?” said John Auers, marketing director of refined fuels at data analytics firm Novi Labs. “The assumption is it’ll be opened by then, and Russian refineries will be back to normal. So, it doesn’t really matter what’s happening now or next year when making plans for a major expansion project.”

Wars squeeze refining output

Refining capacity that is limited worldwide, rather than just in the United States, is a major reason for the spike in fuel prices this year, even more so than the Iran war cutting off crude oil shipments in the Strait of Hormuz.

“In my 35 years in the refining business, there’s been an excess (refining) supply,” ExxonMobil CEO Darren Wood told CNBC earlier this summer. “(But now) we have a refinery constraint. So, pump prices are being established by supply and demand of refining products — not crude.”

Vehicles queue at a a Gazpromneft petrol station in Moscow on August 18, 2026. Russian authorities acknowledged that some regions faces new gasoline shortages, as Ukraine steps up attacks on the country’s oil refineries. Alexander Nemenov/AFP/Getty Images

Refineries in the Middle East and Russia have been damaged by military attacks. Russia, long a major exporter of refined fuel, is now a net importer due to fuel shortages at home, and even the facilities still operating in the Persian Gulf can’t export as much product due to ongoing shipping disruptions.

It’s not the modest drop in US refining capacity in recent years that has increased prices, Auers said. “The problem is we’ve lost 2 million barrels per day of supply combined between Russia and the Middle East to global markets. That is huge in a market that was already fairly tight.”

Oil prices have surged this year, recently climbing back above $100 a barrel. But despite the higher input cost for refiners, the sky-high prices for the products they sell have inflated their margins to record levels.

US refiners now bring in about $100-a-barrel profit for diesel, and about $40 to $50 a barrel for gasoline, said Tom Kloza, an independent oil analyst and advisor to Gulf Oil.

“These numbers aren’t just off the chart — they’re out of the galaxy,” he said.

That’s made the economics of running a refinery incredibly profitable, so US refineries have been running at nearly 100% capacity this year, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Exxon’s Wood told investors earlier this year that the company had even deferred any maintenance to maintain output and profitability. The company raked in $14.5 billion in profit in the second quarter, more than double compared to the same quarter last year. But it can’t safely defer maintenance forever.

“The utilization that we’ve seen can’t be sustained for the long term,” Wood told CNBC.

Temporary shutdowns for maintenance will be inevitable later this year, said Auers. That will result in some reduction in the supply, pushing up prices.

No easy solutions

Despite a sharp drop in the number of refineries over the last 45 years, the US has been able to get all the gas it needs from those that remain.

Many of those that closed were smaller, less competitive refineries, Auers said. Plus, improved technology and efficiency — along with the expansion of the surviving refineries — meant that US capacity actually grew over time.

Output rose 16% from 1999 to a record high of 18.6 million barrels a day in 2019, according to the EIA. It’s only down 3% since then. Meanwhile, Americans use less gasoline due to better fuel efficiency, more electric vehicles on the road and the rise of remote work.

US gas prices rose quickly after the start of the Iran war in late February and have remained high, climbing more than crude oil prices.

The national average price for gas on Saturday was $4.31 a gallon, according to data from AAA, the highest price on record for September. Diesel just crossed the $6-a-gallon mark for the first time on record. Jet fuel has been at its highest point since April.

A sign displays the price of unleaded gasoline at an Exxon gas station in Washington, DC, in May 2026. Gas prices have remained high since the start of the war in Iran are are at the highest level ever recorded in the month of September. Alex Wroblewski/Bloomberg/Getty Images

But don’t expect more US refineries to change that anytime soon.

First and foremost, it takes at least three years to significantly expand existing oil refineries, even longer for a new one.

Auers noted that even if a refinery has been designed and ready for environmental review, “you’re still looking at four to five years until it’s going to start producing.”

Also, that extra capacity would need to be operational for decades for the investment to pay off. Uncertainty about future US regulations and demand makes such long-term investments risky.

Excluding the pandemic, “gasoline demand this summer will probably be the lowest for a summer period since 2001,” said Kloza.

“North America is the best continent to be a refiner at the moment, and probably for the next five to 10 years,” he said. “Beyond that, who knows?”

That’s likely why oil companies are more interested in taking their current windfall profits and investing in oil exploration or pipelines, which have more immediate payoffs, or returning the money to shareholders.

“They’re putting it back in (stock) buybacks and dividends,” said Auers. Even when oil companies such as Marathon and Phillips 66 invest their windfall profits back into their business, “most of their capital expenditures over the past few years have been in midstream (such as pipelines), not on the refining side. That’s because that’s where Wall Street wanted them to put their money.”

World.title: Iran-Gulf talks without US participation on reopening the Strait of Hormuz postponed, Omani official says
World.content:
Gulf diplomats and Iranian officials were set to meet Monday to discuss an Omani plan for reopening the Strait of Hormuz to regular tanker traffic, a conversation that would have happened without a critical player: the United States.

But, as news of the meeting circulated on Sunday, it was indefinitely postponed, according to the Omani foreign minister.

“In the interests of consensus the regional meeting set for tomorrow in Salalah has been postponed,” Badr Albusaidi, the foreign minister, wrote in an X post. “We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting cooperation in our region.”

Despite shipping traffic remaining depressed, President Donald Trump has insisted the state of the waterway is acceptable for now with the US military escorting oil tankers.

The meeting that was scheduled for Monday would have underscored that — despite active efforts to develop alternative corridors for passage through the strait — countries in the region are unwilling to accept the status quo as the new normal. After months of private discussions on a complicated possible legal framework to reopen the strait that could allow Iran and Oman to collect fees, diplomats hoped the gathering could create some momentum for a deal.

“There is no imminent breakthrough expected, but resolving the strait issue is the most pressing issue, so we need to start somewhere,” a regional source said.

Saudi Arabia submitted amendments because it had concerns that the proposed language could effectively establish a new status quo that would not be acceptable to it or the other Gulf Cooperation Council states.

The possibility of Iranian tolls is still widely rejected, but there is a willingness to consider voluntary contributions for directing passage through the strait, the sources said. The Omani legal framework includes voluntary payment for providing navigational safety and environmental protection, according to three sources familiar with the plans.

Trump administration officials have privately told those in the Gulf region that they want to refocus any future US-Iran negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear program and not reopening the strait, according to three sources familiar with the matter.

“I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Tuesday night, after Iran retaliated following US strikes. “I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing.”

One goal for the Monday meeting was to agree on maps for routes going through the strait, one of the sources said. Still, the likelihood of the Gulf Corporation Council countries and Iran getting behind a comprehensive plan to open the waterway would be virtually impossible without the US at the table. The administration did not seek to oppose the gathering, maintaining that they would closely monitor discussions.

“The United States is in close communication with all of our regional partners and will remain so before, during, and after the meeting. Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz and never will,” said a US official on Sunday about an hour before the Omani foreign minister’s announcement.

While the US initially underestimated Iran’s willingness to close the strait in response to the US and Israel launching combat operations earlier this year — a strategic error that Tehran has capitalized on by leveraging its ability to threaten commercial shipping and prolong the war — American forces believe they have now reached a point where they, militarily, have the upper hand in the waterway, a different US official said.

“We don’t want to talk about the strait, and that is the position of the administration right now — we’re only going to talk to you if you want to talk about nuclear file,” the official said.

Iranians have signaled to regional players that they would be open to nuclear negotiations with the US when the strait issue is resolved, including lifting the US blockade, the regional source said. As a result, getting the ball rolling on a framework to reopen the waterway is likely a critical step to pave the way for nuclear negotiations and an overall end to the war.

The possibility of mandatory fees or tolls for tanker traffic will be a major sticking point. Before the conflict broke out, the waterway was open to commercial traffic without any required charges. And in the early days of the conflict, the US and regional players were adamant about one thing: The postwar status of waterway could not include new fees, especially fees that would financially benefit Iran.

Now, after months of surging global energy prices and intensive work on a legal framework to reopen the strait, the absolutist nature of this sentiment has faded, according to multiple European and Gulf diplomats.

“We won’t accept something that was not there before, but there could be symbolic new rules that allow both sides to save face from both sides,” said a European diplomat briefed on the Omani proposal.

Trump administration officials have reviewed the plans being drafted by Oman in recent months, sources said, but they have not publicly signed onto the framework. Instead, Trump and members of his administration continue to claim that the US is the only player that can facilitate an open waterway.

“We are the only country in the world that can ensure, as you heard the president say, the control over the Strait of Hormuz,” Vice President JD Vance said last week.

In recent weeks, the number of oil tankers moving through the strait has greatly increased due to US military escorts enabling passage, though commercial ships continue to be struck by Iranian attacks as they attempt to transit.

There are questions, however, around how long the US military can credibly maintain its substantial commitment of ships and resources to aid in moving ships through the Strait.

The US Navy has successfully escorted as many as 40 commercial vessels on a given day, but the complexity of those operations underscores how Iran still poses a real threat to those ships and the American military personnel tasked with protecting them.

As a result, US diplomats and regional sources privately conceded that the Gulf effort to develop a framework to reopen the strait is a necessary endeavor — even if the US is not at the table for the first meeting.

The administration has also sought to downplay just how vital the waterway may be in the years to come, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently claiming the strait will become “like a worthless piece of water” within two years.

While regional players and US officials say resiliency in developing alternative routes for energy exports has been impressive, they argue that finding a long-term solution for the strait should remain a priority. The need to develop that plan is even more necessary given recent Huthi military successes that have threatened passage out of the Red Sea, the sources said.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

World.title: Opposition set to halt Sweden’s slide to right
World.content:
Reuters — Sweden’s center-left opposition on Monday looked set to form the next government as preliminary election results projected a narrow three-seat lead over the Sweden’s center-left opposition on Monday looked set to form the next government as preliminary election results projected a narrow three-seat lead over the right-wing ruling parties with most of the votes counted after Sunday’s vote.

A win for the opposition would halt a slide to the right over the last four years which has transformed Sweden from one of Europe’s most ⁠welcoming countries for immigrants to one with among the toughest asylum regimes.

While a center-left government may take a softer line, it is unlikely to return to the generous, open-door immigration policies of past decades, analysts say. It would also stick to Sweden’s pro-Western and pro-Ukraine stance.

Left-leaning parties headed by Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson were projected to win 176 seats in the 349-seat parliament while Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing bloc ⁠was seen winning 173 seats, the election authority said.

“If this result remains valid, Sweden will get a new government,” Andersson told supporters after the preliminary results were published on Sunday night.

The far-right Sweden Democrats, who hoped to join a government for the first time in the event of ‌a win for the ruling bloc, ⁠lost an estimated 11 seats, projections showed.

Party leaders, however, have been cautious about claiming victory or accepting defeat with 353 election districts still to be counted and overseas votes not likely to be tallied until Wednesday.

In 2022, exit polls initially gave a narrow victory to the center-left which proved premature and Kristersson showed no sign of conceding when he spoke after Sunday’s election.

The blocs were separated by just 0.4% of votes ‌on Monday morning.

Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson talks to members of the media in September. Denis Balibouse/Reuters

If a centre-left win is confirmed, forming a government could take some time.

While Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson will be prime minister, it remains unclear which other parties will be in her government. The Center ⁠Party has refused to share power with the Left Party which says it must be a part of any coalition.

“It could very well be a complicated process to form a government,” the speaker of the parliament, Andreas Norlen, ⁠told Swedish television.

The leader of the Sweden Democrats, Jimmie Akesson, speaks at a campaign event ahead of the election in Nykoping, Sweden. Tom Little/Reuters

The result of the election is unlikely to change the course of Sweden’s pro-Western and pro-Ukraine stance and its effect on immigration and economic policy is unclear.

Andersson has ⁠promised ‌voters more spending on welfare, a fairer tax system and a focus on social cohesion. But while the Greens and Left parties want the rich to contribute ‌more, ‌the Center Party is against a billionaires’ tax.

The Social Democrats are unlikely to ease immigration rules, as campaigned for by the Left and Green parties, with Andersson saying Sweden has to continue its tough line.

Asylum numbers have dropped to a 40-year low under the current government which has abolished permanent residency for refugees, tightened welfare rules and stepped up expulsions of those without a right to stay.

World.title: Why Democrats’ blue wave might not be as big as expected
World.content:
The 2026 election will be decided where the wave meets the wall.

Signs are accumulating that the blue wave of Democratic support this year may be even higher than in the 2018 election, when a backlash against President Donald Trump’s tumultuous first term carried the party back into control of the House of Representatives. But the defensive wall that Republicans are constructing against that Democratic tide also looks bigger than in 2018.

The height of the wave gives Democrats legitimate reasons to expect they can win races deep into previously reliably Republican territory. The depth of the wall gives Republicans plausible reasons to hope they can contain their losses to a modest level.

For Democrats, the wave is being powered primarily by turnout and Trump: clear signs that their partisans are more energized than Republicans about voting this year and that voters are now more negative on the president’s performance than not only in 2018, but also in other modern midterms that broke sharply against the party holding the White House, such as 2010 and 2006.

For Republicans, the central bricks in the wall are money and the map: a financial advantage magnified by crucial recent decisions from the Republican-appointed majority on the Supreme Court, and an electoral battlefield that is playing out almost entirely in places Trump carried in 2024.

“This election is home field advantage for Republicans, and they’ve got to exploit that,” says former Republican Rep. Tom Davis, who chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee. “On the other hand, this is a referendum on the president, and he’s had a confluence of very bad things coming together.”

What’s powering the wave

A wide assortment of measures suggests the electoral environment this year is more perilous for Republicans than it was in 2018 — and during other recent midterms that produced significant losses for the party holding the White House.

Those warning lights begin with attitudes about the economy. Compared with 2018, Americans today are much more negative about current economic conditions and much more pessimistic about the future. Inflation has become an inescapable strain on daily life: AAA, for instance, reported that gas prices last week reached $4.28 per gallon, compared with $2.75 on Election Day in 2018 (that’s $3.65 in today’s dollars, factoring for inflation). In the latest CNBC poll this summer conducted by a bipartisan Democratic-Republican pollster team, just 27 percent of Americans described the economy as excellent or good, compared with 73 percent who viewed as fair or poor. In CNBC’s October 2018 poll, 58 percent described the economy in positive terms and only 40 percent in negative ones.

Micah Roberts, a Republican pollster who conducts the CNBC survey with a Democratic partner, says far more Democrats, independents and even Republicans are negative on the economy than in 2018. Just as striking, he says, the share who are not only down on today’s conditions but pessimistic about tomorrow’s is twice as large now as then. “That’s a radically different environment,” Roberts says. “Everybody everywhere is feeling an economic pinch.”

Today’s economic assessment is also gloomier than the results measured in CNBC polls before the midterm election that produced historic losses for Democrats in 2010, and in the exit polls when Republicans lost control of both chambers in 2006.

The Democrats’ 2006 gains were fueled as well by widespread disillusionment over the Iraq War that then President George W. Bush launched in 2003. In the 2006 exit poll, 59 percent of voters said the war had not improved American security — and over three-fourths of those skeptics supported Democrats for the House. Today, the Iran War is facing comparable public opposition in most polls.

Some of Trump’s other initiatives have been more popular, such as his efforts to regain control of the Southern border and the provisions in the “One Big Beautiful Bill” temporarily reducing taxes on tips and overtime. But to a much greater extent than before the 2018 election, Trump has pursued a wide range of other specific policy choices that have provoked opposition from a significant majority of Americans, including his tariffs and the Medicaid cuts in that reconciliation bill.

All of this — especially the economy and the war — has predictably eroded Trump’s support. The negative views of Trump’s economic management “didn’t really exist in 2018,” said Democratic pollster Nick Gourevitch. “2018 was like: ‘He’s a bad guy, crazy guy, but the economy is good.’ Now it’s: ‘He’s a bad guy, crazy guy, and the economy is bad.’”

The latest CNN poll of polls found just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s performance, with 63 percent disapproving. If those levels hold among this November’s electorate, they’ll be much worse than Trump’s standing in the 2018 exit poll, when 45 percent of voters approved and 54 percent disapproved. Trump’s approval rating is also much weaker than that of other presidents in recent midterms when their party suffered losses, including Joe Biden in 2022, Obama in 2010, George W. Bush in 2006 and Bill Clinton in 1994.

Trump’s decline poses a clear and present danger for Republicans: During his first term, Democratic House candidates won 90 percent of voters who disapproved of him in 2018, and 93 percent in 2020, per the exit polls. Likewise, in Senate races over those elections, every Democratic incumbent or challenger except Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ opponent in 2020 won at least 89 percent of voters who disapproved of Trump.

Probably the most worrisome sign for Democrats this year is that many of their candidates are not yet matching those benchmarks among Trump disapprovers. But so many voters now disapprove of Trump — not only in swing states but even such red-leaning places as North Carolina, Texas, Ohio and Georgia — that Democrats can reach 50 percent even with support from fewer of them.

Democratic pollster Anna Greenberg says that in her surveys and focus groups, red-state voters are often the most disenchanted with Trump’s return. They point above all, she says, to inflation, the Iran war and Trump’s focus on his own preoccupations — from making money to gilding the capital with his construction projects.

“In the red states… it feels like independent voters, Hispanic voters, White non-college women to some degree, are really, really angry at Trump,” Greenberg says. “And, in guilt by association, with Republicans. When you do focus groups … they feel betrayed and lied to.”

Whit Ayres, a veteran Republican pollster, says that Trump’s hold remains undiminished on voters who identify as part of his Make America Great Again movement. But he notes, about half of Republican voters don’t identify with MAGA. And among those non-MAGA Republican voters — a group that includes both traditional country-club Republicans and the new, mostly younger and nonwhite, voters Trump attracted in 2024 — Trump “has slipped a lot,” Ayres says.

The turnout gap

Some of those disillusioned 2024 Trump voters (especially people of color) may cross over to vote for Democrats, Ayres and other strategists say. But as American politics have grown more polarized, fewer voters are willing to cross that line. Roberts says that in the CNBC polling, the share of non-MAGA Republicans who say they are still voting for Republicans this fall is about 20 points higher than the portion who approve of Trump’s performance.

“There are a lot of people who may think, ‘I don’t like Trump but … I don’t agree with the policies of the other party and where they would take us,’” Roberts says.

Most analysts agree the biggest risk for the GOP among disillusioned Trump supporters is that they will not vote at all. “That’s one of the major challenges for Republican candidates,” Ayres says. “Democratic enthusiasm is substantially higher than Republican enthusiasm at the moment.”

That potential turnout gap represents the other major component of the possible Democratic wave. Not only do polls consistently show that more Democrats say they are very motivated to vote than Republicans, but more Democrats are voting since 2024.

Political data analyst John Couvillon has calculated that through last week’s New Hampshire contest, 56 percent of all the votes in primaries nationwide this year have been cast in Democratic contests. That’s an even bigger share than their 54 percent in 2018. By contrast, Couvillon found that in 2014 and 2022 — when Republicans made midterm gains — they cast at least 53 percent of primary votes nationwide.

Similarly, Democrats are performing even better in special elections leading into this midterm than they did before 2018. The Downballot, a political website, calculates that in 110 state and federal special elections since 2024, Democratic candidates on average have run 12.5 points better than Kamala Harris did in the same jurisdiction; in 2017 and 2018, Democratic candidates ran 10.6 points better than Hillary Clinton did in 2016.

Two other factors could widen this year’s potential Democratic turnout advantage. One is that across almost all the key battleground states, racial minorities and/or White college graduates, two generally good groups for Democrats, have increased their share of eligible voters since 2018, while Whites without a four-year college degree, the core Trump constituency, have diminished, according to census figures analyzed by demographer William Frey. And while people of color usually make up a smaller share of the vote in midterms than presidential years, the opposite is true for college graduates. These shifts will likely matter only at the margin, but that could be enough to tip some very close races.

The GOP’s bricks in the wall

Amid all these forces churning against them, the Republican wall begins with the map of states and districts at play this year.

Heading into the 2018 election, House Republicans held 23 seats that voted for Clinton two years before and ultimately lost 20 of them. This time, before the redistricting wars, Republicans were defending just three seats that voted for Harris. Looking more broadly, Republicans this year must defend 30 seats that narrowly voted either for or against Trump in 2024, compared with 36 in 2018, according to calculations by the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics. And the GOP’s redistricting drive has left 13 House Democrats defending districts where Trump ran at least 5 points better than his share of the national vote, compared to just four in such districts in 2018. Moreover, fewer House seats overall than in 2018 remain competitive — which leaves Democrats, while still strongly favored to capture the majority, with less room to overcome idiosyncratic stumbles (such as scandals or otherwise vulnerable nominees).

Attendees from Texas watch the proceedings during the second day of the Republican National Committee midterm convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas on Thursday. Kent Nishamura/AFP/Getty Images

On paper, the Senate map is even more forbidding. Of the Republican-held seats Democrats are most seriously contesting, Maine is the only one in a state that supported Harris; North Carolina is the sole other state on the Senate map where Harris even came close. Trump prevailed by double digits in every other state whose Senate seat Democrats are targeting — Alaska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, much less Kansas and Nebraska (where Democrats are supporting an independent candidate.)

Even in these states, Trump’s approval has generally fallen into negative territory, which provides Democrats their opening. But to win on this stony soil, Democratic candidates must overcome years of alienation from their national party. In these red states, Democrats “have to establish yourself as a really unique candidate who is going to change the way things are,” says Democratic pollster Celinda Lake. “It isn’t going to be the party that wins; it is going to be a vote for change that wins.”

After the map, money is the next major component of the GOP wall. In 2018, Democratic House and Senate candidates significantly outraised their Republican opponents, according to OpenSecrets.org. And while Republican party committees and independent expenditure groups raised more than their Democratic counterparts that year, that advantage was dulled by federal election rules which limited their direct coordination with campaigns and allowed broadcasters to charge those groups more for ads than they charged candidates.

But two rulings by the Republican-appointed Supreme Court majority this year have swept away those constraints, which will allow Republicans to maximize the big financial advantage their party committees and outside groups have established over their Democratic rivals.

Also working for Republicans is the decline in the Democrats’ own image. In Pew Research polling, favorability ratings for the Democratic Party have hovered in the high 30s for the past three years, a downtick from 2018. But the GOP image is no better-and historically attitudes toward the president in the White House have shaped midterm results much more than views of the party outside it.

Trump’s efforts to tilt electoral rules toward the GOP represent the final section of the GOP wall — the spikes on the battlements. That effort began with his successful pressure on multiple red states to gerrymander their House districts. Still looming are his attempts to restrict mail voting and possible deployments of federal law enforcement at polling places in Democratic areas.

All of this could limit Democratic gains. But strategists in both parties agree that attitudes toward the incumbent president have become the most powerful force influencing midterm outcomes. No wall may be high enough to fully contain the wave of public disenchantment cresting through Trump’s storm-tossed second term.

This headline has been updated.

World.title: Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon quits, sparking greater concerns about AI safety
World.content:
When Jacob Coxon, a researcher at the AI ​​startup Anthropic, publicly announced his resignation on Tuesday—citing concerns about the rapidly emerging technology—a flood of messages poured in within the company.

Commenting on Coxon’s statements in an internal group chat viewed by The New York Times, one employee wrote: “This is what we’ve all been saying; the only difference now is that it’s gone public.”

Another wrote: “Jacob has taken the discussion from the internal group chat to the public stage, and that’s a good thing.”

The New York Times highlighted in a report on Sunday the widespread debate sparked by Coxon’s resignation and the reactions among AI researchers at Anthropic—sentiments that resonated with their counterparts at OpenAI, Meta, and Google.

These reactions went so far as to characterize the fears surrounding a loss of control over the rapid pace of AI development—in the absence of safety standards—as a “doomsday scenario.”

Some researchers turned to analyzing Coxon’s social media posts—including one in which he explained how OpenAI and Anthropic are gambling with human lives through this technology.

Many AI employees had resorted to internal messaging channels, encrypted chats, and private dinners to organize efforts aimed at raising awareness about the risks of artificial intelligence, according to about a dozen employees from OpenAI, Meta, and Google.

Among these efforts was a move by AI professionals to urge senior executives at their companies to pause the technology’s development—buying time to ensure it could be worked on safely—while others followed Coxon’s lead and voiced their concerns publicly.

A safety researcher at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, said in a social media post that he believes there is a greater than 10 percent chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade.

Another safety researcher at OpenAI, Julie Stiel, called for AI companies to slow their pace.

And an employee at Google DeepMind, Andreas Kirsch, expressed concerns about the possibility of AI wiping out humanity—whether through “imminent risks,” “long-term risks,” or both.

World.title: Aggression against Arab nations must cease, says Sisi to Iran’s president
World.content:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi reaffirmed his nation’s firm position in support of efforts to restore stability in the region.

The president emphasized Egypt’s expectation that Iran will exert all possible efforts to halt escalation and reach a comprehensive, sustainable, and peaceful settlement to the war—one that ensures the sovereignty of regional states and protects the resources and well-being of their peoples.

These remarks were made during a meeting between Sisi and his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian, on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS summit held in New Delhi, India.

The Egyptian President underscored the imperative of halting any acts of aggression against Arab nations, in order to maintain good relations and and strengthen the historical and cultural ties uniting the region.

Meeting with Modi

Sisi on Sunday also met with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to discuss ways to advance Egyptian-Indian relations and build upon the growing momentum witnessed since ties were elevated to strategic partnership in 2023.

He emphasized the importance of taking concrete steps to strengthen this partnership, including increasing the volume of trade to $12 billion and boosting Indian investments in Egypt—particularly in the manufacturing, technology, clean energy, and automotive sectors.

The Indian Prime Minister affirmed his country’s commitment to further developing bilateral relations across various fields.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Video: Celine Dion breaks down in tears at first concert after six-year hiatus
World.content:
Canadian superstar Celine Dion experienced an emotional moment on stage in Paris, moved to tears during her comeback concert—her first live performance before an audience after a years-long absence due to health issues.

The star affirmed that she had kept her promise to return to the stage and stand once again before her fans.

Dion performed at the La Défense Arena in Paris on Saturday, kicking off a series of shows in the French capital and marking her return to a full concert performance for the first time in nearly six years.

Her emotion was palpable as she stood before tens of thousands of fans who welcomed her with cheers and applause— a reflection of the immense anticipation surrounding her return to the stage.

Addressing the audience, Dion said: “I made a promise to return.”

“It is wonderful to be together,” she added, amidst an enthusiastic response from the crowd, before continuing: “Here I am, singing for you and singing for myself.”

The superstar thanked her fans for standing by her over the past few years, saying: “Thank you so much for your support and patience. I am who I am today thanks to your love.”

Dion’s return to the stage follows a long hiatus from performing, which began after she announced in December 2022 that she had been diagnosed with Stiff-Person Syndrome (SPS)—a rare neurological condition that affects movement and causes muscle stiffness and spasms.

Her health condition forced the Canadian artist to cancel her “Courage” world tour; she had previously cancelled a series of Las Vegas concerts in 2021 due to health issues.

Since announcing her diagnosis, Dion has spoken on several occasions about the difficulties she endured, all while maintaining her desire to return to singing and perform before her audience once again.

Paris Olympics

Despite a long hiatus from performing, Céline Dion made a public appearance in 2024 when she took part in the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympic Games, delivering a vocal performance that garnered widespread global attention.

Her appearance at the Olympics signaled her readiness to gradually resume her artistic career after years of focusing on her health.

Sixteen-Concert Run

Dion’s comeback has generated immense public interest, reflected in her Paris concert schedule; the series of shows has been extended to a total of 16 performances, running through October 14.

During these concerts, the artist will perform a selection of her most notable songs in both French and English, including “My Heart Will Go On,” “Think Twice,” and “It’s All Coming Back To Me Now.”

The announcement of Celine Dion’s return to the stage was made on her birthday, March 30, via an Instagram post in which she expressed her excitement about returning to her audience.

World.title: Scientific committee in Egypt recommends dismantling Ramesses II statue
World.content:
A specialized Egyptian scientific committee has recommended re-evaluating the sections used to complete the statue of King Ramses II, located in front of the Second Pylon at the Karnak Temple Complex in Luxor, RT reported on Sunday.

The committee also recommended studying the feasibility of dismantling the restored section atop the statue’s base, so long as it is confirmed that doing so will not impact the original part of the statue.

This recommendation follows from the committee’s comprehensive study of the statue, which revealed discrepancies in the type and color of certain blocks used in the restoration compared to the statue’s original sections.

Furthermore, the committee recommended conducting laboratory analyses on samples taken from the statue’s base—a section still in its original position—and comparing them with samples from the blocks used in the restoration.

This aims to verify whether the blocks belong to the same statue; should the results fail to match, those pieces would be excluded as having no confirmed connection to the statue.

Re-evaluation needed

The study also revealed discrepancies in the anatomical proportions of the restored section; its dimensions exceeded the statue’s presumed natural proportions.

Consequently, the committee recommended a scientific study to assess the feasibility of detaching this section, while ensuring the preservation of the original part and avoiding any damage to it.

At the same time, the committee instructed specialists at the archaeological site to search for missing fragments of the statue—including the upper part of the crown and a portion of the leg—and to examine any such pieces found to verify that they belong to the statue.

If the missing original parts are not found, an archaeological study will be conducted to determine their probable form and proportions, followed by an assessment of the archaeological feasibility of completing the statue, in accordance with international laws and charters governing restoration work.

The study concluded that completing the statue is not feasible; therefore, the discovered archaeological fragments will be preserved and stored rather than used in a speculative reconstruction of the statue.

World.title: Liberia: VP Koung says Liberia must move from NPL conference promises to reforms that unlock lending, investment and jobs
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Liberian government is moving to confront the country’s non-performing loans (NPLs) problem with the establishment of a National Non-Performing Loans Task Force, in a bid to unlock credit, strengthen banking stability and expand financing for businesses and entrepreneurs.

Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung Sr. announced the task force at the close of a national conference on non-performing loans, saying the accumulation of bad debts has become more than a banking-sector problem and is now a broader economic constraint.

“What has emerged from these discussions is a clear consensus: resolving non-performing loans is not simply about improving commercial bank balance sheets; it is about unlocking economic opportunity, expanding access to finance, encouraging investment, supporting entrepreneurship, and creating jobs for the Liberian people,” Koung said.

The conference brought together policymakers, financial regulators, commercial banks, development partners and other experts to examine the causes of non-performing loans and identify reforms to strengthen Liberia’s financial system.

According to Koung, participants identified weaknesses in credit systems, delays in legal proceedings, governance concerns, limited enforcement mechanisms and broader economic pressures on borrowers and lenders as key factors contributing to the problem.

He warned that elevated levels of bad loans are restricting credit growth, limiting private-sector expansion and increasing the cost of borrowing.

“The conference materials have reminded us that elevated levels of non-performing loans constrain lending, restrict private sector expansion, increase the cost of credit, and ultimately undermine economic growth,” he said.

Task Force to Coordinate National Response

The National Non-Performing Loans Task Force is expected to bring together the Central Bank of Liberia, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, the Ministry of Justice, financial institutions and other relevant stakeholders.

Koung said the task force will provide a coordinated framework for addressing the NPL problem while strengthening the resilience of the financial sector and restoring confidence in Liberia’s banking system.

“I am pleased to announce on behalf of His Excellency, Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr., President of the Republic of Liberia, the establishment of a National Non-Performing Loans Task Force,” he said.

The Vice President disclosed that President Boakai has instructed relevant institutions to move quickly to finalize the task force’s composition, terms of reference and implementation action plan.

The plan, he said, should include clear responsibilities, timelines, monitoring mechanisms and reporting requirements.

“By directive of the President, the relevant institutions are requested to move expeditiously to finalize the Task Force’s composition, terms of reference, and implementation action plan, with clear responsibilities, timelines, and mechanisms for monitoring and reporting progress,” Koung said.

Government Targets Lending Constraints

The government’s intervention comes as Liberia continues to grapple with limited access to affordable financing, particularly for small businesses, farmers, women entrepreneurs and youth-led enterprises.

Koung said reforms must go beyond addressing existing bad loans and focus on preventing future accumulation of distressed credit.

He said the government supports measures to strengthen prudential supervision, improve credit-risk management, modernize credit infrastructure and make debt recovery more effective.

“We support efforts to strengthen prudential supervision and credit risk management. We support reforms aimed at modernizing Liberia’s credit infrastructure. We support initiatives that improve debt recovery, insolvency administration, collateral enforcement, and commercial dispute resolution,” he said.

The Vice President also emphasized the need to improve financing opportunities for small enterprises and agricultural value chains, arguing that access to sustainable credit is essential to broad-based economic growth.

“No country can sustain economic transformation without an efficient financial system,” Koung said. “And no nation can achieve broad-based prosperity if businesses, farmers, women entrepreneurs, young innovators, and small enterprises lack access to affordable and sustainable financing.”

Beyond the Banks

Koung stressed that resolving Liberia’s NPL crisis cannot be left solely to the Central Bank or commercial banks.

He called for coordinated action among the Executive Branch, Legislature, Judiciary, financial institutions, borrowers and development partners.

“The responsibility for implementation does not rest with any single institution. It belongs to all of us,” he said.

He specifically pointed to the Legislature’s role in supporting legal reforms and the Judiciary’s responsibility in strengthening contract enforcement and commercial justice.

Delays in debt recovery and commercial dispute resolution, he noted, can weaken lenders’ willingness to extend credit and increase the risks associated with borrowing.

From Conference to Implementation

While acknowledging the challenges confronting Liberia’s financial sector, Koung said the country has the expertise and institutional capacity to address them.

“The policy options have been identified. The reform priorities have been articulated. The responsibilities of stakeholders have been clarified. What remains is implementation,” he said.

That implementation, he suggested, will ultimately determine whether the conference produces meaningful economic results.

“History will not judge this conference by the quality of the presentations delivered in this hall. History will judge it by the reforms implemented after we leave,” Koung said.

He said the real measure of success would be the amount of credit unlocked for productive sectors, the number of businesses able to expand, jobs created and confidence restored in Liberia’s financial system.

The Vice President concluded by urging stakeholders to move beyond resolutions and recommendations toward measurable action.

“Our commitment extends beyond today’s closing ceremony. Our commitment is to implementation of the outcome, the recommendations and the commitments from all stakeholders. Our commitment is to reform. And our commitment is to delivering tangible benefits for the Liberian people,” he said.

“As we depart this conference, let us move forward not merely with resolutions, but with resolve. Not merely with recommendations, but with responsibility. Not merely with aspirations, but with action.”

World.title: Liberia: Business Executive Stephen Yekeson Takes Over Liberia’s Commerce Ministry
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — Liberia’s Commerce Ministry gets a new face today as businessman and former Deputy Public Works Minister Stephen Marka Yekeson Jr. assumes the acting ministerial post, bringing with him a career that has moved between government, corporate leadership and entrepreneurship. With Liberia seeking to expand local enterprise, strengthen trade and create more value from what the country produces, Yekeson enters a portfolio where his private-sector experience could prove particularly relevant.

By Philip Freeman, contributing writer

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai appointed Yekeson Acting Minister of Commerce and Industry on September 11, replacing Magdalene E. Dagoseh, who is being reassigned. His appointment was part of a wider reshuffle announced by the Executive Mansion.

The appointment places an experienced business executive at the head of a ministry whose work directly affects the country’s business community, consumers, traders and entrepreneurs.

Yekeson’s professional background stretches across business development, strategic planning, entrepreneurship, management consultancy and infrastructure development. CitiTrust Liberia describes him as a senior executive and business leader with more than 20 years of experience across those areas.

He is also the Group Chief Executive Officer of South Atlantic Capital Group, according to the company’s official leadership profile.

That private-sector experience could prove significant as the Commerce Ministry seeks to balance regulation with the need to create an environment in which businesses can grow.

A businessman returning to government

Yekeson is not new to public service.

He previously served as Deputy Minister for Administration at the Ministry of Public Works between 2012 and 2013 under former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.

His return to government therefore brings a combination of private-sector management and previous experience inside the Liberian public sector.

That combination could give him a different perspective on the relationship between government regulation and the realities businesses face.

At South Atlantic Capital Group, Yekeson has served in a corporate leadership role, while his professional profile highlights experience in strategic planning, entrepreneurship, management consultancy and infrastructure development.

His educational background also includes an MBA, with North Carolina Central University listed in his professional profile.

Why the business background matters

The Commerce Ministry is more than a regulator of markets.

Its responsibilities touch business registration, trade, consumer protection, market regulation, competition and efforts to create opportunities for local businesses.

That makes business experience particularly relevant to the portfolio.

Liberia’s private sector continues to operate in an environment shaped by high operating costs, limited access to finance, infrastructure constraints, dependence on imported goods and difficulties accessing larger markets. A minister with direct experience running a business could bring a practical understanding of some of those pressures into policy discussions.

The opportunity will be to translate that experience into policies that make commercial activity easier, while maintaining the government’s responsibility to protect consumers and enforce market rules.

A chance to strengthen the business environment

Yekeson’s appointment comes at a moment when the conversation around Liberia’s economy is increasingly focused on local enterprise. The country has taken steps to increase Liberian participation in certain reserved business sectors, while the Commerce Ministry has also been working to expand business registration services and support entrepreneurs.

The bigger challenge is turning those policies into an environment where Liberian businesses can actually compete and grow.

That requires more than simply reserving sectors.

Businesses need access to finance, reliable infrastructure, markets, information, skills and predictable regulations.

Yekeson’s experience in business development and strategic planning could give the ministry an opportunity to look at these issues from a broader commercial perspective.

From regulation to growth

One of the central questions surrounding his appointment will be whether the Commerce Ministry can strengthen its role as both a regulator and a facilitator of economic growth.

Market inspections, price monitoring and consumer protection will remain important. But the ministry also has a role in helping businesses understand regulations, formalize their operations, access markets and prepare to compete.

The potential advantage of Yekeson’s private-sector background is the possibility of placing greater emphasis on the practical realities behind those policies.

A business registration system, for example, becomes more meaningful when newly registered businesses can find financing, customers and opportunities to expand.

Likewise, trade policies become more valuable when Liberian producers can meet quality standards, access regional markets and compete with imported products.

The local production opportunity

Liberia remains heavily dependent on imported goods, while many of its agricultural and natural resources leave the country with limited processing and value addition. That presents one of the biggest opportunities within the Commerce portfolio.

A stronger focus on local production could connect farmers, manufacturers, traders and entrepreneurs to a larger domestic value chain. Instead of simply importing finished products, Liberia could create more opportunities to process and package goods locally, build businesses around domestic resources and eventually position more Liberian products for regional export.

Yekeson’s background in business development and infrastructure development could be useful in navigating some of the commercial and structural questions involved in that process.

A bridge between government and business

The private sector will also be watching how the new minister engages with businesses. Commerce policies can have immediate consequences for traders, manufacturers, importers, retailers and consumers.

A ministry that understands the concerns of businesses while maintaining strong regulatory standards could help reduce friction between government and the private sector. That balance will be important.

Businesses want predictable rules and a government that listens.

Consumers want fair prices, safe products and protection against abusive commercial practices.

The ministry sits directly between those interests.

The opportunity ahead

Yekeson begins his tenure with an existing policy agenda and a commercial sector looking for stronger results.

His background does not automatically guarantee success, but it gives the new acting minister experience from both sides of the public-private divide.

He has worked inside government, led a private-sector organisation and built a career around business development, strategic planning and management.

That combination could offer the Commerce Ministry an opportunity to bring a more business-oriented perspective to some of Liberia’s longstanding commercial challenges.

The immediate task will still involve regulation, consumer protection and market oversight.

The larger opportunity, however, lies in strengthening the conditions under which Liberian businesses can survive, expand, employ more people and compete beyond Liberia’s borders.

As Yekeson takes office today, attention will shift from his appointment to his approach. The coming months will show whether his private-sector experience, government background and management expertise can translate into stronger implementation, greater business confidence and a more competitive commercial environment.

The portfolio is demanding. But with a businessman now at the helm, the Commerce Ministry enters a new chapter with an opportunity to put business growth, local enterprise and stronger trade at the heart of Liberia’s commercial agenda.

World.title: Liberian SMEs Urged to Seize Regional Markets as Accelerate 360 Dialogue Ends
World.content:
Monrovia, Liberia — Liberian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have been urged to take advantage of regional and international trade opportunities while improving the quality, management and marketability of locally produced goods.

By Patience M. Jones,[email protected]

The call was made during the conclusion of a three-day dialogue under the Accelerate 360 Liberia Program, which brought together SMEs, government officials and development partners at the Ministry of Commerce and Industry in Monrovia.

The final day provided participating businesses an opportunity to showcase their products, share their entrepreneurial journeys and engage directly with officials of the Ministry of Commerce on challenges affecting private-sector growth.

The Chief of Party of Accelerate 360 Liberia, Prosper Doe Melomey, said the three-day engagement was designed around three major areas: public-sector procurement, access to finance and closer engagement between SMEs and government.

Melomey said the program identified more than US$100 million in potential annual public procurement opportunities that could benefit SMEs, based on a possible 25 percent allocation from procuring agencies.

He said the first day focused on public-sector dialogue, including discussions with the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC), while the second day focused on connecting SMEs with financial institutions and available financing opportunities.

According to Melomey, access to finance remains one of the major constraints confronting Liberian businesses. He referenced World Bank enterprise survey findings indicating that about 40 percent of Liberian SMEs identify access to finance as a major obstacle to business growth.

He said Accelerate 360 has also submitted about 45 SMEs to the Enterprise Acceleration Project for consideration and is supporting participating businesses in engaging financial institutions to access funding.

“Today, the emphasis is to bring proximity between the SMEs and the ministry,” Melomey said, noting that the final day also marked the completion of the core intervention journey for the program’s first cohort.

Entrepreneurs Share Their Journeys

Among the entrepreneurs sharing her experience was Angia Talo-Davis, founder of Angia Agri-Hub, an agriprocessing company that transforms locally grown agricultural products into ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook products.

Talo-Davis said her entrepreneurial journey was inspired by her mother’s health challenges, particularly hypertension.

Angia Davis Founder of Angea Dgro Hub

She explained that she began producing salt-free mixed spices using ingredients such as rosemary, garlic, ginger, bay leaf and cloves as an alternative way of adding flavor and potential nutritional value to food.

“My motivation came from my sick mother,” she said.

She said her business now produces powdered ginger and mixed spices without salt, preservatives or additives, targeting consumers who want convenient and healthier food options.

However, Talo-Davis identified access to markets and competition from imported products as major challenges facing locally produced goods.

She said Liberian consumers must be encouraged to support locally produced products, stressing that the country’s agriprocessing sector has significant potential despite the challenges.

Through Accelerate 360, she said, her business has benefited from technical support in areas including governance, staffing, funding opportunities and market access.

“Let’s grow, eat Liberia and add value to what we’re eating instead of just depending on what is coming in,” she urged Liberian business

Local Manufacturing Faces Market and Raw Material Challenges

Maxwell George Manager of New Horizon INC

Maxwell Sensi George, Portfolio Manager at New Horizon Incorporated, also shared his company’s experience.

New Horizon, which has experience in construction and building-material sales, recently diversified into the production of toiletries in Liberia.

George said the company sees significant potential in local manufacturing but continues to face challenges, particularly the high dependence on imported raw materials and limited market penetration.

He said the company has machinery capable of producing nearly 400 tonnes per day, but is currently operating at only about 25 percent of that capacity due largely to raw-material constraints, distribution challenges and competition from imported finished products.

“We want to increase our distribution outlets so that Liberians in different parts of the country can be able to access our products,” George said.

He also encouraged Liberians to abandon the perception that successful businesses must be foreign-owned.

“Liberians have talents. Liberians have capacity,” he said, arguing that local entrepreneurs can produce quality goods while creating employment and contributing to national economic growth.

George said one of his major takeaways from the three-day dialogue was learning that funding opportunities exist, but many Liberian businesses lack sufficient information about where and how to access them.

Young Entrepreneur Calls for Quality and Government Contracts

Stephame M. Dunean, Co- Founder of Stebel’s Classic

Stephanie M. Duncan, co-founder of Stabelle’s Classic Shoes, a Liberian-owned company producing leather footwear, shoes, slippers and sandals, also called for greater support for local brands.

Duncan said business has been moving slowly but remains promising, emphasizing the need for Liberians to support locally manufactured products.

She said Accelerate 360 provided her business with technical assistance, including business and financial management training.

“Because we want the money, but we also want to be able to maintain the money,” Duncan said, stressing that financial assistance alone cannot guarantee business success without proper management.

She also called on government to create more opportunities for Liberian businesses to compete for government contracts.

Duncan encouraged young people to embrace entrepreneurship by identifying problems and developing solutions.

“Be able to start something from scratch. Be able to turn this thing into another thing,” she said.

Commerce Ministry Pushes Regional Trade

Deputy Minister for Commerce and Trade Remond Reeves challenged Liberian businesses to look beyond the domestic market and take advantage of trade opportunities across West Africa and beyond.

Reeves emphasized that private-sector growth must be at the center of Liberia’s economic transformation, noting that micro, small and medium-sized enterprises play a significant role in economic activity and employment.

He stressed that access to finance must be accompanied by access to markets.

“You can have access to finance and produce your products so much, but have no market to sell the products,” Reeves cautioned.

He encouraged export-ready businesses to take advantage of regional trade mechanisms, including the ECOWAS Trade Liberalization Scheme, which allows qualifying products to move within the West African region without customs duties once the required certificate of origin is obtained.

Reeves also highlighted opportunities under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and other trade preference arrangements.

He said the Ministry of Commerce, together with the Small Business Administration and Accelerate 360, would work toward organizing dedicated sessions to help SMEs understand how to access regional, continental and international markets.

Ministry Urges SMEs to Manage Businesses Before Seeking More Funding

Deputy Minister for Administration Tarnue Jeke, speaking on behalf of the Minister of Commerce and Industry, said the government is prioritizing private-sector development, particularly the growth of SMEs into larger industries.

Jeke said structural barriers affecting businesses are being addressed through collaboration involving the Ministry of Commerce, the Central Bank of Liberia, the World Bank, African Development Bank and other partners.

He highlighted the enhanced collateral registry system introduced by the Central Bank, which allows businesses to potentially use movable assets such as machinery as collateral when seeking financing.

However, Jeke cautioned entrepreneurs against focusing solely on obtaining loans without understanding their businesses’ financial position.

He urged business owners to properly calculate their expenses, maintain accurate records and determine whether they are actually making profits.

“You may think the business is going on, but that’s not sustainability,” Jeke warned.

He encouraged SMEs facing challenges to make use of the Ministry’s Small Business Administration, particularly in the areas of capacity building, finance and market access.

Government Seeks More Liberian Businesses in Export Market

Jeke said the government’s broader objective is to create an environment in which Liberian businesses can move beyond survival and become competitive manufacturers and exporters.

He challenged the Ministry and its partners to ensure that more SMEs become capable of accessing regional, continental and international markets.

The Accelerate 360 dialogue ended with calls for stronger collaboration between government and the private sector, increased awareness of financing and procurement opportunities, improved product quality and packaging, and greater support for locally manufactured goods.

For the participating entrepreneurs, the three-day engagement was not only about accessing funding but also about building the knowledge, systems and market connections needed to make Liberian businesses sustainable.

As Liberia seeks to transform its economy, participants agreed that the growth of locally owned businesses will require both government support and greater commitment from entrepreneurs and consumers to buy, build and promote Liberian products.

World.title: Liberian Officials Post Vulnerable Children’s Data to “Prove” Aid Programs Work
World.content:
Monrovia – In Liberia, showing your work used to mean something simple — a photo of a handshake, a ribbon-cutting, a smiling child holding a new backpack. This week, several government officials, among them Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, took “showing your work” somewhere it should never go: they published spreadsheets. Full names. Ages. School enrollment lists. Home addresses. The names of caregivers. All of it, posted to Facebook, as proof that the government’s social protection programs for vulnerable children are real.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

The backlash was immediate. Commenters accused the officials of playing politics with children’s lives. But the deeper story here isn’t really about a bad social media post. It’s about what happens when a country still carrying the scars of two civil wars treats a child’s location as a talking point.

A generation that has already been found — and lost — before

Look closely at who’s on these lists, and a pattern emerges. These aren’t just any children. Many were flagged as “out-of-school” or “street-connected” — bureaucratic terms that, in Liberia, often sit quietly on top of a much harder story: family separation, displacement, exploitation. Decades after the guns went silent, the trauma from those years hasn’t simply evaporated. It shows up today in the same places — kids without stable homes, kids vulnerable to being used, moved, or sold.

These are precisely the children a protection program exists to shield. Publishing their addresses and school names doesn’t just embarrass an agency. It can hand a map straight to whoever they were removed from in the first place.

The law is not vague about this

Cllr. Moriah Yeakula, an outspoken voice in the opposition Alternative National Congress, didn’t mince words: “Vulnerable children’s data cannot be used as a chess piece in the cesspool of political buffoonery,” she said. “Not only were their names published, but their schools, addresses, and even their parents’ and caretakers’ information. That’s a violation of the Children’s Law, and the Ministry must investigate this breach.”

She’s not reaching. Liberia’s Children’s Law of 2011 grants every child a right to privacy, and the guidelines built into that law specifically address the disclosure of a child’s personal information to outside parties — the exact thing that happened here. This isn’t a gray area dressed up as one for political effect. It’s the kind of breach the law was written to prevent.

UNICEF’s fingerprints are on this too — and that matters

The project behind these lists is funded by UNICEF, which raises the stakes further. The international standard that guides child protection work in exactly these situations — the Minimum Standards for Child Protection in Humanitarian Action, built with UNICEF’s own participation — says that information on vulnerable children should only move with informed consent from children and their caregivers, and only under real confidentiality protocols. Nobody asked these families first. UNICEF’s own global data policy says much the same: personal data on the people it serves should only be processed for a legitimate, protective reason — not to win an argument on Facebook.

That gap between policy and practice is now a donor’s problem too. A breach at this scale — names, schools, addresses, caregiver contacts, all in one place — is the kind of thing that tends to trigger uncomfortable questions from funders about who, exactly, their local partners are trusting with sensitive data.

The quiet damage no one’s talking about

Beyond the legal violation, there’s a slower harm that will outlast this week’s outrage cycle. A child publicly tagged as “removed and reunified” carries that label into a new school, a new neighborhood — a target for bullying, or worse, for someone who remembers a name from a Facebook post. Caregivers who took in a child at real personal risk — grandmothers, aunts, foster families — now have their contact details sitting in public view, reachable by whoever they were protecting that child from.

And there’s a longer-term cost still: trust. Families who might otherwise report abuse or accept help from these programs will think twice if the lesson they’ve just learned is that their children’s private details can end up as a political prop. Once that trust breaks, it is notoriously hard to rebuild — and the children who need these programs most are the ones who pay for it.

For a country still working to heal from war, that’s not a cost Liberia can afford to shrug off.

World.title: Liberia: Saclepea Mayor Under Fire After Admitting GOL Awarded MDR Contract in Nimba, Then Backtracks
World.content:
SACLEPEA, Nimba County — In Saclepea, Nimba County, the promise of newly paved streets should ordinarily be a welcome development. Instead, a government road project has become the subject of an increasingly heated political argument after the acting city mayor initially identified the Movement for Democracy and Reconstruction as the successful bidder, only for the party to later reject the claim and the mayor himself to clarify his earlier statement.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The controversy has transformed what began as an announcement about the pavement of five streets into a broader debate about government procurement, political influence, and the responsibility of public officials to provide accurate information about projects financed with public resources.

Acting Saclepea City Mayor Wallace Zigbuo was initially categorical in describing the development. According to his first account, MDR had submitted a bid for the road project and emerged successful.

He said preparations were already being made for implementation, including a meeting concerning the project, and indicated that construction could begin within weeks. For residents awaiting better roads, the announcement carried the promise of visible change.

But the name attached to the alleged winning bid immediately made the development politically sensitive. MDR is a political party, not a conventional construction company. Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, one of the most influential figures in President Joseph Boakai’s administration, hailed from the party.

That political connection transformed the story from a local infrastructure announcement into a national governance question. If the party itself had won a multimillion-dollar government road contract, critics argued, the issue would extend beyond Saclepea’s streets to the integrity of Liberia’s public procurement system.

The opposition Congress for Democratic Change quickly seized upon the report. In a September 12 statement, the CDC accused the government of awarding what it described as a US$3.5 million road contract to MDR and characterized the alleged arrangement as an unacceptable conflict of interest.

The party questioned how a political organization could participate in a government construction project and raised concerns about whether the contract had been competitively advertised and awarded. For the CDC, the controversy was not merely about whether roads would be constructed.

It was about the possibility that political affiliation could influence access to government resources. The opposition argued that MDR’s position as a political party and its association with the ruling Unity Party establishment made the reported contract especially troubling. The party also questioned whether MDR possessed the legal and technical standing to operate as a contractor for a public road project.

The CDC called for the alleged contract to be terminated and demanded greater transparency from the government. But before the political storm could settle around the original statement, MDR issued its own response.

In a statement signed by National Secretary General Jonathan S. Jackson, MDR said it had taken note of reports and social media posts claiming that the party had won a Ministry of Public Works bid to pave five streets in Saclepea. The party described those reports as false, misleading and inaccurate. MDR emphasized that it remains a political party registered and accredited by the National Elections Commission and said it has never been, and will not become, a construction company.

The party further insisted that it does not participate in bidding for public works contracts. That denial fundamentally changed the nature of the controversy. What had initially appeared to be a question of whether a political party should have won a government contract became a question of whether the party had been correctly identified in the first place.

And that is where Mayor Zigbuo’s subsequent clarification became significant. The acting mayor later returned to clarify his earlier comments concerning MDR and the road project. Rather than maintaining that MDR, as a political party, had been awarded the contract, the clarification sought to explain that his initial statement should not be understood as confirmation that the party itself was the government’s road contractor.

The attempt to clarify the matter, however, did not erase the original statement. Instead, it left the public facing two competing versions of the same development. The first was that MDR had submitted a bid and won. The second was that the reference to MDR should not be interpreted as the political party itself receiving a construction contract. MDR’s own statement went even further, saying the party had not participated in such a bidding process at all.

That gap between the initial announcement and the subsequent denial is now at the center of the Saclepea debate. The Ministry of Public Works is therefore being placed under increasing pressure to provide the documentary answer.

The ministry’s procurement records establish that road rehabilitation in Saclepea and Bahn was the subject of a formal government procurement process. An open domestic bidding notice was issued for the project, with prospective bidders invited to submit bids under established procurement requirements.

The existence of that process is important because it shows that the road project itself was not invented by the controversy. There is a real government infrastructure project.

The unresolved issue is the identity of the successful bidder and whether the name “MDR” was ever legitimately connected to the bidding process. A procurement notice does not automatically mean that the organization named in a political statement won the contract.

Similarly, a mayor’s announcement does not substitute for an official award notice, evaluation report, or signed contract. Those documents are what would ultimately determine what happened.

The Ministry of Public Works, as the government institution responsible for the project, holds the most important piece of the puzzle.

If MDR was not a bidder, the ministry can establish that through its bid records. If another construction company won the contract, the ministry can identify that company. If the procurement process reached only the evaluation stage, that too can be clarified. For the Ministry of Public Works, the matter should ultimately be resolved through procurement documents.

A simple announcement about road construction has become a controversy involving the opposition, a political party led by the vice president, a local government official, and the Ministry of Public Works. It is also a reminder that public officials operate in an environment where their words can carry consequences far beyond their immediate audience.

For Mayor Zigbuo, the challenge is now not merely to clarify what he meant but to help explain how the original information came to be presented as fact. For MDR, the challenge is to demonstrate through the procurement record that its denial is supported by the official process. For the CDC, the challenge is equally clear: to substantiate its allegation with documentary evidence rather than political suspicion.

And for the Ministry of Public Works, the simplest route out of the controversy may be the most powerful one—release enough information for the public to independently determine who bid, who won, and who is legally responsible for constructing the five streets.

World.title: Liberia: Former Solicitor General Cephus Calls on Boakai to Apologize to Ex-VP Taylor Over Arrest
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former Solicitor General of Liberia, Cllr.
