Sayma Syrenius Cephus, has called on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to publicly apologize to former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor over what he described as the degrading manner in which she was arrested and detained in connection with Liberia’s multimillion-dollar drug investigation.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Taylor, a former First Lady, Senator and Vice President, has been charged with drug trafficking, money laundering and other offenses following the government’s investigation into a major cocaine seizure.

She was initially placed in pretrial detention at the Monrovia Central Prison before the court later granted her compassionate release.

In a national address before her release, President Boakai said Taylor would be afforded due process and a fair trial, while reaffirming his administration’s commitment to leaving no stone unturned in the fight against drugs and other illicit substances.

But Cephus, while expressing support for the administration’s anti-drug campaign, said the government’s pursuit of justice must not come at the expense of due process, dignity and the presumption of innocence.

In a strongly worded statement titled “Mr. President, You Owe Madam Jewel Howard Taylor an Apology,” Cephus said he was not asking the President to apologize for the allegations against Taylor, but for the manner in which she was treated during her arrest.

“I fully support the President’s war on drugs,” Cephus said. “If anyone, including former officials, is found to be part of a drug network, let the full weight of the law apply.”

However, he argued that “process matters as much as outcome,” warning that the treatment of former officials accused of crimes must not resemble practices associated with Liberia’s past military regimes.

“The way Jewel was arrested is exactly how the PRC operated in the 1980s,” Cephus said, referring to the People’s Redemption Council, which seized power in 1980.

He questioned whether a former constitutional Vice President needed to be arrested in a manner he said appeared degrading while the allegations against her remained subject to judicial determination.

“Do we need to effect the arrest of a former First Lady, a former Senator, and a former constitutional Vice President in a manner that appears degrading, when what is being said about her remains an allegation?” he asked.

‘Why Was She Arrested That Way?’

Cephus also questioned aspects of the government’s handling of Taylor’s case, including its decision to seek bail after initially placing her in detention.

“If the government has ‘overwhelming evidence,’ why did the same government that arrested her file a Bill of Information to admit her to bail?” he asked. “Is the government now acting as both prosecution and defense in the same case?”

He further questioned whether Taylor had been considered a flight risk and whether authorities had first invited her for questioning before carrying out what he described as a highly publicized arrest.

Cephus said he was particularly troubled by what he characterized as the government’s public-relations campaign following Taylor’s arrest.

“Government apologists went on air saying, ‘Jewel should confess, the evidence is overwhelming,’” he said. “Confess to what?”

According to Cephus, publicly declaring a suspect guilty before trial undermines the justice process.

He compared the situation to “catching a man, beating him, calling him a ‘rogue,’ and then demanding that he confess to being a rogue,” arguing that such treatment amounts to public humiliation rather than justice.

“This is a serious misstep in the ARREST Agenda,” he said.

‘Let the Court Determine That’

Cephus stressed that his criticism should not be interpreted as opposition to the government’s drug campaign or as a declaration of Taylor’s innocence.

“I am not asking for an apology for the allegations linking her to drugs. No, far from it,” he said. “Let the court determine that and let the chips fall where they may.”

Instead, he said the President should apologize for what he considers the government’s treatment of Taylor as though she had already been convicted.

“I am asking for an apology for the manner of treatment meted out against a former Vice President,” Cephus said, criticizing what he described as a “near-naked spectacle before television cameras” that portrayed Taylor as though she were already condemned.

“For treating a former Vice President like a convicted criminal awaiting execution before trial,” he added.

Cephus also invoked a previous conversation he said he had with Boakai during the Alexander Benedict Cummings trial, when Boakai was Vice President.

According to Cephus, Boakai had then emphasized the importance of having people around the presidency who would tell the President when his actions were wrong and prioritize truth over friendship.

“Mr. President, you owe Madam Jewel Howard Taylor a public apology,” Cephus concluded. “And I mean it.”

World.title: Liberia, Morocco Deepen Military Ties as AFL Secures Commando Training, Vehicles and Air Wing Support
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL) is moving to deepen military cooperation with Morocco, with Chief of Staff Major General Davidson F. Forleh securing commitments for commando training, military vehicles, training equipment and support for Liberia’s efforts to establish and operationalize an Air Wing.

Major General Forleh is in the Kingdom of Morocco on an official visit from September 6–14, 2026, at the invitation of the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces (FAR), as Liberia seeks to translate the two countries’ military cooperation agreement into concrete programs and capabilities.

According to a release from the AFL, the visit is focused on strengthening bilateral defense relations and implementing the Liberia–Morocco Military Cooperation Agreement signed in Rabat on October 21, 2025.

The agreement provides for cooperation in military training, exercises, technical assistance, military health, and the exchange of experience and expertise. It also establishes a Joint Military Commission tasked with identifying priorities, coordinating implementation, and developing a structured framework for military cooperation.

Morocco Offers Training, Equipment Support

One of the immediate outcomes of General Forleh’s visit is Morocco’s commitment to facilitate commando training for an AFL composite company-sized element in Morocco.

The training is expected to expose Liberian troops to advanced individual and collective training, fieldcraft and operational techniques, according to the AFL.

Morocco has also committed to providing four vehicles, including a command vehicle, along with training aids and selected equipment to strengthen the AFL’s training and operational capabilities.

The measures form part of a broader package of cooperation encompassing professional military education, specialized training, military exercises, technical assistance, equipment support and personnel exchanges.

Support for AFL Air Wing

During the first phase of the visit, the Liberian delegation toured the Royal Moroccan Air Force Inspectorate, Air Transport Base and Royal College of Higher Military Education.

The engagements focused on professional military education, aviation and air transport capabilities and institutional development.

Of particular significance to Liberia is Morocco’s commitment to support the AFL’s efforts to establish and operationalize an Air Wing, including the training and development of qualified personnel.

The Royal College of Higher Military Education also indicated its readiness to provide opportunities for AFL officers at appropriate staff and higher defense education institutions.

High-Level Military Talks

On Tuesday, September 8, Major General Forleh held high-level discussions with General of Army Corps Mohammed Berrid, Inspector General of the Royal Armed Forces and Commander of the Southern Zone, at the FAR General Staff Headquarters in Rabat.

The discussions centered on practical modalities for cooperation in military training, exercises and exchange visits, consistent with the October 2025 military cooperation agreement.

The Liberian delegation subsequently visited the 1st Parachute Brigade and Mohammed V Military Hospital to examine operational training, military health capabilities and potential areas where Moroccan expertise could contribute to AFL capacity development.

Military Health Cooperation

Military health has also emerged as a key area of bilateral cooperation.

During the visit to Mohammed V Military Hospital, AFL Medical Command Commander Major Dr. Albertha Clark briefed Moroccan authorities on the state of Liberia’s military health services, including existing capabilities and key challenges.

The discussions identified opportunities for training and exchanges involving AFL medical personnel, technical cooperation and arrangements for specialized medical referrals.

The initiative is expected to strengthen the health-support component of military cooperation between the two countries.

Maritime Security on the Agenda

The AFL delegation is also scheduled to engage with additional Moroccan military institutions, including the Royal Military Academy in Meknes, the Royal Moroccan Navy Inspectorate, the Royal Moroccan Naval Academy and other naval facilities.

The engagements are expected to explore cooperation in maritime security, naval operations, professional military education, technical training and the development of Liberia Coast Guard capabilities.

The Royal Moroccan Naval Academy has served as a venue for professional maritime training and engagement with international naval partners.

Turning Agreement Into Action

A central objective of General Forleh’s visit is the establishment of a structured mechanism to implement the 2025 military cooperation agreement.

The Joint Military Commission is expected to serve as the institutional framework for converting areas identified during the visit—including command and staff education, commando training, air capability development, maritime training, military health, exercises, equipment support and personnel exchanges—into annual cooperation programs.

Such programs could include agreed priorities, training quotas, timelines, focal points and responsibilities for both countries.

The AFL said the approach is consistent with discussions between the two military leaderships, which identified training, exercises and exchange visits as immediate areas for advancing bilateral cooperation.

Delegation

General Forleh is accompanied by his Military Assistant, Lieutenant Colonel Francis O. Gbodi, and Major Dr. Albertha Clark, Commander of the AFL Medical Command.

Liberia’s Ambassador to the Kingdom of Morocco, Joseph Johnson, has also participated in the engagements.

The AFL says the visit represents an important step toward transforming Liberia and Morocco’s longstanding relationship into measurable military capability, professional development and improved operational readiness for the Liberian military.

The cooperation also opens opportunities for sustained institutional engagement between the two armed forces.

According to the AFL, the support being extended to Liberia is being provided pursuant to the High Royal Directives of His Majesty King Mohammed VI.

World.title: Liberia: Africa College of Bishops Ends Liberia Meeting, Calls for Bigger Church Footprint Across Africa
World.content:
Monrovia — The 2026 Africa College of Bishops Meeting of The United Methodist Church has concluded in Liberia with bishops from across the continent renewing their commitment to expanding the Church’s mission, strengthening institutional sustainability and partnering with governments and civil society to address Africa’s social and development challenges.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The five-day gathering, held in Monrovia from August 31 to September 4, marked the first time Liberia hosted the Africa College of Bishops, bringing together active and retired bishops and other senior church leaders from across Africa.

Held under the theme, “Deepening Ecumenical Engagement, Expanding Continental Influence and Strengthening Institutional Sustainability,” the meeting focused on the future of The United Methodist Church in Africa and its role in promoting peace, justice, reconciliation and sustainable development.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the bishops issued a statement anchored in Isaiah 54:2: “Enlarge the site of your tent… lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes.”

Regionalization Taking Root

The bishops said the Church’s regionalization process is now taking effect across Africa, allowing United Methodists to conduct mission and ministry in ways that better reflect local contexts while maintaining connections with the worldwide denomination.

They said African regions are updating their Books of Discipline and establishing judicial courts as part of the transition.

The bishops also recognized the continued role of United Methodist general agencies in supporting the Church’s mission and maintaining connections across the denomination.

Several major denominational institutions provided updates during the meeting, including the General Council on Finance and Administration, Global Ministries, United Methodist Committee on Relief, United Methodist Communications, the General Commission on Religion and Race, Wespath and Africa University.

New Bishop Expected for West Africa

The bishops also celebrated what they described as continued growth of The United Methodist Church in Africa, pointing to plans for the election of a new bishop in the West Africa Regional Conference in December 2026.

According to the statement, the additional episcopal leadership is expected to help address the vast geographical responsibilities of the regional conference, which encompasses Liberia, Sierra Leone and Nigeria, as well as mission districts in Senegal and Cameroon.

Guinea-Bissau, the bishops said, is also in the process of formally rejoining the West Africa Regional Conference and is expected to become part of the Sierra Leone Conference.

Discussions were also held on the feasibility of adding more bishops in Africa during the next quadrennium.

Bishops Push Wider Ecumenical Role

The gathering reaffirmed the Church’s commitment to ecumenical engagement, particularly on issues of peace, reconciliation, violence and public health.

The bishops said United Methodists across Africa continue to work with other Christian denominations and ecumenical organizations to confront major challenges facing the continent.

They specifically cited efforts to end wars and violence, promote peace and reconciliation, and respond to pandemics, including Ebola outbreaks in parts of Africa.

The meeting brought together prominent Liberian Christian leaders, including the President of the Liberia Council of Churches and keynote speaker, Rev. Dr. Samuel B. Reeves; Roman Catholic Archbishop of Monrovia, Most Rev. Gabriel Blamo Snosio Jubwe; and Bishop of the Episcopal Church of Liberia, Rt. Rev. Dr. James Bombo Sellee.

Africa Eyes General Conference 2032

The Africa College of Bishops also received an update on preparations for the 2028 United Methodist General Conference.

The bishops welcomed efforts by the Commission on the General Conference to ensure that African delegates can participate fully and effectively in the global gathering.

But they went further, urging the wider Church to consider hosting the 2032 General Conference in Africa.

The call could give the continent a greater role in shaping the future direction of The United Methodist Church as its membership and influence continue to expand across Africa.

Backing AU Agenda 2063

The bishops also expressed support for the African Union’s Agenda 2063, “The Africa We Want,” saying its objectives are reflected in development and social initiatives being pursued within various United Methodist episcopal areas.

They called on African political leaders to champion equality, justice, peace, reconciliation and the wellbeing of citizens.

The Church, they said, remains committed to partnering with governments, civil society, ecumenical institutions and local communities to help build a peaceful, just, prosperous and sustainable Africa.

Call for Accountability

On church administration and finances, the bishops highlighted what they described as increased giving and apportionment contributions across their episcopal areas.

They also commended support for the Regional Conferences Theological Education Fund.

At the same time, they urged United Methodists to maintain high standards of accountability, transparency, generosity and responsible financial management, stressing that resources entrusted to the Church must be properly managed in support of its mission.

Liberia Receives Special Commendation

The bishops expressed profound gratitude to the Government and people of Liberia for hosting the historic gathering.

They said Liberia occupies a special place in the history and mission of The United Methodist Church in Africa, making the country an appropriate setting for the meeting.

During their stay, the bishops interacted with President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. and former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, Africa’s first elected female president and a lifelong United Methodist.

The College also commended the Government of Liberia, ecumenical partners, United Methodists, the Liberia National Police, development and institutional partners, sponsors, media organizations and individuals whose financial, logistical, moral and spiritual contributions helped make the gathering possible.

Host Committee Closes Its Mandate

The Special Committee established to host the meeting also formally concluded its mandate, expressing appreciation to all individuals and institutions that contributed to the event.

The committee was headed by Cllr. Amb. Medina A. Wesseh, Chairperson; Cllr. Ruth Jappy-Samukai, Co-Chairperson; and Jeremiah S. Swen, Secretary.

As the bishops returned to their respective episcopal areas, they said they were leaving Liberia with renewed commitment to the mission of Jesus Christ, stronger fellowship and a shared determination to “enlarge the tent” of the Church’s mission across Africa.

World.title: Govt eyes gold reserves to drive economic growth
World.content:
Government has reiterated its commitment to transforming the country’s economy through the effective utilisation of Zambia’s gold reserves.

Speaking during a stakeholder engagement meeting in Mufumbwe District today on the Kikonge Mining Project, Ministry of Mines Permanent Secretary Hapenga Kabeta said Government wants proceeds from gold mining operations such as Kikonge to contribute directly to the national economy.

Dr Kabeta said Government has made significant progress in ensuring that gold mined in Zambia is properly accounted for and contributes to the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

He has since urged Zambians to embrace patriotism and a nationalistic mindset as the country works to transform the lives of local people.

Meanwhile, ZCCM-IH Chief Executive Officer Kakenenwa Muyangwa told stakeholders that about 80 percent of the main road leading to the Kikonge Mine has been completed, while construction of the dam is expected to commence soon.

And representatives of cooperatives from Mufumbwe and Kasempa districts have appealed to the Ministry of Mines to prioritise local cooperatives when allocating mining tenements before considering applicants from outside the two districts.

World.title: Kabompo grandpa jailed 7 years for manslaughter
World.content:
A 60-year-old man of Indeco Compound in Kabompo District has been sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment with hard labour by the Solwezi High Court for causing the death of a man he found naked in his house with his wife.

Kennedy Liwema was convicted of manslaughter, contrary to Section 199 of the Penal Code, Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia.

Solwezi High Court Judge Comfort Mulenga sentenced Liwema following an incident that occurred on February 23, 2024, at about 21:00 hours in Kabompo District.

According to facts presented by State Advocate Francis Mphanza, Liwema had returned home from his farm and found his house locked.

Upon opening the door, he discovered Luka Mutoho, who was naked and in the company of his wife.

The court heard that a confrontation ensued, during which Liwema assaulted Mutoho with fists and kicks which made Mutoho to fall to the ground and sustained a serious head injury and bled profusely.

Liwema called for help from neighbours, who assisted in taking Mutoho to hospital. However, Mutoho later died from the injuries he sustained.

In mitigation, Liwema’s lawyer, Ethel Banda, Deputy Chief Legal Aid Counsel from the Legal Aid Board, asked the court for leniency, citing his client’s advanced age, remorse and status as a first offender.

Ms Banda said Liwema had readily admitted the charge and had saved the court’s time and resources.

She also pointed to his actions after the assault, particularly calling neighbours for help and assisting in taking the deceased to hospital.

But in sentencing, Justice Mulenga said although she had considered the mitigation, the severity of the head injuries sustained by the deceased could not be overlooked.

Justice Mulenga subsequently sentenced Liwema to seven years’ imprisonment with hard labour, effective from the date of his arrest, and informed him of his right to appeal.

World.title: AAC congratulates new ministers
World.content:
Alliance Against Corruption (AAC) Executive Director has congratulated newly appointed Cabinet Ministers on their assignments wishing them wisdom, strength and commitment as they serve the people.

Noel Chisebe who is also a Governance Activist says the new portfolios are central to the successful implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda for 2026 to 2031.

Dr. Chisebe has called on the Ministers to make the fight against corruption a priority and uphold the rule of law without selective application.

He has further urged the Ministers to ensure that public resources are used with integrity and that every kwacha allocated to their ministries delivers value to Zambians in both the formal and informal sectors.

The AAC Executive Director also said that his Organisation is ready to support Government through civic education, monitoring and advocacy to promote accountability and ensure that public office is used for the public good.

World.title: Governance expert urges MPs to start work
World.content:
Local governance expert Wesley Miyanda has called on newly elected Members of Parliament to immediately begin working in their respective constituencies.

Mr Miyanda said the election and campaign period was over and that leaders should now focus on the broader task of developing the country.

He said Zambia should be ready to embark on the “Grow Zambia Agenda” in line with presidential pronouncements.

Mr Miyanda was speaking in a walk-in interview with ZANIS in Lusaka.

He said the goals of the Grow Zambia Agenda need to be actualised in order to translate into economic growth, create jobs and open up business opportunities for Zambians.

Mr Miyanda further called on the general public to hold newly elected leaders accountable, saying citizens should not wait until the next election period to demand accountability from those they elected.

“Our Members of Parliament are starting work and my request to all of us is to start holding them accountable now and not wait for the 2031 elections,” he said.

World.title: Illegal gold processing threatens Kasempa water supply
World.content:
Mufwashi Member of Parliament Brian Kakonkanya says illegal gold processing activities have blocked the Dengwe Stream, a key water source for Kasempa District, threatening water supply to the district’s treatment plant as the dry season approaches.

Mr Kakonkanya said the Dengwe Stream is a major source of water for Kasempa, with water flowing downstream to the treatment plant operated by North-Western Water Supply and Sanitation Company.

He said this today when he inspected the Dengwe Stream in Kasempa.

Mr Kakonkanya described the situation as unfortunate, warning that the extent of the blockage poses a serious threat to communities that depend on the water downstream, particularly as the dry season is expected to begin in October.

“What we have seen today is quite unfortunate. Dengwe is a major source of water for Kasempa District and downstream is where we have the water treatment plant, where the North-Western Water Supply and Sanitation Company treats water for supply to the district,” he said.

Mr Kakonkanya said the blockage was a direct result of illegal gold processing activities and should not be allowed to continue.

He said the situation demonstrates the dangers of illegal gold mining, particularly where environmental safeguards are not observed.

“This is purely the effect of illegal gold mining and when the President stands strong to talk against illegal gold mining, this is exactly what he means, because this is going to affect many lives,” he said.

Mr Kakonkanya said clearing the blockage would require resources, adding that the situation could have been avoided if action had been taken earlier.

He, however, proposed that miners be organised into groups and provided with designated and controlled areas where they could undertake gold processing without damaging water sources.

Mr Kakonkanya stressed that such measures should not be viewed as government support for illegal mining, but rather as an effort to balance livelihoods with environmental protection and the need to safeguard water sources.

“What we don’t want is to encourage illegal activities. They have no space in the new government, and we appeal strongly to our colleagues doing this, because it’s dangerous, no proper environmental safeguards have been considered here,” he said.

Mr Kakonkanya has since urged Kasempa District authorities to urgently engage relevant stakeholders to find a lasting solution and restore the stream to normal flow.

World.title: Midlands Boxing Association to host boxing league tournament
World.content:
More than 100 pugilists from 15 boxing clubs within Lusaka are expected to take part in the boxing tournament organised by the Midlands Boxing Association (MABA).

MABA Secretary Morgan Mwansa says the competition to be held in conjunction with Exodus Boxing Academy, will host a boxing league tournament in Lusaka on Saturday, September 26, 2026.

Mwansa told the media that the tournament will be held at the Inter Bus Station from 09:00 hours to 18:00 hours as part of the Association’s 2026 boxing calendar.

Mwansa said this as a notice to club secretaries that all participating clubs are expected to abide by the rules of boxing.

He said MABA has also directed participating club sponsors to meet the costs of transportation, meals and other logistics for their respective clubs.

“A participation fee of K100 has been set for each participating club,” he said.

Mwansa said the tournament is expected to provide boxers with an opportunity to gain competitive experience as MABA continues with its 2026 boxing programme.

World.title: Govt completes wetland inputs distribution in Lusaka
World.content:
Government has completed the distribution of wetland farming inputs to vulnerable but viable households across all six districts of Lusaka Province, in a move aimed to strengthen household and national food security.

Lusaka Provincial Administration Principal Public Relations Officer Logic Lukwanda said the completion of the distribution is part of Government’s continued efforts to promote food production and enhance the resilience of farming households against drought and erratic rainfall.

Mr Lukwanda said a total of 5,710 beneficiaries across the province had received wetland farming inputs under the programme.

He said Lusaka district has 500 beneficiaries, Chilanga, Rufunsa, Kafue and Luangwa have 1,000 beneficiaries each while Chongwe District has the highest number of beneficiaries, standing at 1,210.

“The package of inputs includes Compound D and UREA fertiliser, white hybrid maize seed for early- and medium-maturing varieties, as well as medium-maturing Vitamin A-fortified hybrid maize seed,” Mr Lukwanda said.

He said beneficiaries have also received various vegetable seeds, including red onion, okra, rape, cabbage, butternut, tomato and eggplant, together with bactericides, insecticides, fungicides and agricultural lime.

Mr Lukwanda explained that the core objective of the wetland inputs intervention is to mitigate the effects of drought and erratic rainfall by encouraging farmers to utilise dambos, rivers and wetlands for continuous food production.

He said the initiative was designed to enable vulnerable but viable farming households to continue producing food during the dry season and throughout the year.

“At national level, the Government is targeting 120,000 vulnerable but viable farming households for dry-season and year-round cultivation,” Mr Lukwanda said.

He further commended the Department of Community Development under the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services for remaining steadfast in the implementation of the programme.

He said the intervention would help strengthen food production at household level while contributing to the broader national objective of improving food security and building resilience among farming communities.

World.title: Two die in Kalabo road accident
World.content:
Two men have died in a road traffic accident involving a Toyota Wish and a cyclist in the Muyumbana area along the Mongu-Kalabo Road.

Western Province Police Commissioner Godfrey Mwanza confirmed the incident in a statement to media , saying it occurred around 19:30 hours.

Mr Mwanza said the accident involved a 36-year-old driver, Mike Mwangu of Litambya, Senanga, who was driving an unregistered Toyota Wish, and an unidentified cyclist riding an unmarked Buffalo bicycle.

He said both the vehicle and bicycle were travelling in the same direction, from south to north, when the driver lost control of the vehicle due to excessive speed, hit the cyclist and subsequently collided with a tree.

Mr Mwanza said both the driver and cyclist sustained fatal injuries and were pronounced dead at the scene.

He said the Toyota Wish and bicycle were extensively damaged, while the bodies of the deceased were deposited at Kalabo District Hospital mortuary pending post-mortem examinations.

The Police Commissioner has since urged motorists and other road users to observe road safety measures at all times.

He advised motorists to maintain controllable speeds, particularly at night when visibility is reduced, noting that excessive speed affects reaction time and vehicle control.

Mr Mwanza also urged cyclists to use reflectors, reflective jackets and functional lights when riding at night to improve their visibility to other road users.

World.title: Mali: The Success Mali Must Move Beyond
World.content:
Mali built a cotton sector capable of producing, ginning and exporting at scale. Mossadeck Bally argues that this success must now support a more demanding ambition: retain more fibre, begin with spinning and finance industry for the long term.

In Mali, cotton is everywhere except where its value multiplies. It supports between four and five million people and sustains transporters, banks, insurers and fuel distributors. The country has ranked among Africa’s leading producers for years. Yet, according to Mossadeck Bally, nearly 98 per cent of the fibre it produces still leaves the country without passing through a Malian spinning mill.

At first glance, this appears to be a story of industrial failure. Bally offers a more useful and more unsettling reading. The sector did not fail. It performed the mission for which it was designed: produce cotton fibre, gin it and export it. The problem is that Mali is now asking that architecture to accomplish a new mission without having built the ecosystem the new mission requires.

“We succeeded in making Mali one of Africa’s leading producers of cotton fibre. Now we need a vision of Mali as an industrial textile country.” — Mossadeck Bally

An agricultural success and an unfinished value chain

Bally speaks with the perspective of an entrepreneur who has invested across West Africa for nearly four decades. His diagnosis begins with history. Mali’s cotton sector was organised around farmer support and fibre exports. After independence, that orientation was consolidated with considerable success. Cotton became one of the country’s broadest sources of economic spillovers.

But producing fibre does not automatically lead to yarn, fabric and garments. The experiences of COMATEX, Fittina and ITEMA show why an isolated factory is not enough. Between a bale of cotton and a finished shirt stand reliable and competitively priced electricity, roads, technical skills, markets, guarantees and, above all, financing whose duration matches the life of the industrial asset.

Start with yarn

Bally is not proposing that Mali build an integrated industry overnight and attempt to compete with Asia at every stage. For a landlocked country located roughly 1,200 kilometres from some ports, sequencing matters. His first priority is spinning: convert fibre into yarn, even if the yarn must initially be exported.

Pixabay Cotton branch

The logic is industrial and logistical. Cotton fibre is bulky and flammable. Yarn is a higher-value product that is easier to transport and can attract textile manufacturers in a second phase. Once spinning capacity is established, Mali can progressively develop weaving and then garment production.

Public procurement can provide an initial market through military uniforms, school clothing and other government needs. Over time, Bally also sees scope for just-in-time production for Europe, using air freight when speed and proximity can offset some of the disadvantages of being landlocked.

“Instead of exporting cotton fibre, let us begin by exporting yarn. The yarn will then attract textile industries.” — Mossadeck Bally

When loan maturity programmes failure

The main barrier is not only the amount of capital. It is the form that capital takes. A spinning mill may require ten to fifteen years to amortise, while commercial banks rarely offer maturities beyond five to seven years. When repayment begins while a factory is still learning to produce efficiently, financing does not reduce risk; it organises failure.

Equity requirements create another barrier. For a textile plant costing CFAF 15 billion, Bally illustrates, a 30 per cent contribution represents CFAF 4.5 billion. Few entrepreneurs can immobilise that amount. When a project must raise US$20 million to US$50 million from a development finance institution, appraisal may take eighteen to twenty-four months—long enough to exhaust a promoter before the first machine turns.

Bally identifies four recurring disconnects between lenders and industrial operators: loan maturities that are too short; collateral requirements based on the promoter’s existing property rather than the future cash flows of the factory; lengthy appraisal processes; and a cost of credit incompatible with manufacturing margins. He adds a broader structural pressure: private borrowers can be crowded out when government securities offer banks attractive returns with fewer capital constraints.

AllAfrica The Economic Impact of Mali's Cotton Industry, Summarized in Three Key Figures

“You have barely begun production when repayment starts. That means failure is guaranteed.” — Mossadeck Bally

Finance the project not only the promoter’s assets

The answer requires more deliberate financial engineering: first-loss guarantees, political-risk cover, equity investment and semi-concessional resources. Bally points to the World Bank’s Private Sector Window and to political-risk guarantees available through specialist institutions. These tools do not eliminate risk. They allocate it in a way that can make investment possible.

He also identifies Mali’s Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations, once fully operational, as a potential source of long-term capital. Pension funds can play a similar role because their liabilities extend over ten, fifteen or twenty years—the same horizon industry needs. Bally argues that the Private Sector Guarantee Fund should be capitalised more strongly so an institutional guarantee can replace at least part of the land title or other fixed collateral demanded from entrepreneurs.

A strategic state and a private operator

For Bally, the model is not a state that owns and operates factories. It is a strategic state: one that defines the trajectory, secures land, organises infrastructure, simplifies tax and customs administration, and then attracts private capital and expertise through public-private partnerships.

The Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone in Benin is a reference point, but not a template to copy mechanically. Benin’s zone is close to a port; Mali must absorb the costs of being landlocked. A Malian textile zone would need to be designed around competitive energy, internal logistics, a single-window service and an initial specialisation in spinning.

Two public decisions recur in his argument. The first is a cotton single window bringing together government, power utilities, producers, investors, banks, development institutions and insurers. The second is a revised public-private partnership law that gives investors the stability and visibility required to commit capital for twenty or twenty-five years.

TCM / AllAfrica Large-scale spinning and yarn preparation: the first link in the industrial chain that Bally wants to prioritize.

“The state must be strategic and visionary, but it must not be the operator.” — Mossadeck Bally

Risk viewed from a distance

Bally does not deny geopolitical tension or logistical constraints. He challenges the way those realities are converted into a risk premium. His experience across eight West African countries has taught him that external narratives often confuse difficulty with impossibility.

His message to investors is direct. Cotton responds to enduring global demand. Despite crises and disruptions to transport corridors, Mali continues to produce, gin and export. If that chain functions in a difficult environment, local transformation is not a fiction. Investors must visit, examine the assets, assess the operators and follow the real flows rather than stop at a general story about African risk.

“If you stop at what you see on television or hear on the radio, you will miss an opportunity.” — Mossadeck Bally

A vision measured over thirty years

The industrial ambition Bally describes cannot be reduced to a five-year campaign promise. It requires a measurable trajectory over several decades: progressively reduce the share of fibre exported, expand spinning capacity, use public procurement to establish an initial market, and then attract textile and garment production as the ecosystem gains competence.

A long horizon is not an argument for waiting. It is an argument for beginning now. Mali already has the raw material, organised producers, entrepreneurial experience and a regional market. The failures of earlier factories should be treated as evidence for better design, not as a verdict against industrialisation.

The first chapter of Mali’s cotton story was about volume. The next will be about value. The passage between them is not a leap but a sequence of concrete decisions: power, yarn, a guarantee, a law and a market. Bobbin by bobbin, the success of yesterday can become the industry of tomorrow.

“We must come together around a thirty- or forty-year vision: move from a producer and exporter of cotton fibre to a country industrialised around cotton.” — Mossadeck Bally

World.title: Kenya: Can Kenya Turn Its Cotton Comeback Into A Genuine Industrial Revival?
World.content:
Kenya is growing cotton again. But the bigger question is whether it can turn the crop into an industrial engine and keep more of the value at home.

The machines have stopped. Inside Luanda Ginnery in Busia, the belts and rollers that separate cotton fibre from seed sit motionless. The noise that would normally fill the building has disappeared. For about four months, there has been no cotton to process.

Outside, however, the next story is already taking shape. Across the farms of Busia, cotton plants are about two months old. Farmers are watching the skies, waiting for the rains they hope will give the crop the push it needs.

The landscape is hot and dusty. The roads leading to some of the farms are rough, forcing farmers and visitors to rely on boda bodas (motorcycle taxis) to reach fields hidden away from the main roads. Yet there is optimism. The cotton is growing. And with it, the hope that the industry that once supported thousands of families can find its way back.

Vincent Akumu wants to expand. His ambition is to grow cotton on five acres, up from the one and a half acres he farms today. The problem is getting there. Land preparation remains difficult because machinery is scarce. Farmers often depend on county equipment, hire machines when available or resort to labour-intensive manual preparation. Then there is seed. A late delivery can push farmers outside the narrow planting window.

Vincent knows what that means. “The rainy season cannot wait for farmers,” he says.

That simple observation captures one of the biggest challenges facing Kenya's cotton revival. The country may have farmers willing to grow the crop. It may have ginneries. It may have textile mills. It may have a market. But all those pieces have to work at the same time. Because cotton is not really a story about a plant. It is a story about what happens after the plant is harvested.

Kenya's cotton industry has been here before. According to research by the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO), national cotton production reached an all-time high of about 70,000 bales in 1985/86. By 2001, production had fallen to about 20,000 bales. The collapse was not caused by one problem. KALRO's research points to a combination of factors, including poor agronomic practices and pest control, delayed payment to farmers, mismanagement of cooperatives, exploitation by middlemen, poor pricing and poorly managed ginneries.

Rising imports of second-hand clothes, known in Kenya as mitumba, also weakened demand for locally manufactured cotton garments. The result was a vicious cycle. Farmers stopped planting. Ginneries struggled for raw material. Factories lost reliable supplies. Investment became harder to justify. And the industry shrank further.

For communities that had once depended on cotton, the consequences were profound. Farmers switched to maize and other food crops. And the machines built to process cotton increasingly became monuments to an industry that had lost its way.

But Kenya is attempting another turnaround. This time, the ambition is considerably bigger.

The government's vision is to increase production while strengthening certified seed development, textile mills and garment manufacturing, with the private sector playing a bigger role in the value chain. But between the 500,000-tonne ambition and Vincent's one-and-a-half-acre farm lies the difficult part: production, processing, investment, markets, infrastructure, skills and time.

Small farms, big ambitions

In Busia, most cotton farmers are not operating on large commercial plantations.

That small scale creates a problem for an industry that wants predictable volumes. Luanda Ginnery can process cotton. But a ginnery cannot run on machinery alone. It needs farmers. And farmers need markets. Barasa puts it bluntly: “If they don't grow cotton, then we don't have raw materials. That means we won't move on.”

It is the central contradiction of the revival. Kenya needs more cotton to make its ginneries viable. But farmers need functioning ginneries, reliable markets and predictable prices to make cotton worth growing. That is why the cooperative is critical. It is the bridge between the smallholder and the industrial system.

Bernard Ojiambo, the union's chairman, says cotton has been grown in the region for decades. But years of delayed payments and weak markets pushed farmers towards maize. Today, he believes cotton can once again provide a stronger cash income. “Cotton is more of a value than maize,” he says. But farmers need support to expand.

AllAfrica The upgraded Luanda Ginnery in Busia county awaiting the next ginning season (2)

Ojiambo says a lack of machinery delays land preparation. “We delay because we don't have machines like tractors and other things to support farmers.” The cooperative has been seeking investment in machinery and transport to improve its ability to serve farmers. For Vincent, mechanisation would mean the opportunity to expand. For the ginnery, it would mean more raw material. For the textile mill, it would mean more cotton. And for the economy, it could mean another step towards rebuilding an industry.

For farmers such as Mama Aisha Mohammed, the change is not measured in tonnes. It is measured in school fees. Food. Livestock. And the ability to improve a household.

Aisha, from the Bajuni community, had largely grown maize and green grams for household consumption before cotton became a commercial opportunity. After her first harvest, she was able to pay school fees and provide for her grandchildren. Julia Njuguna tells a similar story. Income from cotton enabled her to build a new house and improve her family's living standards. She now sees cotton as a crop her children can build a future around.

These stories matter because they show what happens when the first link in the chain begins to work. But the real test comes after the farmer sells the cotton.

A garment can be assembled in Kenya using imported yarn or imported fabric. It is Kenyan-made. But the value chain behind the garment may stretch across several countries. Kenya's bigger opportunity is to shorten that chain. Cotton grown in Busia or Lamu. Ginned in Kenya. Spun in Kenya. Woven in Kenya. Dyed and finished in Kenya. Cut and stitched in Kenya. Sold in Kenya or exported. That is how one crop becomes an industrial ecosystem.

As Olweny puts it: “The more stages we keep in Kenya, the more employment we create.”

Those stages create opportunities far beyond the farm. Transporters move cotton. Engineers maintain machinery. Technicians operate textile equipment. Workers spin yarn. Others weave and dye fabric. Garment workers cut and stitch. Packaging companies supply factories. Retailers sell the finished product. Graduates of technical and vocational training (TVET) institutions and university researchers become part of the industrial workforce. The cotton plant may begin in a field. But its economic footprint can stretch across an entire country.

The import paradox

There is, however, a striking contradiction in Kenya's cotton story. While the country wants to dramatically increase domestic cotton production and rebuild its textile industry, it continues to import large quantities of cotton products.

A factory cannot plan production around uncertainty. It needs cotton when it needs it. It needs quality that can be predicted. It needs enough volume to justify machinery and workers. And it needs markets for the finished products.

That makes the problems farmers describe — delayed seed, inadequate machinery, limited finance and small acreage — industrial problems too. A farmer waiting for seed is not just an agricultural story. It is a textile factory waiting for raw material months later. A cooperative without a tractor is not simply a rural development issue. It is a supply-chain bottleneck. A silent ginnery is not merely an idle building. It is evidence that one link in the industrial chain is missing. And a textile mill relying on imported yarn tells another part of the story. The value chain remains incomplete.

KALRO's research demonstrates both the potential of cotton and the painful history of its decline. Farmers in Busia are returning to the crop. Lamu has demonstrated that farmers can respond when the economics improve. Cooperatives are asking for machinery and finance. Ginneries are waiting for raw material. Textile companies are asking for reliable supply and investment. And the government is talking about taking production from tens of thousands of tonnes of lint towards half a million tonnes.

As the sun sets over Busia, the cotton fields remain quiet. The plants wait for rain. Vincent waits too. He wants his five acres, and a crop that will educate another generation of his family. A few kilometres away, Luanda Ginnery waits for cotton. The machines will eventually start again. The challenge is making sure they never again fall silent because farmers have abandoned the crop. And beyond the ginnery, another set of machines waits at textile factories. Their future depends on what happens in fields like Vincent's.

World.title: Nigeria: Dangote Refinery Plans US Listing in Three to Four Years

"By doing so, because the company will be very, very large, we will be having 10 per cent of the total America's capacity," Mr Dangote added.

Africa's richest man aims to list his 700,000 barrel-per-day oil refinery, which commenced its initial public offering Monday morning, in the United States in the next three to four years, he told the investing public in Lagos during the Fact Behind the Offer event at the Nigerian Exchange.

"In the next three years, by the grace of God, three to four years or thereabouts, we will try and also list outside the African continent, most likely in the U.S," he said.

"By doing so, because the company will be very, very large, we will be having 10 per cent of the total America's capacity," he added.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The IPO hopes to democratise wealth creation across Africa by allowing the mass market that is dominated by retail investors to own a piece of the cake in the refinery, which is looking to increase capacity twofold by 2030 from the proceeds of the transaction.

Mr Dangote said the IPO is not out to raise money in the strictest sense of the word, given that it has other means of sourcing, with $46 billion already in the pipeline for the expansion of the plant and the actualisation of its 2030 strategic vision.

Rather, the share sale aspires to extend the ownership of the refinery to as many people as possible, he went further to say.

"Even if there is mishap, devaluation, the business you are investing in is a dollarized business. Don't let the train leave you at the station," he noted, assuring that the investment of local investors will be shielded from currency headwinds, with dividends planned to be distributed in dollars.

The $2.5 billion that was eventually raised from the private placement was the original size the refinery aspired to raise from both the placement and the IPO.

"We refused to take one single currency other than the dollar. With the private placement, we have already met our demand," he stated.

Come the end of the year, the refinery will be the largest company in Africa, not just in Nigeria, Mr Dangote remarked, adding that an asset of that magnitude should create value, not for a few people, but for millions of people.

The refinery and petrochemical plant is also looking to build the first train ever in the world of linear alkaline benzene, a major raw material in detergent making, with a capacity of 400,000 metric tonnes, surpassing Egypt's 50,000 tonnes and Algeria's 100,000 tonnes.

JOHN RICH CLAIMS JELLY ROLL KNEW HE’D LOSE HALF HIS FANS OVER POLITICAL COMMENTS

That's why they were left out of the playoff, they didn't deserve to be included.

As a result of this abhorrent "disservice," Sark went off about scheduling teams like Ohio State. In December 2025, he said he would "re-evaluate" future schedules because he didn't believe tougher strength of schedule was properly rewarded.

Now? He's pounding his chest over playing Ohio State instead of an FCS team, because the Longhorns won. Had they lost, and finished the season 9-3 and missed out again, he'd be complaining.

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

To be fair to him and the Longhorns, it's a tricky balancing act, weighing schedules. Because, on the one hand, both teams can and should be credited for playing this game. On the other hand, Sark is essentially arguing that the outcome shouldn't matter. Winning or losing is irrelevant, because credit for scheduling it should come first. That's effectively what he said on Monday, per The Athletic.

"Quite frankly, Ohio State should be rewarded for playing in this game against us, and so that’s my goal," Sarkisian said. "Time will tell, you know. And this isn’t crying over spilled milk. I don’t think we got rewarded for going to Columbus last year in Week 1."

We all want more games like this, but if there are no stakes, no reward based on performance and outcome, what's the point? What might make sense is some concrete criteria, a combination of forward-looking efficiency ratings, and strength of resume rankings, along with human evaluation of that combination, to pick the playoff teams. At least then subjectivity would be diminished, there would be more rewards for playing tough schedules, and Sark would have less to complain about after his undeserving team isn't selected.

But that makes too much sense for college football, so don't expect any changes anytime soon.

World.title: China dismisses AI slowdown calls and blasts ‘fearmongering’ from U.S. tech leaders
World.content:
HONG KONG — China has dismissed urgent calls to slow down the development of AI, rejecting the grave warnings as a bid to hobble the progress of America’s rival superpower rather than safeguard humanity’s future.

Beijing on Monday dismissed the intervention from U.S. tech leaders as “fearmongering” and part of a “Cold War playbook.”

It’s the latest sign that competition between the two countries could outweigh mounting safety concerns, after President Donald Trump also rebuffed the warnings from industry leaders and said his focus was on beating China on artificial intelligence.

The comments followed a lengthy essay published Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk.

Amodei said that companies should deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve their models given the potential risks. He also said that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world,” and called for the U.S. to restrict sales of key tech to China.

That message was not welcomed by Beijing.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve no one’s interests,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters at a regular news briefing Monday.

The state-run Global Times newspaper had a more blunt tone Sunday, blasting the call for an industrywide slowdown as “packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘Cold War playbook’ for the AI sector.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay on his website over the weekend entitled "We Must Pace The Frontier." Krisztian Bocsi / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

AI has advanced at a breakneck speed, with models rapidly getting smarter, faster and cheaper. They have also frequently outpaced technical safeguards, fueling security fears.

Those fears have now reached a crescendo, but also exposed just how far apart Beijing and Washington seem to be on cooperating to address them.

Amodei himself likened the situation to the Cold War arms race, telling CBS’ ‘Sunday Morning’ that the two sides should work together, but that he didn’t hold out much hope.

Altman similarly said on X late Sunday that “where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said his company would adopt one of Amodei’s proposed safeguards. Kyle Grillot / Bloomberg / Getty Images

But that might not be compatible with Trump’s approach.

“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” the president told reporters Sunday. He criticized “very negative forces” for bringing up things “that won’t happen.”

While Trump rebuffs safety concerns, Beijing has acknowledged AI security risks.

State Security Minister Chen Yixin said Sunday that China must “accelerate the establishment of a system for preventing and controlling AI security risks.” Chen also said in the state-run China Cyberspace magazine that “we must engage extensively in international cooperation,” identifying AI as “a new track for strategic rivalry.”

The difference in approach on tackling AI progress is likely to be a central issue when Xi and Trump meet Sept. 24 in Washington.

Amodei’s essay came just a few days after U.S. agencies published an alert saying that top China AI companies have systematically copied cutting-edge AI models from American companies.

Beijing rejected this accusation that its companies had been “distilling” U.S. models.

President Donald Trump with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing in May. China says the warnings are aimed at slowing its progress. Evan Vucci / Pool /AFP via Getty Images

China has also rejected any outside take on how its companies should pace development.

“They want to write the rules. I don’t think they want to follow anybody else’s,” Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a nonresident scholar at Carnegie China, told NBC News in a phone interview.

“There’s the sort of talk of cooperation, but the behavior suggests otherwise, and underlying that behavior, I think, is this deep mutual suspicion,” Chong said.

Chinese companies now offer advanced AI performance at a fraction of the cost of U.S. models, with President Xi Jinping pitching China as a pioneer of open-source models in contrast to those produced by most leading American companies.

At the BRICS summit in India on Sunday, he offered member nations help to develop open-source AI. Xi has also outlined a potential global governance framework on AI among the Global South.

00:00 00:00 How exactly could AI cause widespread danger? 02:35

Chong said the distillation clash highlighted the suspicion toward China in both the White House and Silicon Valley.

“It’s a bit like an arms race. And to get de-escalation there needs to be simultaneous neutral self restraint and it’s difficult to see how that would come about in this kind of environment,” Chong said.

But not everyone is so pessimistic.

While a U.S.-China agreement on curbing AI progress may be a long shot, the countries could separately pursue greater regulation, said Theo Bertram, director of the London-based Social Market Foundation.

“The idea that we could see the domestic introduction of some safeguards in both countries is not impossible,” Bertram said in a phone interview.

“You do it domestically and it’s in everyone’s interest to learn and share and for there to be accountability,” he said. “Some greater accountability is one way of trying to mitigate what is inevitably going to be a growing political and public demand globally.”

World.title: Pentagon watchdog says Iran war has led to munitions shortfall
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Pentagon’s inspector general on Monday released its first report on the war with Iran, saying the conflict has resulted in a shortfall of U.S. munitions and “bottlenecks” in supply chains as the Trump administration works to replenish weaponry.

“To mitigate these constraints,” the report said the Defense Department is “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has denied reports that the U.S. is running low on munitions.

The congressionally-mandated report covers from the start of the war on Feb. 28 through June 30. It is one of the first public accountings from any government agency detailing the cost, scope and scale of the U.S. and Israel-led conflict to the U.S. military, the State Department and other agencies. It follows reports of low morale among U.S. troops deployed to the Middle East, a depleting stockpile of key munitions and extensive damage to American military and intelligence assets in the region.

Among the findings, the report provides one of the first government confirmations that Iran targeted the U.S. Navy’s main logistics hub in the region, in Bahrain, with drones and ballistic missiles.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.

It does not address a likely U.S. strike on an elementary school in Iran during the initial hours of strikes. The military has yet to release an internal investigation into the bombing, though NBC News reported in June that the report on the probe was being finalized.

The report details the damage to military equipment, aircraft and other materiel over the first four months of the war, including the destruction of at least 30 large U.S. drones.

The watchdog’s report said the war with Iran has cost roughly $33.4 billion, though that number does not account for repairing damaged facilities. It does include $22.3 billion in expended munitions, $3.7 billion for equipment losses and $7.4 in other expenditures.

NBC News reported in July that the war with Iran had so far cost between $80 billion and $100 billion, according to three U.S. officials and three people familiar with the internal cost estimates. The Pentagon publicly said in July the war cost $37.5 billion. The Pentagon’s estimate does not include the cost for replacing aircraft, repairing U.S. bases and replenishing critical weaponry.

Trump initially said the war would only last for weeks. But over the weekend he said it might not end until “right after” November’s midterm elections or perhaps before.

Strike damaged residential buildings in Karaj, southwest of Tehran, in April. Atta Kenare / AFP via Getty Images

The report also finds that the war has displaced more than 20,000 U.S. military and diplomatic personnel, who were relocated at the outset of the conflict and in the days and weeks after.

Most medical evaluations of injured U.S. forces were carried out on the ground, including by local ambulances and they were taken to local treatment facilities because air lift capabilities had been moved because of concerns.

And U.S. forces flew as many as 5,000 flights from European bases in support of the war, though President Donald Trump has bitterly complained that European allies have not done enough to help support the war.

Sailors conduct flight operations aboard the USS George H.W. Bush in July. Seaman Apprentice Lucas Krug / U.S. Central Command

The report catalogues some of the damage to U.S. aircraft and other military gear as well as some of the American bases in the region. Aircraft, for example, includes destruction or extensive damage to four F-15E jet fighters, one F-35A Joint Strike Fighter, and an A-10 Warthog, which was also destroyed, according to the report. Twelve KC-135 refuelers, and nine other aircraft were also destroyed, the report said. More than 30 MQ-9 drones were also destroyed, as of June, according to the report, citing the Congressional Research Service.

The State Department suffered more than $208 million in damages in four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, according to the report. That includes $184 million in damages to “diplomatic facilities” and another $25 million due to delays in construction projects, the report said.

The damage Iran inflicted on U.S. military bases had been far more extensive than is publicly known, NBC reported in April. Iran also caused more damage to America’s intelligence and surveillance assets in the region than U.S. spy agencies have ever endured and is estimated to cost billions to repair, NBC reported last month.

The report does not touch on the morale of U.S. troops who’ve been deployed as part of the war effort.

In recent weeks, concerns about deteriorating conditions for troops serving in the Middle East on the USS Abraham Lincoln during an extended deployment had escalated, and the Pentagon announced it was replacing the aircraft carrier.

The USS Lincoln is now en route back to its port in San Diego after making a stop in Thailand.

World.title: Macklemore says he was dropped from Ed Sheeran tour after Robert Kraft organized boycott
World.content:
Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran’s tour after he says New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft organized a boycott among stadium owners over the rapper’s remarks in support of Palestinians.

The “Thrift Shop” rapper posted a lengthy statement to his Instagram on Monday alleging that Sheeran was called by Kraft to inform the singer Macklemore was not welcome at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play at the venue, which is owned by Kraft Entertainment + Sports Group.

“Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues,” Macklemore wrote.

The decision was reached after comments made by Macklemore at the tour’s New Jersey shows and “a broader history of rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community,” Kraft said in a statement provided to NBC News on Monday.

Gillette Stadium seeks to create a “welcoming environment for all guests,” he added.

“I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same — peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate,” Kraft said.

He added that that the decision was not about trying to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminishing the suffering of Palestinians. Kraft blamed Hamas, which the United States, Israel and the European Union have designated as a terrorist organization, for the actions that “have caused immeasurable suffering for Palestinians and Israelis alike.”

“Much of my time and attention for the last decade has been focused on the fight against antisemitism and hate of all kinds, and I feel a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed,” Kraft said.

Kraft, who is Jewish, created the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism in 2019 and is a longtime supporter of Israel. There is a page dedicated to his Israel-related philanthropic efforts on the Kraft Group’s site.

“The Kraft family has supported and launched numerous programs that create a connection to Israel and Jewish life,” the site said. “Their commitment has helped build a robust economic relationship between Boston and Israel, the results of which have created jobs and fostered technological innovations in both communities.”

Macklemore added that Sheeran, who he described as a friend, was in a “f---ed up position.” The two have had “difficult” conversations over the past week, according to Macklemore, that ended in a place of “fundamental disagreement.”

“He told me that the words ‘Free Palestine’ and the image of the Palestinian flags were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with,” Macklemore wrote. “I told him that if those words were more offensive than the tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood.”

According to Macklemore’s account, Sheeran was not able to get past his desire to remain an apolitical public figure.

Ms. Rachel, the wildly popular children’s content creator whose real name is Rachel Griffin Accurso, criticized Sheeran. She wrote in an Instagram post that the “Thinking Out Loud” singer had an opportunity to show “that we won’t be bullied” into punishing people who support Palestinians.

“Instead he caved to people who refuse to accept what the world knows,” Accurso wrote. “A genocide is happening in Gaza. We all need to speak out against it.”

A United Nations commission said that Israel is committing genocide is Gaza in findings from an independent inquiry published last year. Israeli government officials have denied the allegations, calling them “distorted and false.”

Macklemore has been deeply outspoken about social and political issues throughout his career, releasing the 2012 song “Same Love” in support of same-sex marriage three years before it was legalized in a Supreme Court decision. He released a song called “Hind’s Hall” in 2024, referencing an anti-war protest at Columbia University in which students took over a building and renamed in honor of a Palestinian child who was killed after being trapped in a car by Israeli fire in Gaza.

“The problem isn’t the protests, it’s what they’re protesting,” the song lyrics say. “It goes against what our country is funding.”

He performed the song while opening for Sheeran at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey earlier this month. According to video posted by Macklemore, he told the crowd that part of why he wanted to be on the tour was to be able to be in stadiums to say “Free Palestine.”

The clip of Macklemore drew controversy and criticism, including from fellow artist Pink, who identifies as Jewish. She put out a statement Friday explaining why she reposted a social media post critical of Macklemore’s performance.

She wrote that she was not trying to get any artist fired or silence anyone, but she took issue with Macklemore putting “violent images” of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza up in a stadium filled with families and then telling Jews in the audience that “it wasn’t about them.”

“You don’t get to decide that for us,” she wrote Friday. “That’s what prompted my repost. Not ‘Free Palestine,’ and not anyone’s right to say it.”

Representatives for Pink and Sheeran did not immediately responded to requests for comment Monday. The company working on Sheeran’s tour, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone on Monday that it was informed that multiple venues “will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup.”

Cancellations would “impact hundreds of thousands of fans,” the statement said, confirming that Macklemore would no longer perform on his previously scheduled dates.

Macklemore told his followers that he is not a victim, nor are Pink or Sheeran. He wrote that the victims are the Palestinian people who have been “forced to live through unimaginable violence.”

He also said he understood why many people do not take a side, but pointed out that he has been outspoken in his position for three years prior to the tour. The decision to remain outspoken about the Gaza war has become something Macklemore said he considers a duty.

“An entire people being displaced, starved, and killed while the world debates which words we allowed to use to describe it, how those words make us feel, and whether our discomfort matters ore than the people living through a genocide,” he wrote.

Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killed about 1,200 people and saw 250 others taken hostage, prompting a multiyear military offensive by Israel in the Gaza Strip.

More than 73,000 people in Gaza have died as a result of Israel’s military campaign in the enclave, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry. That includes at least 1,273 people killed in Gaza since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October, according to the ministry.
