In a 2016 paper crunching their new dataset, the Tax Ninjas put numbers on just how consequential the shift had become: they estimated that in 2011, pass-through business income faced an average federal income tax rate of just about 20 percent — dramatically lower than the nearly 32 percent average rate faced by traditional corporations.

Even today, after significant changes to the tax code, earning income through a pass-through business can carry considerable tax advantages over earning it through other types of businesses — or as an employee. The economists suggest the tax rules are arbitrary and unfair. For example, Zwick says, a doctor who owns a practice may pay a significantly lower tax rate than one employed by a hospital — even when they're essentially doing the same work.

Meet the Main Street Millionaires

In their book, The Everywhere Millionaire, when Zidar and Zwick talk about "Main Street Millionaires," they're talking specifically about the rich owners of private businesses.

"Collectively, Main Street Millionaires have more than thirteen times the wealth of the Forbes 400," they write. For every member of that famous list of multibillionaires, there are more than four thousand private business owners who each have at least $10 million in net worth.

Sponsor Message

And, appropriately for this book's title, these multimillionaires can be found basically everywhere.

"Half the Forbes 400 live in New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Miami, and the other half tend to live in such big cities as Chicago, Boston, Atlanta, Washington, Dallas, and Houston," they write. "Main Street Millionaires, by contrast, live in hundreds of communities all over America."

Zidar and Zwick began wondering who the actual people were behind these numbers and what their stories were. The tax data they were using, however, kept their identities anonymous.

So they began searching for these Main Street millionaires in the real world. And they turned to public sources where people could be identified, including magazine profiles and — our personal favorite — registries of private jet and yacht owners.

Zidar and Zwick found a colorful cast of characters, including the owner of a yacht named Top Dog.

Top Dog's owner is Dick Portillo, an entrepreneur and former Marine in the Chicago area who came from nothing and poured his family's savings into a humble hot dog stand and turned it into a billion-dollar restaurant empire over his lifetime.

Another inspiring story: Karen Bentlage, who, instead of buying a car, spent $3,000 on a tanning booth and rented it out. That led her to build a company that became the nation's second-largest distributor of tanning beds. She became a tanning multimillionaire, and then made even more money by pivoting to waxing salons after tanning fell out of fashion.

But not all of these fortunes can be chalked up to just good old-fashioned hard work, ingenuity, and entrepreneurial hustle in delivering better products and services to consumers.

The Middle Garchs

Some Main Street millionaires have also gotten rich in industries where government rules restrict competition, protect incumbents, and help keep profits high.

For example, as we've reported before in the Planet Money newsletter, economists have long blasted doctors and their professional groups for working to reduce the supply of medical providers and increase costs for patients. That has included efforts to restrict the number of medical residency slots and opposition to letting nurse practitioners and other providers take on work that doctors do.

Sponsor Message

Another example that Zidar and Zwick provide is alcohol distributors. With the help of government regulations, they've ensconced themselves as middlemen between alcohol makers and retailers — a system that can raise distribution costs and ultimately the cost of drinking. The economists tell a similar story about real estate brokers, who have fought to protect their role as middlemen and the hefty commissions that come with it.

Being a politically protected middleman, it turns out, can be a pretty lucrative business. Probably the best example is car dealerships, which their data showed were money machines propelling their owners into the top of the income distribution. Car dealers are middlemen between manufacturers and consumers. They do provide valuable services like, for example, handling warranty claims for automakers and allowing consumers to test-drive vehicles before buying them.

But many car dealerships also benefit from a slew of protections against competition, particularly state franchise laws that restrict automakers from selling directly to consumers and protect the turf of dealerships to sell their affiliated brand of cars.

On top of this, many dealerships pursue profits through notoriously shady business practices, including deceptive marketing tactics, hidden fees, and overpriced add-ons, like alarm systems, anti-rust undercoating, and floor mats. The worst offenders are sometimes branded as "stealerships."

We've reported on the shady economics of car buying before in the Planet Money newsletter. After my Toyota Tacoma was stolen in 2022, I encountered many of their profit-making shenanigans myself as I sought to buy a new truck.

As we reported back then, Tesla, under Elon Musk, sought to circumvent the dealership model and sell directly to consumers. He has had success in some states, but car dealers have proved to be formidable opponents.

Car dealers, like many other Main Street millionaires, have significant political clout. Not only do they have money, but they are geographically dispersed in political districts and employ lots of people. They often sponsor local little leagues, football games, and community events. They are influential donors and constituents for a slew of politicians. Even the richest man in the world — whom many label as an "oligarch" — has had trouble defeating them.

Sponsor Message

Zidar and Zwick provide another example of Elon Musk losing while Main Street millionaires win. Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars helping elect Donald Trump and then literally served in his administration. Yet the One Big Beautiful Bill, signed into law by President Trump last year, eliminated federal tax credits for electric vehicles, hurting the bottom line for Tesla. Meanwhile, owners of pass-through businesses got a major win: the law made permanent a lucrative deduction that allows many of them to subtract up to 20 percent of their business income when calculating their federal taxes.

Everyone is talking about the "oligarchs." But Zwick jokes there's another powerful group of rich people in America: the "middle-garchs."

Main Street millionaires in the halls of power

It's not just the money. It's not just the lobbying. It's not even just that Main Street millionaires are all over the nation and serve as important donors and constituents for politicians.

As Zidar and Zwick document in their book, Main Street millionaires often become politicians themselves. Business owners make up just 3 percent of the U.S. population, they write, but they are dramatically overrepresented in elected office.

Decamillionaires — worth at least $10 million — "are more than ten times as likely to serve in Congress as their share of the population would suggest," they write. Centimillionaires — worth at least $100 million — are 62 times as likely. "These wealthy politicians," Zidar and Zwick write, "are predominantly Main Street millionaires."

Their overrepresentation is even more extreme at the state level. "In 2023–24 state legislatures, 40 percent of legislators came from business backgrounds — and that figure rises significantly if we include lawyers and doctors who own their own practices," they write. "Twenty-one state legislators across the country were auto dealers in 2023–24."

To be clear, there's nothing inherently wrong or corrupt about wealthy business owners serving in government. Many bring valuable experience and expertise to public office. And these millionaires are often popular with the electorate.

But Zidar and Zwick offer examples in the book of how being both a business owner and politician can create potential conflicts of interest.

For instance, they tell the story of Bob Corker, a Republican from Tennessee who served as a U.S. senator. Corker was a real estate developer, and when he was elected, he was one of the richest members of Congress. He proved to be a critical vote for the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, a major legislative accomplishment of President Trump's first term.

"He decided to support President Trump's huge tax cuts in 2017 only after lawmakers inserted a provision — later dubbed the 'Corker kickback' — from which he was destined to benefit greatly due to his rental income from real estate–related LLCs," Zidar and Zwick write. Corker denied these accusations.

Another example they provide, from the other side of the aisle: Michael J. Madigan, a powerful Illinois Democrat and wealthy lawyer who maintained a private legal practice while serving as speaker of the Illinois House of Representatives. In 2025, Madigan was convicted on federal corruption charges involving schemes that used his political power to steer business to his law firm.

There are, of course, many honorable people who own businesses and choose to become politicians. But the fact is that Main Street millionaires are a politically important class of people. They're not just influencing politicians. They often are politicians.

America's billionaires obviously have extraordinary wealth and political power. But Zidar and Zwick argue they're eclipsing a much larger — and, collectively, much richer — class of wealthy Americans who also wield enormous influence over our economy and politics.

Their businesses may be more boring than those that launch rockets into space or have algorithms that influence how we shop or view the world. They may not be celebrities. But they may be worth paying more attention to.

World.title: Beijing hits back at Anthropic CEO's call to curb China's AI development
World.content:
Beijing hits back at Anthropic CEO's call to curb China's AI development

toggle caption Ng Han Guan/AP

BEIJING — China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday bristled at the Anthropic CEO's call for the U.S. to curb China's artificial intelligence capabilities as part of a wider argument for a global slowdown on AI development.

In a lengthy essay published Saturday, Dario Amodei warned that a "Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world." To enable the U.S. to keep its technological edge, Amodei called for maintaining restrictions on sales to China of the most advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment.

A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Amodei's dire warnings about China were counterproductive and that all parties should work together on AI.

"Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance -- which serves no one's interest," spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press conference in response to a question about Amodei's essay.

Sponsor Message

For their part, Chinese leaders have also sounded the alarm about AI, warning of the risks posed by foreign entities with advanced capabilities. A top security official in China's government published an essay on Sunday in which he accused "certain nations" — a reference to the U.S. — of leveraging AI advantages to hinder other countries' innovation.

On Monday, President Donald Trump pushed back against calls for his administration to step in to slow down AI development, saying such efforts were part of a "SICK conspiracy" which could allow China to eclipse the U.S. on AI.

Trump and Xi could discuss AI governance at summit

Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to discuss AI governance, among other topics, at a meeting planned on Sept. 24.

Chinese companies have developed powerful AI models that are often cheaper to use than advanced models from U.S.-based companies; by some measures, they are just as capable.

Among the concerns outlined in his essay, Amodei predicted that a swarm of AI "agents" could be able to take over the internet in six to 12 months unless researchers agree to slow down. He said that "global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities."

Sponsor Message

Xi has called for the setting up of a global AI governance framework among the Global South, while pitching China as a pioneer in establishing an open-source AI community.

Beijing accuses U.S. of trying to hold it back

In an editorial published Sunday, China's state-run Global Times newspaper dismissed Amodei's essay as a veiled call to "contain" China. It said that Amodei's essay may appear on the surface to be focused on global AI security, but, that it is "packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a 'Cold War playbook' for the AI sector."

Amodei's essay was published a few days after the FBI, National Security Agency and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a joint cybersecurity advisory last week. That advisory said Chinese AI developers had engaged in "aggressive, malicious" efforts in extracting, or "distilling," capabilities from some of the most advanced AI models in the U.S. like Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's GPT.

China's Commerce Ministry dismissed the U.S. claims as groundless and said "distillation" has been commonly used by many AI companies. It also said that the U.S. was pursuing a "monopoly of the AI industry."

Both China and the U.S. want "to make sure the other side cannot establish a tech chokepoint over them," said Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis.

"So from Beijing's perspective, there is an obvious question: if the U.S. wants China to cooperate on frontier safety while also restricting its access to frontier compute, what exactly does that cooperation look like?" Lee said.

China has worries about AI in the hands of "hostile forces"

In an essay posted Sunday on social media, Chen Yixin, head of China's Ministry of State Security, warned that, in the hands of "hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives," this technology could pose a direct threat to "our political, institutional, and ideological security."

Sponsor Message

Citing the capabilities of powerful technologies from U.S. companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, Chen warned that "certain nations and organizations" now have the capabilities to "rapidly discover vulnerabilities at scale ... and execute complex hacking tasks." That, he wrote, poses "serious risks to my country's critical information infrastructure."

Foreign spying agencies are turning to AI to "aggressively harvest sensitive data, including critical national data, trade secrets, and citizens' personal privacy information," Chen wrote.

World.title: What we know about Carney's push for a 'unique alliance' with the EU
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that Canada plans to begin discussions on a "unique alliance" with the European Union.

Carney was responding to a Wall Street Journal article that said Canada was seeking to become an "associate member" of the 27-nation bloc.

That report included this quote from Finnish President Alexander Stubb: "Wouldn’t it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?"

In response to the article, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and other MPs in his party said on X on Sunday that Canadians should be concerned about becoming the "28th EU state."

Here is what we know about the Canada-EU partnership as Carney prepares to deliver a speech to the European Parliament on Thursday morning.

Is Canada planning to join the EU?

No, Carney says. The prime minister reiterated at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday that that is not the plan.

"We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," Carney said, adding that officials are instead looking to begin discussions on a "unique alliance."



"We share the same values, we have the same priorities, and we have very complementary strengths," he said.

WATCH | See Carney's comment here: Canada looking into 'unique alliance' with EU, not membership: Carney | Duration 0:33 Prime Minister Mark Carney was asked on the red carpet of the Toronto International Film Festival about a Wall Street Journal report that suggested he was exploring whether Canada could become an 'associate member' of the European Union. He said Canada plans to begin discussions for a 'unique alliance' with the bloc, but will not seek membership.

Has the idea of full EU membership been floated?

Not officially, but the idea has made the rounds among media and some people in power as Canada seeks to become less dependent on its relationship with the U.S.

One public instance was a comment by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, who said in March that "maybe Canada at some point" could 

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, shown in Helsinki on Monday, casually floated the idea of Canada joining the EU in March. (Mikko Stig/Lehtikuva/The Associated Press)

Barrot's comments at a European conference in Berlin generated laughs and applause at the time, though Carney has consistently said, as early as June 2025, that membership is not on the table.

He said then that he wants to "co-operate much more clearly and broadly to our mutual benefit."



"Not as a member, but along that continuum."

What is an 'associate' member?

Saturday's Wall Street Journal article said Carney is pushing his team to take Ottawa's relationship with the EU "to the next level" — including having Canada take on a new title: "Associate Member of the European Union."

"Associate member" is not a legal designation.

A senior Canadian official, who offered information to CBC News on a not-for-attribution basis, said the "associate member" label is one of a few that have been considered and that Canada did not propose it.

The official added that the government is still examining what the relationship could look like, and hopes to more clearly sketch it out at the EU-Canada summit at the end of October.

The official said they did a deep analysis of the EU's relationships with non-members Norway, Switzerland, the U.K. and Georgia and said none of those would work because the Canadian government does not want to give up independence in return for access.

What do we know about deepening ties between the EU and Canada?

Carney and the EU's ambassador to Canada, Geneviève Tuts, have both used the same word: "unique."

But there have been few on-the-record details beyond a willingness on both sides to work something out.



Carney said on Aug. 22 that the two sides would talk this fall about building a "much stronger and deeper" security and economic partnership. This is on top of their only partially applied free-trade deal (CETA) and the non-trade Strategic Partnership Agreement, as well as the Security and Defence Partnership they signed in June 2025.

Tuts said what that looks like is still being worked out.

WATCH | Canada should increase trade, Dion says: Canada will 'not become a member of the EU,' Stéphane Dion says | Duration 1:21 Former Liberal leader and Special Envoy to the European Union Stéphane Dion says the idea of Canada joining the EU 'will never happen,' but Canada must look to increase trade with the EU above eight per cent. Conservatives and Liberals 'should all agree it's the thing we need to do,' he added.

The Wall Street Journal report says Canada and the EU are "eyeing ways" for Canada to move closer on energy, AI, critical minerals and defence.

The Canadian official said they're aiming for more options on where Canadians study, travel, do business and retire.

What are the possibilities?

Tuts said she expects only discussions about any new partnership at this point, possibly with more detail from speeches by Carney on Thursday and by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday.

Achim Hurrelmann, co-director of the Centre for European Studies at Carleton University, says it seems the new agreement is being put together in a hurry.

He said the plan might include things like collaboration on a European stockpile of critical minerals, university student exchanges through the Erasmus program and a digital trade agreement.

Hurrelmann said this all might amount to a series of agreements instead of a major pact, or a grab bag of ideas assembled under the label of "co-operating on strategic capabilities."

"There are lots of initiatives, but they don’t at this point really amount, from what I can see, to this systematically new step in the relationship," he said. "I’m not really sure if the substance will actually justify the new label."

World.title: 'Cool to be Canadian': Leaders optimistic their pitch to invest here will pay off
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada is a safe and competitive place to do business, teeming with hundreds of capital-ready major projects to pour dollars into — at least, that's the pitch Canadian business leaders and politicians are in the midst of making to some of the world's top money managers.

And as this week's Canada Investment Summit kicks off, there's plenty of optimism on the Canadian side that investors are starting to see the country that way.

The multi-day summit is bringing financiers from abroad responsible for managing trillions of dollars worth of capital to Toronto, where they'll be pitched on major Canadian projects.

Led by the Prime Minister Mark Carney, the exclusive summit is set to feature a Monday night dinner at the Art Gallery of Ontario, talks from high-profile Canadian business leaders and closing remarks from former prime minister Stephen Harper.

The list of invitees spans Canadian business leaders, foreign investors and politicians past and present. Chief executive of investment bank Barclays C.S. Venkatakrishnan, Blackstone president and CEO Jon Gray, president and CEO of CIBC Harry Culham, and head of countries for OpenAI George Osborne are among them.

On the political side, National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, CEO of the government's Major Projects Office Dawn Farrell and former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien will also attend.

WATCH | Carney hosts investment summit amid trade war: Carney hosts investment summit amid trade war | Duration 2:44 Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting a two day investment summit in Toronto in an attempt to attract foreign capital to the country amid an escalating trade war with the United States.

Though foreign investors haven't always viewed Canada as the best place to pour their money, Goldy Hyder, president and CEO of the Business Council of Canada, says that attitude is changing.

"It's really cool to be Canadian right now. People I've been meeting with are excited about what they're hearing and what they're seeing," Hyder said.

The government has already made moves aimed at showing they're serious about building big things, too.

Minister of Finance François-Philippe Champagne on Monday announced the Canadian Revenue Agency will prioritize advanced income tax rulings for investments over $1 billion.

The program, which goes into effect immediately, will allow investors to know how income tax law will apply to a proposed investment before they commit money to it, reducing risk, according to a government release.

"When investors are considering major projects, certainty matters," Champagne said.

Companies see changes

In recent years, long turnaround times for major projects and uncertainty about whether or not projects will get approved have hurt Canada's reputation in the eyes of investors, business leaders say.

A recent report by the CPP Investment Insights Institute collected responses from global investors and found that while Canada ranked high in terms of stability, regulatory complexity and permitting timelines were big concerns, especially among energy and mining projects — the areas where investors saw some of the most value in Canada.

But provincial and federal governments seem to be working better with the private sector to clear the way for big projects, Hyder said, and bringing Indigenous nations on board with new projects.

Mark Selby, CEO of Canada Nickel Company, has seen the change from within, too.

He says changes to the permitting process have helped his company secure key federal permits for the Crawford nickel project, which is included in the government's pitchbook for the summit, in about half the time it would have taken previously.

That 66-page pitchbook obtained by CBC News last week listed more than 160 projects that will be on the table at the summit, 11 of which were listed as shovel ready and about two dozen more in an advanced stage.

Frank McKenna, deputy chair at TD Securities and former Canadian ambassador to the U.S., said many of the projects are "fully baked" opportunities ready for financing, which could help meet the moment for investors.

WATCH | McKenna says Canada proving to investors its a trustworthy place to invest: Prime minister's investment summit 'breathtakingly audacious': former ambassador | Duration 9:34 As the world's richest investors head to Toronto next week, former Canadian ambassador to the U.S. Frank McKenna tells Power & Politics that Prime Minister Mark Carney's investment summit is 'more audacious and more ambitious' than previous government attempts to attract foreign investment, especially at a time when investors are looking for reliability in the face of global uncertainty.

And while Canada finds itself in a moment of trade upheaval with the U.S., which some have worried could make Canada look less stable, McKenna points out the rest of the world is going through that upheaval in tandem — which could work in Canada's favour.

"We represent those other options, and we represent a country with a well-developed rule of law and stability," McKenna told CBC's Power & Politics on Friday.

"All of that makes us an attractive … alternative place to invest."

Deals could take time

Selby is seeking $2 billion to help fund the Crawford mining project included in the prospectus, but he's not expecting to walk away from the two-day event with it in hand.

"The summit for most mining companies is really a door-opener," Selby said.

Mark Selby, CEO of Canada Nickel Company, says the government's work to make Canada more attractive to businesses is working. (Abby Hughes/CBC)

He says some of the really big international investors likely won't be looking to put their money in projects that only need a few billion, like his. Still, he says the attention of the prime minister will make Canadian industries including mining more attractive, and will open more doors for the future.

Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly said she was hopeful "good deals" and memorandums of understanding pledging future investment will come out of the summit, though the full impact of those deals might only be apparent in time.

"What I'm hearing and based on many of the conversations I've had, it's a great momentum," Joly said. "We will see the impacts of this summit in three months, in six months, in a year."

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt echoed the message, saying the meetings happening at the summit are like a "first date."

"You're getting to know someone, making sure that they're marriage material and they're doing the same with us," Holt said.

She says success will come in the form of follow-up meetings that lead to deals on paper.

World.title: 2 more people have died exploring Banff National Park, police say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two people died in Banff National Park in the last week while exploring the outdoors, police say.

A 24-year-old climber died after a significant fall from Recondite Peak in Banff National Park on Wednesday, while a 33-year-old hiker died on Saturday near Devil's Thumb and the Big Beehive area by Lake Louise, said local RCMP detachment commander Susan Richter.

Richter said the climber had hiked into the remote area on Sept. 7 to ascend Recondite Peak and was in contact with people via a communication device. They reported him missing on Sept. 9, and police said Parks Canada rescue specialists found him dead the same day.

Richter said he was on his own, but "very trained and experienced in the back country."

Recondite Peak is in the eastern part of Banff National Park and roughly 3,350 metres high. The area is north of Lake Louise and to the east of the Icefields Parkway. It sits along the provincial border at the Siffleur Wilderness Area.

Parks Canada's Banff field unit didn't respond to CBC's request for information and an interview.

Second death near Lake Louise

On Saturday afternoon, a 33-year-old Calgary man was hiking with three friends near Devil's Thumb and the Big Beehive close to Lake Louise, said police.

He went on his own to Devil's Thumb. When his friends lost sight of him, Richter said they reported him missing. Parks Canada rescue specialists were sent out, and confirmed the man had died.

Parks Canada's Lake Louise, Yoho and Kootenay field unit is working to get additional details.

A view of Lake Agnes near the tea house in the Lake Louise area of Banff National Park. The Devil's Thumb is the third peak to the right and considered a scramble. (Greg Colgan/CBC)

A grim summer

Banff National Park and Kananaskis Country have had five other hiking-related deaths this summer combined. A 47-year-old woman died hiking Mount Bryant in June, while a 65-year-old man died on Mount Temple in July, and a woman in her twenties died falling from Marvel Peak that same month.

In August, a woman died on Mount Yamnuska, and a female hiker died on Tent Ridge.

There have also been three drownings in the Bow Valley in the past few months: a 25-year-old American man at Johnston Canyon, a 29-year-old Banff resident at Johnson Lake and a 33-year-old man at Quarry Lake in Canmore.

Richter said regardless of skill level, all people should plan ahead, know the trail and know their abilities when recreating outdoors. She said it's safer to travel in a group and stick to "well used trails with higher visibility."

World.title: Sydney Sweeney's 'sexualized' sports betting ad slammed by Canadian athletes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. actor Sydney Sweeney is once again facing backlash over an .

This time, she has enraged female athletes around the world with a nude sports gambling ad — and her response.

The ad for Novig, a peer-to-peer prediction exchange focused exclusively on sports, was posted online Sept. 9 and viewed nearly 39 million times by Monday morning. It features Sweeney holding various pieces of sports equipment in front of what looks like her otherwise naked body, as bass music plays in the background.

"Think you know sports? Prove it," says the star of Euphoria and The Housemaid at the beginning of the ad as she holds a football in front of each breast.

In other shots, she perches on a basketball net while spinning a ball with only her hair covering her, holds a football in front of her pelvis, lies nude on a bench with a soccer ball resting on her feet and swings a golf club wearing only white underwear.

It set off a backlash from female athletes and Olympians who say the ad sexualizes women in sport and sets them back. The criticism crosses borders and a range of sports, with many posting "Dear Sydney Sweeney" videos on social media in response.

It also elicited a strong response from a number of Canadian athletes.

"Dear Sydney Sweeney, this is women in sports," Canadian sprint canoeist Sophia Jensen posted on TikTok on Sunday, alongside a video where the world champion competes on the water and trains in the gym.

"Hey Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Canadian figure skater Madeline Schizas posted on Instagram with a similar video where she competes and trains on and off the ice.

Canadian high diver Molly Carlson posted that "this one hits close to home." She wrote on Instagram that she spent years struggling with how her body looked in sport, "because I didn’t think I looked like the athlete I was 'supposed' to be."

"Young girls deserve to grow up seeing female athletes celebrated for their strength, courage, talent and what their bodies are capable of," she wrote alongside a video where she dives out of a helicopter.

Canada's Molly Carlson dives at the World Aquatics Championships in Singapore, Thursday, July 24, 2025. Carlson is among the Canadian athletes who have spoken out again Sydney Sweeney's sports betting ad. (Vincent Thian/The Associated Press)

Canadian gymnast Ellie Black added her voice to the throng, quoting the ad in her Instagram post — "Think you know sports? Prove it." — with a video where she flips and flies through competitions and lifts weights in the gym.

"This is women’s sport: powerful, skilled, courageous and so much more interesting than being treated as something to look at," Black wrote.

"Let’s celebrate the athletes, the work and the sport itself."

Global response from athletes

Athletes from around the world had their say, too.

"IDK what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what a woman in sport looks like," posted U.S. gymnast Gracie Kramer over a similar montage.

British sprinter Amy Hunt got a word in during a post-race interview on Sunday, after she finished fourth in the 200-metre final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

" Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Hunt told BBC Sport, adding "h ard work, blood, sweat, tears."

Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus, the reigning Olympic champion in the 400-metre freestyle, called the ad "a kick in the face" on Instagram.

"H ow do we live in a world where monetizing a woman's body and sexualizing women's sport is still a thing?" she said, according to Australia's ABC News.

Novig CEO and co-founder Jacob Fortinsky praised the brand campaign for highlighting a platform that's "singularly focused on sports."

"Sydney helped bring that message to life in a way that’s impossible to ignore," Fortinsky said in a press release the same day the ad launched.

In the same press release, Sweeney called the campaign "a fun idea" that "brings that idea to life with confidence, humour and a playful edge."

Sydney Sweeney poses for photographers at the Armani beauty event during the Venice Film Festival on Sept. 3, 2026. (Scott A Garfitt/Invision/The Associated Press)

Not her 1st controversial ad

If this is sounding familiar, Sweeney faced similar backlash last year over an American Eagle  that was criticized for promoting white standards of beauty at best, and eugenics at worst.

In the ad, Sweeney makes a play on words between jeans (the clothing item) and genes (the genetic material).

“Genes are passed down from parents to offspring, often determining traits like hair colour, personality and even eye colour. My jeans are blue,” Sweeney said in the ad.

Some internet commentators read the ad as alluding to eugenics. Eugenics is a discredited idea that the human race could be improved by selectively breeding for certain traits.

At the time, the blond-haired, blue-eyed actor stood by the ad and downplayed the reaction, which included support from U.S. President Donald Trump, who called it the "HOTTEST ad out there."

Sweeney appeared to take a more overt approach to the backlash against her new ad, posting a series of photos on Instagram on Sunday that showed magazine covers with male and female athletes posing in little to no clothing.

WATCH | What Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle ad says about marketing: What Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle ad says about the brand's marketing | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 6:07 Morgan Westcott, a marketing professor at the British Columbia Institute of Technology, says the American Eagle ad does not signal a 'shift,' but rather reflects a 'recycled concept' and a clear call to their target market.

This move prompted even more backlash. Canadian alpine skier Cassidy Gray called it "idiotic" and "senseless."

"It's not a joke when your life is actually you being a female athlete, and you being sexualized or not taken seriously and not given the same opportunities, and then you see one of the most famous actresses in the world going and completely wiping away all the work that you have done to be taken seriously," Gray posted in an emotional video on TikTok.

Gray also responded to those who might say it's just a commercial and not meant to be taken so seriously.

"I fear you're just out of touch, because it really is that deep."

Female athletes have historically been marketed in an over-sexualized manner, with a greater focus on t heir appearance than their skills.

This also extends to sports coverage, with women at the Tokyo 2021 Olympics 10 times more likely to be "visually objectified" with a camera angle than men, according to a report from The Representation Project . Researchers defined visual objectification as when a camera panned across an athlete's body or focused on a specific body part in a sexualizing way.

The same study found female athletes were more likely to be infantilized by commentators, often called "young ladies" and "girls."

Another recent study from World Athletics found that female athletes were consistently targeted by online abuse more than their male counterparts at four global sporting events, including the 2024 Paris Olympics.

World.title: Music festival apologizes after Flo Rida uses alcohol props at sober event in Thunder Bay, Ont.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Wake the Giant Music Festival is facing backlash after Grammy-nominated headliner Flo Rida used alcohol props on stage at the sober event in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Saturday.

The annual festival, which was launched in 2019, raises awareness to create a safe, inclusive environment for hundreds of Indigenous youth from remote northern communities who attend school in the city.

CBC Thunder Bay reached out to the Wake the Giant Musical Festival for comment, and was referred to a statement it released on social media on Sunday .

The statement said the festival's team apologizes and acknowledges the harm done by the American rapper's performance.

“The props used were not approved by organizers and we clearly communicated to the artist’s team that this was a sober event and that alcohol is not permitted on our stage,” the statement said.

The team also said it shared in the “hurt and disappointment” that many people felt, and wanted to assure the public that this performance does not align with the values of Wake the Giant or the Northern Nishnawbe Education Council, an Indigenous-run education authority.

“We take responsibility for booking the artist and we will take the lessons learned from this experience to ensure our core values will be at the forefront in choosing artists in the future,” the statement said.

Superior Morning 8:27 Sarah Law: Wake The Giant 2026 Recap The seventh annual Wake the Giant Music Festival took place in Thunder Bay over the weekend.Hear more about the meaning behind the movement, which aims to support Indigenous students in the city.

Other performers at the festival included the American group the Wallflowers, featuring Jakob Dylan, Bob Dylan's son, and Tia Wood, a Cree and Salish pop singer-songwriter from Canada.

A ‘very shocking’ performance

Esther Maud, a city resident who was in the VIP section during the performance, attended to show her support for the event, and for her son and his youth drum group, Charging Thunder, which opened the event.

Maud said it might have helped if she had relistened to his music to reflect on what it means and whether she should support it.

“I just went in thinking and being excited that I get to see someone in person that I kind of grew up listening to. So it didn’t even dawn on me what he represents, and what he sings and puts into his music at all."

Maud said she's going into six years of sobriety from alcohol. She said her mind was blown the moment she saw the first alcohol bottle on the stage during the show, in a space she has grown to love because it’s an alcohol- and drug-free event, and more bottles kept coming.

She could only think about people who are in early recovery or not as strong, and children thinking about what’s going on and if it was normal behaviour, Maud said.

Shortly after Flo Rida performed his third song, Maud left with her family and a friend.

If she were an organizer of the event, she said, “I probably would have put out the message to maybe the security and asked them to come and help us — tell them that we need to remove the bottles off the stage or ... get somebody to maybe do a little pause, and then quickly regroup and let him know that this is not the place for that."

Flo Rida, shown carrying two alcohol bottles, was the headliner at the festival Saturday. (Nicky Shaw/CBC News)

Maud said she appreciated the music festival's efforts in the wake of Flo Rida's controversial performance, and understood they had communicated to him what the event is about.

But she said the apology could have been better, as the performance was “really heavy and very triggering for a lot of people.”

Maud said she isn't angry at the festival itself and hopes what happened serves as a learning experience.

“I’m disappointed. I’m upset that this happened, but at the same time, I don’t want this one event and this performer to ruin everything else that they work so hard to do."

Organizers still have a chance to continue this work, she said, noting that she still wants to support them no matter what, as she sees their vision and knows how important it is.

“There are so many purposes and reasons to why this festival still needs to go and keep the momentum for the youth."

World.title: Macklemore cut from Ed Sheeran U.S. tour after onstage 'Free Palestine' remarks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Macklemore has been dropped from the U.S. leg of English singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran's tour after several venues in the United States threatened to cancel the scheduled concerts if the American rapper — and outspoken advocate for Palestinian rights — was not removed.

Benjamin Hammond Haggerty, better known as Macklemore, joined Sheeran for the first two U.S. shows on the Loop Tour on Sept. 4 and 5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The Seattle-born Grammy winner was slated to open for the remaining eight of Sheeran's 10 U.S. shows before he was dropped from the tour.

Macklemore's onstage remarks at MetLife — including chanting "Free Palestine" and expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank — drew criticism from pro-Israel groups.

The rapper also wore a keffiyeh, a checkered black-and-white scarf long worn by Palestinians, and performed his song Hind's Hall, one of two songs he released in 2024 in support of student protesters on university campuses and to decry Israel's military actions in Gaza following the Hamas-led attacks on Israel of Oct. 7, 2023.

The Israeli American Council (IAC) also launched a petition calling for Sheeran to remove Macklemore from the rest of the tour. In a statement issued following the announcement he would be cut, the IAC said it welcomes the decision.

"Anyone who chooses to turn an 80,000-person concert into a vehicle for advancing a one-sided political agenda must stand behind that choice," it said. "A concert stage is not a platform for anti-Israel and antisemitic propaganda."

Macklemore blames Robert Kraft

Messina Touring Group, the promoter of the U.S. leg of the tour, told Rolling Stone magazine that the decision to remove Macklemore came after "discussions with stakeholders."

"As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran's U.S. Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming U.S. tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans," the group said on Monday.

Macklemore responded Monday in a lengthy statement posted on Instagram, blaming his removal from the tour on New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who owns owns Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts. He claimed Kraft said Macklemore would not be allowed on stage and rallied other stadium owners to threaten to cancel scheduled concerts if he was not taken off the bill. The threats placed Sheeran, his friend, in a difficult position, Macklemore said.

"Ed [Sheeran] was in a f--ked up position. He knew it. His typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before. He told me that the words 'Free Palestine' and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with," Macklemore said.

"I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood. But he couldn't get past his public facing, 'I don't take sides.'"

CBC News reached out to representatives for Sheeran for comment but did not immediately hear back.

Kraft responds to Macklemore

In response to Macklemore, Kraft said Gillette Stadium does "not provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of divisiveness and hate by sharing "selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas," in a statement shared with CBC News.

"Based on Macklemore's recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran's shows in New Jersey and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line," Kraft said in an email.

"I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same – peace for all people, an end to suffering and an end to all hate.”

In his onstage speech at the first show, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine.

"I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them."

New England Patriots owner Robert Kraf responded to Macklemore on Monday after the U.S. rapper said that Kraft had rallied other stadium owners to not allow the pro-Palestinian advocate to perform at their venues, saying Gillette Stadium does not allow 'hate speech.' (Brynn Anderson/The Associated Press)

Macklemore said that his criticism was directed at Israel's government and was not an attack on Jewish people.

"To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you," he said in his speech onstage at the second show on Sept. 5. "My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality."

Following his comments, singer-songwriter Pink reshared a social media post from StopAntisemitism calling for him to be removed from the tour. She later said that the post "said things in words I didn't write, and I wouldn't have chosen all of them," but defended her criticism of the rapper.

"He stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn't about them. You don't get to decide that for us," Pink said on Friday in a lengthy statement on Instagram.

"That's what prompted my repost. Not 'Free Palestine,' and not anyone's right to say it. I have never asked for another artist to be silenced and I'm not asking now," she wrote.

Pink also recalled a 2014 performance by Macklemore in which he wore a costume onstage that was widely criticized as offensive and antisemitic. The rapper later apologized, saying, "I respect all cultures and all people," and that the costume was not meant to be a caricature of a Jewish man.

Humanitarian groups have said Israel's actions constitute genocide

Reaction to Macklemore's statement on Monday included support for the rapper.

"The way you stand in solidarity here is an absolute model. Thank you for walking through this fire while centering Palestinians," commented Noura Erakat, a Palestinian-American activist, professor and human rights attorney.

"Thank you for recognizing your relative power and privilege. Thank you for having the humility to be changed by Palestinians, enough to learn not just a phrase but a pillar of our continuity — thank you for not abandoning this duty."

U.S. singer-songwriter Lauren Jauregui, who has also been an advocate for Palestinians, said: "So much love and respect for you."

Popular children's content creator Rachel Accurso, known as Ms. Rachel, has similarly faced intense public reaction and antisemitism accusations for using her platform to highlight the humanitarian needs, safety and rights of children in Gaza.

"Ed Sheeran had an opportunity [to] show that we won't be bullied into punishing people for supporting Palestine," she wrote on Instagram. "Instead he caved to people who refuse to accept what the world knows. A genocide is happening in Gaza. We all need to speak out against it."

Humanitarian organizations, including Amnesty International and a United Nations commission have said Israel's actions in Gaza constitute a genocide.

World.title: Former Saskatoon private school admin, pictured with paddle in 1997, testifies at former principal's trial
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A photo of a former administrator for a Saskatoon private Christian school holding a wooden paddle, published in Maclean's magazine 30 years ago, is now evidence in the assault trial of a former principal at the school.

Duff Arthur Friesen faces five counts of assault with a weapon. He has pleaded not guilty to all of them.

Friesen is accused of hitting students with a wooden paddle. The charges stem from his time at Christian Centre Academy from 1997 to 2007.

The school was later renamed Legacy Christian Academy, then Valour Academy. It's closely associated with Mile Two Church, now called Encounter Church.

Duff Arthur Friesen makes his way into Saskatoon Court of King's Bench last week for the start of his jury trial. He faces five counts of assault with a weapon. (Travis Reddaway/CBC)

Lou Brunelle, the man in the magazine photo from 1997, was the first defence witness at the trial. He testified Monday that paddling was school policy and parents signed off.

Brunelle worked at the school from 1989 to 2001, first as a supervisor and then an administrative assistant, reporting to the director and senior to the teachers. He said the role can be compared to that of a vice-principal.

He said the paddle was one of multiple methods, alongside things like demerits and detentions, that the school used to enforce discipline for things like stealing, lying or cheating.

“We would chat with the child. If warranted — three swats,” he told the jury.

He said the student and the discipliner would then pray together.

Brunelle also testified that none of the staff at the school at the time were certified to work as teachers. He added that the curriculum was approved and that students received Ministry of Education transcripts that allowed them to go on to university.

Crown witnesses

The Crown closed its case Friday after calling five former students, each of whom testified about being struck with a wooden paddle.

Robyn Mandell said Friesen spanked her hard enough to leave bruises for days. She said it was extremely "humiliating, shameful and terrifying."

Coy Nolin, who testified on Wednesday, told the jury he was called to Friesen's office during a school day after Friesen sent a letter to his mother about his schoolwork, and was told he would be taken off the basketball team if he didn't catch up.

He said Friesen told him he’d be getting paddled and sent back to class. Nolin said he then put his hands on the seat of a chair and bent over.

“He struck me three times,” Nolin said.

The trial is set for two weeks, with Justice Daryl Labach presiding.

World.title: Ice wine producer in Ontario's Niagara region says U.S. buyers 'flabbergasted' by Trump's booze ban order
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump has ordered a ban Canadian booze effective later this month, but for one winery in Ontario's Niagara region, his tariffs have already killed the possibility of selling to Americans.

"There's no product in the world that could compete in a marketplace with a tariff that high," said Jamie Slingerland, director of viticulture for Pillitteri Estates Winery, pointing to the 50 per cent tariff imposed as of Aug. 22 .

His Niagara-on-the-Lake,-Ont., company has five main buyers in the U.S. who love their "very Canadian" product, but have been left "flabbergasted."

Last Tuesday, Trump signed five proclamations, including banning import of alcoholic drinks and other goods as of Sept 29. and adding 50 per cent tariffs to other items, such as whey, molasses, furniture, and paper and wood products.

The move comes after 20 months of escalating trade action between Canada and the U.S.

Winery shipped early to beat latest tariffs

Knowing tariffs were coming, Slingerland said, the winery pivoted. Instead of preparing wine to export in the fall before the holiday shopping season, Pillitteri accelerated its schedule and exported four months early. Slingerland said their buyers are keeping the product in storage until closer to Christmas.

He said the family-owned winery was able to act quickly in part because it's smaller and independent. Other wineries, he said, likely don't have that option.

"We're not laying anybody off. We're not reducing production. We're pushing ahead."

WATCH | B.C. wine industry calls on Canadians to support local producers: U.S. alcohol ban sets ‘dangerous precedent,’ B.C. wine industry warns | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 3:24 The U.S. is set to ban imports of most Canadian alcohol starting Sept. 29 as the trade war with Canada escalates. Wine Growers B.C. president and CEO Jeff Guignard calls the move 'unprecedented and deeply frustrating' and says Canadian consumers should support domestic producers.

Ontario wineries support 22,000 jobs: association

There are 186 wineries in Ontario, and they generate about $711 million in revenue and support about 22,000 jobs, according to industry association Grape Growers of Ontario.

The association website says its industry generates an economic impact of $5.49 billion for the province, including through taxes, tourism and suppliers, per a 2019 study by Wine Growers Ontario.

Grape Growers has said it recommends businesses impacted by trade disruptions look into federal support programs such as the government of Canada's Regional Tariff Response Initiative.

John Boynton is president of Arterra Wines, which owns wineries including Jackson-Triggs and Inniskillin, and retail chain Wine Rack. He told CBC his team is "disappointed" by the import ban.

"More than anything, businesses need stability and predictability to plan, invest and grow, and unfortunately the level of uncertainty facing our industry continues to increase rather than decrease," he said in an emailed statement.

Alcohol products have been used as leverage on both sides of the border, Boynton said, creating challenges for businesses, workers and customers.

He said it's too early to determine the full impact of Trump's latest ban plan, but in the meantime, his company will focus on "supporting our customers and partners while we assess the implications of this latest measure."

Slingerland and Boynton both called on the federal government to renew its Wine Sector Support program, which is set to end March 31.

CBC Hamilton asked Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada (AAFC) if the government plans to renew the program or is considering doing so.

In an email on Monday, AAFC said the government "remains committed to active engagement with the Canadian wine industry on how best to support its competitiveness and resilience in the current context."

AAFC said the program has supported wineries with $343 million over five years.

World.title: Adam Pankratz: Mark Carney’s elitist quest to turn us into Europeans
World.content:
Article content

While not all of those items may be desirable, some unequivocally are. On the negative side of the ledger would almost certainly be the free flow of workers between Canada and the EU. We have seen this play out in Europe before, notably in the United Kingdom. The simple reality is that more people in Europe (and the world) speak English as a second language than vice-versa. That affects the direction of travel of the workers. On pure linguistic grounds alone, it is nearly certain that Canada, as a primarily English-speaking nation, would be opening its workers up to far more competition from English speaking Europeans, than, say, Greek or German workers would face from Greek or German speaking Canadians. Any politician who avoids the difficulty of that question alone is in for a massive shock when push comes to shove. A “free flow” of people and workers goes both ways and isn’t an unalloyed good for Canadians.
