World.title: Pemex contains another oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico
World.content:
An oil spill was detected at Pemex facilities north of Ciudad del Carmen, Campeche, last Thursday, prompting the Navy to activate a contingency plan to help the state-owned company control the leak quickly enough to assure the public that no oil would reach the coastline.

Unlike the major Gulf Coast incident that occurred earlier this year, Pemex quickly confirmed that crude was leaking from one of its pipelines.

En la Sonda de Campeche, Pemex inició instalación de la envolvente metálica, a 50 metros de profundidad, para la reparación de la sección afectada del ducto submarino en campo Ek-Balam, ocurrida el jueves 10 y que puso en alerta ante derrame de crudo en aguas del Golfo de México. pic.twitter.com/dNDHANG8kA — Quadratín Tabasco (@QuadratinTa) September 14, 2026

“Immediate action was taken to depressurize the pipeline and isolate it by closing safety valves at its ends,” Pemex said in a statement released on Saturday. “Since then, it has remained without flow and without any leakage.”

Complementing Pemex’s security measures, the Navy deployed its ARM “Guanajuato” Ocean Patrol Vessel, four additional boats and two aircraft, along with 255 naval personnel.

Additionally, continuous observation is being carried out to monitor the evolution of the slick — which measured 4 square kilometers on Thursday — and forecast its movement so as to apprise state authorities and the public.

Agency for Safety, Energy and the Environment (ASEA) scientists were analyzing three drift forecast models, all projecting a net westward shift over the next five days. ASEA has also been conducting overflights to document the containment, the clean-up and repair efforts.

The Permanent Observatory of the Gulf of Mexico — which discovered and reported the leak — is an integrated, real-time environmental monitoring system created by the federal government in April.

It was launched amid fallout over a massive leak in February that Pemex officials originally hid from upper management and then was made worse when the oil company denied responsibility.

This time, authorities have been more transparent. Pemex acknowledged that the incident occurred at its Ek Balam platform system, part of the Cantarell oil field, one of the most productive in Mexican history

By Sunday, the dredging of the seabed had been completed and Pemex said pipeline repairs would be completed in the coming days.

With reports from LopezDoriga.com, El Economista, Vanguardia and El País

World.title: Spanish exchange student killed in Morelos
World.content:
A 21-year-old Spanish university student was murdered in the state of Morelos, Mexico, on Saturday in a crime that is being investigated as a femicide.

Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, a University of Granada (UGR) student who was studying at the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos (UAEM) on an exchange program, was stabbed at the Casa de la Cultura cultural center in Cuautla, a city around 40 kilometers southeast of Cuernavaca.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by adn Noticias (@adnnoticiasmx)

The cultural center was hosting an event focused on medicinal plants when the murder was perpetrated. Casa de la Cultura de Cuautla said in a statement that Tacoronte was the victim of an “alleged robbery with a bladed weapon.”

Morelos Attorney General Fernando Blumenkron told reporters on Sunday that the crime was being investigated as a femicide as authorities seek to determine whether the victim’s gender was a motivating factor. As of Monday morning, no one had been arrested in connection with the murder. Blumenkron said on Sunday that the aggressor hadn’t been identified.

He said that Mexican authorities immediately notified the Spanish Consulate in Mexico of the death of Tacoronte, who was studying early childhood education. She began her exchange program at the UAEM campus in Cuautla last month.

UAEM and UGR condemn the murder

In a statement, the UAEM expressed its “profound anger” over the “femicide” of Tacoronte, a native of the Spanish island of Gran Canaria.

“The Autonomous University of the State of Morelos expresses its most sincere condolences to her family, her friends, her classmates, the University of Granada, … the Spanish government and Spanish society,” the UAEM said.

“We stand in deep solidarity with all of them in the face of this irreparable loss and we share the grief that overwhelms them today,” the university said.

The UAEM called on the Morelos Attorney General’s Office to carry out an “immediate” and “exhaustive” investigation “with a strict gender perspective” in order to “guarantee justice and avoid impunity.”

In its own statement, the UGR expressed its “absolute” condemnation of the murder of Tacoronte.

“The university community wishes to convey its deepest condolences, solidarity and affection to Claudia’s family, friends and classmates at these times of such profound pain,” the university said.

The Conference of Rectors of Spanish Universities also condemned the murder of Tacoronte, saying she was a “victim of an intolerable act of violence that has shocked all Spanish universities.” At a press conference in Andorra on Monday, the Spanish Minister of Foreign Affairs, the European Union and Cooperation José Manuel Albares said that the Spanish government will seek to shed light on what happened so that “those responsible are brought to justice.”

The rector’s office of the University of Granada later announced the cancellation of the exchange program with UAEM, impacting three students who were set to study in Morelos next semester.

Tacoronte is the 4th UAEM student to be murdered this year

Tacoronte is the fourth UAEM student to be murdered this year. All of the other victims were women.

An average of around 10 women are murdered daily in Mexico. Around one-quarter of those murders are prosecuted as femicides, according to the EFE news agency, which cited statistics from Mexican authorities and non-governmental organizations.

In the first seven months of 2026, a total of 380 femicides were committed in Mexico, according to official statistics.

More than 40% of the cases occurred in just five federal entities: Sinaloa, Morelos, Chiapas, Mexico City and Tamaulipas.

With reports from EFE, El País, Cadena Ser, El Economista, El Financiero and DW

World.title: Mexico, US aiming to resolve trade issues before US midterms
World.content:
The fourth round of trade talks between Mexico and the United States will take place next week, with officials from both sides expressing eagerness to hammer out a deal before the U.S. midterm elections in November, according to sources interviewed by Reuters.

A framework for a deal would benefit both parties.

U.S. President Donald Trump is looking for a win on the economic front (a bilateral deal may bring down consumer prices in the U.S.) as he faces the possibility of losing control of Congress when ballots are cast on Nov. 3. Meanwhile, the Mexican government is struggling with investor unease and a cooling economy.

Mexico’s push to reach a deal comes after U.S.-Canada trade talks — the other half of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) review process — collapsed last month.

The U.S.-Mexico talks are seen as an effort to reach an interim bilateral deal while issues with the USMCA on the whole are ironed out.

President Sheinbaum chatted with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last Wednesday to assess the progress of the negotiations, after which Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard flew to Washington, D.C., to finalize details ahead of the fourth round. Next week’s bilateral meetings will be the first formal return to the negotiating table since the third round of talks was held in Mexico City from July 21-23.

Upon his return to Mexico City on Friday, Ebrard met with José Medina Mora — president of Mexico’s Business Coordinating Council (CCE), the principal organization representing Mexico’s private sector before federal and local governments. It groups 14 major business umbrella organizations that represent more than 2,000 trade associations comprising roughly 80% of Mexico’s GDP.

Medina Mora told the newspaper El Universal that the elimination of Section 232 tariffs, which place duties on aluminum, steel and automobiles, is expected to be a primary focus next week.

He expressed confidence that the two sides will avoid the problems that arose during the U.S.-Canada dialogue, saying they would not affect negotiations with Mexico.

“The bilateral relationship between the United States and Canada is different from our relationship [with the U.S.],” he said, adding that Sheinbaum “has clearly defined the limits of what is unacceptable, while maintaining a cordial … relationship” with Trump.

“[Sheinbaum’s strategy] has yielded results and our negotiations are moving forward,” he said.

On Saturday, when asked whether the United States would leave the USMCA, Trump told the Irish press that “we’re going to have a great relationship with Mexico” and that a deal with Canada would come soon.

With reports from El Universal, Bloomberg and Reuters

World.title: Sheinbaum attributes rise in national pride to 4T governments: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🛣️ Accountability tour hits 18 states: Speaking after her latest “honesty and results” assemblies, Sheinbaum said her nationwide accountability tour has drawn more than 300,000 attendees across 18 states so far, calling the experience “very moving” and framing it as a way to speak to citizens directly about her government’s achievements.

📰 Media outlets are “propaganda of the right”: Sheinbaum accused much of the Mexican press of acting as “propaganda outlets” for the political right, claiming important stories go unreported and that commentators coordinate their criticism of her government in a group chat.

🇲🇽 National pride climbs to 90%, Sheinbaum says: Citing an El Financiero poll, the president said pride in being Mexican rose from 58% in 1990 to 90% today, crediting the shift to “fourth transformation” governments.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Monday morning press conference after completing the second leg of her “accountability tour,” a nationwide effort to report directly to citizens on her government’s achievements during its second year in office. To date, Sheinbaum has held so-called “honesty and results” assemblies in 18 of Mexico’s 31 states and will make public speeches in the 13 remaining ones before concluding her tour in Mexico City’s central square, the Zócalo, on Sept. 27.

As was the case last year, the president is undertaking her accountability tour after delivering her annual government report to the nation. The assemblies Sheinbaum holds while “on tour” are similar to her weekday mañaneras insofar as she can bypass intermediaries — such as media outlets — and speak directly to Mexicans, including some of her biggest supporters, about government actions and achievements.

At today’s mañanera, the president sought to underscore the importance of such communication as, in her view, many Mexican media outlets are biased against her administration.

Also of note at today’s press conference were Sheinbaum’s remarks about Mexican patriotism ahead of Mexican Independence Day this Wednesday. On Tuesday night, the president will lead the traditional Grito de Independencia (Shout or Cry of Independence) from the National Palace balcony.

Sheinbaum: Accountability tour has been ‘very moving’

Sheinbaum told reporters that her accountability tour has been “very moving” because large numbers of people have come out to see her everywhere she has gone.

“What I talk about when I speak is the history of Mexico and the patriotic month [mes patrio], and people are very aware of what’s happening, and of the importance of defending independence and sovereignty,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that more than 300,000 people have attended the 18 events she has held so far on her accountability tour.

Sheinbaum: Many Mexican media outlets serve the political right

Sheinbaum asserted that the “objective” of many Mexican media outlets is “to be propaganda of the right.”

“They’re not news outlets, they’re propaganda outlets. That’s what they are,” she said.

” … If something very important happens in the country, it doesn’t appear [in the media],” Sheinbaum claimed.

She subsequently accused media outlets of “distorting reality in a way that agrees with their propaganda.”

“… They seek to distort everything, adapt everything to what they want, create political propaganda for the right,” Sheinbaum said.

The president also accused media commentators of coordinating their attacks on the government.

“They have a [group] chat where they talk about what everyone is going to say during the week,” she said.

“This week, the INE. The INE is not an institution that guarantees clean elections,” Sheinbaum said, referring to the National Electoral Institute and seeking to provide an example of the kind of coordination she believes occurs.

In the context of alleged media bias and distortion, the president portrayed her accountability tour as a presentation of the truth, although her administration also faces allegations of bias.

“What do we do? Disseminate [information], talk. Why do I go to all the states to report [to the people]? So that they hear what we’re doing in all the federal entities,” Sheinbaum said, asserting that if citizens relied solely on the media, it would be difficult for them to find out what her government is actually achieving.

Sheinbaum: There is ‘deep pride’ in being Mexican

Citing poll results, Sheinbaum highlighted that pride in being Mexican is much more prevalent today than it was in 1990.

“The other day we brought out an El Financiero newspaper poll where it said that in 1990, 58% of Mexicans felt proud of being Mexican. Today it’s 90%,” she said.

🗣️ “El 90% está orgulloso de ser mexicanas y mexicanos” 🇲🇽 Claudia Sheinbaum resaltó que el trabajo de la Cuarta Transformación ayudó a que la población sea más orgullosa del país; “algo que no lo dio el neoliberalismo”, agregó pic.twitter.com/kfTuPxe3hH — El Universal (@El_Universal_Mx) September 14, 2026

“I like the poll [result] precisely because it’s what I see every day, especially when I go out on tour,” Sheinbaum said before asserting that there is “deep pride” in being Mexican.

“This didn’t happen during neoliberalism in Mexico,” she said, referring to the period between 1982 and 2018.

Rather, “deep pride” in being Mexican became more prevalent with “fourth transformation” (4T) governments in office, said Sheinbaum, who now leads the 4T movement founded by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

“And it’s very powerful — very powerful because when a people knows their strength and their history, there is nothing that can stop them,” she said.

World.title: Opinion: Mexico is AI’s secret weapon
World.content:
A few days ago, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, published an essay arguing that AI is advancing so fast that we need to slow down — not stop, but ensure safety keeps pace with capability. Within hours, Sam Altman of OpenAI responded: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.” Elon Musk followed: “Dario is right.”

When those three agree on something, you pay attention.

Amodei’s warning is specific: “In 6-12 months, a swarm like the one in the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet, potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage — and the scale of damage would continue to increase if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.”

His proposed solution has three steps: embedded third-party evaluators inside AI companies, democratic coordination among allied countries on safety standards and eventually, global coordination. The phrase “democratic coalition” appears repeatedly in his framework.

That’s where I can actually say something useful.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that “nothing would matter if China wins the AI race.” Amodei agrees. A Chinese lead in AI, he argues, would pose grave danger, economically, but most importantly: militarily, through AI-driven weapons systems and geopolitical dominance. At its core, this is a national security conversation dressed in technology clothing.

And national security conversations have physical requirements. AI runs on hardware: servers, chips, data centers, power, cooling systems, specialized cables, transformers, processing units. It runs on supply chains. It runs on energy. It runs on engineers.

The United States needs all of those things faster than it can build them domestically, and it needs them from partners it can trust.

Which brings me to Mexico.

In the first half of 2026, Mexico’s computer-related exports reached US $82.9 billion, a 172% increase from the same period a year earlier, putting computing equipment ahead of automobiles and auto parts ($74.8 billion) for the first time in thirty years.

Mexico doesn’t export algorithms and code. It is building the physical layer that makes AI possible; the unglamorous, essential plumbing of the AI data center buildout. The United States accounted for 93.9% of those exports, which tells you everything about the strategic nature of this relationship.

This new nearshoring wave is not a buzzword; it is an AI supply-chain strategy embedded in a global security race. BTW: I’ve written about this before.

U.S. data center investment reached $102.2 billion in 2025, growing nearly 30% year over year. Mexico’s export growth tracks that figure almost perfectly — the architecture of an integrated continental co-production system responding to a common demand signal. Folks, this is actually okay! Not just that, it is strategic and necessary.

Amodei calls for cutting off powerful AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment from China and cracking down on smuggling operations. He’s right. But that strategy only works if you have an alternative. Mexico — integrated into North American supply chains, operating under USMCA digital trade rules, with a manufacturing base that pivots fast — is a large part of that alternative.

Now, here’s the number that makes Washington uncomfortable: Mexico’s imports from Taiwan surged 220% in the first half of 2026. Computer equipment imports from Asia into Mexico are booming. Since those components are assembled into goods that cross north into the United States, this shows up, mechanically, as a larger U.S.-Mexico trade deficit.

I can already hear the reaction in certain corners of Washington, D.C.

But this is precisely the kind of number that demands context before it demands a tariff. What is actually happening is that North America — through Mexico’s manufacturing base — is progressively substituting Asian-sourced inputs and redirecting them through a regional production platform that delivers the servers, components, and infrastructure American firms need to build AI data centers faster, cheaper and without the geopolitical risk of direct dependence on Taiwan or China.

A tariff on Mexican electronics would tax precisely the substitution away from China that U.S. policy is trying to achieve. It would be, in effect, a tax on America’s own AI infrastructure — and on America’s own capacity to win this race.

The deficit is not a sign of a broken relationship. It is a sign of an integrated continental production system doing exactly what it was designed to do.

The “democratic coalition” Amodei calls for doesn’t need inventing. It needs to be deepened — starting with the country that shares 2,000 miles of border with the United States, a trade agreement that explicitly covers digital trade, deep supply chain integration, and a talent base that is the envy of the world.

Every day the North American neighborhood spends fighting over tariffs, USMCA renewal mechanics and trade deficits that don’t mean what people think they mean is a day China runs faster on AI infrastructure, critical minerals, energy policy and diplomatic reach.

The question is not whether Mexico is relevant to the AI race. The question is whether the people making policy decisions in Washington are looking at the right numbers and the right strategic angle.

You don’t win a race by slowing down your most integrated and reliable partner.

Pedro Casas Alatriste is the Executive Vice President and CEO of the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico (AmCham). Previously, he has been the Director of Research and Public Policy at the US-Mexico Foundation in Washington, D.C. and the Coordinator of International Affairs at the Business Coordinating Council (CCE). He has also served as a consultant to the Inter-American Development Bank. Follow his Substack here.

World.title: MND Local: Independence Day in Puerto Vallarta and Nayarit
World.content:
It’s Independence Week in Puerto Vallarta and Nayarit, Mexico, and there’s no shortage of ways to celebrate.

From civic ceremonies and charro parades to mariachi, fireworks and the inevitable late-night Grito, the next few days will be about as Mexican as it gets. Even if you’re not planning to attend every event, it’s hard not to get caught up in the atmosphere. Flags appear on balconies and shopfronts, restaurants bring out special menus and the whole region seems to shift into a more festive mood.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Don Capellani (@doncapellani)

Here’s what’s happening around the region this week:

Puerto Vallarta

Puerto Vallarta’s official Fiestas Patrias celebrations run Sept. 13-16, with the Plaza de Armas, Malecón and downtown area serving as the main stages.

Monday, Sept. 14, brought the traditional charro parade at 10 a.m. The parade began on Ignacio L. Vallarta Street, traveled along the Malecón and wrapped up near the Ley store in Cinco Diciembre.

A formal City Council session is scheduled for 8 a.m. Tuesday, Sept. 15, followed by the evening’s celebrations in the Plaza de Armas. DJ Zuar, accompanied by batucada and pre-Hispanic dancers, takes the stage at 6:30 p.m., followed by the Ballet Folklórico Cuauhtémoc and Mariachi Internacional Real de América.

Grupo Caché performs at 9:30 p.m. Then, at 11 p.m., it’s time for the Grito de Independencia from the Municipal Presidency.

Fireworks will follow at 11:30 p.m. over the Malecón, with Banda Vallejo scheduled to close out the night at midnight. That sounds like a long evening, but this is one of those occasions when nobody seems in much of a hurry to go home.

Wednesday, Sept. 16, begins with an 8 a.m. civic ceremony in the Plaza de Armas, followed by the Independence Day civic-military parade at 9 a.m. The parade will follow the same general route as the charro parade.

Bahía de Banderas

Across the river in Nayarit, Bahía de Banderas will have its own Independence celebrations, with the municipal festivities centered in Valle de Banderas.

On Tuesday, Sept. 15, the municipality will hold its Noche Mexicana in the town’s main plaza, including the traditional Grito led by Mayor Israel Santillán.

The evening’s entertainment will include Mariachi Internacional de México, Banda La Taberna “La Más Guapa” and Banda Arkangel R-15.

On Wednesday, Sept. 16, the traditional civic and military parade will take place. Municipal officials are advising residents to check official traffic notices for the parade route and any resulting road closures.

Nayarit

The state government is also preparing for two days of celebrations in Tepic.

The program begins Tuesday, Sept. 15, with the raising of the Mexican flag and Honores a la Bandera at 8 a.m., followed by the lowering of the flag at 6 p.m.

At 7 p.m., the artistic program, “México Vivo, Nayarit Eterno,” begins, featuring the Ballet Nuevo Nayarit, the Traditional Youth Mariachi of the State School of Fine Arts, the State Symphony Band and singer María Dolores, along with Mariachi Nayarit Contemporáneo and Son de Mi Pueblo.

The public celebration gets underway at 9 p.m., with 7,000 free portions of food and drinks planned.

At 11 p.m., Governor Miguel Ángel Navarro Quintero will lead the Grito de Independencia, followed by a musical fireworks display and performances by Banda Ráfaga and norteño group La Session.

The celebrations continue Wednesday with the traditional parade in the morning. At 5 p.m., Marimba Orquesta Águilas de Chiapas will perform in Plaza Benito Juárez, in front of Casa de Gobierno.

So, for the next few days, expect much of the region to be focused on flags, food, music, fireworks and the familiar cry that brings everyone together for at least one night: ¡Viva México!

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Biodiseño MX at the Franz Mayer Museum explores more-than-human design
World.content:
When visitors enter the “Biodiseño MX” exhibition at the Franz Mayer Museum, earthen tones and other elements evoke the feeling of “entering an ecosystem.” Later, the exhibition transforms from its earthy finishes as color and light shift toward white, creating the atmosphere of a laboratory.

The exhibition’s power is reflected not only in this juxtaposition, but can also be seen in the curated design pieces, spanning popular art and practices rooted in ancestral knowledge to technological innovations, such as 3D-printed memorial reefs made from human ashes.

Curated by Taina Campos, “Biodiseño MX” brings together more than 60 creatives who explore design from a more-than-human perspective — in “collaboration with and for nature.”

What is biodesign?

Design is the creative approach to solving a problem. But since the Industrial Revolution, designers have been put at the service of the market, argues Campos. The Mexico-based designer and curator explains that biodesign is a fundamental shift in current design practice from an anthropocentric approach toward a symbiotic worldview, where nature is not only exploited for resources but integrated into the design process.

In interdependence with flora, fauna, microbes and fungi, and drawing from bio-inspiration, design pieces at the exhibition explore a world beyond anthropocentrism.

More-than-human design

Although symbiotic, biodesign is still susceptible to human ideas and needs. Campos acknowledges that, when approaching biodesign from an anthropocentric perspective, the tendency to create objects that cater to human needs persists.

But although a substantial part of the exhibition is centered around objects for human life — like tableware made from eggshells — certain pieces explore a more-than-human design.

The “Memorial Reef” by the U.K.-based company Resting Reef consists of 3D-printed artificial reef structures made from human ashes and calcium carbonate. According to Resting Reef, introducing those phosphorus-rich sculptures to underwater sites is meant to nourish marine communities. This project adds another question to biodesign: How can biodesign move toward regeneration?

The exhibition’s juxtaposition

The exhibition juxtaposes biodesign for functional objects like biofashion with pieces that help restore marine ecosystems or create oxygen.

“Jardín lacustre” by Mariana Paredes and Molecular Lab takes microalgae from Lake Texcoco and feeds them carbon dioxide from Mexico City’s polluted air. Through photosynthesis, these algae produce oxygen, escalating biodesign from a utilitarian need to a question of ecological survival.

The pieces of popular art made by Indigenous peoples of the Global South reflect an understanding that nature is “intrinsic to us,” while contrasting with technological innovation abundant throughout the exhibition.

Design as a revolution

When speaking about Campos’ motivation for biodesign, she mentions that design has an impact on how we understand the world through objects, systems and everyday applications. Biodesign is not only a design practice but another way to see the world.

“For me, biodesign is the language or practice — the material expression of design — that can lead us toward this other pursuit of design,” she explains. “It is no longer only about solving human problems or making beautiful products to sell; it is about generating another understanding of the world.”

She cites Arturo Escobar’s “Designs for the Pluriverse:” “Design designs worlds, and the worlds it designs design us back.”

“Biodiseño MX” is on display at the Franz Mayer Museum until Oct. 25, 2026.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Taste of Mexico: The curious history and myths of chile en nogada
World.content:
September, known as the “mes patrio” or patriotic month, has begun. This is the month when Mexicans commemorate the consummation of our independence, which took place in 1821. During the official celebration on Sept. 15, the president reenacts the way the independence movement began with what we call the “grito” — the cry of independence.

We also celebrate the grito at home, accompanied by family and friends. We dress up to look even more Mexican with sombreros, fake mustaches and braids. We drink tequila, sing Mexican songs, shout “Viva México” and, of course, eat.

Perhaps the most famous seasonal dish, and the one that generates the most intrigue for me, is chile en nogada.



The dish is essentially a stuffed poblano pepper covered in a walnut sauce. The stuffing is a mixture of beef with fruits such as apple, peach, banana and pear, along with almonds, pine nuts, walnuts, onion and garlic. Its flavor profile, combining sweet and salty, is outstanding.

And now, the intriguing part

As a historian, I am fascinated by how official history is shaped, and I find it puzzling that chile en nogada is included in September’s menu as the quintessential Mexican dish.

According to information from an official government page, on Aug. 28, 1821, the Augustinian nuns of the Convent of Santa Mónica in the state of Puebla welcomed the first Emperor of independent Mexico, Agustín de Iturbide, with a newly created dish that represented the colors of the new national flag: green, white and red. This, the tale goes, is how chile en nogada came to be.

The historical records, however, tell a different story: Agustín de Iturbide did travel to Puebla in 1821, but he arrived on Aug. 5. The list of supplies purchased for the emperor’s reception shows that the ingredients needed to make the chile en nogada weren’t acquired, so it is highly unlikely that he ever tried the dish. Nevertheless, he did enjoy a splendid banquet.

The idea that the nuns created the dish for Iturbide is a myth: Historical records indicate that the recipe was already being prepared in the early 1800s. Researcher Lilia Martínez has discovered that nogada is a European sauce with documented origins going back to the 15th century.

It’s important to note that without the Spanish Conquest, this dish would be impossible, since most of the ingredients used in chile en nogada originate in Spain or were brought over in the intercontinental trade of the time. These ingredients include the English walnut, a protein option of pork, beef or chicken, pomegranate, almonds, apples, pears, peaches and bananas.

The poblano pepper is the sole ingredient native to this land — a huge and vital contribution, if I may add.

So why is it considered the quintessential Mexican dish?

“Je ne sais pas,” the French would say. Wouldn’t it make much more sense if we ate a mole madre or a “tlacoyo?” Or maybe we eat it because it’s the conjunction of two great culinary traditions. Regardless of the reason, I can promise you two things: first, it is one of the most delicious dishes in Mexican cuisine you’ll ever try. Second, once I find out when it became the quintessential Mexican dish, I will create a video and write an article about it.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mexico News Daily (@mexiconewsdaily)

Where can you eat it?

Any Mexican restaurant will have its version of chile en nogada. However, in my opinion, the best chiles I’ve had are found in Puebla. If you can’t go there, look for a thick, ivory-white sauce on your plate, and you’ll probably have an amazing chile en nogada.

I considered sharing the recipe, but every family has its own version, and I don’t want to offend anyone by claiming that mine is the ultimate recipe. This recipe is over three centuries old, from a time when people had the luxury of peeling walnuts with their fingernails and taking time to appreciate the landscape, so it requires a lot of time and patience; as in, two whole days. My parents had two comadres who prepared chile en nogada for the entire family, a party of 80 including us. A group of six women had to spend a whole week in the kitchen. We were fortunate, no doubt.



Do you have a good chile en nogada recipe to share with us, or is the one you use a family secret? Do you know where the best chile en nogada can be found? Share in the comments below.

María Meléndez is a writer and art historian. She works at the Mexican Cultural Institute of the Embassy of Mexico in Washington, D.C.

World.title: A Drone Hit a Saudi Pipeline, Oil Prices Passed US$108, and Brazilian Banks Paid for It
World.content:
MARKETS · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Drones hit a Saudi oil pipeline. The price of a barrel went above US$108.

— Why Latin America cares The region both sells oil and buys fuel. Monday moved both sides at once.

— The pipeline It was built to carry Saudi crude away from the Gulf, avoiding the world’s tightest shipping lane.

— The second squeeze That lane, the Strait of Hormuz, is already carrying about a third of its normal traffic.

— In São Paulo Petrobras shares rose. The stock market still fell, dragged down by banks and miners.

— The catch Neither the Chilean nor the Colombian peso gained, though both countries sell commodities.

The pipeline that was attacked exists because of the shipping lane that is also blocked. That is why one drone moved so much money.

Crude on the water. The pipeline now shut was built so that tankers could avoid the Gulf. (Photo: “00 3357 MAXINE DEYMANN – Tankschiff” by W. Bulach, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. Sometime in the dark between Thursday and Friday, drones launched from southern Iraq crossed into Saudi Arabia and found a pipeline. Oil prices have not stopped moving since.

By Monday lunchtime the consequences had reached a trading floor in São Paulo. They did not land where anyone expected.

Oil prices went above US$108 a barrel, against a Friday close of US$104.61. The Brazilian stock market opened more than three thousand points lower.

The Pipeline That Exists Because of the Strait

The line the drones hit runs 1,200 kilometres from Abqaiq in eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu on the Red Sea. The industry calls it Petroline.

It was built for one reason. Oil loaded at Yanbu never has to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and Oman.

Hormuz has been the single point of failure in the oil trade for fifty years. Petroline was the answer to it.

So the pipeline is not an ordinary piece of infrastructure. It is the hedge, and the hedge is what has been taken out.

Saudi Arabia says the line was stopped as a precaution. The energy ministry spoke, and Saudi Aramco itself said nothing.

The foreign ministry blamed drones flown from Iraq and reported injuries. Iraq’s prime minister confirmed launches from Maysan province and dismissed the local commander.

Nobody has claimed the attack. Between four and five million barrels a day were moving through the line, close to one barrel in twenty worldwide.

Why the Hedge Mattered This Week

In a normal month those barrels would simply take the other route. They would sail out through Hormuz instead, and the market would shrug.

This is not a normal month. Traffic through the strait has fallen to roughly seven million barrels a day, against about twenty before the current conflict.

Ships are reported to need Iranian permission to pass. On Sunday a merchant vessel was struck there, killing one crew member and injuring three.

Counting what actually moves has become contentious. Commercial trackers log ten to thirteen transits a day, while United States officials give figures several times higher.

Monday’s trigger was not military at all. Oman postponed talks between the Gulf states and Iran over shipping, and set no new date.

That was enough. With the bypass shut and the strait rationed, traders had nowhere to put oil prices except higher.

Petrobras. Its shares rose on Monday while the wider Brazilian market fell. (Photo: “At Rio de Janeiro 2019 435” by Photograph by Mike Peel ( www.mikepeel.net )., via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

It operates through three segments: Exploration and Production; Refining, Transportation & Marketing; and Gas & Low Carbon Energies. The Exploration and Production segment explores, develops, and produces…

What Brazil Actually Did With the News

The obvious expectation was that Brazil’s oil producer would carry the market. The opposite happened.

Petrobras rose, with its preferred shares up about 1.1%. PetroRio, Brava and PetroReconcavo gained alongside it.

The Ibovespa fell anyway. It touched 183,813 before recovering to around 185,400 by early afternoon in Brasília.

The weight came from the lenders and the miners. Bradesco, Santander Brasil, Vale, Itaú, B3 and Banco do Brasil each lost between 1.8% and 2.4%.

Three forces pressed at once. Expensive crude, a United States ten-year yield above 5%, and a global retreat from technology shares.

Brasília supplied a fourth. The Supreme Court meets on Tuesday in a crisis that has run a fortnight, and money dislikes watching institutions fight.

The real slipped to around 5.17 to the dollar. These were intraday levels, taken before the session closed.

The Currencies That Refused to Cooperate

There is a tidy version of this story in which oil exporters’ currencies strengthen. Monday declined to provide it.

The Chilean peso fell for a fourth straight session, reaching 957.45 to the dollar. It has not been that weak since October 2025.

Copper explains part of it. The metal dropped 1.37% and has now fallen four days running, which matters more to Chile than any barrel does.

Colombia has no such excuse. It sells oil, and its peso still weakened to around 3,105 against an official rate of 3,072.27.

The dollar was simply stronger than everything. Its index rose 0.57% as investors positioned for Wednesday’s Federal Reserve decision.

Argentina did not move at all. The parallel dollar finished at 1,545 pesos, flat, with the gap to the official rate near 1%.

The Colombian Windfall That Is Not One

One number is travelling fast in Bogotá. A figure of 35 to 40 trillion pesos, about US$13bn, has been attached to this week’s rally.

It came from Frank Pearl, who runs Colombia’s petroleum and gas association. It is the industry’s estimate, not the treasury’s.

It also describes the sector’s total contribution across the whole of 2026, rather than any windfall. And it assumes oil prices average US$90 to US$100 for the year.

Colombia’s own financial plan assumes US$85.50. One violent Monday does not make an annual average, and the fiscal year has three months left to disagree.

More: Latin American business and markets, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did oil prices rise so sharply?

Drones hit Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline overnight between 10 and 11 September, and it was shut. The line carried four to five million barrels a day, close to 5% of world supply.

Is the Strait of Hormuz closed?

No. It is open but heavily restricted, carrying roughly seven million barrels a day against about twenty million before the conflict. Reports of a closure are not supported by shipping trackers.

Why does one pipeline matter this much?

Because it was built to avoid Hormuz. With the strait already rationed, the route that existed as insurance against it is the one now out of service.

Did Petrobras shares fall with the Brazilian market?

No. Petrobras rose about 1.1% on Monday. The Ibovespa was pulled down by Vale and the large Brazilian banks.

Will Colombia collect 40 trillion pesos in extra royalties?

That figure, about US$13bn, is an industry association estimate of the sector’s total 2026 contribution rather than extra income. It assumes a full-year average price of US$90 to US$100.

Sources: Trading Economics, Euronews, Al Jazeera, EnergyNow, InfoMoney, Seu Dinheiro, La Tercera, El Espectador, La Nacion and La Republica.

World.title: Brazil Supreme Court Meets Tuesday to Decide Whether One of Its Own Can Be Investigated
World.content:
BRAZIL · JUDICIARY

Key Facts — The situation Brazil’s highest court is deciding whether to investigate one of its own eleven judges.

— The judge Alexandre de Moraes, who led the prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

— The allegation A bank that collapsed last year paid millions to a law firm owned by his wife.

— The bank Banco Master failed in November owing about US$2.3bn to some 1.6 million ordinary savers.

— What happens Tuesday The judges meet in emergency session. On paper they are ruling on the federal police chief.

— The catch Any single judge can stop the whole thing by asking for more time to read the file.

Courts everywhere protect their own. Brazil is about to find out, in public, whether its highest one will.

Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court, where eleven judges sit for life until the age of 75. (Photo: “Brasilia Supreme Federal Court of Brazil 2009” by Cayambe, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

At ten o’clock on Tuesday morning, the eleven judges of the Brazil Supreme Court take their seats in Brasília. One of them is the reason the session was called.

The Brazil Supreme Court has spent a fortnight tearing at itself in public. Tuesday is the day it either stops or does not.

How a Failed Bank Reached the Bench

Banco Master was a mid-sized lender in São Paulo that sold savers high-yield deposits it could not cover. Regulators shut it down on 18 November 2025.

The hole is estimated at 12bn reais, about US$2.3bn, and roughly 1.6 million people had money in it. Its owner, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested the day before, boarding a private jet to Malta.

Police took his phone. That is where this story really begins.

On 1 September a judge named André Mendonça unsealed a 218-page report drawn from that phone. It described a contract between the bank and the law firm of Viviane Barci de Moraes.

She is married to Alexandre de Moraes, the judge who led the prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro. He is the most powerful and most disliked figure on the court, depending on who you ask.

In most countries a judge’s spouse may practise law. What made this different was the sum, the timing, and who was paying.

The Week the Court Turned on Itself

What followed was not a legal process so much as a slow-motion collision. Mendonça ordered the removal of the head of Brazil’s federal police.

A second judge, Flávio Dino, reinstated the man the same week. A third, the chief justice Edson Fachin, suspended both decisions and called Tuesday’s emergency session.

Thirteen retired justices wrote to Fachin demanding an immediate investigation. They called it the most acute crisis in the court’s history, and they are the people best placed to know.

The prosecutor-general’s office has filed twice, in opposite directions. It first sought to void the police report, then asked for related bank records to be made public.

On Sunday a fourth judge, Cristiano Zanin, ordered the police to hand him the raw phone data by eleven that night. Evidence, he wrote, belongs to the whole court and not to any one member.

It arrived on Monday morning and his staff began reading. Nobody else on the bench has confirmed receiving it.

The Square of the Three Powers. Court, congress and presidency face each other across it. (Photo: “Imagens de Brasília – Praça dos Três Poderes – 49732065671” by Senado Federal, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

What Is Actually on the Order Paper

Here the drama and the paperwork diverge. Tuesday’s session is listed as Petition 16,662, which concerns the removal of the federal police director-general.

That sounds like an administrative squabble, and legally it is. But it is also the file inside which every step against Moraes was taken.

Strike down what was done in that petition and the investigation touching Moraes goes with it. That is why a procedural vote has become a national event.

Not everyone accepts the framing. Gilmar Mendes, the court’s longest-serving member, has objected that the matter has no defined procedural shape at all.

One more detail has escaped most accounts. Mendonça is no longer in charge of the case.

Fachin took it over on Saturday, reasoning that the session might raise the question of Moraes stepping aside. Under the court’s rules, that question belongs to its president.

The Single Word That Could End It

Brazilian judges have an instrument called a vista. One of them asks for more time to study a file, and the judgment stops where it is.

It can last weeks. In an election year, weeks are everything.

Brazilians go to the polls in early October. A case suspended now would not return until the votes are counted.

Mendonça is reported to want his vote recorded early, before anyone can reach for that lever. Allies of Moraes are expected to reach for it anyway.

No such request has yet been filed. It is the move everyone is watching for rather than one that has happened.

Why This Matters Beyond Brazil

Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America and its court is unusually powerful by any international standard. It has removed a president, jailed a former one, and regulated social media.

That power was tolerable while the court appeared united. A bench that investigates its own members in public is a different institution.

Investors noticed on Monday, when the São Paulo market fell about 1% with banks leading it down. A Brazil Supreme Court at war with itself has a price.

Whatever the eleven decide, the tearing is already visible. Tuesday determines only whether it is done quickly or slowly.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Brazil Supreme Court deciding on Tuesday?

Formally, a case about the removal of the federal police chief. In practice, whether the investigation touching Justice Alexandre de Moraes survives, because every step in it was taken inside that case.

Why is a judge being investigated?

A police report drawn from the phone of a collapsed bank’s owner describes payments to a law firm owned by the judge’s wife. The judge has not been charged.

What was Banco Master?

A mid-sized São Paulo bank that sold savers high-yield deposits without the assets to cover them. Regulators shut it in November 2025, leaving a hole of about US$2.3bn affecting some 1.6 million people.

Could the session be postponed?

Yes. Any judge may request a vista, which suspends the judgment while that judge studies the file. With elections in early October, a suspension now would push a decision past the vote.

Who is in charge of the case?

Chief Justice Edson Fachin, who took it over on 12 September from Justice André Mendonça. Many accounts still name Mendonça and are out of date.

Sources: Supreme Federal Court press note of 9 September, ConJur, Migalhas, CNN Brasil, Poder360, Agência Pública and O Povo.

World.title: Two Brazil Runoff Polls Put Different Men in Front. The Difference Is a Telephone.
World.content:
BRAZIL · ELECTION

Key Facts — The election Brazil votes for a president in early October, and few expect it to end in one round.

— The contenders President Lula, now 80, against Flávio Bolsonaro, senator and son of the previous president.

— Poll one Quaest sent interviewers to people’s homes. It found Flávio Bolsonaro ahead, 42 to 40.

— Poll two Nexus telephoned a similar sample on overlapping days. It found Lula ahead, 47 to 46.

— The agreement Both give Lula the same five-point lead in the first round. That margin is identical.

— The catch Neither lead clears the margin of error. Both races are ties dressed up as results.

Both polls were in the field on the same days, testing the same names. Then they published headlines that contradicted each other.

The Planalto palace in Brasília, the prize both men are contesting in October. (Photo: “Imagens de Brasília – Praça dos Três Poderes – 49732065671” by Senado Federal, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

On Monday Brazil woke to two Brazil runoff polls that appeared to describe different countries. One had the challenger winning, the other had the president holding on.

Both were taken in the same week, testing the same six candidates. The explanation is not politics but the way the questions were asked.

The Election Everyone Is Measuring

Brazilians vote for a president on the first Sunday of October. If nobody clears half the vote, the top two meet again three weeks later.

Nobody expects anyone to clear half. So the polls that matter are the ones testing that second round.

On one side is Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80 years old and in his third term. He has been the dominant figure in Brazilian politics for a quarter of a century.

On the other is Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and the eldest son of Jair Bolsonaro, the president Lula replaced. He carries his father’s movement and his father’s legal problems.

What the Two Brazil Runoff Polls Found

Quaest, published for the Globo media group, put Flávio Bolsonaro ahead by 42% to 40%. Its interviewers went to people’s homes with tablets.

Nexus, published for the investment bank BTG Pactual, put Lula ahead by 47% to 46%. Its interviewers used the telephone.

Quaest was in the field from 10 to 13 September, Nexus from 11 to 13. Three of the four days overlap.

Both tested the same six names. Both surveyed just over two thousand people.

Neither result is outside the margin of error, which both put at two points. In the language of polling these are two ties.

The Number Nobody Led With

Turn to the first round and the two surveys stop disagreeing entirely. Quaest has Lula on 36% and Flávio Bolsonaro on 31%.

Nexus has them on 42% and 37%. The levels differ by six points in both cases.

The gap between the two men is five points in each poll. Two firms, two methods, one answer.

The other candidates line up as neatly. Cury takes 7% and 6%, Caiado 4% and 5%, Zema 1% in both.

Brazil’s congress. Polls here must be registered with the electoral authority before publication. (Photo: “Brasilia Congresso Nacional 05 2007 221” by Mario Roberto Duran Ortiz, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.)

Why the Telephone Changes the Answer

A person on the telephone is talking to a stranger and wants the call to end. Asked to choose between two names, most choose one.

A person on their own doorstep has time to say they have not decided. The interviewer waits, and the answer stays open.

The arithmetic shows it plainly. In the Quaest second round, 42 plus 40 leaves 18% of voters unassigned.

In the Nexus second round, 47 plus 46 leaves 7%. That eleven-point gap is the entire disagreement.

The same pattern appears in the first round, where Quaest records 10% undecided against Nexus on 2%. Neither firm is wrong.

They are measuring the same electorate through different instruments. Instruments have personalities.

The Trend That Is Real

Comparing two firms tells you about polling. Comparing one firm with itself tells you about voters.

Quaest has now run the same question three times in a fortnight, the same way each time. On 2 September Lula led by one point.

On 7 September it was level at 41 each. On 14 September Flávio Bolsonaro led by two.

That is a drift of three points towards the challenger in twelve days. It is small, and unlike the headline contradiction it is genuine.

Other Brazil runoff polls bracket it. Datafolha had Lula ahead by two on 11 September, while AtlasIntel, polling online, had Flávio Bolsonaro nominally ahead.

One Number to Read Carefully

Both polls asked about the government twice, in ways that are not interchangeable. Quaest found 43% approving and 50% disapproving.

Asked instead to rate the government, 38% of the same sample called it bad or terrible. That is twelve points below the disapproval figure.

Nexus shows the same effect more gently, with 49% disapproving and 44% rating it badly. Approval and rating are different questions about the same president.

In the weeks ahead both numbers will be quoted as though they were one. They are not, and the gap between them is wide enough to win an argument with.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which of the two Brazil runoff polls is right?

Both, within their own margins. Each shows a statistical tie, and each gives Lula the same five-point first-round lead over Flávio Bolsonaro.

Why do the headline numbers differ?

Quaest interviews people at home and leaves 18% of second-round voters unassigned. Nexus telephones and leaves 7%. A telephone call pushes undecided voters into naming someone.

Who are the candidates?

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, seeking a fourth term, and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Four other names are polling in single figures.

When does Brazil vote?

The first round falls on the first Sunday of October, with a runoff three weeks later if nobody wins more than half the vote. No candidate is close to that.

Has Flávio Bolsonaro taken the lead?

Not in any meaningful sense. His two-point margin sits inside a two-point margin of error, and a poll published the same day has Lula ahead.

Sources: Nexus Pesquisa e Inteligência release of 14 September, Poder360, Gazeta do Povo, Brasil de Fato, CartaCapital, Metrópoles and Correio Braziliense.

World.title: Falkland Islands Jet Claim Collapses: Four Typhoons Out, Four In, in Late 2027
World.content:
SOUTH ATLANTIC · DEFENCE

Key Facts — The islands A windswept British territory of 3,600 people, 500km off Argentina, which claims them as the Malvinas.

— The history Argentina invaded in 1982. The 74-day war killed 649 Argentines, 255 Britons and 3 islanders.

— The islanders In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% voted to stay British. Three people voted against.

— The claim this week That Britain is sending extra fighter jets in response to Argentina’s president.

— The document Four ageing Typhoons will be swapped for four newer ones, in late 2027.

— The catch Argentina’s protest note to Uruguay is dated before the speech it supposedly answers.

A written answer to a backbench question in London became, by the time it reached Buenos Aires, a military response to Argentina.

The Typhoon. Four are stationed in the South Atlantic, and four will remain. (Photo: “A retired Royal Air Force (RAF) F-4M Phantom FGR.2 aircraft formerly of No. 1435 Flight RAF as the gate guardian at the entrance to the air terminal at Mount Pleasant Complex in the Falkland Islands, 2007” by The joy of all things, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

On 7 September a Conservative backbencher in London put a written question to the Ministry of Defence. He asked about the aircraft stationed in the Falkland Islands.

A junior minister answered three days later, in the flat prose these replies always use. By Monday that answer had become, in Buenos Aires, a British military response to Argentina.

What the Answer Actually Says

Four Tranche 1 Typhoon fighters are currently assigned to British forces in the Falkland Islands. They are to be replaced by four Tranche 2 Typhoons drawn from the existing fleet.

The rotation is planned for late November to early December 2027. The four older aircraft will then be scrapped.

Four before, four after. The newer airframes have better radar and weapons, so it is a modernisation.

It is not more aeroplanes. It is the same number, of a slightly younger vintage, in fourteen months’ time.

The reply ends with a standard sentence noting that British F-35 aircraft remain available for global tasking. That formula appears in dozens of answers a year and commits nobody to anything.

Why the Framing Does Not Survive Contact

This was not a government announcement. There was no press release, no ministerial statement and no photograph of anyone standing in front of a jet.

It was a minister answering an opposition backbencher in writing, one of hundreds such replies each week. Nobody in London intended it as a signal.

It also predates the argument it is said to answer. The ministry said in April 2025 that those four aircraft would stay until 2027.

It confirmed on 13 July 2026 that they would remain at Mount Pleasant as part of a wider upgrade programme. That was seven weeks before Argentina’s president made the speech this is framed as a reply to.

Mount Pleasant normally hosts three small flights. Four Typhoons for air defence, a tanker and a transport aircraft, and a few helicopters.

The one genuinely new movement runs the other way. A tanker returned on 3 September after five months in the Middle East.

That restores the normal establishment rather than adding to it. It was spotted by aircraft trackers, not announced.

Stanley, capital of a territory with more sheep than people. (Photo: “Town Hall in Stanley, Falkland Islands” by Liam Quinn, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

The Bill That Has Not Been Written

President Javier Milei announced a sovereignty package on television on 3 September. Two decrees followed the next day.

One shifts money within the defence and security budget. The other makes the foreign ministry responsible for enforcing a 2011 law on oil drilling around the islands.

A bill was also promised, and the bill is what has been reported as formalised. On Monday the government was still deciding what it would contain.

It had not settled whether to present one bill or two. Nothing has been introduced in either chamber of congress.

What is known of the intent: heavier penalties reaching suppliers, shareholders and directors of oil companies operating there. Also trials in absentia, a national security council, and a naval base at Ushuaia.

The cabinet decided it should enter through the lower house. This is a government that has been losing votes there.

The Protest Montevideo Receives Every Year

The third front is a trade fair. Expo Prado, Uruguay’s big agricultural exposition, opened in Montevideo on 11 September.

Inside the British embassy stand was a small Falkland Islands desk promoting commerce and tourism, with gin to taste. Argentina objected in writing.

The objection was an embassy note to Uruguay’s foreign ministry. No ambassador was summoned, and the note is dated 31 August.

Milei‘s speech was on 3 September. A letter written three days earlier cannot be a response to it.

Uruguay’s deputy foreign minister, Valeria Csukasi, was asked about it at the Prado on Monday. She called the affair a confusion and said Argentina makes the same representation every year.

The Falklands have been showing up at Expo Prado since 2015, and Argentina has objected each time. A foreign ministry release from September 2017 says almost exactly the same thing.

What London Actually Said to Buenos Aires

Britain did reply to Milei, on 4 September, and the reply contained nothing military. The islands are British, the defence secretary said, because the islanders choose to be British.

He called the commitment absolute and unshakeable. The islanders’ own assembly issued an unsigned statement the same day saying their future is theirs to decide.

Underneath all of it sit two immovable positions. Argentina’s constitution makes recovering the islands a permanent national objective.

Britain rests its case on what the 3,600 people living there want. Neither side has moved in forty years.

In the 2013 referendum, turnout was 99.2% and 99.8% voted to remain British. Three people voted the other way, and nothing since has moved either government an inch.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Britain sending more fighter jets to the Falkland Islands?

No. A written parliamentary answer of 10 September describes four Typhoons being replaced by four Typhoons from the existing fleet, in late 2027. The number stationed there does not change.

Why does Argentina claim the islands?

Argentina says it inherited them from Spain and that Britain seized them in 1833. The claim is written into its 1994 constitution as a permanent national objective.

Has Milei sent a sovereignty bill to congress?

No. Two decrees were published on 4 September, but the bill was still being drafted on 14 September, and the government had not decided whether to present one bill or two.

What was the protest to Uruguay about?

A Falkland Islands desk inside the British embassy stand at the Expo Prado agricultural fair. The protest was an embassy note dated 31 August, and Uruguay says Argentina files one every year.

How many people live there?

About 3,600, mostly in the capital Stanley. In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% voted to remain a British overseas territory.

Sources: UK Parliament written question 27623 answered 10 September, RAF Mount Pleasant station pages, MercoPress, Infobae, Teledoce and the Argentine foreign ministry.

World.title: The Dark Horse Forensic Report Clears the Bolsonaro Film’s Money Without Tracing Its Source
World.content:
BRAZIL · INVESTIGATIONS

Key Facts — The film Dark Horse is an American biopic of Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil’s president until 2023.

— The question Brazilian police want to know whether public money and bank money financed it.

— The bank Banco Master collapsed last November. Its owner is accused of running a criminal enterprise.

— The report A forensic expert concluded the film’s US$13.3m was clean and traceable.

— Who paid for it The production company’s own defence lawyers commissioned it.

— The catch The same expert told a Brazilian outlet he never examined the fund the money arrived from.

The expert’s conclusion and the expert’s own interview describe two different pieces of work.

Dark Horse opened in the United States on 11 September. Brazil has no release date. (Photo: “Blackmagic Production Camera 4K” by Smashing Film, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Last Thursday a film about Jair Bolsonaro opened in American cinemas. In Brazil, a Dark Horse forensic report landed saying its money was clean.

Jim Caviezel plays the Brazilian president who governed until 2023. Police in Brasília are less interested in the acting than in the accounting.

The story covers the 2018 campaign and the knife attack that nearly killed him. The film has no release date in Brazil, only a federal police inquiry into who paid for it.

The Clean Bill of Health

Into that investigation has arrived a Dark Horse forensic report with a reassuring conclusion. The film cost US$13.3m, of which US$3.7m came from Brazil and US$9.6m from the United States.

No public money entered the production, it says, and every sum can be followed. The first investor is named as the Havengate Development Fund, a Texas property vehicle.

It was written by Anísio Costa Castelo Branco, who runs a private forensic institute. It was commissioned and paid for by the production company’s defence team.

That last fact is ordinary. Defendants everywhere hire their own experts, and the resulting report is evidence like any other.

The Interview Three Weeks Earlier

On 26 August, before his conclusions reached the press, the same expert gave an interview to the Brazilian outlet Poder360. He was asked where the money had come from.

He said he had not tracked the fund and had no contact with it. That information, he explained, was confidential to the fund itself.

What he had examined was the production company’s spending. Money going out, not money coming in.

It is a real piece of work and it answers a real question. It simply does not answer the one the investigation is asking.

Police consider the origin of the money fundamental, because the inquiry is about money laundering. Havengate is linked in police material to roughly 61m reais, about US$11.8m, associated with Daniel Vorcaro.

Vorcaro owned Banco Master, the São Paulo lender regulators shut in November 2025 with a hole of about US$2.3bn. He was arrested boarding a private jet to Malta.

Brazil’s lower house. A parliamentary grant of about US$390,000 sits inside the inquiry. (Photo: “Construção de Brasília Congresso Nacional e Câmara dos Deputados 1959” by unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.)

The Congressman and the Handwriting

A second thread runs through Brazil’s congress rather than its banks. It concerns a parliamentary grant of 2m reais, about US$390,000.

The grant was secured by Mário Frias, a former actor who served as Bolsonaro’s culture secretary. He now sits as a federal deputy, and is credited with the film’s story.

Justice Flávio Dino is overseeing an investigation into whether that public money reached the production. Frias has answered the court’s questions about the grants.

In June, São Paulo police searched the home of Karina Gama, who produced the film. Among the items seized were handwritten notes.

Estadão reports that those notes sketch a flow of funds between three entities. A name written as Mário is marked as a partner, and whether that is the congressman rests on a first name.

On 13 September, Dino authorised the use of financial intelligence reports in the police investigation of the production company. That is a separate authorisation from any examination of the film’s own books.

The Producer Who Will Not Talk

Karina Gama has become the pressure point, and she knows it. On 13 September she told CNN Brasil she is being pushed to cooperate and will not.

Her phrase invoked Mauro Cid, the army officer whose plea bargain shaped the coup-plot case against Bolsonaro. She will not, she said, be the new Mauro Cid.

Outlets render the wording slightly differently, some as the new one and some as the next. The meaning does not move.

What the Report Can and Cannot Settle

Nothing here suggests the expert was dishonest. He described the limits of his work plainly when a reporter asked.

The distance is between those limits and the headline his conclusions have produced. An audit of outgoings has been reported as a clearance of the funding.

Gazeta do Povo has separately argued that Dino’s investigation rests on vague suspicions and coincidences. That view belongs in the record alongside the rest.

No charges have been filed over the film’s financing. What exists is an American release, a Brazilian inquiry, and a report that answered a narrower question than the one being asked.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Dark Horse?

A biographical drama about Jair Bolsonaro, directed by Cyrus Nowrasteh and starring Jim Caviezel, covering the 2018 campaign and the stabbing. It opened in the United States on 11 September 2026 and has no Brazilian release date.

Who commissioned the Dark Horse forensic report?

The defence team of GoUp Entertainment, the production company. It is not a court-appointed or police examination.

Does it prove no public money funded the film?

It asserts that, but its author told Poder360 in August that he did not trace the fund the money arrived from. He examined the company’s outgoings rather than the origin of its income.

What is Havengate?

A Texas property fund named in the report as the film’s first investor. Police material links it to roughly 61m reais, about US$11.8m, associated with the owner of the collapsed Banco Master.

Has anyone been charged?

No charges have been reported over the film’s financing. The producer has publicly refused to enter a plea agreement.

Sources: Gazeta do Povo of 14 September, Poder360 of 26 August, Estadão, InfoMoney, Money Times and Metrópoles.

World.title: Sixteen Former Supreme Court Justices Are Left Alive in Brazil. Thirteen Signed. Three Did Not.
World.content:
BRAZIL · JUDICIARY

Key Facts — What happened Thirteen retired judges of Brazil’s highest court publicly demanded it investigate one of its own.

— Why that is rare Former judges almost never comment on their old court. Brazil has sixteen still living.

— The crisis A collapsed bank is alleged to have paid millions to the wife of a sitting judge.

— Their words They call it the most acute crisis in the court’s history and want an immediate inquiry.

— Who stayed out Two declined for different reasons. A third says nobody ever asked him to sign.

— The catch That third man is also Brazil’s serving justice minister, which makes his silence awkward.

Retired judges are famously silent. Four out of five of Brazil’s surviving ones just signed the same piece of paper.

Every one of the thirteen signatories once sat inside this building. (Photo: “Supremo Tribunal Federal building in Brasilia – DSC00288” by Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Former Supreme Court justices, in most countries, are the quietest people in public life. They write memoirs and decline to comment.

On 7 September, thirteen of Brazil’s wrote to the chief justice together. What went unreported is how few were left to ask.

The Arithmetic Nobody Published

Brazil has sixteen living former justices of its Supreme Federal Court. Thirteen signed the letter.

Of the remaining three, two publicly declined and one says he was never approached. That is 81% of everyone available.

No source states the figure of sixteen outright. It comes from adding the signatories to the named refusals.

Two men often assumed to be among the living are not.

José Carlos Moreira Alves died in October 2023. Sepúlveda Pertence has also died.

What They Wrote

The letter runs to a few paragraphs and does not name the judge at the centre of the affair. It does not need to.

It expresses full confidence in the seriousness, discernment and firmness of chief justice Edson Fachin. Then it asks for an immediate and rigorous investigation.

The signatories describe the situation as the most acute crisis in the court’s history. Coming from people who served through a military dictatorship and two impeachments, that is a considered phrase.

They say the events have been damaging the prestige and authority of the court. They add public confidence and the stability of democratic institutions to the list.

Celso de Mello, who sat for thirty-one years, issued a separate note of his own. No authority, he wrote, is above the law.

The court, he added, cannot be turned into a protective shield for individual deviations. He named nobody, and nobody needed him to.

The Three Who Did Not Sign

Luís Roberto Barroso is a former president of the court and the most internationally visible Brazilian jurist of his generation. He said no.

Signing an external manifesto, he explained, would cost him the ability to contribute from inside. He is reported to be talking quietly to serving judges on both sides.

Marco Aurélio Mello refused on grounds of manners. He said he would not have wished to receive such a document himself, were he still in the chief justice’s chair.

Ricardo Lewandowski gives a different account altogether. He says nobody asked him.

That claim carries weight, because Lewandowski is not only a retired judge. He is Brazil’s serving justice minister, in a government entangled in the same affair.

Whether the organisers skipped him deliberately has not been explained by anyone. Neither he nor they have offered a reason.

Brasília. The affair has drawn in the presidency, the police and the prosecution service. (Photo: “Palacio do Planalto” by Annemariebr at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.)

The Second Letter, and Why the Two Keep Merging

Six days later a different letter appeared, backing the same chief justice. It is routinely reported as the same document, and it is not.

This one demands transparency, stronger collective decision-making and rules on conflicts of interest. It says the court must not be captured by hidden interests.

Most outlets count 198 signatures, one counts 199, and nobody has resolved it. The signatories are jurists, businesspeople, economists, trade unionists and former government ministers.

There lies the confusion. In Portuguese, a cabinet minister and a supreme court judge are both called ministro.

The first came from thirteen former Supreme Court justices who sat on that very bench. The second came from a broad civic coalition, and the two carry different weight.

What Set It Off

On 1 September a serving judge, André Mendonça, unsealed a 218-page police report. It had been drawn from the phone of Daniel Vorcaro, owner of the collapsed Banco Master.

The report described payments from that bank to the law firm of Viviane Barci de Moraes. She is married to Alexandre de Moraes, the judge who led the prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

A week later Mendonça ordered the removal of Brazil’s federal police chief. A second judge reinstated him and the chief justice suspended both orders.

The letters were written into that gap. On Tuesday the eleven serving judges meet in emergency session, and the retired thirteen will be watching like everyone else.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many former Supreme Court justices signed?

Thirteen, on 7 September 2026. This newspaper counts sixteen living retired justices, reached by adding the signatories to the three who are on record declining or saying they were not asked.

Who refused to sign?

Luís Roberto Barroso, who said signing would prevent him contributing from inside the institution, and Marco Aurélio Mello, who cited respect for the current chief justice. Ricardo Lewandowski says he was never approached.

What does the letter ask for?

An immediate and rigorous investigation of the crisis, together with an expression of confidence in chief justice Edson Fachin. The signatories call it the most acute crisis in the court’s history.

Is this the same as the letter with 198 signatures?

No. That is a separate document from 13 September signed by jurists, businesspeople and former cabinet ministers. Portuguese uses the same word for both kinds of minister, which is why they are confused.

What triggered it?

The unsealing on 1 September of a police report describing payments from a collapsed bank to the law firm of a sitting judge’s wife, followed by conflicting orders over the federal police leadership.

Sources: ConJur, Rádio Pampa, Brasil em Folhas, Poder360 and A Tarde. The count of living former justices is this newspaper’s own, reconstructed from named signatories and named refusals.

World.title: The Kast Cadem Grade Is 3.4 Out of 7, and in Chile That Is a Failing Mark
World.content:
CHILE · GOVERNMENT

Key Facts — The president José Antonio Kast, a hard-line conservative, took office in March with the biggest vote Chile has ever cast.

— The question Pollsters asked Chileans to grade his first six months on the scale used in their schools.

— The answer An average of 3.4 out of 7. Four is the pass mark, so this is a fail.

— The cause he names A fuel price shock in March and unemployment now running at 9.5%.

— What people name The same two things. They simply disagree that the fuel decision was necessary.

— The catch His grade has not fallen. This is the first time anyone asked the question.

Chile marks schoolwork from one to seven, and four is a pass. Everyone in the country understood the number instantly.

La Moneda in Santiago. Kast reached six months in office on 11 September. (Photo: “Palacio de La Moneda – miguelreflex” by Miguel hernandez, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)
