World.title: Nationalist chiefs sign pact to make Burnham ‘the last UK prime minister’
World.content:
But all three agreed that Trump’s sentiments reinforced their own sense that the time was right for independence referendums in Scotland and Ireland, and a push for greater devolution of powers from Westminster to the Welsh Assembly.

“Each of our nations has the right to determine its own future, through democratic means and in accordance with the wishes of its people,” the three parties said in a joint statement.

They met in Cardiff to acknowledge the fact that all three devolved administrations in the U.K. are now led by nationalists for the first time following May’s electoral trouncing by Plaid Cymru of Burnham’s Labour, long the party of government in Wales.

Sweeney, Scotland’s leader since 2024, is seeking a second independence referendum following the failed 2014 vote. Burnham, who holds the levers on permitting such a ballot, has ruled it out.

“I think he [Burnham] will be the last prime minister of the United Kingdom, because the people of Scotland, if given the choice of independence in a referendum, will take that choice,” Sweeney said, citing recent polling trends.

World.title: Record number of Brits have unfavorable view of Nigel Farage
World.content:
Newly-installed Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham continues to be viewed favorably by 46% of Brits — the same figure as last month — though the proportion who view him unfavorably has risen six points to 39% in the last month.

YouGov sampled 2,099 adults in Great Britain between Sept. 9 and 10.

The findings come at a difficult time for Reform UK.

Farage’s party — which stormed ahead in local elections earlier this year in a grim night for the governing Labour Party — is now under investigation by parliamentary authorities over an undeclared £5 million gift from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

Two of Farage’s aides — Dan Jukes and policy chief James Orr — stood down earlier this month pending an investigation into an undercover donations sting.

But the outfit has just been buoyed by a record £72m cash injection from two financiers. It has promised to use the funding — which has triggered a row over political financing in the U.K. — to beef up its policy and campaigning operations.

World.title: Eurocrat salaries, staff numbers face cuts in next long-term budget
World.content:
The Irish presidency, which is steering the budget talks, wrote that “reductions could be made, with many [countries] questioning the justification of the proposed increase in staff levels” at a time when they’re making domestic personnel cuts.

The Commission proposed hiring an extra 2,500 officials over the next seven years, fueling discontent from nine countries led by Austria.

In the Commission's proposal, which was drawn up in July 2025, administrative costs will be worth €118 billion from 2028 to 2034, which is around 6% of the overall budget.

However, Ireland is facing strong resistance to cutting other areas of the budget. The Irish presidency wrote in the document that most capitals oppose reductions in agricultural spending and regional payouts, which it described as countries' “most important priority.”

Ireland hinted that the overall budget might face cuts as countries opposed increasing their national contributions and challenged new EU-wide taxes to finance the budget.

“These factors point to a need to reflect on our level of ambition for expenditure increases,” the Irish wrote.

During a meeting on Wednesday, Dublin will sound out the EU’s 27 ambassadors on which budget items they want to downsize.

"Are there any other elements in terms of changes to the Negotiating Box [the working document that guides budget talks] that would be helpful in formulating your views regarding the expenditure level?" it wrote.

World.title: Finland joins France's forward nuclear deterrence initiative
World.content:
Finland and France committed to deepening their defence partnership on Monday, with Helsinki formally joining a French initiative aimed at strengthening European security through forward nuclear deterrence.

 

In a joint statement, the two nations called the decision an "important step for European security, and for bilateral cooperation."

"It will strengthen their partnership, and offer opportunities for strategic signalling, as well as the ability to manage escalation below the nuclear threshold," it continued, adding that a "Nuclear Steering Group" would be set up within the next few months to "begin the implementation of this cooperation."

In a post on X, Finnish President Alexander Stubb stressed that Finland’s "foremost priority" was still to act as part of NATO and the EU and that the French initiative would not "replace or overlap with NATO’s nuclear deterrence."

"Finland does not intend to station nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime," he added.

The United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Denmark, and Norway have already signed up to France's initiative, which aims to deepen nuclear cooperation across Europe through joint exercises.

Under the framework, participating countries could also potentially host French nuclear-capable aircraft on a temporary basis.

Paris would, however, retain exclusive control over its nuclear arsenal, with the final decision on its use resting with the French president.

Estonia could be next

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told AFP that Tallinn was also "in discussion" with Paris over possible cooperation on the matter.

"This is not this kind of (initiative) that you just join ... It needs certain capabilities, readiness and so on," Michal told the news agency on the sidelines of the European Arctic Summit in northern Finland.

"We are under NATO's nuclear umbrella already. And France is also backing up our independence with the troops in Estonia. So if the cooperation can be deeper in nuclear field, that probably will go so," he added.

Since March 2017, France has maintained a military presence of around 300 troops in Estonia as part of NATO's enhanced forward presence in the Baltic states.

World.title: Former Moroccan spy reportedly offered Spain intelligence information in bid to avoid extradition
World.content:
Former Moroccan intelligence officer Mehdi Hijaouy contacted people close to ex-Venezuelan spy chief Hugo Carvajal in the summer of 2024, offering information to Spanish authorities in exchange for protection from a potential extradition to Morocco, The Objective reported.

 

At the time, Hijaouy, who was reportedly forced into exile following a conflict with some of his intelligence colleagues, was in France, but he would move to Spain over fears for his safety and that of his family.

Hijaouy turned to a lawyer who had taken part in efforts to persuade Carvajal to cooperate with Spanish authorities as he sought to prevent his own extradition to the United States.

Carvajal, a former director of Venezuela’s military intelligence agency, was arrested in Spain in 2021 and later extradited to the US on narco-terrorism and drug trafficking charges.

According to sources cited by The Objective, the former Moroccan agent claimed to have information on how Morocco's intelligence services operate and was willing to share it.

The offer reached the public prosecutor's office at the Audiencia Nacional, headed by Jesús Alonso, via an intermediary. According to documents disclosed by "ABC," an email was sent on 7 October 2024 formally presenting it.

Hijaouy said he could provide information on the use of Pegasus spyware to target Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, as well as on terrorism and organised crime.

The prosecutor's office responded on 28 October. An assistant to Alonso said that since the Pegasus case was already before the courts, the information had to be passed on to the investigating judge. According to judicial sources quoted by "ABC," the offer never reached Judge José Luis Calama.

After giving up on the option of cooperating with Spanish authorities, Hijaouy began considering leaving Spain.

The Objective reported that he looked at moving to Canada or Algeria, among other countries.

He eventually left Spain via a ship and private plane before reaching Turkey. He has since continued on to another destination, and his current whereabouts is unknown.

World.title: France seeks Usmanov delisting in bid to secure release of French nationals detained in Azerbaijan
World.content:
France is pressing for Russian-Uzbek businessman Alisher Usmanov to be removed from the EU sanctions list in an effort to secure the release of an unspecified number of French nationals detained in Azerbaijan, according to several officials and diplomats familiar with the negotiations.

 

The French position has complicated efforts in Brussels to renew EU sanctions on Russia, which cover almost 3,000 individuals and entities accused of supporting Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The measures are due to expire this month.

The deadlock was initially driven by Slovakia, which has long called for Usmanov to be removed from the sanctions list, for separate reasons.

France joined Bratislava in calling for his delisting on Friday to the surprise of diplomats, Euronews reported.

EU ambassadors agreed on Monday to extend the sanctions for one week, until 22 September, giving member states more time to reach an agreement. If no agreement is reached, all Russian nationals will be delisted, adding to the sense of urgency.

"France isn't for budging, but it would send the absolute wrong message at the wrong time," one official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

"I'm not sure what will change in a week."

Most member states remain opposed to removing names from the sanctions list while Russia continues its war in Ukraine and amid concerns over hybrid attacks in Europe.

However, some officials acknowledge that France has cited national security concerns, a principle applied to critical issues. The French government declined to comment.

"Everything has an explanation," one diplomat said.

Still, the last-minute move has frustrated diplomats who oppose removing any Russian nationals from the sanctions list.

One diplomat familiar with the talks said Paris' quid-pro-quo approach effectively amounted to a veto of a common EU position, reminiscent of tactics employed by Hungary under Viktor Orbán.

France, meanwhile, insists it remains one of the bloc's strongest supporters of sanctions against Russia.

The Financial Times first reported about the prisoner swap in Azerbaijan.

Usmanov was added to the EU sanctions list in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The EU Council cited his "close ties" with Russian President Vladimir Putin and his interests in "key sectors" of the Russian economy.

Usmanov denies the allegations and has vigorously pushed to be removed from the list.

Slovakia has also long called for Usmanov and fellow Russian businessman Mikhail Fridman to be removed from the sanctions list. Other EU member states have so far rejected the request, which they regard as politically motivated.

Earlier this year, a media investigation published a two-page letter sent by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, asking for assistance in ending what Erdoğan described as the "unfair practice" involving Usmanov.

"Your support in removing him from the EU sanctions list and restoring his violated rights would be extremely valuable," Erdoğan wrote in the letter, dated 2 March 2026.

The document said Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan also supported Usmanov's removal.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticised the state of negotiations in his evening address on Monday, name checking Usmanov and Fridman.

"This is definitely not the time to lift sanctions, to rescue Russian oligarchs from them, and definitely not the time for Europe to give Russia gifts," Zelenskyy said.

"Usmanov, Fridman, and other Russian figures like them have not made their moves against the war so far. This is not the time for Europe to forget what is happening."

World.title: Turkish Airlines drops Luanda as Angola's new airport struggles
World.content:
Turkish Airlines has permanently axed its Luanda route, the latest in a series of international carriers to drop the Angolan capital since Angola inaugurated its new airport in 2023.

 

The Istanbul-based carrier removed Luanda from its future schedule earlier this month, along with Juba, Kinshasa, Libreville and Lusaka, after those services had been suspended through 24 October.

Turkish Airlines initially described the suspension as temporary when it announced the move in April, citing fuel costs.

It had operated a triangular service through Kinshasa rather than a direct connection, but the route gave Luanda passengers onward access to destinations across Europe, Asia and beyond via Istanbul.

Brussels Airlines ended its Luanda service on 25 March 2025 as part of a restructuring within the Lufthansa Group, redirecting passengers onto Lufthansa's direct Frankfurt–Luanda flights.

TAAG Angola Airlines suspended its Madrid route — codeshared with Iberia — in January 2024 and later removed a planned return from its schedule.

Iberia never reversed its decision to suspend flights to Luanda, in place since 2016, opting instead to codeshare with TAAG since 2022. That link is now gone as well.

South African Airways (SAA) also only places its code on TAAG-operated flights.

Low passenger numbers plague new airport

The departures come as Angola's Dr António Agostinho Neto International Airport, about 45km from central Luanda, struggles to establish itself as the regional hub the government promised when it inaugurated the facility in November 2023.

Built by Chinese state-owned company AVIC and designed for a maximum annual capacity of 15 million passengers, the airport handled 756,028 passengers in all of 2025, according to figures from the airport's temporary operator ATO.

By 24 February of this year, total passenger numbers since the first domestic flight in November 2024 stood at 1,090,861, including 444,212 international passengers.

The full transfer of services from the old Quatro de Fevereiro airport was completed on 1 March — more than two years after the inauguration — when South African carrier Airlink moved its Johannesburg flights to the new facility.

In December 2025, ATO's Director of Planning and Quality Vissolela Chivunda said the airport expected around 4 million passengers in 2026.

Luanda remains served by TAP Air Portugal, Air France, Lufthansa, Royal Air Maroc, Ethiopian Airlines, Qatar Airways, Airlink and TAAG, alongside Compagnie Africaine d'Aviation, which began two weekly flights from Kinshasa on 21 August.

World.title: Italy and wolves: living with a growing population amid myths and alarmism
World.content:
From the attacks in Puglia to sightings in Emilia-Romagna, Umbria and Lazio, the summer of 2026 was dominated by alarmism about wolves.

 

The wolves currently present in Italy are around 3,500 according to the data from the latest national monitoring exercise carried out by Ispra (source in Italian), the Higher Institute for Environmental Protection and Research, which dates back to 2022. Since then the population has increased by around 150 animals, mainly in the Alpine area.

However, it is not only the growing number of wolves or the sightings near built-up areas that have reopened the debate about the species.

In March 2026 Italy transposed the 2025 EU directive on the wolf's protection status, which amends the previous 1992 rules. The animal has thus gone from "highly protected species" to "protected species", raising questions among experts about how useful this downgrading really is.

Are there too many wolves in Italy? How real is the risk for people living in towns and cities and how should they behave? Euronews asked experts in the field to respond, debunking myths and scaremongering.

Should we be afraid of wolves?

"Wolf attacks remain an extremely rare phenomenon, so there is no real risk to people, but in recent years we have seen an increase in these cases, which we monitor very closely," says Piero Genovesi, head of the wildlife coordination service at Ispra, speaking to Euronews.

The institute was the first to carry out nationwide monitoring of the number and distribution of wolves in Italy using rigorous scientific methods. In the past, animals were counted at local and regional level on the basis of sightings and estimates, but the methods were not standardised.

Ispra's study was conducted between 2018 and 2022 and used a single protocol for sampling and data analysis across the country, as well as the most sophisticated statistical methods currently available. The figure of 3,500 animals is therefore an accurate estimate of the number of wolves actually present in the country; it is not a minimum figure, the experts stress.

"Numbers tell only part of the story: wolves are territorial animals that live in packs and they do not accept other animals in their territory. This means that numerical increases are not explosive, but that the species tends to colonise any area left free," explains Genovesi, noting that the wolf has gone from being a species almost extinct 50 years ago to one that is now found virtually everywhere, from the beaches of Rome and Puglia to the Po Valley.

The species' remarkable adaptability is the reason why sightings near cities are no longer so rare.

There were 19 incidents of wolves attacking humans between 2017 and 2024, according to Ispra data gathered thanks to cooperation with Life Wild Wolf, (source in Italian) an EU co-financed project that supports the authorities in preventing and managing interactions between humans and wolves.

The most significant figure, however, concerns the number of wolves involved in these attacks: only seven animals were responsible for all the cases, and a single female wolf committed 11 of them. Looking at the numbers, it is clear that these episodes are exceptional and that these particular wolves have developed abnormal behaviour, as confirmed by experts and by studies that have been focusing on this species for decades.

What is "confident behaviour"?

"In reality there is no need to be afraid of wolves: it is a species that keeps its distance; it is a shy, nocturnal animal that tends to avoid coming into contact with humans," says Marco Antonelli, zoologist and large carnivore specialist for WWF Italy.

Ispra has drawn up a specific protocol for the management of urban and 'confident' wolves, classifying wolf behaviour according to the level of risk it poses. While sightings near homes have always occurred and pose no risk, permanent settlements close to people carry a higher level of risk, up to increasingly worrying behaviour such as the predation of domestic animals and, ultimately, aggressive reactions towards humans.

"There may be different reasons why this kind of behaviour develops: certain human actions lead wolves to become used to and comfortable around people," explains Antonelli, adding that in some cases these are individual traits of specific animals that develop behaviour that departs from the norm.

Image of a wolf captured by a camera trap Foto concesse dall'Istituto di Ecologia applicata, in collaborazione con il progetto Life Wild Wolf

Downlisting and legislation in other European countries

The major novelty in 2026 is the so-called "downlisting", the move from the category of "highly protected" species to "protected" species. The difference is just a single word, but we will have to wait and see what changes in practice.

In March Italy approved the transposition of the 2025 EU directive and will have to bring previous rules into line with it by January 2027. The decision is triggering a wave of changes at national level: Germany, for example, has already transposed the new directive and is preparing to amend its national hunting law.

"It was a political choice, pushed by President von der Leyen. It was not necessary; wolves could already be culled under derogation, as provided for in the legislation," says Luigi Boitani, emeritus professor at La Sapienza University in Rome and one of the world's leading wolf experts.

His view is backed up by some figures: in Italy there have been cases of culls authorised as derogations from the rules, and there are countries where they took place regularly, such as France, which culled 250 wolves every year.

According to Piero Genovesi, by contrast, in the Italian system the downgrading brings technical changes, as it simplifies the bureaucratic procedure.

"Whereas previously authorisation from the Environment Ministry was required, based on a technical opinion from Ispra, now the regions can decide autonomously, still on the basis of a technical opinion," says Genovesi.

The current system should therefore be much more flexible, but it does not solve the real problem created by the growing number of wolves in Europe.

"The downgrading was essentially a political decision driven by very powerful farming lobbies at European level, in an attempt to solve the age-old issue of conflict between wolves and livestock farming," says Marco Antonelli, speaking to Euronews.

The difficult coexistence between wolves and farmers

Zootechnics is the science that deals with livestock breeding. And it is livestock farmers who have always been on the front line in denouncing the damage caused by wolves to their sector and the dangers faced by farm animals.

"Over the past 10 years, wolves are thought to have been responsible for preying on 0.6% of the livestock present in Europe, and the figures for Italy are very similar," says Antonelli, adding that the phenomenon should not be underestimated and should in fact be tackled with appropriate prevention strategies.

One of the most effective strategies is the use of so-called livestock guardian dogs, specially selected breeds of sheepdogs that look after and guard flocks. One of the best breeds for this job is found in Italy: the Maremma-Abruzzese sheepdog.

Other, more modern strategies include electrified and buried fences or raised night shelters, which provide effective protection for animals. Culls can be a solution to deal with animals that develop abnormal behaviour, but taken together these protective measures can ensure everyday coexistence between wolves and farmers.

"The data show that prevention strategies are much more effective than any culling strategy. A solution does exist, but it is not as simple as many make out, which is why the commitment of the authorities is also needed," Antonelli concludes.

Pack of wolves monitored by camera traps for the Life Wild Wolf project Foto concesse dall'Istituto di Ecologia applicata, in collaborazione con il progetto Life Wild Wolf

Beyond polarisation: "coexistence means compromise"

City dwellers can also play a part and need to know the right preventive behaviour to adopt. Above all, it is essential to ensure proper waste disposal, as rubbish is highly attractive to all kinds of wildlife.

Another important factor is the management of pets: in areas where sightings are frequent, experts advise against leaving pets unattended and, above all, against leaving pet food on the street, as it could attract wolves.

"The most dramatic change we are seeing today is the polarisation of opinion about wolves: the number of people wanting to defend them has grown a lot, and so has the number of people wanting to see them culled," says Luigi Boitani.

"The middle ground is still very small, yet that is what we should be aiming for: coexistence means compromise," the professor concludes. Knowledge of the species beyond opinions and myths is still limited, but pursuing it is the only long-term solution.

World.title: Iran seizes assets of 240 dissidents and journalists as protest arrests top 6,000
World.content:
Iran's judiciary has seized assets belonging to 240 dissidents, journalists and public figures and frozen 182 of their bank accounts, the judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency reported, as Police Chief Ahmadreza Radan announced on Sunday that more than 6,000 people had been arrested over the January protests.

 

Of the asset seizures, 143 took place in Tehran. Those targeted were accused of "propaganda activities or actions against the country and in favour of hostile governments," according to Mizan.

The agency said some of the assets belonged to journalists working for Persian-language opposition broadcasters Iran International and Manoto, as well as activists and public figures living abroad.

The asset seizures include the case of Sadegh Saeedi-nia, whom Iranian media described as an entrepreneur, whose property was confiscated and who received a custodial sentence in one of the most high-profile proceedings against regime opponents.

The judiciary has also made more than 2,000 inquiries to Iran's Central Bank regarding defendants' accounts and warned that additional seizures and proceedings are under way.

Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran new supreme leader AP Photo

Radan said his forces had arrested three members of the Mojahedin-e Khalq (MEK), an exiled Iranian opposition organisation seeking to overthrow the Tehran regime, in an operation the previous night.

He said MEK members had played a role in what Iranian authorities describe as a coup, the term the Islamic Republic uses for the December-January protests.

"We will not forget the rioters and coup-plotters, we continue to monitor them and take action against them," Radan said.

He also said security forces had prevented a repeat of Chaharshanbe Suri — the Persian fire festival marking the last Wednesday of the year — from being used to trigger further unrest.

"One of the enemy's extensive plans was to use the last Wednesday of the year to create a scenario similar to the incidents (in January), but that did not happen," he said.

Related Iranian café chain mogul jailed and stripped of assets for backing January protests

Iran has executed at least 532 people since January, according to Iran Human Rights, a Norway-based monitoring group, including at least 29 people in connection with the January protests. The rate has accelerated since the start of the war with the US in late February.

The late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, killed in a US strike on his residence at the start of the war, had been among those who publicly described the protests as a coup attempt.

World.title: Parliament pushes tougher energy permit deadlines, setting up clash with EU countries
World.content:
The European Parliament is pushing for tougher EU-wide deadlines and automatic approvals to speed up energy infrastructure, setting the stage for a clash with EU countries seeking more flexibility over how their national permitting systems work, according to an internal document seen by Euronews.

 

The divide is emerging as EU lawmakers negotiate new permitting rules designed to cut years of delays — sometimes up to ten years — that have held back renewable energy, electricity grids, storage and other infrastructure needed for the bloc's energy transition.

The Parliament's position is more rigid than the Commission proposal and the Council's mandate, particularly on electricity grids. While the Commission proposed a maximum two-year authorisation period for transmission and distribution infrastructure, Parliament wants distribution projects approved within one year and transmission projects within two years. The Council would retain a two-year ceiling for both, with extensions allowed in extraordinary circumstances.

However, the sharper dispute is over what happens when authorities miss those deadlines.

The Parliament backs a stronger use of tacit approval, under which certain administrative steps are deemed approved if authorities fail to respond on time. But the Council has narrowed this approach, saying EU countries may provide for tacit approval for specific intermediary administrative steps, while excluding environmental decisions and grid-connection permits.

EU lawmaker Niels Fuglsang (S&D/Denmark), leading the file in Parliament, said the bloc's power grids need to be built faster if the EU is serious about the climate and energy transition and lowering electricity and fuel bills.

"The European Parliament’s position delivers faster permitting without compromising legal certainty or public confidence. I will defend that approach in the negotiations, and I don’t think weakening the rules on tacit approval is the right solution,” Fuglsang told Euronews.

Overriding public interest

The co-legislators also differ on how far energy projects should be prioritised when they conflict with other interests. Both sides want faster permitting and support tighter deadlines, digitalisation and simpler procedures. However, they differ over how much discretion should remain with national authorities.

The Parliament mandate seeks to broaden the presumption that renewable energy projects and related infrastructure are of overriding public interest, limiting member states' ability to create exceptions.

On the other hand, the Council retains the broader presumption but allows more explicit exceptions — including where cultural heritage needs protection or where a project would have significant environmental effects that cannot be mitigated or compensated for.

The Parliament also wants a more standardised administrative system, including stronger requirements for a single point of contact for project developers, while the Council is more willing to let EU governments decide how to combine existing national authorities and contact points.

Nonetheless, the Council goes further than the Commission in some areas.

According to the document, the Council mandate raises the threshold for some small-scale installations benefiting from simplified permitting, including small solar systems, to 200 kW from the Commission's 100-kW level.

Ultimately, the emerging compromise will go beyond a political battle between faster and slower permitting and be about who controls the clock.

Parliament wants EU rules to make missed deadlines costly and approvals more predictable, while EU governments want to accelerate projects without giving Brussels —or the automatic approval mechanism — too much power over national permitting decisions, avoiding undesired precedents.

The next political talks on the permitting rules under the Grids Package are scheduled for early October.

World.title: Carcassonne: Police officer under investigation after video shows man violently thrown to ground
World.content:
A French police officer is under investigation after a video emerged showing him violently throwing a man to the ground in Carcassonne in southern France, days after a separate scandal involving recordings of officers in the city making racist, misogynistic and conspiracy-related remarks.

 

A judicial investigation was opened on Sunday for "intentional violence by a person vested with public authority."

The footage, shared on social media by MP Thomas Portes, shows several police officers standing around before one walks up behind a young man and hurls him to the ground.

Once down, the man can be seen holding his head in his arms as other people appear and protest, while someone says: "It's being filmed."

"In Carcassonne, the police are out of control!" Portes wrote.

The incident occurred on 21 June during the Fête de la musique music festival. The police officers were responding to reports of "noise disturbance".

In a statement issued on Monday, the public prosecutor's office said the man, identified as a 29-year-old homeless person, was not the subject of the intervention. He was not arrested and did not lodge a complaint.

On 3 July, he was found "in cardiac arrest" at his camp. An investigation was then opened to determine the cause of his death. But according to the findings of the autopsy carried out on 9 July, "any suspicious traumatic injury pointing to the involvement of a third party" has been ruled out.

The Inspectorate General of the National Police (IGPN) has also been called in.

The prosecutor's office said it had referred the case to the Marseille branch of the IGPN on Sunday, "as soon as it became aware of this video".

César R., one of the four officers suspended following the release of a previous video by the newspaper Midi Libre on 8 September, also appears in the new footage.

He is a witness at the scene but does not intervene.

In the first video, he was reportedly responsible for nearly 90% of the hateful remarks recorded during the patrol. He was a volunteer with the National Rally's security detail.

Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella's party has condemned the remarks made by the police officers, which included racist insults, a call for a coup and the repetition of a transphobic conspiracy theory targeting Brigitte Macron.

In a statement sent to several media outlets, including Euronews, the National Rally announced that the officer had been expelled from the party and removed from its security team.

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: Arctic power plays: EU searches for a new strategy
World.content:
Russia’s aggression, Trump’s threats against Greenland and the race for critical raw materials are pushing the Arctic to the top of Europe’s agenda.

Known as the "Gateway to the Arctic," the Finnish city of Rovaniemi sits directly on the Arctic Circle. Its forests are glowing in autumn colors as European leaders gather here at the invitation of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to discuss a new EU strategy for the Arctic. Climate change and Russia’s war against Ukraine have thrust the High North into the center of European attention.

"There is a high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic," Orpo said. "Our security environment has changed fundamentally. The Arctic has emerged as a central arena of great power competition."

The prime minister added that the Arctic's critical natural resources are also "attracting interest."

A changing security environment in the High North

The changing security environment was a central theme throughout the summit. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Russia is reopening former Soviet military bases in the region and conducting missile exercises in the High North.

"We also see that China is increasingly more interested in the region, so we have to remain vigilant," Kallas said.

The leaders gathered at Finland's northernmost air force base, looking up into a cloudless blue sky as Finnish fighter jets took to the air for a demonstration. Security has been placed at the heart of the discussions by Prime Minister Orpo. From Rovaniemi, Finland's Air Force monitors the skies along Europe's Arctic border with Russia ― 24/7.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who attended despite facing significant political pressure at home, described the region as increasingly important to Europe's security: "This region has become a geopolitical hotspot. Russia is building up its military capabilities here and… uses its presence for hybrid activities every day."

Merz added that the Arctic is not only a security issue, but also offers major economic opportunities, particularly when it comes to critical raw materials.

European leaders learned about Finnish fighter jets during the Arctic summit as well Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Confrontation replaces cooperation

"From the Putin era onwards, Russia has been developing its military capacities everywhere, but also in the Arctic," said Timo Koivurova of the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland.

For years Western countries still continued cooperating with Moscow on scientific research and climate issues. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought that era to an end. Finland and Sweden joined NATO as a direct consequence of the war. Finland's 1,340-kilometer border with Russia is now also a NATO border, fundamentally changing the security landscape in northern Europe.

The European Commission plans to update its 2021 Arctic Strategy as early as October 2026. The summit's joint declaration calls for greater investment in military mobility, cross-border connectivity and critical infrastructure in the EU's northernmost regions, including transport links, digital networks and satellite technologies.

Koivurova said that Russia's current focus on Ukraine and that war takes its military capacities.

"But obviously when that war is over, and someday it will be over, there will be a lot of investments from Russia, very likely also in the northern regions, because they are so important for its overall security," Koivurova told DW.

The United States as an additional stress factor

The Arctic is also being affected by tensions among Western partners, Koivurova said. In particular, he argued that US President Donald Trump's proposals regarding Canada and Greenland have strained cooperation among Arctic allies.

"Trump's proposal to have Canada as the 51st state of the United States, or the purchase of Greenland, these are really major problems for the cooperative relations between the western Arctic states," Koivurova said. "That is a kind of additional stress factor for Arctic governance cooperation."

Veteran Arctic observer Markku Heikkila believes the region is increasingly divided.

"In my opinion, [the] Arctic is now slowly dividing into three parts," Heikkilä told DW.

He said Russia forms one bloc, while countries such as EU member states, Norway, Iceland and Canada continue to defend a rules-based international order, climate action and Indigenous rights.

"Officially the position of the USA is now very much different from what it used to be," said Heikkila.

Inside NATO's Arctic operation preparing for a Russia crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Climate change is transforming the Arctic

At the same time, climate change is reshaping the Arctic faster than any other region on Earth. Scientists expect the central Arctic Ocean to become largely ice-free during summer sometime around 2040 and 2050. As sea ice retreats, the region is gaining strategic importance with new shipping routes and significantly shortening distances between major trading centers, creating new economic and geopolitical opportunities, says Koivurova.

Yet climate policy has become another source of disagreement between the United States and many of its Arctic partners.

"Climate change is, of course, a hugely important thing in the Arctic. It's warming four times the rate as compared to the global average. So everything we do in the Arctic nowadays, one way or the other, is related to climate change," Koivurova said.

He added that the Trump administration's approach has had a significant impact on international cooperation, including within the Arctic Council: "The US is torpedoing any mention of climate change at the moment. So that was certainly a big, big change."

Orpo: 'We should strengthen Arctic resilience'

At the close of the summit, Prime Minister Orpo called for greater investment to strengthen the region's resilience.

"We should strengthen Arctic resilience by strategic investments in Arctic infrastructure, dual use transport networks, critical raw materials, icebreaking and technological innovation," Orpo said.

Rovaniemi is known worldwide as the hometown of Santa Claus. Not far from the "Arktikum" museum and science center where the leaders met lies "Santa Claus Village." It's home to the official Santa Claus Post Office, which remains open year-round. Visitors can also meet Santa himself. Whether any of the summit participants paid him a visit ― and if so, what they wished for ― remains unknown.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Ukraine, Russia set for new round of US-mediated talks
World.content:
New trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US could begin in October, according to Kyiv and Moscow. Few expect a breakthrough, but Ukraine is seeking a partial de-escalation to help it get through the winter.

Ukraine and Russia have signaled their readiness to resume trilateral talks under US mediation.

"We're preparing. For October," said Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian president's office.

Similar signals came from Moscow: "We do not rule out such a possibility. We are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner aimed to revive trilateral talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, visiting Moscow and Kyiv in the first week of September.

The last round of trilateral talks took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, without producing a breakthrough, as the issue of territory control in eastern Ukraine remained unresolved.

Territory remains a difficult subject

Vladimir Putin still demands more territory than Russia currently controls, Kushner confirmed on September 12, speaking online at the YES security conference in Kyiv.

"President Putin [has] laid out his line of what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. Ukraine right now does not want to do that," the US envoy said.

The Ukrainian government has indicated it is willing to freeze the fighting along the current frontline in exchange for security guarantees. Such a step could be supported by 60% of Ukrainians, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology conducted in summer 2026. A similar majority of respondents rejected giving up territory that Russia hasn't been able to conquer. 33% said Ukraine should give up territory that Putin demands.

Russia's air superiority is a problem for Ukraine

Few expect a breakthrough anytime soon.

"For there to be a negotiated end to the war, there has to be parity. Right now, there's a stalemate on the front lines and not much is changing there, but in the air war, unfortunately, Russia currently has a significant advantage," Volodymyr Fesenko, a Kyiv-based political scientist, told DW.

Ukraine is running low on interceptors for Russian ballistic missiles. Russia has also stepped up attacks with new jet-powered drones, which fly faster than older gasoline-powered models and are harder to intercept.

Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russian airstrikes are increasingly targeting Ukraine's economy, including warehouses, energy facilities, gas stations and railway infrastructure.

The Kremlin has accused Ukraine of opening a "Pandora's box" by targeting Russia's economy and fuel and energy facilities with deep strikes since the summer. Ukraine says the attacks are intended to force Russia to the negotiating table.

Ukraine is worrying about the winter

Ukraine's supporters say Kyiv's strategy is working.

"The escalation ... is not a problem. It's a sign of success," said Jonathan Powell, the United Kingdom's National Security Adviser, speaking at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv on September 11. "Of course [Putin] doesn't go straight to negotiations, he tries to escalate in the ways that he can."

The West must "keep its foot on the gas" to make Putin negotiate in earnest, Powell said.

Such optimism contrasts with concerns in Ukraine about the upcoming winter. In 2025, Russian attacks on energy infrastructure caused extended blackouts and left people without heating in freezing temperatures.

"We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country," said Ukraine's Economy Minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko.

Zelenskyy calls for partial de-escalation

Russia rejected the idea of a ceasefire during the upcoming talks. Ukraine is now calling for a de-escalation of attacks on energy infrastructure and the unblocking of grain exports via the Black Sea instead.

"What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So, energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told DW in an interview aired on September 12.

Zelenskyy backs Putin meeting at Miami G20: 'Results matter' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Political scientist Fesenko says an agreement on grain exports could prove the easier task: "In the Black Sea, both Ukraine and Russia are facing major problems. Grain exports have been blocked; ports have been shut down and therefore both sides have a stake in the matter."

An energy truce, however, remains elusive, as Ukraine's vulnerability in the winter gives Putin leverage he would not give up easily, Fesenko said.

At the same time, the US is increasing pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy facilities.

"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: He has to ‌stop ⁠knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Donald Trump said on Sunday. "There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel. That's hurting the world."

A day later, Trump claimed on social media that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy truce.

“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. However, neither Ukraine nor Russia immediately confirmed the reported agreement.

Kremlin rejected Zelenskyy-Putin meeting

The Kremlin has already rejected another of Zelenskyy's proposals: a meeting between the Ukrainian and Russian leaders in December on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Miami.

"Putin doesn't want to negotiate with Zelenskyy. It's been obvious since last year that he wants to reach an agreement with Trump," said Fesenko. "If Trump insists, Putin may agree to a meeting between the three leaders. But he has no intention of negotiating with Zelenskyy."

If negotiations start in October as expected, negotiating teams rather than the leaders themselves will conduct them. But Ukraine insists that only the presidents can decide the territorial issue.

"The territorial question remains a pressing one... Complex issues such as this are only resolved at the level of leaders," Zelenskyy said during the US envoys' visit to Kyiv.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

This article was updated to include a claim by Donald Trump that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking energy targets. Neither government immediately publicly confirmed that.

World.title: Trump seeks halt to energy attacks by both Russia, Ukraine
World.content:
Donald Trump, under fire for record US diesel prices, claims Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking energy targets. Russia said nothing; Ukraine said "we expect specifics from our partners" on any such move.

US President Donald Trump claimed a breakthrough on Monday in diplomacy between Ukraine and Russia, although his unsubstantiated declaration only elicited a very reserved comment from Ukraine and no immediate word from the Kremlin.

The assertion comes amid indications from both Russia and Ukraine that they would be willing to continue with US-brokered negotiations, which have been largely stagnant throughout Trump's second term.

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week told DW that he would be willing to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the G20 summit in Miami in December if rumors of Putin being invited materialized.

What did Trump say?

Trump appeared to claim that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop hitting each other's energy targets.

"Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!" Trump or his team wrote.

"The World's Diesel price is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War [sic], not Iran," the Truth Social comment continued, demonstrating — as a quickfire series of agitated follow-up posts would reinforce — a desire to downplay rising US oil prices, the role of Trump's war in Iran in pushing them skywards, and economic pressures closer to home.

Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What, if anything, did Ukraine and Russia say?

There was no immediate comment on the matter from Moscow.

Ukraine's presidency declined to comment but President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issued a more guarded statement online.

He did, however, say that he had recommended seeking such an accord, as winter approaches — if Russia's cooperation could be ensured after years of it targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

"Ukraine has proposed that its partners secure an agreement with Russia that would stop the destruction of critical infrastructure," Zelenskyy wrote online. "Food, energy, and other basics that sustain life must be protected, and Russian strikes are directed primarily against them."

But Zelenskyy cautioned that Kyiv "is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by an agreement," if one could be reached.

"If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes."

He said Kyiv would need assurance that this was a lasting deal and not just a bid to secure temporary relief in fuel prices in Russia ahead of elections at the end of the week.

"We expect specifics from our partners," Zelenskyy concluded, without naming names.

Ukraine has been targeting Russian warehouses, refineries amid Iran war

As Trump's war in Iran pushed oil prices to highs not seen since the immediate aftermath of Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv has started using long-range drone strikes to target Russia's refinery and petroleum supply infrastructure.

This has caused isolated shortages and price increases, even in oil-rich Russia.

Ukraine has also launched a series of high-profile strikes on Russia's best-known online retailer Wildberries, accusing it of providing logistical support to the military.

The US miltiary action of the last six months in the Gulf has also left Ukraine poorly placed to defend itself against Russian ballistic missiles, because of US Patriot missile supplies being depleted in the Middle East.

In recent winters, Russia has frequently targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure to try to exacerbate difficulties of dealing with the cold. Last winter, as a particularly fierce cold snap hit Kyiv and other parts of the country, Trump announced a brief halt to strikes on Kyiv which only held for a few days.

World.title: Donald Trump dismisses concerns about dangers of AI
World.content:
The president called efforts to slow the development of artificial intelligence a "sick conspiracy," claiming they only serve China. Market leaders have warned of the dangers of the pace of the technology's development.

US President Donald Trump has called concerns that artificial intelligence is progressing too quickly a "SICK conspiracy."

Trump's statement followed calls by tech leaders such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman for more governmental regulation of AI. In recent months, several incidents have highlighted the risk that AI agents could go rogue.

What Trump said about AI 'guardrails'

"The only control or ‘guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump posted on his Truth Social account.

Anthropic is the developer of the popular AI model Claude Image: IMAGO/ZUMA Press

Trump added that his administration has already prevented Anthropic from "doing bad, or potentially bad" things with the technology.

The Pentagon previously tried to brand Anthropic's models a security risk and posed a temporary ban on one of its more advanced models.

"There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China," Trump wrote.

Anthropic boss Amodei warned against uncontrolled global AI development over the weekend saying that there's a risk of AI-led agents taking over the entire internet within six to 12 months. Microsoft published its own code of conduct to ensure human control over AI.

This led to AI stocks falling worldwide, including those of chip maker Nvidia (3.5%) and Elon Musk's SpaceX (1.7%).

World.title: Yemen's Houthis attack Saudis, seize crucial Red Sea islands
World.content:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels have tightened their grip on a key shipping route, capturing two strategic Red Sea islands. The closure of another global transport route is the latest ripple effect of the US war with Iran.

Iranian-backed Houthi rebels on Monday announced they had captured Greater and Lesser Hanish Island in the southern Red Sea.

The move bolsters the group's ability to choke traffic in another key global maritime shipping route as the ripple-effect of the war in Iran grows.

The strategic advance comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces try to regain territory recently lost near the Bab el-Mandab Strait, an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz — which Iran has held closed since US President Donald Trump began bombing the Islamic Republic on February 28.

The closure of the Hormuz Strait, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the US began hostilities, has led to a global economic and energy emergency, driving up prices around the world and forcing petro-monarchy Saudi Arabia to move its oil exports through Bab el-Mandab.

But the Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and last week seized strategic Mayun Island and the Red Sea port of Mokha, cutting off the alternative route.

The capture of Greater and Lesser Hanish now puts even more pressure on Saudi shipments and thus global oil supplies and prices.

Beyond putting the squeeze on Saudi Arabia — the Houthis' proxy enemy for backing the internationally recognized government in the Yemen's reignited civil war — it could also provide Iran added leverage in defending itself against the US.

Houthis seize Red Sea chokepoint: What can Saudi Arabia do? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Houthi offensive continues to escalate as Iran war expands

The Houthis pressed on with their offensive Monday, launching missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets.

A spokesman for the group said the strikes had caused "significant damage" and had come in response to "more than 300 [Saudi] airstrikes in [Yemen over] the past five days."

Despite being a longtime backer of the Houthis as part of its anti-Israel "axis of resistance," Tehran has denied any involvement in Yemen's revived civil war.

"Iran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs," said Tehran's Foreign Ministry on Monday, with spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei telling reporters the Houthis are "entirely independent actors who make their decisions based on their own interests."

Yemen's civil war — dormant for four years until the conflict in Iran broke out — began in 2014, when Houthi rebels seized large parts of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, and forced the government to flee to Aden in the south.

In 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition aiding the government, launching wave after wave of airstrikes as the conflict escalated into one of the worst humanitarian disasters in the world.

Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Concerning situation for US and its Saudi, Gulf State allies

On Monday, Admiral Brad Cooper of US Central Command (CENTCOM) was in Jeddah to discuss "the latest developments in the region" with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

US news site Axios reports that Cooper has been in the kingdom since Thursday, dealing with urgent coordination meetings as the situation in the Red Sea escalates.

US media outlets reported last week that President Trump had rejected a request by the crown prince for the US to directly intervene.

Despite turning down the request to unleash US firepower, Trump reportedly agreed to provide intelligence sharing and targeting assistance.

Iran war: Analyzing the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran blames Saudi Arabia for stalling Hormuz talks

Iran on Monday accused Saudi Arabia of delaying talks aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Baghaei called a meeting set to take place in Oman, a "real opportunity" to restore security in the region and added that an agreement between Iran and Oman on opening the passage had been finalized and would be announced later.

Saudi Arabia reportedly has concerns over the lasting implications of a deal for the Strait of Hormuz and how it might negatively impact Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries.

Tehran says Riyadh is using Yemen as a "pretext" to delay talks on how the Strait will be governed now that the status quo has been upended by the US.

Currently, the only secure routes allowing Saudi Arabia to deliver its oil to Asian markets are via the Suez Canal or around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope.

On Monday, China's Foreign Ministry called attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure "unacceptable," saying Beijing is "deeply concerned" about further escalation.
