World.title: Passengers evacuated after train hits lorry on level crossing
World.content:
Around 150 passengers have been evacuated from a train after it collided with a lorry on a level crossing in Gelderland.

Two people on the train and the lorry driver suffered minor injuries in the collision on Horsterweg, Elmelo, train operator NS said.

The Sprinter train was heading towards Harderwijk when the crash happened just after 10am on Monday. The passengers were escorted to the station before buses were arranged to take them to their destinations.

The lorry was transporting concrete blocks on a low loader. NS said the clean-up operation would take several hours and all trains between Amersfoort and Zwolle have been cancelled for the rest of the day. Replacement buses are running between Putten and Nunspeet.

Police said the lorry driver was taken to hospital for treatment. The investigation into the cause of the crash is ongoing.

World.title: Brainwash: Anatomy of a Dutch language course
World.content:
Ready to start speaking Dutch? The Dutch Brainwash school, which sponsored this piece, invited DutchNews’ Lauren Comiteau to visit a class.

On the sweltering August day I visit Albert Both’s Brainwash class on the Keizersgracht in the heart of the Jordaan, you can hear the laughter before you even enter the room.

During this last class of Both’s current one-week intensive Dutch language course, eight students – Both’s maximum per course – sit around a huge white table that takes up most of the room. Amidst the organised chaos are stuffed animals, books and games, all props to help the students learn Dutch, or as Albert says, “they’re part of the story to get people talking”.

Armed with fans, water bottles and notebooks full of the handouts they’ve been given throughout the week, all eyes are on Both, who is working a whiteboard via his computer and talking about the past tense.

“It’s the first thing people teach you when you’re learning Dutch,” says Both, “but it’s like giving cauliflower to a baby. The past tense is akin to opening Pandora’s box. If I show it too soon, it will be pure quicksand.”

Instead, after a week of talking and learning, Both gets to the past tense, telling his students the secret to faking it until they make it.

“The trick is you can use the present tense to talk about the past,” he says. You do that, he continues, by saying one sentence in the past tense, pausing, and then continuing in the present tense. “If you do it with elegance and grace, no one knows you’re cheating. I’ve been doing it for a very long time.”

Informal, fun and funny

“I’ve done six different types of courses trying to learn Dutch,” says American independent researcher Lauren Vargas (45), who currently lives in Leiden. “This is the first one where I’ve learned more in seven days than I have in six years.”

She chalks that up to Albert’s teaching style, a far cry, she says, from her other classes where teachers focused too much on structure without theory and application. “Here, you build up to better understand the mechanics, and we’re encouraged to be playful with the language, to make mistakes, to accept that we can actually speak more and understand more than we think we do.”

They can do that because of the informal atmosphere Albert has honed over the years. “We sit around a table like a group of friends,” he says. “My students inspire each other to learn. We create a safe and fun atmosphere, as compared to their past traumatic experiences learning Dutch, which were often impersonal and had students sitting there like they were in a factory.”

The casual conversations – which focus on anything the students want, including the sex toy a sex worker once brought in or a headlining murder investigation that led to a murder-themed discussion – uniquely bind the students. The stuffed Jesus toy is to stimulate conversations about religion.

“That really helped break the ice and get us more comfortable with each other,” says student Jamie Tipelto. “Then we’re able to be more open and freer about speaking and making mistakes. It’s a safe space.”

Fellow student Jesse Corcoran (47), an American researcher at UMC Utecht, who’s lived in the Netherlands for only four months, ditched her more structured and academic Dutch class and followed her husband into Albert’s Brainwash.

“My old class always filled me with anxiety because there wasn’t a lot of ice-breaking, and I wasn’t really comfortable with the people that I was in class with,” she says. “Here, from the first day, the ice is broken, and then you’re more comfortable making mistakes and trying new things.”

“It’s definitely given me more confidence to speak to my neighbours. And that’s a big thing for my husband and I because we want to integrate and become part of the culture. So getting that courage and that confidence to speak to Dutch people is paramount.”

65,000 mistakes

Even for those who have been in the Netherlands longer, like Romanian product manager Sudi (46), who has lived here for 15 years, Albert’s class was a gamechanger.

“I’d taken inburgering classes before, but they created a fear in me of making mistakes,” she says. “Coming to this course made a big difference, because we signed a contract to make 65,000 mistakes. I think I’ve made 30,000, so I still have 30,000 to go!”

Sudi had been following Albert on social media and related to his postings that seemed to echo her situation – getting over the speaking-Dutch hump.

“Now, in the process of making my mistake quota, I’m more confident speaking Dutch and being part of the community. It was a great choice.”

For American Shemby Nagel, who took the course with her friend Lauren Vargas, Albert’s class gave her an unexpected energy boost. “With every language course I’ve tried to take in the past, after about an hour or two, your energy level just goes down. You tank and you’re just dreading coming in the next day. You don’t have time or energy for homework,” she says.

“This is the very first language class – or any class – I’ve taken where my energy level has just gone up and up and up. So by the time I finish, Lauren and I travel back to Leiden and continually work on what we learned in class. And when I get home, I’ll have conversations with my partner and my daughter in Dutch, which I never would have done before.”

Ongelooflijk!

“We have an amazing time together,” says Sandra from Mexico, a procurement manager who has lived in the Netherlands for 10 years.

Albert is legendary among those looking to learn Dutch, and she liked the reviews that talked about his jokes and non-traditional way of teaching. She made the daily commute from Rotterdam, “feeling so happy to be here and excited that he broke through my fear of speaking”.

At the same time, she says his class “opened her ears” to listening to Dutch on the streets, something she had previously avoided because she didn’t understand the language. “That’s how I found my new favourite word: ongelooflijk (unbelievable)!”

Only the beginning

As class winds down, Albert reminds his students one last time to keep on talking. “You can do more than you think,” he tells them. “You must! At some point, you must just say it, even if you think it’s wrong. That’s the reality.”

One by one, the students go around the table saying, “Ik spreek Nederlands,” or “I speak Dutch”.

Albert hands them their diplomas, and then they gather their belongings and head out to a local café for a well-earned drink.

“Het is niet het einde, maar het begin,” he tells them. “It is not the end, but the beginning.”

For anyone looking for a Dutch refresher class, struggling with stalled motivation or wanting to start truly speaking Dutch, Both’s class has proven invaluable. You can sign up here for the next Dutch Brainwash!

World.title: Scientists develop “tickle robot” to solve touching mystery
World.content:
Researchers in Nijmegen have set up a laboratory to try to answer one of the oldest questions known to science: why are people ticklish?

Aristotle, Erasmus, Galileo and Darwin all tried to put their finger on the purpose of tickling, or gargalesis to use its scientific name, without finding a definitive reason.

Now two researchers at Radboud University in Nijmegen are using robots and sensors to try to shed more light on the phenomenon.

Tickling exists across cultures and throughout history, but with few variations and little difference between men and women, indicating that it has its roots in biology. Tickling has been observed in other primates such as bonobos and chimpanzees.

Ziliang Xiong and Konstantina Kilteni have set up their lab in a windowless basement in the Maria Montessori building, an environment stripped of any other stimuli that could make their test subjects laugh.

The robot uses a metal pin to simulate tickling, with settings that can be adjusted to measure the effect of different types of contact from gentle stroking to prodding. The participants wear a cap equipped with electrodes that measure their brain responses.

Families and partners

The researchers also asked the 448 subjects to fill in surveys about how they experienced tickling, which revealed strong similiarities.

Most tickling is by adults on children, usually within families, or between siblings. Partners and friends also tickle each other, but this is less common.

Most respondents said they reacted to tickling by laughing, squirming or trying to turn away. The vast majority named the same body parts as most susceptible to tickling: the sides, armpits, belly and the soles of the feet.

The researchers noted that while tickling is associated with play and laughter, many people find it unpleasant and it can quickly become overwhelming. The Nazis even used it as a torture method.

There are indications that people diagnosed with autism are more sensitive to tickling and that ticklish people may even live longer.

Other theories suggest a link between tickling and sexual stimulation, given that couples often tickle each other and it tends to be directed at body parts that are rarely exposed.

Thin skinned

Darwin speculated that tickling felt uncomfortable because it involved touching parts of the body that are unused to being touch, while Aristotle believed it worked on places where the skin is thinner.

But the researchers in Nijmegen said none of the theories provided a complete answer to the reasons why people are sensitive to tickling. “You rarely get touched on your back, but the back is pretty resistant to tickling,” Xiong pointed out.

World.title: Notorious fugitive Dutch arms dealer dies in South Africa
World.content:
A timber merchant turned arms dealer, one of the Netherlands’ most infamous international fugitives, has died peacefully in South Africa after evading justice for years.

Guus Kouwenhoven, who facilitated weapons shipments to the Liberian dictator Charles Taylor in the early 2000s, was sentenced in absentia to 19 years for illegal arms smuggling and complicity in war crimes in 2017.

Despite being arrested in Cape Town, he was released on bail and avoided extradition, living a life of luxury, until his death last week.

Taylor, who was himself given a 50-year prison sentence in The Hague for crimes against humanity, waged civil wars in Liberia until 2003 that killed over 150,000 people. Kouwenhoven’s dealings with him were seen as instrumental to the fighting, which was notorious for its brutality and widespread use of child soldiers.

The Liberian press described Kouwenhoven as a reminder of the country’s violent past, referring to “blood timber”, and asked how someone could get away with turning the timber trade into a currency for war.

So far nothing has been said by Dutch justice minister David van Weel, despite the scale and notoriety of the case. Efforts to have him extradited were complicated and delayed even after South Africa revoked his visa, and his exuberant lifestyle reportedly went unhindered.

Given the recent efforts by Van Weel to push for Sierra Leone to extradite fugitive drugs baron Jos Leijdekkers – even by asking the EU to cut off development aid to the country until it hands him over – Kouwenhoven seems to have escaped proportional scrutiny in his final years, a Volkskrant column argued.

World.title: Woman arrested after trying to hire hitman on dark web scam site
World.content:
A woman has been arrested for allegedly trying to recruit a hitman on the dark web to kill her ex-husband.

Police confirmed that the 45-year-old woman was arrested in Rotterdam at the weekend for being “involved” in organising a contract killing after the case came to light during an investigation by RTL Nieuws.

The website turned out to be a scam that advertised non-existent “contract killing” services and the attack was never carried out, despite the client transferring US$1,400 (€1,200) in bitcoins as a downpayment.

The man, who was given the cover name of Jerom by RTL, told the broadcaster he was “incredibly relieved that the police have identified a suspect”

The client instructed the website “burn him alive and make sure he doesn’t survive.” When told that the attack would cost $9,000, they replied: “OK, how much does it cost to cut off his arms and legs or shoot him?”

Elderly mother

The instructions included Jerom’s home address, a recent photograph and information about the house, including the alarm system and the fact that his elderly mother lived with him.

“The only demand is that he has to die. I don’t care what happens to the mother,” the client wrote.

Police said arranging the killing was still a crime even though the hitman did not exist. They did not confirm if the request had come directly from the businessman’s ex-wife.

In 2021 a man from The Hague was given an eight-year jail sentence for trying to arrange a murder on the same website. A judge said he had acted “coldly and clinically” in instructing the killing and could take no credit for the fact that the victim was still alive.

A moose wandered onto the tracks at Warsaw Central Station on Sunday evening, disrupting rail services in the Polish capital for more than 80 minutes before it was safely removed. The animal first appeared on a platform before moving onto the tracks, forcing Polish Railway Lines (PLK), the company responsible for Poland’s rail infrastructure, to suspend, cancel and divert several train services. View this post on Instagram A post shared by TVP3 Warszawa (@tvp3warszawa) Videos and photographs shared online showed the moose lying on the tracks and running along the railway line at Warsaw Central, the capital’s busiest station, which is mainly underground and therefore not easy for such a large animal to access. Police do not know how the moose ended up at the station, reports broadcaster TVN24. Officers were first alerted at 7:10 pm on Sunday and cordoned off the platform where the animal was located. When emergency services arrived, the moose was tranquilised. It was then placed on a large sheet and carried out of the station by police officers and emergency workers before being loaded onto a specialist vehicle to be returned to a forested area. PLK, which named the moose Emil, later confirmed that the animal had been safely removed and that normal train services were being restored. The company added that the disruptions lasted just over 80 minutes, using a pun combining the Polish words for moose (łoś) and 80 (osiemdziesiąt) to produce the word “łosiemdziesiąt”. ❗Aktualizacja❗Zwierze zostało bezpiecznie zabrane z torów. Przywracana jest rozkładowa organizacja ruchu pociągów. Utrudnienia trwały przeszło łosiemdziesiąt minut. https://t.co/Xui2B6SxyU — PLK SA (@PKP_PLK_SA) September 13, 2026 The Eurasian moose (also known as the Eurasian elk) has long been native to Poland, but by the mid-20th century hunting and habitat loss had brought the species close to extinction in the country. Its population subsequently recovered, reaching an estimated 6,000 animals by the 1980s and around 30,000 by 2019, helped by a moratorium on moose hunting introduced in 2001. Several hundred live in the Kampinos national park on the northwestern outskirts of Warsaw. They are therefore relatively frequent visitors to the capital, according to the Interia news website, although venturing onto train lines in the centre is unusual. The growth in the moose population, combined with urban expansion and changes to its habitat, has led to other high-profile encounters in areas inhabited by humans. In 2022, a moose was spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in the northern Polish city of Elbląg. A moose was this morning spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in Poland. World.title: Poland issued EU’s third most residence permits to immigrants in 2025
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland issued first residence permits to almost half a million immigrants in 2025, which was the third-highest figure in the European Union, behind Spain and Germany but ahead of Italy and France. However, the number of permits issued by Poland fell for the fourth year running, as the country continued to tighten its migration rules. Previously, between 2017 and 2022, Poland had led the EU figures for six years running, reaching a peak of almost one million permits in 2021. The new data, released on Friday by Eurostat, the EU’s statistical agency, show that Poland issued 467,314 first residence permits to immigrants from outside the EU in 2025. As was the case last year, Spain (635,438) issued the most, followed by Germany (605,292). Poland was then followed by Italy (433,099) and France (377,462). However, whereas in those four other countries the number of permits rose in 2025 (by 13.1% in Spain, 11.1% in Germany, 25.0% in Italy and 9.2% in France), in Poland the figure fell by 4.4%. That decline has come amid a tougher new migration strategy by the current government, a coalition that ranges from left to centre right, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Ahead of elections in 2023, Tusk, then in opposition, accused the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which had ruled Poland since 2015, of allowing “uncontrolled” migration, including through widespread abuses of the visa system. Shortly after coming to power in those elections, Tusk, a former president of the European Council, declared that the “survival of Western civilisation” depends upon preventing mass migration. His government has since introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students, suspended asylum rights for migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus, and stepped up deportations of immigrants who have committed crimes or entered the country unlawfully. Poland has introduced tougher new rules regulating the entry of foreign students and immigrant workers. “This is another step towards regaining control over migration and increasing the safety of Poles," says the government https://t.co/gYdikpc6pL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2025 The new 2025 data show that, in relative terms (the number of permits issued in relation to countries’ populations), Poland was only ninth in the EU (12.8 permits per 1,000 people), behind Malta (56.9), Cyprus (46.7), Portugal (27.3), Lithuania (18.5), Ireland (13.4), Croatia (13.2), Luxembourg (13.1) and Spain (12.9). That marks a significant decline since 2021, when Poland issued 967,345 permits, which was the highest in the EU in absolute terms but also second-highest in relation to population. In 2025, as in previous years, Poland issued the most first residence permits to Ukrainians (241,126, 51.6% of the total), who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. They were followed by Belarusians (128,468, 27.5%), Georgians (10,249, 2.2%), Indians (9,230, 2%) and Turks (7,533, 1.6%) – the same top five nationalities as in 2024. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Following a decade of unprecedented mass migration, the number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland this year passed two million for the first time, making up just over 5% of the country’s population. Around 1.5 million of those are Ukrainians. In June, the number of foreigners working in Poland reached 1.14 million, making up almost 7% of the workforce. While Ukrainians constitute two thirds of the total, the fastest-growing nationalities are Colombians and Indians, who are now the third- and fourth-largest groups of foreign workers. The rise in migration has come as Poland’s economy has boomed but the country has also faced a demographic crisis, with a shrinking, ageing population and one of the lowest birth rates in the world. In 2023, the state Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) calculated that, in order to maintain its ratio of working-age population to retirees, Poland would need to attract almost two million immigrant workers over the following decade. However, it admitted that that target was “unrealistic”. World.title: Poland and other V4 countries will block EU climate policies that raise energy costs, warns Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that the Central European Visegrád Group (V4) would seek to block any European Union climate policies that push up energy prices. Speaking after a meeting with the leaders of the other V4 countries, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, Tusk said that they could not accept policies that further weakened competitiveness at a time when they were already facing high electricity costs. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Bratysława ⤵️ Polska i grupa #V4 nie pozwoli na żadne zmiany i na żadne propozycje instytucji europejskich, czy innych państw, które mogłyby wpłynąć na pogorszenie sytuacji energetycznej w naszych państwach. Ceny energii w tym regionie muszą spaść. pic.twitter.com/BFnRx8Clse — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 10, 2026 In recent months, Poland and some other member states have been pushing for a softening of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a cap-and-trade scheme launched in 2005 that makes polluters pay for carbon emissions in sectors such as power generation and heavy industry. They have also secured a postponement of the introduction of ETS2, which will cover emissions from road transport and buildings. “Whether we are talking about ETS1, ETS2, or other proposals, anything that brings a risk of more expensive energy for us will be blocked by us,” said Tusk on Thursday at a press conference alongside the other V4 prime ministers, as well as Ireland’s Micheál Martin. “Poland and the V4 will not allow any changes or any proposals from European institutions or other countries that could worsen the energy situation in our countries,” he added. “Energy prices in this region, including in Poland, must fall.” Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Tusk argued that high energy prices pose a threat not only to Central European economies but also to the competitiveness of the EU as a whole. “We can forget about any dreams of competing with China or the United States if our energy prices remain as they are right now,” warned Tusk. Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico likewise said the V4 countries were united in their approach to the emissions trading system. “We will be very active, and we will also engage in discussions outside the meetings of the European Council and the Council of Europe to discuss what steps to take to bring down these energy prices,” he said. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also expressed frustration with rising energy costs. “All of us in our industrial region pay a lot of money for emissions allowances. And what did the commission tell us in 2020? That the price of this allowance in 2030 will be €26.50. Right now, it’s €80,” he said. According to the Eurostat data, households in Poland paid €27.09 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh), including taxes and levies, for electricity in the second half of 2025. That was the 11th highest figure in the EU and below the figure of €28.96 across the bloc as a whole. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in costs of living, Polish households faced the second-highest electricity prices in the EU, at 37.15 PPS per 100 kWh, behind only Romania (49.52 PPS) and the Czech Republic (39.16 PPS). The effects of ETS on electricity bills has moved to the centre of political debate this year after the main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from the system, saying it makes “Poles a cash machine for the EU’s absurd leftist climate policy”. The opposition-aligned conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, has also twice sought to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policies, including ETS, arguing they are too expensive. Both his efforts were rejected by the government’s majority in parliament. While the government has rejected the idea of withdrawing from ETS – which it says would result in large, ongoing fines being levied against Poland – it has pushed for reforms to the system. In July, the European Commission outlined proposals to soften ETS in response to pressure from countries such as Poland, allowing industries to continue emitting CO2 for longer while providing more financial support for investment in clean technologies. Yet there are also a number of other EU member states that argue against weakening ETS, saying it would penalise those who moved early to cut emissions. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Just before the European Commission unveiled its proposal in July, Poland’s climate minister, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said she had assembled a coalition of 10 countries calling for ETS reform and a more realistic emissions-reduction path. They also want ETS funding mechanisms to account for national differences, including energy mixes and GDP per capita, to ensure a fairer transition for lower-income countries starting from a more challenging position. Poland, for example, has a historical reliance on coal, which it still uses to produce around half of its electricity, helping make it one of the EU’s biggest emitters. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. For more, read our full report: https://t.co/XjD9hfhabo pic.twitter.com/WklP7dYL78 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 2, 2026 However, the country has made significant progress in expanding renewables in recent years, particularly solar and onshore wind. In 2025, renewables accounted for just over 29% of Poland’s electricity generation, almost three times the share recorded a decade earlier. Further progress is expected this year, after Poland began to generate electricity from offshore wind farms for the first time. Under a national energy and climate plan approved by the current government in June, it plans by 2040 for Poland to generate 18-21% of power from offshore wind and 22-27% from onshore wind. A further 15-16% will come from nuclear, 14-18% from solar, 7-8% from gas and 0-5% from coal. Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun vandalises Ukrainian monument with hammer
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun, who regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, which recently called for a “normalisation of relations with Russia”, enjoys support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. World.title: Polish train drivers announce go-slow protest after deadly crash at rail crossing

Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. Miętek noted that, for over 18 months, the union has been running a campaign, titled “I Want To Live”, focused on safety. Just two days before the accident, it had issued a special appeal to drivers over “growing safety concerns on Polish railways”. “We have been doing everything we can in parliament and at the infrastructure ministry to make sure this problem is noticed,” added Miętek, who also welcomed the fact that, following Wednesday’s accident, Tusk has pledged to take action. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Katastrofa kolejowa w Sokolnikach miała miejsce na przejeździe kolejowym, dlatego natychmiast rozpoczniemy prace nad zaostrzeniem przepisów dla tych, którzy wjeżdżają na przejazdy kolejowe, mimo zapór i czerwonych światel. pic.twitter.com/BgaZQLEPbR — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 9, 2026 In those remarks, the prime minister lamented that the accident in Sokolniki Suche was “yet another case of such a catastrophe happening at a rail crossing”. “We must immediately begin urgent work on tightening regulations,” he continued. However, critics noted that the ministry had already announced such plans in July 2025, and had failed to implement them since then. – Chcemy wprowadzić przepis, na podstawie którego każdy kierowca, który wjedzie na przejazd drogowo-kolejowy kiedy jest zapalone czerwone światło, straci prawo jazdy, zostanie mu ono zatrzymane na trzy miesiące. In total, Poland had by far the highest number of deaths caused by accidents at rail crossings (45), ahead of Germany (26), France (20) and Hungary (18). World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Prague 8 Pirates to Host English-Language Guide to Czech Local Elections
World.content:
EU citizens living in Prague 8 can learn how to vote in the upcoming municipal elections at an event on 17 September.

The Prague 8 branch of the Czech Pirate Party is inviting international residents to an English-language evening explaining how EU citizens can take part in Czech local elections.

The event, titled “Hey, You Can Vote Too!”, will take place on Thursday, 17 September, at 6 PM at Pauza Palmovka in Prague 8.



The evening will offer a practical introduction to the Czech voting system, an overview of the Prague 8 Pirates’ local programme, and an opportunity for international residents to share their views on life in the district.

Organisers say the event is intended to help EU citizens understand their voting rights and discuss what they would like to see improved in Prague 8.

Who Can Vote in Czech Local Elections?

Citizens of other EU Member States can vote in Czech municipal elections if they meet certain conditions.

Voters must:

Be at least 18 years old by the second day of the election.

Have permanent or registered temporary residence in the municipality.

Be entered in the supplement to the permanent electoral register.

EU citizens who are not already registered must apply by 7 October 2026 at 4 PM.

“Many people from other EU countries live in Prague 8, work here, raise their families here and use the same schools, parks, streets and public services as everyone else. Yet many still do not know that they can vote in local elections,” said Martin Štěrba, the Czech Pirate Party’s candidate for mayor of Prague 8.

“We want to explain how it works and hear directly from them what Prague 8 could do better.”

The Czech municipal elections will take place on 9 and 10 October 2026.

Voters in Prague 8 will elect representatives to both the Prague 8 Municipal District Council and the Prague City Assembly.

World.title: Nearly 40 Percent of Young Czechs Experience Financial Stress Every Month
World.content:
Money worries affect almost one in three Czech adults, but younger people are facing a greater burden.

A new survey found that 39 percent of people aged 18 to 26 experience financial anxiety at least once a month, with household income playing a major role in how people feel about their finances.



Financial concerns are common across the Czech Republic. According to a survey conducted by Ipsos for Home Credit, 28 percent of adults experience worries about money at least once a month. Another 35 percent report financial stress several times a year.

Young adults face the greatest pressure

People aged 18 to 26 are the most likely to experience regular financial stress. Nearly four in ten respondents in this age group said they worry about money at least once a month.

Home Credit attributed the pressure partly to the cost of housing and everyday expenses. For young adults trying to establish themselves financially, rising prices in recent years have made it harder to absorb unexpected costs.

An unplanned bill or other expense can therefore create a serious problem, particularly for those who have limited savings.

Household income makes a significant difference

The survey found a clear relationship between household income and financial anxiety.

Among households earning up to CZK 40,000 per month, 41 percent of respondents reported experiencing financial stress. The proportion decreases as household income rises.

People living in households with monthly incomes above CZK 70,000 reported the lowest levels of financial concern.

Age and education also appear to influence how people view their finances. Respondents aged 54 to 65 and university students reported lower levels of stress than some other groups. In both categories, 43 percent said they did not experience financial stress at all.

Financial stress may also affect physical health

The consequences of financial difficulties can extend beyond anxiety and everyday worries.

The material also refers to research published by the American Mayo Clinic in 2025. According to the research cited, long-term financial distress and food insecurity may be associated with poorer cardiovascular health and a higher risk of death.

The findings underline the potential connection between financial security and overall well-being. However, the Czech survey does not establish whether financial stress directly causes health problems.

The survey was conducted by Ipsos in June 2026 among 1,026 people.

World.title: Fresh from France: Meet Benjamin, the Founder of The French in Prague
World.content:
For the past 12 years, Benjamin has been building a life in Prague – and helping bring a taste of France to the Czech capital.

What began as a business supplying wine to hotels, restaurants and wine bars 10 years ago has gradually grown into The French, a food business focused on bringing French products directly to Prague.

The company started with an e-shop selling mainly wine, pâté, jam, honey and foie gras. But Benjamin soon realized there was something missing: fresh French produce.

“The idea, step by step, was that we were missing fresh products to be able to open a physical shop. That’s how, two years ago, we started importing fresh products.”

Today, The French operates two shops in Prague and imports a wide range of products directly from France, with a focus on freshness and quality while keeping prices accessible.

“It cannot be fresher than what we import.”

From Breakfast to Dinner

Fresh fruit and vegetables have become one of the shop’s main attractions. The products are imported weekly, with a truck leaving France every Tuesday carrying oysters, mussels, cheeses, fish, meat, fruits and vegetables.

“Two days ago it was in the sea and today it’s already in Prague, sitting in our fridge.”

The shop aims to cover the entire day, from breakfast to dinner. Customers can pick up croissants and pain au chocolat in the morning, fresh coffee, and a selection of French products for lunch and dinner.

Among the more distinctive products are French crème fraîche and salted butter. Benjamin points out that the natural colour of the dairy products can change during the year depending on what the cows eat. “If you have the same colour of butter or cream throughout the whole year, it’s because they are not eating grass.”

A New Home in Vinohrady

The company recently expanded with a larger shop in Vinohrady, giving customers access to a wider range of ultra-fresh products imported directly from France, as well as cosmetics from Provence.

The French also supplies restaurants and hotels across Prague with products including butter, cream, cheese, ham, sausages and olives. Much of the range comes directly from the Rungis International Market near Paris, one of the largest food markets in Europe.

The company also works with direct farmers, with some products clearly marked as coming from individual producers. “In Prague, you don’t have any shop that is grouping all of these categories of products.”

Customers can also order through The French’s e-shop at francouzske-speciality.cz and either have their purchases delivered or collect them from a shop.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The French.cz (@the_french_cz)

But Benjamin says the experience is intended to be more personal than a standard supermarket. “We are not a shop where people are just behind the cash desk. We have people going into the shop to explain what we have, recommend what to cook and what to pair.”

The shops also have a weekly tasting calendar, giving customers the chance to try different products and discover new flavours.

French Food for Everyone

Although many customers are French, The French is not specifically aimed at the French community.

The Vinohrady shop attracts a large number of expats, while the company’s Prague 4 location has a much higher proportion of Czech customers. Benjamin says the goal is to serve people living in the neighborhood regardless of nationality. “We are not targeting especially expats or especially French. We are trying to target everyone living in the area who like gastronomy.”

There are, however, some differences in what Czech and French customers look for. Stronger French cheeses, for example, can take some getting used to, while certain French cuts of meat differ from traditional Czech ones.

Some types of fish are also relatively unfamiliar. Red mullet, or rouget, is widely used in French cuisine and high-end restaurants but is less common in Czech kitchens.

Growing Across Prague

The French has ambitious plans for the coming years. After opening its Vinohrady location and another shop in Prague 4, the company is preparing to open another location in Prague 9 in January.

The long-term goal is to operate five or six shops across Prague, with Holešovice, Karlín and Dejvice among the areas being considered.

World.title: A Prague Institution: Indian Jewel Celebrates 30 Years of North Indian Flavours
World.content:
The family-run restaurant has been bringing authentic North Indian flavours and warm hospitality to Prague since 1996.

For 30 years, Indian Jewel has been serving authentic Indian cuisine in the heart of Prague. Established in 1996 by Sanjeev Wadehra, the family-owned restaurant is celebrating three decades in the Czech capital in 2026 — a milestone that makes it one of the longest-standing Indian restaurants in the country.



The restaurant’s story began with Sanjeev Wadehra, who brought recipes, cooking traditions and spice blends directly from India to Prague. Today, the kitchen continues to focus on authentic North Indian cuisine, with dishes prepared according to traditional recipes rather than adapted to passing culinary trends.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Indian Jewel Prague (@indianjewelprague)

To celebrate its 30th anniversary, Indian Jewel is offering Prague Morning readers a complimentary welcome drink or dessert. Simply mention Prague Morning when you visit.

Among the highlights are tandoor specialities, prepared in the traditional clay oven, alongside lamb, chicken and shrimp curries. The menu also offers a wide selection of vegetarian dishes, as well as biryanis, freshly baked naan and other Indian classics.

Popular choices include Butter Chicken, Chicken Tikka Masala and Lamb Rogan Josh, while the tandoor menu offers another way to explore the flavours of North India.

But food is only part of the restaurant’s story. Indian Jewel has built its reputation on consistent quality and warm, personal hospitality. Many members of the team have been with the restaurant for years, creating the family atmosphere that Sanjeev and his wife, Mohini, consider an important part of its success.

The restaurant moved to its current location at Rybná 9 in 2021, after many years at its previous home in the historic Týn Courtyard. Despite the change, the philosophy has remained the same: authentic food, attentive service and a welcoming atmosphere.

World.title: From Sri Lanka to Prague: How Tharusha Brought Coconut Culture to the City
World.content:
Tharusha De Silva, originally from Sri Lanka, has spent much of his life between different countries.

Today, he is bringing a taste closely associated with home to Prague through his beverage brand, The Coconut Culture which is also available at select cafés and restaurants across Prague.

We spoke to him about his journey to the Czech Republic, navigating life between cultures, and the story behind The Coconut Culture.



Journey to Prague

Prague was never part of a long-term plan for De Silva. He first came to the Czech Republic in 2016 to study mechanical engineering, after growing up in Sri Lanka and spending his teenage years in Dubai. By his own account, his decision to come here was almost entirely random.

“We had a counselling office that used to help us with university applications, and one day they changed the wallpaper to a map of Prague. I just went into the room, pointed at it and said, ‘Hey, what is that?’ They told me a little bit about Prague, and that’s how I got here.”

At first, Prague was simply where he planned to spend his university years. “I always thought that I would leave after university,” he says. But the longer he stayed, the less certain leaving became.

“It’s very difficult to give you a straight answer to what made me decide to stay. But I think the city has its way of keeping you.”

Freedom and opportunity were part of what made the city difficult to leave.

“You could really make something of yourself here if you really want to,” he says.

Eventually, staying stopped feeling like a temporary decision. “In a way, I found a part of home here. That was enough to make me stay.”

The Coconut Culture

King Coconut, a variety native to Sri Lanka, became the starting point for The Coconut Culture.

Unlike varieties grown primarily for their meat or oil, King Coconut has a more specific purpose. “The other coconuts have multiple uses. Some are used to get the desiccated coconut from the inside, to make milk out of it, to make coconut oil, even some kind of biofuel. But this variant, the King Coconut, has one use: it is to drink it.”

It is sweeter and lighter than regular coconut water, with a taste he compares to subtly sweet spring water.

For De Silva, however, the connection with King Coconut goes back to his childhood. He remembers his grandfather taking him and his sister out on his scooter. On the way back, they would stop beside a road running between paddy fields and have a King Coconut together.

Years later, that childhood ritual became part of the reason he wanted to introduce King Coconut to people who had never encountered it.

“I want to bring King Coconut out more, make more people be aware of it, and give it its place in the world.”

The name The Coconut Culture came later, during a conversation with a friend about Czech and Sri Lankan culture. De Silva remembers describing his background almost casually: “I come from the coconut culture.” The phrase stayed with him.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @coconutculture.eu

Living Between Cultures

Having grown up in Sri Lanka, spent his teenage years in Dubai and lived in the Czech Republic since 2016, De Silva has spent much of his life between different cultures.

There are, of course, things he still misses about Sri Lanka.

“I come from an island, a very fairly simple life. I get to walk around without any shoes. We have the sea, we have the ocean. We have the sun, so many fruits, so many wild animals, forests, mountains.”

But perhaps the biggest difference is language and the sense of belonging that comes with it.

“The most important thing is I communicate in my own language back home. Here, I am the expat. I either communicate in English or with the little Czech I know.”

“Back home, it’s my language. I speak in my language, I’m more comfortable. I feel like I’m a fuller version of myself.”

Distance has also changed the way he sees the place he came from.

“The place that I will make home or call home in the future is just going to be a mix of the cultures that I’ve experienced. It’s going to be some of the things that I picked up from Dubai, some of the things I’ve picked up living in the Czech Republic or Europe, and then, of course, where I come from, my roots.”

Finding a Home in Prague

Prague, naturally, has become part of that mix. After years in the city, De Silva says one of the things he values most is the openness he finds here.

“I think here, Prague is one of the places where you could just walk out feeling or looking any way you want. And it’s very rare that anyone would tell you anything because people accept you as you are.”

Part of that openness, he says, also comes from the people who have made Prague their home from elsewhere.

“Prague has many, many expats and the city is filled with expats. Therefore, all of these expats bring different cultures into Prague.”

Beyond the bigger things that make Prague feel like home, it is also the everyday details that have become part of his life here.

“I would definitely miss the café culture. I love to sit in a café in the mornings, in the evenings, have coffee, read, do some work.”

A First Taste

The first real test came at the launch event, held before The Coconut Culture had even received its full stock. De Silva and his team brought in a small number of bottles specifically for the occasion and invited friends to try the drink.

“We had a launch event with some of our friends, and we got a lot of good feedback about the drink, especially about its taste, about the way it’s packed, about the branding that we’ve done.”

For the team, it was an early indication that the idea could work in Prague.

“This was maybe where we thought, okay, this is actually something that the people of the Czech Republic, all the expats and the locals, will enjoy.”

Beyond King Coconut

King Coconut is only the first of the discoveries De Silva hopes to bring to Europe. He describes The Coconut Culture as “an exploration company”, where “the fruit is the vehicle”.

The idea is to keep the range deliberately small, with the company eventually aiming for five to seven products.

“The Coconut Culture has a very simple vision: to find native fruits. We want to have between five to seven products, and be very specialized in them: find these native fruits that are specific to countries or communities. And we want to go there, we want to discover it, and we want to bring it to the European market and give it to the people here.”

For De Silva, however, the products are also a way of introducing the places they come from.

“We want to find these cultures, tell their story to the world here and, hopefully, respect, as we always try to, where it comes from and also respect the place that it’s being sold at.”

World.title: Czechia Considers One Million-Crown Reward for Second Child as Births Hit Record Low
World.content:
Prime Minister Andrej Babiš is considering a million-crown reward for families who have a second child, along with lifelong tax relief for parents of a third child.

The proposals are among several measures being discussed, including support for parents who are studying, childcare services and more affordable housing. Babiš said he would bring together the relevant ministers to discuss the issue.



The Czech Republic recorded just 77,600 live births in 2025, the lowest figure since statistical records began in 1785. Births fell in every region compared with the previous year.

The country’s total fertility rate also dropped to 1.28 children per woman, while the average age of women having their first child rose to 29.2 years.

Million-crown reward for a second child

Babiš said the government was examining several proposals to encourage families to have more children.

“One million crowns for a second child,” he said, describing a possible incentive for women who already have one child.

He also mentioned a lifelong tax break for a third child, support for studying parents, nurseries and children’s groups.

Babiš also criticized mortgage costs, questioning why Czech interest rates remain 1.5 percentage points above those in the eurozone. He has repeatedly criticized the Czech National Bank, while cheaper mortgages were among ANO’s key election promises.

Debate over assisted reproduction

Babiš also addressed a proposal from the Ministry of Health that would allow single women to undergo assisted reproduction without a male partner.

Responding to criticism from the Alliance for Family, he acknowledged the importance of fathers but pointed to divorce and child-support disputes.

“I know that. But what is the divorce rate here? Fathers leave families and then sometimes do not even pay child support,” he said.

Babiš added that he did not want to comment extensively on the issue because of possible accusations of having business interests in reproductive clinics.

“It’s nonsense. A woman can choose the clinic she wants. If she hates Babiš, then let her not go there. I don’t decide on that at all,” he said.

World.title: Czechia Ranks Fourth Among Russia’s “Enemies” in New Propaganda List
World.content:
Czechia has been ranked among Russia’s top five “enemy” countries in a new list published by Vzglyad, a Russian outlet widely regarded as a Kremlin propaganda mouthpiece.

Czechia has been ranked as the fourth-most “hostile” country toward Russia in a new ranking published by Vzglyad, scoring 65 out of a possible 100 points.



The list places Czechia alongside Romania, Poland, the United Kingdom and Canada, all of which received the same score.

Italy topped the ranking with 80 points, followed by Germany, Lithuania and Finland, which tied for second place with 75 points each. The United States, Latvia and France shared third place with 70 points apiece.

Japan makes the list for the first time

Most of the countries in the top ten appear regularly in the ranking. This time, however, Japan was included for the first time.

According to Vzglyad, Japan’s inclusion was prompted by Tokyo’s “firm protest” over Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Iturup.

Iturup is part of the southern Kuril Islands, which Japan claims as its “Northern Territories.” Russia considers the islands an integral part of its territory.

The territorial dispute dates back to the final days of World War II, when Soviet forces occupied Iturup and neighboring islands in 1945.

Czechia remains a regular presence

Czechia has consistently appeared among the top ten countries in the ranking.

The list was first published in November last year, when Czechia also placed fourth. In May, however, the country briefly dropped to the bottom of the ranking.

The index assigns countries a maximum of 100 points based on six criteria. According to Vzglyad editor Evgeny Pozdnyakov, the most important factor is military-political activity against Russia, which accounts for up to 30 points. Sanctions pressure contributes a further 20 points.

The ranking reflects the perspective of Russian state-aligned media and should not be interpreted as an official assessment of international relations or a measure of actual hostility between countries.

World.title: AIGEL to Celebrate 10th Anniversary with Prague Concert
World.content:
On October 21, electronic duo AIGEL will perform at Futurum Music Bar in Prague as part of a special concert marking the band’s 10th anniversary.

AIGEL was formed by Tatar poet and singer Aigel Gaisina and St. Petersburg producer Ilya Baramiya. Over the past decade, the duo has developed a distinctive sound combining electronic music, trip-hop and psychedelic influences.

Get your ticket here

Their music crosses linguistic and cultural boundaries, with songs performed in Russian, Tatar, English and German.

AIGEL gained international attention with the viral tracks “Tatarin” and “Pyyala.” The latter topped streaming charts in 25 countries and reached No. 1 on the global Shazam chart.

Over 10 years, the duo has released five albums and dozens of singles. They have also received a Cannes Lion for the music video “You’re Born” and toured extensively across Europe and beyond.

Now based in Europe, AIGEL is preparing a special anniversary show in Prague, combining the duo’s electronic sound with Gaisina’s distinctive and expressive vocals.

The concert will take place on October 21 at Futurum Music Bar.

World.title: Brain Bar 2026: Europe’s biggest festival on the future returns to Budapest this week!
World.content:
Brain Bar, Europe’s largest festival on the future, returns to Budapest on 17–18 September. The event takes place at the House of Music Hungary in City Park. The programme includes more than 100 talks, discussions, music and art shows across five stages, plus workshops in the festival’s Talent Hub.

Host Jenn Zeng on what to expect from two days at the House of Music.

Guest author: Anhao Chen

Gergely Böszörményi-Nagy founded the festival in 2015. It brings scientists, politicians, entrepreneurs, and cultural figures together with a mostly young audience, and every session is built so that visitors can ask questions from the floor. Past speakers include PayPal founder Peter Thiel, astronaut Chris Hadfield, and psychotherapist Esther Perel.

Peter Thiel at Brain Bar. Photo: Brain Bar

From Cory Doctorow to Judit Polgár

This year’s speakers include science fiction writer Cory Doctorow, physicist Carlo Rovelli, and Nataliya Kosmyna, the MIT Media Lab neuroscientist studying what ChatGPT does to the brain. Hungarian names on the bill include Minister of Transport and Investment Dávid Vitézy, Minister of Science and Technology Zoltán Tanács, Sziget Festival founder Károly Gerendai, and football coach Zsolt Szoboszlai, father of Liverpool midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai.

Judit Polgár, the most successful female chess player of all time, is also speaking. Her foundation is the festival’s goodwill partner this year and receives all ticket revenue, which it uses to develop children’s thinking and creativity through chess.

Sessions run in English and Hungarian. The agenda marks the language of each session.

“How do humans actually connect?”

Among this year’s hosts is Jenn Zeng, the event’s youngest host and first woman president of the LSE Entrepreneurs’ Society, who will take the stage at Brain Bar for the first time.

Jenn Zeng.

Speaking to Daily News Hungary ahead of the festival, Zeng said she is most looking forward to her one-on-one with Jared Henderson, a philosopher and content creator, on the future of friendship in an age of digital isolation.

“This one specifically stands out because right now we are living in a world where everything we talk about is AI,” she said. “There is less and less emphasis on people and how humans actually connect and bond with each other. How do we form truly fulfilling and meaningful friendships in a world of digital isolation?”

Zeng said the festival’s value lies in putting a young audience in front of the people working at the edge of their fields. “I really hope the people feel inspired, make new friends while they are there, and really think about what they could do to contribute to a better world,” she said.

Tickets for the Brain Bar 2026 Festival

Brain Bar 2026 runs 17–18 September at the House of Music Hungary, Olof Palme sétány 3. Students and teachers can attend for free after registering via a form on the festival website, and teachers can sign up entire secondary school classes by email. Anyone without a pass can still use the open outdoor area. A two-day pass costs 39,900 HUF, with a 25% discount for 4 or more passes. Single-day tickets are 26,900 HUF. You can find tickets and the full agenda at brainbar.com.
