World.title: Hungary’s new child protection bill to scrap controversial anti-LGBTQ provisions
World.content:
The Tisza government has submitted a child protection bill that would remove references to homosexuality and transgender identity from Hungary’s controversial 2021 legislation, while introducing new rules targeting sexual exploitation, harmful content and political advertising aimed at children.

The proposal was submitted to Parliament on Monday by Social and Family Affairs Minister Vilmos Kátai-Németh. It seeks to strengthen children’s rights and safety in both traditional and digital environments.

Controversial LGBTQ references would be removed

One of the most significant changes would affect Hungary’s child protection and guardianship legislation. The current law, adopted by the former Fidesz-led government in 2021, prohibits making content available to under-18s that “promotes” or even depicts “deviation from the identity corresponding to the sex at birth”, changing one’s sex or homosexuality.

The new proposal would remove these references. Instead, the law would prohibit making available or promoting content that is inappropriate for a child’s age or level of development, depicts sexuality gratuitously, or promotes, justifies or encourages sexual violence, sexual exploitation, sexual solicitation or manipulation, or other sexual offences.

The justification says the legislation would therefore focus on actual risks to children rather than sexual orientation or gender identity.

Similar provisions would be removed from Hungary’s media law, advertising legislation and public education law.

Under the proposed changes, lessons covering sexual culture, sexual life, sexual orientation and sexual development would no longer explicitly be prohibited from promoting homosexuality or transgender identity. Instead, they would be subject to the revised child protection rules.

With this amendment, the Tisza government would also repeal the provision in the law that Fidesz used in an attempt to prevent Pride from taking place.

The 2026 Budapest Pride. Photo: MTI

Political adverts targeting children would also face new restrictions

The bill would also introduce new safeguards against political and commercial advertising in public spaces. Political posters and other campaign communications would have to comply with child protection requirements, meaning that campaign materials could not be used if they could seriously harm children’s physical, intellectual, emotional or moral development.

The government also says s that could seriously harm the development of under-18s because of their content, imagery, sound effects or presentation would be prohibited in public spaces and other locations accessible without restrictions.

The rules would apply to both political and commercial advertising. The government has also promised to begin preparing a two-stage pay rise programme for workers in the social and child protection sectors.

Stricter rules proposed for children left in hospital

Another part of the package would address children who remain in hospital even after they no longer require medical treatment.

Under the proposed rules, once a child no longer needs to remain in hospital for health reasons, the guardianship authority would have a maximum of eight days to complete a full assessment of the child’s child protection situation and prepare an action plan.

The stated aim is to prevent children from spending months in hospital simply because the child protection system has not found a suitable placement for them.

The 2021 law triggered an EU legal dispute

The changes would also address a long-running dispute between Hungary and the European Union over the 2021 child protection legislation.

The law, adopted by the Fidesz-majority Parliament in June 2021, was presented by the former government as legislation aimed at combating paedophilia. Alongside tougher criminal and registration rules concerning paedophile offences, however, it introduced restrictions on media content, advertising, school education and publications accessible to minors.

Critics argued that the legislation conflated homosexuality with paedophilia and imposed discriminatory restrictions on LGBTQ-related content.

The European Commission launched infringement proceedings against Hungary in 2021 and later brought the case before the Court of Justice of the European Union. In April 2026, the EU court ruled that Hungary had breached its obligations under EU law with the legislation.

The ruling also resulted in a separate financial issue for Hungary. Around EUR 0.6 billion in cohesion funding has been blocked since the end of 2022 because of the dispute. This amount is separate from the EUR 16.4 billion covered by the political agreement reached in May between Prime Minister Péter Magyar and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on the release of EU funds.

Government says changes could help unlock EU funding

Magyar said in a Monday interview with Hungary’s public broadcaster that the new child protection package could also help Hungary avoid a financial penalty linked to the 2021 legislation. He said the changes could additionally pave the way for the release of around EUR 500 million in EU funding for education, equivalent to roughly HUF 183 billion. The proposed legislation will now have to go through Parliament before it can take effect.

World.title: Hungarian police officer admits beating defenceless man, breaking several bones
World.content:
A police officer in Gyöngyös, Hungary, has received a suspended prison sentence after admitting that he and a colleague beat a defenceless man, breaking his jaw, nose and facial bones. The second officer denies the charges and will face further proceedings in January.

Officer admits to assault in court

A police officer from Gyöngyös has been sentenced to one and a half years in prison, suspended for three years, after admitting that he and another officer assaulted a defenceless man in January 2024.

The officer was convicted at a preparatory hearing before the Military Council of the Budapest-Capital Regional Court. He admitted all the charges against him, allowing the court to issue a final verdict. He was also demoted.

The second officer accused of taking part in the assault continues to deny the charges, meaning his trial will continue in January. The victim is represented by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, which said the case involved an especially serious abuse of power.

If you missed it: Former school guard jailed in Hungary for sexually abusing two vulnerable minors

Police officers allegedly took man to outskirts of Gyöngyös

According to the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, the victim, identified as “András”, is a homeless man living in the Duránda area of Gyöngyös. In January 2024, he was warming himself in the entrance of a bank when the two officers approached him for an identity check. His documents were in order, and no proceedings were launched against him.

The officers then offered to drive him home in their patrol car. Instead, they took him to the outskirts of the town and stopped near a forest.

One of the officers restrained the man while the other punched him in the face. The officer who had initially restrained him then also hit and kicked him in the thigh. The officers pushed him to the ground and allegedly threatened to call a hunter to have wild boars eat him.

The assault continued for several minutes and only stopped when another vehicle approached on the road. The man then managed to escape and return home.

Victim suffered multiple fractures

His mother saw his injuries and called an ambulance. At the hospital, doctors diagnosed him with fractures to his jaw, nose and facial bones, as well as concussion. A criminal investigation was subsequently launched. The two officers initially denied the allegations during the investigation.

However, one of them later admitted the charges in court. He reportedly said that the day of the hearing was also his final day as a police officer. The second defendant continues to maintain his innocence, with his case scheduled to continue in January.

Ivóna Bieber, a lawyer for the Hungarian Helsinki Committee representing the victim, said that around 90% of complaints concerning assaults allegedly committed by police officers do not even result in charges being brought. She nevertheless praised the prosecutors’ work in this case and said the court had delivered a fair judgment, taking into account the officer’s full confession and remorse.

World.title: Russian gas deliveries to Hungary suddenly halved after diplomat expulsions: here’s the reason
World.content:
Gas imports from Russia via the southern route fell to around half their usual level just one day after Hungary expelled ten Russian embassy staff; however, the timing appears to have been coincidental.

Russian gas deliveries suddenly plunge

The amount of natural gas entering Hungary from the south fell sharply last week, reaching levels not seen for years, according to Hungarian economic news outlet G7.

Between Wednesday and Friday, just 11.6 million cubic metres of gas per day entered Hungary via the southern route from Serbia. Since only Russian gas enters Hungary from Serbia, the drop effectively meant that Russian gas deliveries through this route were cut by roughly half.

The timing immediately attracted attention. The decline came just one day after Hungary’s Foreign Ministry expelled ten employees of the Russian embassy, which raised the question: maybe Moscow had responded by reducing gas supplies?

However, the available evidence suggests that the two events were not connected.

A technical restriction was already planned

The southern route has become highly important for Hungary’s gas supply in recent years. Most Russian gas imports now arrive through the TurkStream pipeline, which runs under the Black Sea before passing through Bulgaria and Serbia.

The pipeline has generally operated close to full capacity for around three years, apart from scheduled maintenance periods.

But according to G7, Hungary’s gas network operator, FGSZ, had already included a restriction for this period in its annual maintenance schedule. The document shows that the relevant cross-border capacity would operate at 50 per cent.

In other words, the sharp decline appears to have been the result of a planned technical restriction rather than a political response from Russia.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Russian senator had warned of gas consequences

The possibility of Russian retaliation was particularly notable because a Russian senator had warned about potential consequences following the expulsions.

According to reporting by Világgazdaság, the senator said the diplomatic move could have “unpleasant consequences” for Budapest, including a reduction or even a complete halt to Russian gas deliveries through the TurkStream pipeline.

The timing of the subsequent drop in deliveries therefore fuelled speculation about a possible connection.

However, industry sources and experts contacted by G7 were initially unable to identify a clear explanation for the sudden fall. Most ultimately considered technical or commercial factors more likely, with the planned technical restriction providing the apparent answer.

Have you heard? Péter Magyar would break away from Russian oil, but expects something in return from Brussels

Gas flows have since recovered

The reduced imports did not last. Although the southern route was still not operating at full capacity over the weekend, gas flows have since largely returned to their usual levels. G7 noted that total Russian gas imports for last week amounted to around 122 million cubic metres, making it the lowest weekly figure in almost three years, excluding scheduled maintenance-related shutdowns.

Hungary’s state-owned MVM buys Russian gas from Gazprom under a long-term agreement, while traders have also purchased billions of cubic metres of Russian gas on the spot market in recent years because of its competitive price.

It is therefore possible that short-term commercial purchases were particularly affected by the temporary capacity restriction. However, because Russian gas currently enters Hungary through this southern route, the reduction would have affected at least some of the gas purchased by MVM as well.

All in all, the available evidence points to an unfortunate coincidence rather than a Russian response to Hungary’s diplomatic move.

World.title: PM Magyar says former PM Orbán could face prison over threats against new asset recovery office staff
World.content:
Hungary’s prime minister accused former PM Viktor Orbán of threatening prosecutors, police officers and investigators who may work for the newly established National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office.

Magyar: “This is violence against an official”

Speaking in Parliament, Péter Magyar criticised Viktor Orbán over remarks the former prime minister made about employees of Hungary’s new National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office.

Magyar said Orbán had “specifically threatened Hungarian prosecutors, customs officers, police officers and investigators”, accusing members of the former governing party of remaining silent about the remarks. According to Magyar, Orbán’s statements could amount to the criminal offence of violence against a public official under Hungary’s Criminal Code.

He cited provisions under which anyone who uses violence or threats to obstruct an official carrying out a lawful procedure, or to force them to take action, can face between one and five years in prison.

“What Orbán did is violence against a public official under the Criminal Code,” Magyar said.

He also pointed out that, as a former prime minister, Orbán no longer has parliamentary immunity.

What did Orbán say?

The dispute follows an interview Orbán gave to Hír TV after his closed-door speech in Kötcse at the weekend. In the interview, Orbán referred to the newly established asset recovery office as an “ÁVH-type institution”, 444.hu writes. The ÁVH was Hungary’s communist-era state security organisation.

Orbán warned that if his political side returned to power, people who worked for the office, took part in its procedures or made decisions there would face accountability.

He also said the names of every employee involved would be made public, along with details of their work and the procedures in which they had participated.

Orbán argued that those responsible would have to face financial and legal consequences once, in his words, the rule of law was restored.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Magyar calls for solidarity with officials

Magyar said the remarks were particularly serious because the people being targeted were public servants who would be carrying out lawful procedures. He called on Tisza MPs to express their solidarity with the affected officials and to defend them against what he described as threats.

The confrontation comes as the new Hungarian government prepares to use the asset recovery office to investigate cases involving suspected corruption and recover public assets “lost” during the 16 years of the previous Orbán era.

Orbán also attacks the Tisza government

In the same interview, Orbán criticised the government led by Magyar, arguing that it was handing Hungary’s economy back to Brussels and pursuing policies that would make the country less sovereign. The former prime minister also attacked the planned introduction of the euro, calling it the “biggest scam” and claiming that the stated 2030 target was merely a cover for future austerity measures.

Orbán further argued that the political right could only have a chance of returning to power if it remained united, and said his priority over the next six months would be to reorganise Fidesz rather than focus on Tisza.

World.title: German foreign minister visits Hungary; Budapest and Berlin agree on major new cooperation plans, announce visit
World.content:
Hungary and Germany have agreed on closer political, economic and diplomatic cooperation, while Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s November visit to Berlin is already being prepared.

Budapest and Berlin seek to strengthen ties

Hungary and Germany are preparing to open a new chapter in their bilateral relations, Hungarian Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orbán said following talks with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul in Budapest.

The two sides agreed on a series of measures aimed at strengthening political dialogue, economic cooperation and people-to-people ties. Orbán said the meeting had also begun preparations for Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s visit to Berlin on 9–10 November.

The timing has historical significance: the Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, one of the defining events of the end of the Cold War.

In a joint statement, the two countries said they wanted to renew their partnership and open a new, trust-based chapter in Hungarian-German relations, nearly 35 years after the signing of their friendship treaty in 1992.

If you missed it: FM Anita Orbán reports progress on minority rights for Hungarians in Ukraine

Economic and energy cooperation in focus

Hungary and Germany said they intend to further develop and broaden their economic ties, including beyond the automotive industry, where German companies have a major presence in Hungary.

The two governments also stressed the importance of strengthening the European single market and creating an attractive, innovation-friendly and reliable investment environment.

They agreed that Europe needs to preserve and develop the foundations of a competitive industrial sector so that the continent can remain competitive globally.

Energy security was another key area of cooperation. Hungary and Germany called for greater European coordination to protect the region’s energy security.

The countries also said they face significant migration pressure and share the goal of stopping illegal migration and strengthening the protection of the EU’s external borders.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Closer cooperation between foreign ministries

The two countries agreed on a number of concrete measures to deepen cooperation. These include strengthening the Hungarian-German Forum, which brings together political and civil society representatives. The next forum, scheduled to take place in Berlin in autumn 2026, is being presented as a concrete sign of a new beginning in bilateral relations.

Hungary and Germany will also establish regular professional consultations between their foreign ministries on bilateral relations and European policy, as well as on geo-economic and defence industry issues where relevant.

The ministries plan to increase exchanges on strategic planning and communication, including cooperation on the challenges posed by disinformation. A regular dialogue between Hungarian and German think tanks will also be established.

The two sides additionally agreed to expand exchanges between young diplomats and connect training programmes preparing participants for diplomatic service. The countries also plan to increase the exchange of diplomats between their foreign ministries.

Cooperation in education and culture

Budapest and Berlin also intend to maintain close cooperation with Andrássy University Budapest, youth exchange organisations and other partners in culture, language and education. The two sides will examine the possibility of organising a Hungarian-German Year of Culture in 2028.

The joint statement also highlights the role of science, education, culture, civil society and youth exchanges in strengthening mutual understanding between the two countries.

Germany’s large Hungarian diaspora and Hungary’s German minority will continue to receive particular attention, with the two governments also stressing the importance of the future and accessibility of German-language education in Hungary.

Shared positions on European and international issues

The joint statement says Hungary and Germany want to work together for a strong, secure, free and competitive Europe as EU member states and NATO allies.

On Ukraine, both countries reaffirmed their support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and backed the European Council’s June 2026 conclusions calling for an immediate ceasefire and a comprehensive, just and lasting peace.

They also said they would increase efforts to promote peace and security in the Middle East and South-West Asia, while supporting Israel’s right to self-defence.

On the Western Balkans, Budapest and Berlin said they share an interest in peace, stability, successful EU integration and economic development, and pledged to support candidate countries on their path towards EU membership.

The statement also refers to the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 revolution and uprising, saying it reinforces the two countries’ commitment to European values, including human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and the protection of human rights.

World.title: Road collapses under bus carrying dozens of passengers in Budapest
World.content:
The asphalt gave way beneath a bus in Budapest’s 15th district on Monday morning after water washed away part of the road. Six people, including four children, were taken to hospital.

Road collapsed beneath packed bus

A section of road collapsed beneath a BKK bus carrying around 30–40 passengers in Budapest’s 15th district on Monday morning. The incident happened on Sződliget Street in Rákospalota after water washed away the road surface, according to Hungary’s disaster management authority.

Firefighters and ambulances were called to the scene, while the affected section of the road was closed to traffic. The National Ambulance Service later told Hungarian News Agency MTI that six people were taken to hospital from the scene.

Four children and one adult were transported with minor injuries, while another woman suffered a head injury. She was in a stable condition when taken to hospital.

A photo of the asphalt can be seen here.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Several bus routes diverted

The incident has caused significant disruption to public transport in the area. According to the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK), buses 96, 124, 225, 296 and 296A are currently operating on diverted routes.

As a result, the services are not currently stopping at Géza fejedelem Square, Sződliget Street or Fő Road.

The affected section of Sződliget Street remains closed while authorities deal with the damage caused by the collapsed road.

World.title: Flydubai resumes Budapest flights as airline expands network to more than 125 destinations!
World.content:
Flydubai has resumed its direct Budapest–Dubai flights as the airline restores most of its network and expands to more than 125 destinations across 56 countries. The service is currently operating three times a week, with daily flights planned from late October.

Budapest flights resumed at the end of July

The Dubai-based carrier restarted its direct flights between Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport (BUD) and Dubai International Airport (DXB) on 31 July 2026.

The Budapest route currently operates three times a week on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays. From 25 October, flydubai plans to increase the frequency to a daily service.

The airline operates the route with Boeing 737 aircraft. The service also forms part of flydubai’s partnership with Emirates, giving passengers access to a much wider combined network via Dubai.

According to flydubai, passengers travelling on connecting Emirates flights can benefit from a single booking and checked baggage transferred through to their final destination.

Flydubai network grows to more than 125 destinations

The Budapest service comes as flydubai continues to rebuild and expand its international network. In a press release issued on 14 September, the airline said it had restored operations to 85% of its network and now serves more than 125 destinations in 56 countries, with an average of 2,200 flights per week.

In recent months, flydubai has resumed or launched services to several destinations, including Aleppo, Benghazi and Bangkok. The airline has also increased its Bangkok service to three daily non-stop flights, citing strong demand.

Flydubai is due to add another destination on 23 September, when it launches flights to Pokhara in Nepal, its second destination in the country after Kathmandu.

The carrier said it expects travel demand to remain strong during the upcoming winter season, with Dubai continuing to attract visitors while passengers use the city as a hub for travel elsewhere.

Flydubai’s Boeing 737 MAX 9 in Greece. Photo: depositphotos.com

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Budapest offers connections to destinations beyond Dubai

Flydubai said back in July that the Budapest route also strengthens connections between Hungary and the United Arab Emirates while giving Hungarian travellers easier access to destinations in the Middle East, Africa and Asia.

The airline has previously highlighted destinations such as the Maldives, Thailand, Sri Lanka and Kenya as examples of places that can be reached through Dubai.

The wider Emirates and flydubai network now offers access to more than 214 unique destinations in over 100 countries, with more than 4,600 possible connections through Dubai.

“Despite the challenging operating environment, we have remained focused on restoring our network safely and efficiently, adding capacity where we see demand while opening new markets,” flydubai Chief Executive Officer Ghaith Al Ghaith said.

He added that the airline was encouraged by strong customer demand during the summer and remained positioned to further restore its network in the coming months.

Read more travel news: Good news for passengers: Wizz Air restarts popular flights to multiple destinations from Budapest

Daily Budapest service coming in October

For Hungarian travellers, the most important change will come in late October, when the Budapest–Dubai route is scheduled to become a daily service. Flydubai said it is continuing to add capacity to its year-round routes as more aircraft become available. The airline currently operates an average of 2,200 weekly flights and aims to increase this frequency further.

World.title: BIRN Launches ‘Trial Stories’ Page for Hashim Thaci Verdict
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Illustration: Tijana Dupanovic/BIRN.

Ahead of the verdict in the war crimes and crimes against humanity case against for former senior Kosovo Liberation Army officials at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague on Wednesday, BIRN has launched a special focus page dedicated to the trial and its impact.

The page compiles BIRN’s reporting on the trial since it started in April 2023 – analysis articles as well as news reports from Kosovo and The Hague.

“BIRN is one of the few media outlets that has followed the prosecution of Hashim Thaci and his co-defendants in genuine depth from the beginning, reporting on the latest developments but also examining their potential implications,” said BIRN’s deputy regional director Gentiana Murati.

“The verdict is an event of major significance for Kosovo and the region and BIRN will continue to analyse its consequences as they develop, not only on the day of the judgment,” she added.

Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers are calling for 45-year prison sentences for the four defendants – Kosovo’s ex-President Hashim Thaci and fellow former guerrilla leaders Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi.

They are accused of having command responsibility for a campaign of persecution by KLA fighters during and just after the 1998-99 war, which allegedly included murders, torture, forced disappearances and unlawful detentions.

The defendants have denied the charges and their lawyers are seeking acquittals.

The case has sparked anger in Kosovo, where it is seen as an attempt to vilify the KLA’s war for liberation from Serbian oppression. Supporters of the defendants have staged a series of demonstrations and are expected to rally in The Hague for the verdict.

See the focus page here.

World.title: Turkey Rounds Up 2,447 People in Operation Targeting Crime Gangs
World.content:
Turkish Police and Gendarmerie launched a major operation called “The Streets Are Safe” on Monday, detaining 2,447 people to coincide with the first morning of the new school year in 78 provinces across the country.

“Our streets will not be left to criminal organisations. Our children and young people will not become the human resources of criminal organisations,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said in a statement, defining the detainees as members of “new generation of street gangs”.

The operation targeted criminal groups allegedly involved in offences ranging from drug trafficking, robbery and arms dealing to blackmail, money laundering and illegal betting.

Gurlek said the campaign was intended not only to detain suspects but also to dismantle the criminal groups’ finances, networks, logistical capabilities and ability to recruit new members.

He highlighted the alleged recruitment of young people through social media, accusing criminal groups of seeking to portray involvement in crime as a source of “power and status”.

“We are resolutely continuing our fight against street gangs that threaten the peace of our people, the security of our cities and the future of our children,” the minister added.

In a separate development on Sunday, Turkish police authorities detained members of the LGBTQ+ rights organisation Kaos GL and raided activists’ homes as well as bars and nightclubs in separate operations across 15 provinces, targeting 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses.

Kaos GL said at least 10 of its members were detained. Separately, courts blocked access to websites and social media accounts belonging to a number of LGBTQ+ organisations, activists and rights defenders, including Kaos GL, Lambdaistanbul, Pembe Hayat and UniKuir.

World.title: North Macedonia to Tweak Investment-for-Citizenship Rules, But EU Concerns Remain
World.content:
The European Union has criticised proposed changes to North Macedonia’s Law on Citizenship, saying they fail to go far enough in abolishing a ‘golden passport’ scheme that critics say is widely abused.

In June, the government in Skopje proposed amendments that it said would tighten citizenship rules and satisfy EU concerns over its ‘golden passport’ scheme.

The proposal scraps a threshold of 400,000 euros in investment in exchange for citizenship, as well as a requirement that the person hires 10 people.

However, authorities will still be able to issue citizenship to individuals deemed of special interest to North Macedonia, whether that interest be, for example, economic, cultural, or sporting, as many other countries around the world do, including in the EU.

World.title: In Kosovo’s Guerrilla Heartlands, Impending Trial Verdict Stirs Anger, Fierce Loyalty
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Milazim Thaci survived unscathed, hidden beneath the bodies of those who could not escape the bullets.

On March 28, 1999, four days into a NATO air war to drive Serbian forces from Kosovo, he was among a group of 33 men led away for execution in the Drenica Valley, the heartland of the guerrilla Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA.

He recalled the Serbian policemen and soldiers taunting them: “Where’s Thaci? Where’s NATO?”

By ‘Thaci’ they meant Hashim Thaci, one of the KLA’s top leaders. Milazim knew him better as his younger cousin, a shy, lanky boy always respectful of his elders. “He was a boy of few words,” Milazim told BIRN in his home in Buroje, a village in the Skenderaj/Srbica district.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Presidential Elections Will Test PM Radev’s Grip on Power
World.content:
Following a seemingly endless series of elections and short-lived administrations in Bulgaria from 2021 to 2026, former Bulgarian President Rumen Radev won in a landslide victory in April, successfully formed a government and became prime minister.

But now the country is bracing for presidential elections on October 25. If Radev’s former Vice President Iliana Iotova wins, the prime minister and his Progressive Bulgaria party will secure major political power.

Iotova’s potential win might also have geopolitical stakes for Ukraine and Europe. In a campaign event in Sofia on September 8 she said that “the war in Ukraine cannot be solved through military means” and that “more weapons and wasted billions bring more victims and are pitting Orthodox nations against each other”. This is in tune with Radev’s softer approach to the Kremlin.

The centre-right party GERB – which was the dominant power in Bulgaria from 2008 to 2025 and is now in second place – has surprisingly abstained from nominating a candidate for president. This may be a sign of the party being in free-fall after losing to Radev in April or at least a tactical retreat.

However, several GERB members ended up in Iotova's initiative committee, the list of people endorsing an independent candidate. The committee also included pro-Russia voices, previously socialist-affiliated politicians and various figures in sports and entertainment.

Expectations are building around three of the candidates: the acting President Iliana Iotova, the pro-EU and opposition-minded former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, and the former interim agriculture minister Ivan Hristanov.

All are running as independents, though each is supported, more or less directly, by different parties. This is part of a trend – individual personalities are being foregrounded rather than party members with political baggage.

“We’re about to see a campaign dominated by battling social media narratives, rallying cries adapted for different audiences and quite a lot of populist promises,” said Ivaylo Madzharov from Active Politics, a youth-led organisation popular on Instagram and TikTok for its explainers on Bulgarian politics.

Madzharov sees Iotova as a clear favourite in the election, although, he said, surprises are possible.

World.title: Kosovo Ex-President Thaci’s Defence Seeks Acquittal in Obstruction of Justice Trial
World.content:
The defence teams of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and four others co-accused of obstruction of justice in Thaci’s war crimes trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague have called for their acquittal, accusing the prosecution of charging them based on conversations that did not result in any witness-tampering or intimidation.

The prosecution claims that that during visits at the Detention Centre in The Hague, where Thaci is being held, he told the other four defendants – Hajredin Kuci, Fadil Fazliu, Isni Kilaj and Bashkim Smakaj – to instruct certain witnesses in his war-crimes trial about what to say in court.

But Sophie Menegon, Thaci’s lawyer, told the court during closing statements on Thursday that Thaci was “on trial for having a conversation in the Detention Unit [where he is being held pending the verdict in his war crimes trial]. There is no allegation of a bribe, compulsion, or threat against witnesses.”

She added: “There is no allegation of actual interference with witnesses …There isn’t any victim in this case …The prosecution asks you to send Mr Thaci to prison for six years over conversations inside a detention unit that resulted in zero real-world impact.”

The claims are based on recordings of the visits as well as physical evidence found also at Kilaj’s home in November 2023 – less than a month after Kryeziu and Kilaj met Thaci – allegedly printed via the only printer at the detention centre that Thaci could use.

Thaci and his four-co-accused have denied wrongdoing.

Smakaj’s lawyer, Jonathan Elystan Rees, in his closing statements on Friday, called for the acquittal of all the defendants.

“You should find Mr Smakaj and all the other defendants not guilty, whether individually or collectively,” he said, because Smakaj’s actions did not obstruct or have an impact on the course of justice.

Smakaj “cannot be convicted on the allegation that he intentionally aided in disobeying court orders, because he was completely unaware of the court’s orders”, Rees said.

He added: “There is no evidence from the prosecution, nor any legal obligation, requiring my client to be aware of the operational guidelines and functioning procedures of the detention centres.”

The lawyer for Isni Kilaj, Ian Edwards, told the court on Friday that Kilaj did not take any action after visiting Thaci at the Detention Centre in The Hague, saying he “neither called nor met with any witnesses”, so showing a lack of intent to obstruct justice.

“Everything else is mud that the prosecution is throwing at Mr Kilaj, hoping that some of it will tarnish his reputation,” he added.

David Young, lawyer for Fadil Fazliu, highlighted that his client was not even questioned by the prosecution.

“We can infer that the prosecution adopted a strategic approach of not interviewing them, of not questioning these individuals regarding the allegations. Is this the right way to initiate investigations or bring charges? I believe not. I state clearly that it is not,” Young told the court.

Alexander Admiral, lawyer for Hajredin Kuci, told the court that his client had been charged based on a wrongful translation of a message he sent to one of the witnesses in Thaci’s war-crimes trial, former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA fighter Rrustem Mustafa.

According to Admiral, the message had been misinterpreted as passing a note from a third individual when the rightful translation revealed that Kuci was passing his support to Mustafa and was basically “a man calming an old friend”.

During the prosecution’s closing statements on Thursday, it was claimed that Thaci tried to influence Mustafa and another former KLA, fighter, Bislim Zyrapi, both of whom were testifying in his war-crimes case.

The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament Hit by Fresh Dispute Over Deputy Speakers
World.content:
Kosovo parliament session on September 11, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s parliament failed to find a way out of a fresh crisis on Friday when MPs reconvened in two attempts to elect new deputy speakers.

The legislature derived from the June 7 snap partliamentary elections has not yet been inaugurated because the ruling Vetevendosje party refuses to support proposed candidates from two opposition parties, Vlora Citaku, from the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, and Kujtim Shala, from the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK.

Under the constitutional rules, parliament cannot be considered inaugurated until the speaker and all five deputies are elected.

Albulena Haxhiu from Vetevendosje was elected speaker on Wednesday, Ardian Gola, from the same party, was installed as deputy on Friday.

When Citaku of the PDK received only 44 of a minimum of 61 votes on Friday, her party colleagues left the session and accused Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje of blocking the inauguration of parliament.

“As of today, the PDK has no reason to participate in parliamentary sessions and we will take the case to the Constitutional Court,” Bedri Hamza, the PDK leader, said as soon as speaker Albulena Haxhiu interrupted the session.

In the June elections, Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the chamber, well ahead of the next-placed PDK, which won 22 seats. The LDK came third with 18 seats.

Vetevendosje claims it can call on 62 MPs to form a new government, again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved, as parliament needs to elect a new president of Kosovo within two months of its inauguration. Failure to do so would trigger another election, the fourth within less than two years.

As the post-election blockage enters its second month, Kurti and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku agreed on August 31 to nominate Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and former diplomat, as Kosovo’s president. But, days later, six LDK MPs refused to support his candidacy, making the necessary quorum impossible.

For a president to be elected, a candidate must win at least 80 votes in the first two rounds. In a potential third round, they need a simple majority of only 61 votes.

Arberie Nagavci, head of Vetevendosje’s parliamentary group, said its MPs would not support any candidate for deputy speaker who is against the deal on the new president. Both Citaku and Shala have announced their opposition to Sejdiu’s candidacy.

“Of course, the MPs who are in favour of the Vetevendosje-LDK agreement [on the president] have the support of our 53 MPs,” Nagavci said after the interruption of the session.

Parliament will resume work on Sunday.

World.title: Alar Karis: The president can always count on displeasing MPs
World.content:
The president often has to choose between doing their job and dodging MPs' displeasure, President Alar Karis said in his last speech opening the fall session of the Riigikogu.

Members of the Riigikogu,

Guests,

I am here today to open the Autumn Session of the Riigikogu for the last time.

It has been three and half years since I stood before you to wish the newly elected Riigikogu success. You have heard me repeat year after year how important the role of parliament and the decisions you needed to make are.

I believe it bears repeating because our daily lives and trivial conflicts often stop us from seeing the understated presence held by the highest chamber in a free country. However, today I would prefer to sum up what I have come to realize about the relations of the President of the Republic and the Riigikogu during my office.

My term of office has been mostly spent in the company of the XV Riigikogu. I am sure you have personal opinions on whether the division of roles between the president, parliament and the government has been right in recent years. I have also experienced how general principles, which are often repeated and listed as ideals, actually work in practice.

First of all, I have drawn the conclusion that if the president is doing their job, they can always count on displeasing MPs. I know this feeling from my work as auditor general, and it is impossible to avoid.

Members of the opposition expect the president not to proclaim a law that has been passed after heated debates. But a very important principle is that the parliamentary majority makes most of the national level decisions in a parliamentary democracy.

I have seen that arguments can be found to declare almost any law to be unconstitutional and in need of being vetoed. And yet, if we interpret the Constitution very broadly, all issues of national governance would eventually end up being decided by the court. In that case, the elections would lose much of their point.

Part of the job

When the president vetoes a law — which I have had to do more often than my most recent predecessors — they can be fairly sure that members of the coalition will think they were making a big mistake. It can't be helped; a veto still seems to be taken as criticism by MPs.

I have not always perceived the situation that way because, after all, the president and parliament have the same goal — to make sure our legislation is universally sound, clear as well as correct down to the last detail.

Everyone, of course, generally agrees with this goal, but in practice this can be interpreted as nitpicking and looking for an excuse to shelve a law over some minor detail.

However, I do not think that the president can avoid the question of whether the Riigikogu has explained its requirements to people clearly enough that the law can be respected without needing to wait for interpretation by an official or even a punishment to bring final clarity.

Since the president must respect parliament's political choices, their main job ends up being ensuring whether these goals are translated into precise laws that actually help achieve them.

The second lesson is that if the goal is very important, it tends to overshadow everything else.

President Alar Karis addressing the Riigikogu at the opening of its 2026 fall session. September 14, 2026. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

One example of this is the law that imposed a language requirement on the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF). When I vetoed this law, I was surprised to find myself reaffirming again and again that I was not against imposing a language requirement. Even if I were, as a president I would still have had to respect the opinion of the parliamentary majority that a language requirement was necessary.

It was more so a question of how such a requirement would actually be implemented in reality. The National Defense Committee went on to dedicate significant attention to this issue later, and the Riigikogu eventually passed a thoroughly revised law.

This example ultimately illustrates excellent cooperation between the president and parliament, but it also involved conflict. I do not mean to say that there shouldn't have been any conflict or misunderstandings. Rather, it's yet more proof that the president often has to choose between avoiding MPs' displeasure and doing their job.

In fact, it's kind of a paradox in its own right that parliament elects the president, for whom slowing down, if not outright blocking, the work of the Riigikogu in certain cases is among their most important jobs. From the Riigikogu majority's point of view in particular, there may be doubts as to whether this kind of system is really necessary.

A necessary different angle

I believe it is. Not that I've concluded that MPs aren't doing their jobs well or that the president knows better than they do — not at all. But someone has to look at the legislation from a slightly different angle that doesn't adhere to the usual political conflicts.

Not only parliament but society more broadly focuses primarily on practical goals, be it economic growth, cutting prices, conserving nature, ensuring security or whatever else. That's how it should be, because at the end of the day, we're interested in the results, not the legal provisions.

But if we have our sights on an important goal and feel pressure to achieve it quickly, everything else can end up feeling like a secondary matter. That is when careful consideration may not even be given to whether a law will actually help achieve a goal or end up working in reverse.

Admittedly, there is generally also no consensus on what constitutes a sound and effective law, and in a parliamentary democracy, such debates must also eventually be resolved in parliament. At the same time, national interests extend beyond the political choices made by the parliamentary majority.

At the opening session of the current Riigikogu, I said that the power of the majority cannot start deepening social divides. Herein lies that elusive balance, because the parliamentary majority must nevertheless be able to decide, if we do not want decisions of national importance to not be made at all due to disputes and disagreements.

We can talk about political priorities and practical tasks, but at the end of the day, the very basis of everything, the foundation for both democracy and the development of the country, is that the parliament has the ability to make decisions at all.

I have been reproached for not doing enough during a period of parliamentary obstruction to protect the majority right to vote, and also for not speaking out enough in defense of the opposition's rights.

This kind of two-sided criticism evidently reflects the fact that I have tried to adhere to the principles I mentioned in this hall in April 2023.

President Alar Karis addressing the Riigikogu at the opening of its 2026 fall session. September 14, 2026. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

The majority must have the right to decide, but more MPs having voted in favor of decisions than against them is not enough to justify these decisions or make them clear to the public.

The role of the opposition is not to block the decisions of the majority. Even so, opposition pressure can help ensure that the need for a law is established, alternatives are considered and counterarguments are taken seriously.

So it is no longer primarily a matter of majority and minority. A minority position losing out in parliament is inevitable, as is the social tension that occasionally arises as a result. Such tension is part and parcel of a democracy, and some of it is released in elections.

Lofty words aren't enough

And yet there is another kind of tension, sometimes even deep disappointment, bred by the impression that MPs don't particularly care about citizens' opinions more broadly. However mistaken that impression may be, we cannot deny its existence, and that if it takes root, it can start to threaten the parliamentary system as a whole.

Some may expect the president to respond to such distrust and disappointment with general remarks about the importance of parliamentary democracy — in other words, to educate the public.

I have understood the president's role differently. I have considered it important to prevent distrust of the country's leaders from growing and to ensure that parliament and government decisions are clear to people, at least in terms of their purpose and rationale, because they cannot be sure to please everyone anyway.

In my view, this goal has given practical meaning to the widely expressed general opinion that the president's role is to stand for unity and national spirit in a daily reality that is time and again politically divided.

Yes, that is repeated often. But does that mean the president's role is simply to offer lofty words on national holidays and remind people while touring around the country that, despite all our differences, we are one nation? Is that enough, as society becomes increasingly demanding, self-aware and well-informed?

I don't think lofty words are enough if we want to preserve the feeling of national unity that ultimately underpins respect for even those decisions made in parliament with which people don't agree.

The third lesson, however, is that working toward that kind of consensus framework does not always immediately beget consensus. More often, it gives rise to disputes. The coalition tends to see this as political interference — and in some sense it is, because the president's job is not to simply stand on the sidelines and watch politics unfold.

I repeat: if the president is doing their job, they can always count on displeasing MPs. Maybe that's how it should be; that is how our system of separated powers is built, and it has generally worked very well.

What matters is that our country benefits from all of this.

World.title: Estonian MoD rejects agency's claim it proposed terminating EPF ammo brokerage in 2025
World.content:
Lawmakers continued examining problems with Estonia's defense procurement and financial management Monday, focusing on the role of Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur in controversial ammunition deals.

The Riigikogu State Budget Control Select Committee continued its discussion Monday at a public sitting on problems related to financial management in the defense sector and national defense procurement. The aim was to obtain answers to questions raised by a National Audit Office audit and by information that has emerged publicly in recent weeks.

At the start of the sitting, it emerged that Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform), former Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) Director General Magnus-Valdemar Saar and State Secretary Keit Kasemets, all of whom had been summoned, were not present.

RKIK Director General Elmar Vaher said committee members will be able to visit RKIK on Wednesday where they will be given access to documents protected as state secrets or confidential information.

Committee members will also see a so-called timeline showing various points at which decisions were made, along with related materials. It is still not known precisely who was involved in the decisions or how they were reached.

Elmar Vaher. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Unanswered questions

Committee chair Urmas Reinsalu said he had sent Saar written questions before the sitting. The first concerned conflicting accounts after Pevkur said the ministry did not look into the background of individual transactions in detail and that neither the minister nor the secretary general were responsible for negotiating with market participants.

Saar told Reinsalu that his experience had been the opposite. He added that Pevkur had not kept his distance or merely been kept informed, but had actively intervened in the process. Saar said weekly discussions were held covering new supply opportunities, risks and the progress of projects, during which specific instructions were given.

"He himself brought forward and proposed deals to be made and offers were constantly coming to RKIK through him," Reinsalu continued, reading Saar's response. Pevkur had also allegedly urged that a payment be expedited on at least one occasion after contracts had been signed, shortening the contractual payment deadline and demanding an exception to state accounting rules.

Outgoing Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk was asked to comment and said various ammunition offers had been sent to everyone whose email address was publicly available. Those offers, including ones forwarded by the minister, were passed on to RKIK. The center was then responsible for validating the offers and assessing production capacity, the possibility of obtaining ammunition as aid for Ukraine and the associated risks.

Kuusk said it was common for offers of this kind to be forwarded by various parties, including the minister.

Another unresolved question is who established contact with Datasel. Saar maintains that the contact came through Pevkur who, according to Saar's account, said the contact was reliable. Contact was then established with Oculus, which in turn brought Datasel into the process. Pevkur denies this.

Reinsalu again asked Kuusk for an explanation. Kuusk said he had no reason to doubt the minister's account. "What Magnus-Valdemar Saar has presented does not convince me. There is one screenshot of a conversation in which Magnus himself claims that he received it from the minister, but the other party does not confirm that," Kuusk said.

Kaimo Kuusk. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

From there, the process was supposed to continue with RKIK assessing the offers and securing the ammunition for Ukraine.

Saar further claimed that the final two transactions in the Datasel case were carried out at Pevkur's personal initiative. The minister was particularly interested in concluding the deals through the Greek company Nordeto. Once again, there was pressure to sign the contracts quickly, citing the short validity period of the offer.

Saar added that by that point, RKIK had already been notified of delays in deliveries under the initial contracts. Nordeto was an unknown company and, to Saar's knowledge, its business activities were not related to ammunition or defense goods.

Reinsalu asked whether Pevkur had given instructions regarding Nordeto's involvement as an intermediary. Kuusk again replied that offers reached everyone whose contact details were publicly available.

Reinsalu also asked whether Pevkur or any Ministry of Defense official had urged RKIK to sign additional contracts involving Datasel ammunition after delivery problems with the initial procurements had emerged. Kuusk said he could not confirm that any such pressure had been exerted.

Proposal to stop ammo mediation

Saar also told the media that, as RKIK director general, he proposed in early 2025 that the center stop brokering ammunition through the European Peace Facility. Reinsalu also asked Saar about this and Saar replied that the first delivery problems involving the Datasel contracts emerged in January or February 2025. It had become clear to RKIK that the market had dried up in terms of reliable suppliers and that continuing to support Ukraine in the same way would have required taking even greater risks.

RKIK reportedly submitted a written proposal in late winter 2025 to stop concluding ammunition contracts in this manner using European Union and third-country funds and to return funds that had not yet been committed under contracts. The defense minister did not accept the proposal and decided to continue brokering the aid.

Responding to these claims, Kuusk said it would have to be verified whether such a written proposal had in fact been submitted at the time. He added that even if it had been submitted, contracts with Datasel had already been signed by that point and the first deadlines had already arrived.

Erkki Tori, director of security and national defense coordination at the Government Office, was asked whether the defense minister had informed the Cabinet of the problems in early 2025 when the risks emerged. Tori replied that, to his knowledge, he had not.

Tori also said the government had not discussed the specific problematic ammunition brokerage contracts funded through the European Peace Facility. In fall 2025, the National Audit Office conducted an audit that highlighted risks associated with the ammunition brokerage contracts. Reinsalu asked whether the Cabinet had still not considered it necessary to discuss the issue separately at that point. Tori said he was unable to comment on that.

Erkki Tori and Elmar Vaher. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Ammunition in Romania

During the sitting, Reinsalu also asked about ammunition that has not been entered into inventory and is being held at an interim storage facility in Romania. Vaher said not all of the equipment and ammunition at the facility belongs to Estonia. He added that Estonia nevertheless guards the site to ensure the items remain there. Vaher said there are dozens of containers of ammunition at the facility.

RKIK has inspected the shells on two occasions. The first visit was an expert inspection during which their quality was assessed. The inspection found that the ammunition was not fit to be fired and did not comply with the contract.

The second visit took place about a month ago when the aim was to verify that the goods were still there. "It is true that we did not count every individual shell, but the team confirmed that the number of containers that was supposed to be there was still there," Vaher said.

Background

In 2024, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) signed four procurement contracts with Datasel S.R.L., an Italian company acquired earlier that year by Indian-owned Neco Defence Munitions. Despite neither Datasel nor its parent firm having any prior track record of manufacturing or selling artillery shells, RKIK wired roughly €70 million in advance payments.

The contracts meant to deliver desperately needed ammunition to Ukraine using EU European Peace Facility funding suffered severe delivery delays. Ammunition that did arrive was flagged as incomplete and of substandard quality, leading RKIK to terminate the agreements and launch legal efforts to recoup the money. Datasel has denied wrongdoing, claiming it delivered tens of millions of euros' worth of goods and was left with financial losses.

The European Public Prosecutor's Office has since launched an investigation into the use of European Peace Facility funds by Estonia.

The scandal was part of Minister of Defense Hanno Pevkur's recent decision to resign, alongside wider accounting and oversight issues at the Estonian Defense Forces and other parts of the ministry's administrative area.

World.title: Ave Schank-Lukas: Europe's future in our hands but much remains to be done
World.content:
Europe is working to take the lead in the industries of the future, from artificial intelligence to electric vehicles, while also investing in skills, Ave Schank-Lukas writes.

In September 2025, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen began her annual address by saying: "This must be Europe's independence moment." In other words, in an increasingly unpredictable world, Europe must take greater responsibility for its own future.

Europe has also accomplished a great deal toward that goal over the past year. We are investing more in our security, strengthening our competitiveness, accelerating the transition to clean, homegrown energy and forging new partnerships around the world. Achieving a more independent Europe will take time, but the first effects can already be felt, including in Estonia.

Across Europe, one lesson stands out: We cannot solve problems alone. Whether we are dealing with threats to our security or fundamental values, economic competition and technological change or extreme weather conditions from Spain to Croatia, tackling these challenges requires a strong and united response, as well as solidarity, because they affect us all.

A more competitive Europe

European independence begins with a strong and competitive economy. Over the past year, legislation has been simplified to make it easier for businesses to operate across borders. The "EU Inc" corporate structure will help businesses get started, expand and take advantage of the single market of 450 million consumers. The Savings and Investments Union will help businesses raise capital to develop their operations.

Europe is working to take the lead in the industries of the future, from artificial intelligence to electric vehicles, while also investing in skills. We are reducing energy costs and accelerating the transition to clean, affordable, homegrown energy. As international trade becomes increasingly unpredictable, we must diversify our range of partners and reach new agreements with trusted partners around the world.

Estonia also has many good examples of innovative companies that are strengthening both Europe's economic independence and its overall security with support from the EU budget. The NEO magnet plant built in Narva is unique in Europe, producing magnets needed by strategic sectors including the automotive and renewable energy industries. Jälle Technologies turns used batteries back into a valuable resource, reducing Europe's vulnerability and dependence on third countries.

The AI Leap, which integrates artificial intelligence into the education system, is another area where Estonia can set an example with its ingenuity and forward-looking approach.

A more secure Europe

Europe must take responsibility for its own security. Through SAFE, the EU funding instrument created to strengthen defense capabilities, member states can invest jointly to ensure Europe is better protected. These investments will strengthen the defense industry, close capability gaps and support the creation of skilled jobs.

Estonia will use the €2.1 billion it receives through SAFE primarily to bolster its air defense capabilities, as well as for other defense investments.

Being prepared for potential threats is equally important. With EU support, we are strengthening military mobility infrastructure so that troops and equipment can reach where they are needed as quickly as possible in a crisis. The Eastern Flank Watch and the European Drone Defense Initiative have been launched to enhance Europe's drone technology capabilities.

Europe's security begins in Ukraine. In addition to the more than €220 billion already allocated, the EU will provide a further €90 billion in 2026 and 2027 for Ukraine's civilian and military needs. Twenty-one packages of sanctions against Russia have been adopted and the first negotiating clusters have been opened on Ukraine's path toward EU membership.

Europe's stronger position in the world

Independence means making choices. Europe is working to further strengthen its position in the world and join forces with trusted partners. These partnerships help protect our interests and shape the world around us in line with our values.

Europe must keep its door open. In addition to Ukraine, the first negotiating clusters in the EU enlargement process have also been opened with Moldova, while progress has been made on enlargement toward the Western Balkans. A larger union is stronger economically, politically and strategically and helps prevent gray zones from emerging beyond our borders.

Protecting European values

European independence also means standing by our values and defending them. Several initiatives have been launched across Europe to strengthen democracy, helping to safeguard its foundations and prevent foreign interference.

The proposal for the EU's new long-term budget increases investment in opportunities, skills, innovation and social inclusion, while strengthening protections for the rule of law.

Europe undoubtedly needs to keep pace with developments in the digital world, but we must also take into account the risks that children and young people in particular face online. Here, too, Estonia can set a good example for the rest of Europe. Eesti.ai teaches people how to use artificial intelligence to learn and work more effectively and how to put AI to work for their own benefit and for the economy as a whole.

Although the past year has once again been challenging for Europe, a growing number of Europeans believe we are stronger together. Nearly nine in 10 people, particularly young people, believe European countries should act with greater unity.

We have accomplished a great deal, but if we want to preserve our freedom to decide our own future, we must press ahead with even greater determination. We will hear about Europe's priorities for the coming year on September 16 when President Ursula von der Leyen delivers her 2026 address to the European Parliament.

World.title: WATCH: Estonian National Symphony Orchestra's 100th season opening concert
World.content:
The Estonian National Symphony Orchestra (ERSO) opened its 100th season Friday with a festive concert featuring works by Beethoven, Schumann and Estonia's own Heino Eller.

Conducted by Olari Elts, Friday's program began with Eller's symphonic poem "Dawn" ("Koit"), one of the Estonian composer's most frequently performed works.

South Korean pianist Yekwon Sunwoo then joined the orchestra for Schumann's Piano Concerto in A minor, often described as a musical love letter to his wife, Clara Schumann, who premiered the work.

Sunwoo, an alum of the Curtis Institute of Music and Juilliard, rose to international prominence after winning the 2017 Van Cliburn International Piano Competition and has since performed with leading orchestras and on major stages worldwide.

The evening concluded with Ludwig van Beethoven's iconic Symphony No. 5 in C minor.

More concerts to come

ERSO's season opening concert was broadcast in cooperation with Klassikaraadio, with Nele-Eva Steinfeld hosting.

The award-winning Estonian orchestra's centennial season continues with a South Korean tour featuring works by Schumann and Beethoven alongside Estonian composer Tõnu Kõrvits' "Hymns to the Northern Lights."

In early October, ERSO will perform at the Festival TubIN with conductor Mihhail Gerts and violinist Hans Christian Aavik.

ERR's culture portal will stream more ERSO concerts in full throughout the fall.

World.title: Former agency head: Defense minister actively involved in Datasel dealings
World.content:
Former Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) Director General Magnus-Valdemar Saar has alleged that outgoing Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur personally pushed for several defense procurement deals and rejected a proposal to halt the arrangement.

Former Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) Director General Magnus-Valdemar Saar and outgoing Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) were due to attend a special parliamentary committee hearing on Monday, but neither appeared. Saar said that because the European Public Prosecutor's Office has launched an investigation and he is unable to verify facts against documents, he would prefer to answer questions in writing.

The most significant part of Saar's eight-page explanation concerns Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's role. Saar claims that the defense minister was not a hands-off client in this area who simply waited for reports.

"He personally brought forward and actively proposed deals, intervened in negotiations over contract terms, delivery schedules, the size of advance payments and prices in at least one major case, in some instances negotiated directly with the supplier, urged that payments be expedited after contracts had been signed and gave the contracting authority guidance during discussions held practically every week."

Responding later to follow-up questions, Saar said the final two deals in the Datasel case were concluded at Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's personal initiative.

"The minister also had a specific interest in concluding the deals through the Greek company Nordeto. RKIK was urged to conclude the contracts quickly, with the short validity period of the offer cited as the reason. By that point, delays in deliveries under the first contracts had already been reported."

According to Saar, Nordeto was unknown to RKIK and, to his knowledge, its business activities were not connected with ammunition or defense-related goods.

"The offer had been sent privately to Defense Minister Pevkur. I am not aware of how the defense minister satisfied himself as to the partner's reliability and capabilities. RKIK did not enter into a contract with this intermediary. RKIK entered into a contract with the business entity as close as possible to the origin and ownership of the goods (the general principle), which in this case meant Datasel."

Saar was also asked whether businessman and Reform Party member Jaanus Rahumägi may have played any role in the matter.

Special committee chair Urmas Reinsalu asked: "Delfi has reported on Jaanus Rahumägi's ties to Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur and reported in August 2025 that Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur was in Greece where he spent time at Jaanus Rahumägi's villa and, among other things, met with the Greek defense minister. To your knowledge, were arms deals discussed during this visit, and if so, which ones?"

Saar replied briefly: "I had left office by then and am not familiar with the topics that were discussed."

Minister reluctant to stop mediation

Saar's explanation also shows that, while serving as RKIK director general, he made a formally recorded proposal to end the intermediary arrangement and return funds not covered by contracts.

"In late winter/early spring 2025, RKIK submitted a written proposal to a defense minister's decision-making meeting to stop concluding contracts in this manner and return funds not covered by contracts. Defense Minister Pevkur rejected the proposal and ordered procurement to continue. The minutes of the relevant decision-making meeting are held by the Ministry of Defense and I assume the committee will have an opportunity to review them in writing."

Saar added that the decision showed the minister clearly understood both the need to support Ukraine and the risks associated with providing that support and was by no means unaware of the details of how the aid was being brokered.

ERR was unable to reach Hanno Pevkur for comment by phone.

World.title: Raul Rebane: A field guide to killjoys
World.content:
In his daily commentary for Vikerraadio, Raul Rebane maps out the different types of killjoys and concludes that making society angrier is not easy work — it requires a great deal of time and energy.

I will try to analyze a very common type of person in society: the killjoy. This has nothing to do with the once-popular TV series ("Tujurikkuja — ed.) of the same name; I simply could not find a better term for someone who believes that people, life, Estonia and the world are irreparably messed up and that this misery must constantly be proclaimed to everyone. President Alar Karis drew attention to a similar phenomenon in his Independence Day speech, introducing the term "opinion bullying" into public discourse.

Who are they?

One of my childhood acquaintances suddenly changed about 10 to 12 years ago. It is no longer possible to have a conversation with him. Everything is terrible, any government is stupid, all politicians are crazy, athletes are weak, singers cannot carry a tune, the first lady's dress is ugly and the roads are full of potholes. He began expressing this indignation on social media and it has only gotten worse over time. His Facebook account now contains many hundreds of angry posts. Judging by what he writes, there is no longer anything good to be found in this country.

Sound familiar?

I do not have a study to back this up, but based on the content, I tried to analyze who the most active complainers are. First of all, they are generally older men; there are significantly fewer women. One thing they have in common is that someone else is always to blame for their problems and those of the country.

First: Those who had it better before, especially during the Soviet era. Perhaps their salary was higher or their status greater, but the new era brought them considerable hardship. Their numbers and activity are declining; this group was very large in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

Second: Those whose abilities or talents could not withstand the competition of the new Estonia. They may once have been well-known and accomplished, but encountering a new competitive environment robbed them of their joy. They can be found in every profession, in politics and culture, as well as at ETV and on the radio.

Third: Politicians who are not currently in power. They are extremely angry at everyone and everything until they themselves come to power. Then everything is fine until they are replaced, at which point another cycle of anger begins. The decibel level of outrage rises noticeably before elections. Right now is precisely such a time.

Fourth: Social media influencers and some media personalities who have turned ruining people's mood into their brand. Over time, they enter a so-called spiral of anger in which they must constantly increase the doses of outrage or people will lose interest. This makes them even angrier because what is the point of shouting if no one is listening?

Fifth: The trend of being a killjoy. This is particularly noticeable in the media where outrage is treated almost as a sign of professionalism. If you do not engage in it, you risk being seen as soft. Many have fallen victim to this.

Naturally, this is by no means an exhaustive list. Nor should anyone think this is some kind of national peculiarity. It happens everywhere; the differences stem from history and stages of development. Elsewhere, there are different groups, such as angry consumers or sports fans.

In fact, there are not that many of these serial complainers. I was surprised myself when it emerged that an old acquaintance of mine had written 3,000 angry comments in a short period, believing that using a false name would keep his identity secret. It did not: His style and spelling gave him away. This creates a situation in which a very small segment of the population gains a disproportionately large media presence. Making society angrier is not easy work; it requires a great deal of time and energy.

Thanks to the current fashion for anger, those who think well of Estonia and of our lives here have a problem: They cannot open their mouths without being regarded as blind and stupid.

If someone has chosen being a killjoy as a way of life, facts do not get in their way in the slightest. I conducted an experiment and selected an article that listed all the bad things — tax increases, a stupid government, high prices, Russia's behavior, low pensions and so on — 11 points in all.

I asked people whether they thought it was true. They agreed wholeheartedly: It was all correct. The problem is that the article was published in Eesti Ekspress in September 2008. Whoever was angry then is angry now and will still be angry 10 years from now. It is not about circumstances but about character and the prevailing fashion of the times. Right now, anger is in fashion.

What can be done? The key is actually in our own hands. We simply should not be active consumers of this constant negativity. Let them make noise. Fortunately, most people have already chosen this path: They do not read the comments sections, much less post there themselves. At least that way, they can spare their own nerves.
