World.title: Iran envoy: Georgia not the only destination for Iranians
World.content:
Iranian envoy to Georgia makes pointed remarks

Iranian Ambassador to Georgia Seyed Ali Moujani has responded to a statement by Georgia’s Civil Aviation Agency saying the country would fully comply with sanctions against Iranian airlines imposed by the United States. The ambassador said Georgia had been one possible destination for Iranians, but was not the only one.

On 8 September, the United States imposed sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines. Six of them — Sepehran Airlines, Varesh Airlines, Qeshm Air, Fly Kish Airlines, Taban Airlines and AVA Airlines — also operate flights between Georgia and Iran. “As the expanded sanctions list announced by the US State Department includes airlines that currently operate flights between Georgia and Iran, the Georgian side, as in other cases, will act in full compliance with the international sanctions regime,” the Civil Aviation Agency said.

In turn, the Iranian embassy published a map of the Black Sea region showing only half of Georgia. When the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty asked the Iranian ambassador whether the map was intended to convey a political message, he replied:

“Sometimes a diplomat can say nothing, write nothing and simply share a picture… Water knows no borders; the Caucasus and Iran need a common, interconnected future.”

Map published by Iranian ambassador to Georgia

What Iran’s ambassador said

Seyed Ali Moujani said Iranian tour operators had contacted the embassy’s consular section in recent days with questions about whether tourist trips to Georgia would continue.

“Georgia has undoubtedly been one of the important Black Sea tourist destinations for Iranians,” Moujani wrote, noting that the country had attracted many Iranian tourists in recent years.

He also said Iran respected Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s independent decisions.

“Georgia’s recent decision to introduce certain restrictions in connection with Western sanctions is one that we must respect as the country’s choice. However, respecting the choices of others does not mean disregarding our own right to choose,” the Iranian ambassador wrote.

Moujani said Iranian tourists, like citizens of other countries, considered a range of factors when choosing a holiday destination, including safety, convenience, cost, mutual respect and dignity.

The ambassador also noted that tourism generated mutual economic benefits.

“The arrival of tourists does not simply mean travellers entering a country. Hotels, restaurants, transport providers, shops, tour guides, craftspeople, public services and dozens of other sectors of the economy all benefit,” Moujani wrote.

He said travellers had also historically played an important role in building links between cultures and peoples, and sometimes in creating new opportunities for cooperation and development.

“If a new situation has emerged today, we should not view it solely as a restriction; every restriction can become an opportunity to find new paths,” the ambassador said.

Seyed Ali Moujani said there were other coastal destinations in the Black Sea region besides Georgia that could serve as alternatives for Iranian tourists.

“There are other destinations — other countries worth visiting, other cultures worth discovering and other peoples worth engaging with,” Moujani wrote.

The ambassador described Iran’s respect and friendship for Georgia and the Georgian people as unwavering, but stressed that Iran and the Iranian people’s right to choose also deserved respect.

World.title: Second chance: South Ossetia revives efforts to promote Ossetian amid leadership change
World.content:
South Ossetian Education and Science Minister Aslan Lolayev has announced plans to open a specialist class offering advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

Lolayev said the class would accommodate more than 30 pupils, but did not specify which school it would be based at or which year group it would be for.

“The authorities plan to open another three such classes in the next academic year — two in Tskhinvali and one in one of the districts,” Lolayev added.

He said the authorities hoped the introduction of classes offering advanced Ossetian-language study would “become one of the stages in developing a national Ossetian school system and expanding the use of the native language in education”.

Russian and Ossetian are South Ossetia’s official languages, but administrative work and education are conducted only in Russian. Russian is dominant overall, and is also the language predominantly used by the local population in everyday life.

However, Zarema Ts, a schoolteacher from Tskhinvali, says there is demand among young people for greater promotion of the Ossetian language. She believes the younger generation should therefore be encouraged to study the Ossetian language and literature, as well as Ossetian history and ethnography.

“There should be more opportunities, clubs and classes for studying Ossetian, not only within the education system but also outside educational institutions. For example, why not organise Ossetian-language classes for visitors and Russian specialists working here?”

North Ossetian experience not fully embraced

Zarema says, however, that proficiency in Ossetian is considerably higher in South Ossetia than in North Ossetia. Statistics appear to support her claim: in North Ossetia, which is part of the Russian Federation, the situation surrounding the Ossetian language has been recognised as critical, prompting the local authorities to take serious steps to preserve it.

The Alan Gymnasium, a multilingual Ossetian-Russian boarding school, has been operating in Vladikavkaz for nine years, with most subjects taught primarily in Ossetian. The school was established at the initiative of then North Ossetian leader Vyacheslav Bitarov, who continues to provide it with financial support.

South Ossetian officials, however, have been slow to adopt this model.

In early 2026, Aslan Lolayev was preparing to present a project for a national school in Tskhinvali modelled on the Alan Gymnasium. Reports said the project had already been agreed with the relevant Russian authorities and only needed to be implemented.

Lolayev was subsequently dismissed as education minister, and acting minister Rimma Pliyeva said the North Ossetian gymnasium model was unsuitable for South Ossetia. She argued that South Ossetia’s education system was already “perfectly fulfilling its role in teaching the Ossetian language”.

Second chance

Several months later, however, there was another twist: South Ossetian President Alan Gagloyev resigned early and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov took over as acting president.

Kambolov reinstated former Education Minister Aslan Lolayev, giving him another opportunity to implement at least part of his programme to expand advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

How successful the initiative will prove remains unclear, with South Ossetian experts so far reluctant to make predictions.

Three years ago, in September 2023, Aslan Lolayev raised concerns about a shortage of Ossetian-language textbooks.

“These textbooks cannot be purchased commercially because they were published under a state procurement programme. All copies were distributed to educational institutions. Moreover, the textbooks were published in 2019 and, if handled with care, have a lifespan of five years. After that, they need to be replaced,” he said at the time.

Lolayev added that the republication of the textbooks was included in a three-year programme that was due to be submitted to parliament and the government for consideration.

“I hope it will receive support and that we will be able to resolve this issue,” Lolayev said in 2023. There have been no reports of new textbooks since then.

South Ossetia is due to hold a presidential election on 18 September. Whether the change of leadership and the arrival of a new team, which includes Aslan Lolayev, will alter the situation remains to be seen, although there are hopes within society that it will.

Madina Valiyeva, a finalist in the Team of the Future personnel programme, for example, says that if she is appointed to an official post, one of her goals will be to establish a South Ossetian version of the Alan Gymnasium.

“There is a very apt saying: ‘No language, no nation.’ We must preserve our native language and pass it on to future generations. That is the future of our people,” Valiyeva said.

World.title: Abkhaz president voices blacksmith in cartoon
World.content:
Abkhaz President Badra Gunba has voiced a character in the animated film Nart Sasrykva, dedicated to a hero of the Abkhaz epic. Gunba provided the voice of one of the film’s characters, the blacksmith Ainar.

Work on the 36-minute animated film, which has taken five years to complete, is nearing its end, with its official premiere due in a month. Director Astamur Kvitsinia adapted the heroic epic, which has several versions, into a format designed to be engaging and accessible to children.

It is unclear why the president became involved in voicing the film. One possible explanation is the longstanding friendship between Badra Gunba and Astamur Kvitsinia, dating back to Gunba’s time as Abkhazia’s culture minister from 2011 to 2014.

Astamur Kvitsinia is widely regarded as the father of Abkhaz animation and has created more than a dozen animated films based on Abkhaz fairy tales and myths.

Versions of the Nart epic, about warrior brothers who battle giants, are found among many peoples of the Caucasus. Most scholars date the epic to the 8th-7th centuries BC.

Each people’s version has its own distinctive features and reflects its particular worldview. In the Abkhaz version, the Narts are a family of 100 brothers and their only sister. Sasrykva, the youngest of the brothers, is the epic’s main hero.

World.title: “Injustice prevails under oligarch Ivanishvili” — video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Azerbaijani “Bridge of Peace” initiative group reacts to Armenian media's biased position
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. The "Peace Bridge" Initiative Group on Azerbaijan has expressed deep disappointment regarding the biased attitude of Armenian media and the unacceptable tone of public discussions concerning the visit of the diplomatic corps to the Karabakh and East Zangezur regions of Azerbaijan on September 11–12, 2026.

Trend presents the statement issued by the group regarding this matter.

"The Azerbaijani 'Bridge of Peace' initiative group expresses deep disappointment regarding the hostile media reaction and the unacceptable tone of public discourse in Armenia concerning the visit of the diplomatic corps to the Karabakh and East Zangezur regions of Azerbaijan on September 11–12, 2026.

First and foremost, the visit of the diplomatic corps to the sovereign territory of Azerbaijan should not, in itself, be a subject of dispute. In particular, verbal attacks directed at ambassadors and countries for participating in such a visit are concerning and contradict the fact that Armenia recognizes Azerbaijan's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Azerbaijan and Armenia are currently in a post-conflict period, and both countries face the complex task of overcoming decades of confrontation. As representatives of civil society, and with the support of the governments of Azerbaijan and Armenia, we are taking steps—within the framework of peace initiatives—to facilitate the peace process, encourage dialogue, and support confidence-building measures.

Cultural heritage within the territory of Azerbaijan belongs to the Azerbaijani people and is protected by the state.

To ensure fairness, issues regarding cultural heritage must be discussed on the basis of reciprocity and open dialogue. To advance these goals, civil society representatives have established a platform for professional discussion of issues that form an integral part of the peace process agenda between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

The peace process must not be allowed to come under pressure from revanchist forces, as this would seriously jeopardize further progress toward peace. We call upon Armenian society to demonstrate a responsible approach to this issue and not to succumb to the provocations of those harboring malicious intent, whether in Armenia, as well as beyond its borders.

Farhad Mammadov

Kamala Mammadova

Rusif Huseynov

Dilyara Afandiyeva

Ramil Iskandarli,” the statement said.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev donated the $500,000 prize he received as part of the Zayed Award for Human Fraternity to the Garabagh Revival Fund.

This was reported by the Press Service of the President of Azerbaijan.

According to the information, on September 14, during a meeting with President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, Mohamed Abdelsalam, Secretary-General of the Muslim Council of Elders, presented the certificate of the Zayed Award for Human Fraternity to the head of state.

World.title: Flying fox influx overruns Mount Isa suburb 'like a cloud coming over'
World.content:
As dusk settles over the outback city of Mount Isa a dark plume rises from the trees surrounding homes in the suburb of Sunset.

Thousands of flying foxes stream into the evening sky.

For 24-year-old doctor Aaron Gray the spectacle has lost its initial sparkle.

Dr Gray moved to Mount Isa this year for postgraduate medical training and bought his first home as "a little present to himself" in June.

The established garden was part of the attraction, but within about a week there was "an explosion" of flying foxes.

His garden is now covered in droppings, dead flying foxes, leaves and fallen branches.

At one point he was spending three to four hours a day cleaning.

"I've just given up and just let it go," Dr Gray said.

Aaron Gray bought his first home in Sunset in June, shortly before the flying foxes arrived. (Supplied: Aaron Gray)

'Like a cloud coming over'

A few doors away, long-time property owner Tony Tolke has watched the colony grow.

"It's just like a cloud coming over," Mr Tolke said.

"It's never been as bad as this."

Branches have blocked Mr Tolke's driveway and droppings cover cars, the roof and a boat.

Residents say falling branches have damaged properties and blocked access around some Sunset homes. (Supplied: Aaron Gray)

His pregnant daughter is a paramedic and shift worker, and the family had to move her baby shower away from the house.

"You can't even enjoy your own home," Mr Tolke said.

He said wet season insurance repairs had also been delayed because builders were unwilling to work at the property while the flying foxes remained.

Residents want action

The residents want authorities to encourage the flying foxes away from homes and provide more help with the aftermath.

Dr Gray said the problem had left him increasingly confined to his home.

He said the council environmental officers had visited his property but told him their "hands are tied", legally.

He later asked for visiting state wildlife officers to meet affected residents but said they instead drove through the area.

"A drive-by is not really the same as going into the property and speaking with the actual residents affected by it," Dr Gray said.

The Queensland Department of Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation confirmed a little red flying fox camp had formed in trees across private properties.

It said it expected the animals to move on once the trees finished flowering.

The state environment department says a little red flying fox camp has formed across private properties in Sunset. (Supplied: Aaron Gray)

A department spokesperson said wildlife rangers had inspected the site and met with Mount Isa City Council to provide advice on management options.

Under Queensland conservation laws, landholders can use deterrents including noise, lights and water sprays to discourage flying foxes from returning, provided the animals are not harmed.

Council considers moving flying foxes

Mount Isa City Council chief executive Tim Rose said new state advice had established the flying foxes were not breeding at the site.

"We can start having a look at moving the bats on because they're not breeding there, which is a positive outcome," Mr Rose said.

Options include noise and potentially reducing vegetation, with the council considering a coordinated approach with residents.

"They call it nudging," Mr Rose said.

Mount Isa City Council is considering measures to encourage the flying foxes away from residential areas. (Supplied: Tony Tolke)

The council received a $38,500 state government grant last year to develop a flying fox management plan.

Mr Rose said the draft plan, developed following community consultation, was now with the department for feedback.

Residents have criticised the council's response to the influx but Mr Rose said, "I think we've done everything we can."

He said the council had needed state advice about what it could legally do because flying foxes were protected.

Mr Rose said the council was unlikely to financially assist residents with cleaning, increased water bills or property damage.

"Probably not, to be perfectly frank and honest," he said.

" We're probably not responsible for bats being there. "

Residents have questioned whether the council's vegetation clearing along Breakaway Creek contributed to the flying foxes moving into the area.

Mr Rose said the clearing was undertaken because of flooding concerns.

"We can't really say one way or the other whether it made any difference or not," he said.

For Dr Gray, the issue is increasingly about the life he came to Mount Isa to build.

"I understand the benefit to the environment, but should it really come at the cost of our livelihood and our homes?" he said.

World.title: Live: 'Deeply disturbing day': Bowen lashes Gupta over Whyalla
World.content:
(ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Industry Minister Tim Ayres has taken aim at the former owner of the Whyalla steelworks after it was confirmed hundred of workers will lose their jobs after the blast furnace was shut down.

The blast furnace has been offline since April. Workers have not been able to restart it.

Ayres tells ABC News Breakfast it was left in a terrible state of disrepair.

"The finger of blame here should be pointed squarely at GFG for their maladministration and underinvestment in this blast furnace," he says.

Ayres pushed back at criticism from the Coalition the closure was a result of an energy failure by the federal government.

"It is just not remotely the reason why this blast furnace has failed. The blast furnace failed because the foreign owner … deliberately didn't invest in the capability of the blast furnace," he says.

The South Australian government wrested control of the steelworks from Sanjeev Gupta's GFG alliance in early 2025. The federal and state governments have injected funds to keep it going while an administrator prepares it for sale.

Ayres says there are two bidders in the process to take over.

World.title: Gambling authority looked to offload controversial pokies tax scheme
World.content:
Every year, clubs around the state operating poker machines throw parties where they present money to community groups and charities.

Giant novelty cheques are handed to people who smile for the cameras.

But rarely is it mentioned that the money comes from the type of gambling the NSW government considers to be most harmful; poker machines.

The clubs operating 65,000 poker machines in NSW are given tax discounts under the ClubGrants scheme, if they donate a fraction of the $5 billion in annual profits to community organisations.

The NSW government considers poker machines to be the most harmful form of gambling. (ABC News: Gregory Nelson)

But the scheme has proven controversial, dogged by reports that clubs have been awarding grants to their own groups, facilities and projects.

Now, documents shared with the ABC reveal the Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority (ILGA) believed there were "constraints and issues" with the ClubGrants scheme, and that it wanted to offload oversight to another agency.

The bundle of documents were obtained by Greens MP Cate Faehrmann, who used a parliamentary process known as a Standing Order 52 to compel the NSW government to release them.

'Constraints and issues'

Ms Faehrmann used a Standing Order 52 to compel the NSW government to release the documents. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

The ILGA wanted to relinquish oversight of the ClubGrants scheme due to compliance concerns, according to its submission to a recent review.

It cited the yearly "burden" of having to conduct preliminary checks on applications submitted by more than 500 clubs, within a period of two weeks or less.

Chairperson Caroline Lamb said the workload "practically limits the authority's ability to most effectively monitor the compliance with the Scheme".

"The Chief Commissioner [of State Revenue] is best placed to administer a tax rebate program," she said.

The independent watchdog is not the only body concerned about the ClubGrants scheme.

It agreed with the "constraints and issues" raised in a discussion paper by the regulator, Liquor and Gaming NSW.

One of them is that clubs and community groups do not need to verify how the grant money is spent.

Do you know more? If you have any information about the story, contact Tony Ibrahim.

Another is that clubs can ignore recommendations by local committees to award a particular type of grant to "any organisation or program".

Most of the grants awarded by clubs went to sporting groups, according to the ClubGrants 2025 contribution report.

Of the $127 million awarded that year, $53.3 million went to sporting programs and facilities.

This is more than the combined grants for health, disability inclusion, education and early learning, domestic violence, mental health, veterans, emergency services and homelessness.

Both the independent authority and regulator of poker machines believed there were problems with the set up of the scheme. (Supplied: YouTube)

The industry lobby group, Clubs NSW, did not respond to questions and requests for comment.

Clubs responsible for 'scheme's integrity', ILGA says

The ABC asked the ILGA if it still held concerns about the ClubGrants scheme.

A spokesperson said its role was to support clubs as they were the "stewards of the scheme's integrity".

It said the guidelines ensured "there is accountability for expenditure of the tax revenue foregone".

The NSW government ordered the first formal review of the ClubGrants scheme in more than 10 years, after coming into office in 2023.

It received a final report in January 2025, but it has not released it or shared its findings despite repeated requests.

The independent authority said it wanted to relinquish oversight of the scheme due to compliance concerns. (ABC)

The office of the NSW Minister for Gaming, David Harris, said the findings were still being considered.

"We have … updated the guidelines to clarify funding for statewide services and ensure tax obligations are understood," a spokesperson said.

Ms Faehrmann said the ClubGrants scheme allowed clubs to pay less tax while buying community goodwill, despite the harm caused by poker machines.

"The changes to the guidelines are just tinkering around the edges. I can't even see the difference, frankly, when I've compared the two," she said.

"ClubGrants is what the clubs rely upon to push back against any reform. The fact is they're not generous, they're a rort."

The allegation was put to Clubs NSW, but it did not respond.

A rehab waits for the final report

Some non-profits have been left in limbo as they wait for the state government to release the review's final report before deciding if they should participate in the ClubGrants scheme.

NSW government sits on report into controversial gambling scheme The ABC has learned the final report into the controversial ClubGrants scheme has been sitting on the state government's desk since January 2025.

An example is Odyssey House in Sydney's south-west, which operates one of the largest alcohol and drug rehabilitation services in the state.

Among the documents shared with the ABC is an email from Odyssey House's chief executive to the office of the minister for gaming.

"For many years we participated in the ClubGrants scheme," chief executive Carmel Tebbut said in the email on November 7, 2025.

" The Board took a decision last year to pause our participation in the scheme due to both governance concerns and potential conflict of interest, given we support people with addiction issues. "

Ms Tebbut, the state's former deputy premier, had asked for an update on when the review would be released.

"The Board agreed they would reconsider the matter when the Governments (sic) review of the ClubGrants scheme is finalised," she said.

The ABC contacted Odyssey House, but the organisation declined to comment.

World.title: Apple growers fear economic and biosecurity wipeout as US eyes market
World.content:
Australia's apple industry has held urgent talks in Canberra as the United States edges closer to exporting its fruit to Australia.

Following decades of lobbying, American growers were given the green light by Australia in 2022 to send their apples across the Pacific.

Before shipments begin, the Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) needs to publish import conditions on its biosecurity website.

That has not happened yet.

But according to industry group Apple and Pear Australia Limited (APAL), it is getting closer.

"The US government has just recently … brought it back to the table to discuss with the federal government," APAL general manager Jeremy Griffith said.

"So that's got a lot of growers in this country very, very concerned."

The Australian apple industry is valued at about $650 million a year. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Apple giant

The United States is the second-largest apple-growing country in the world behind China, with the bulk of production in the Pacific Northwest, including Washington.

"They export a lot of them," Mr Griffith said.

"Our understanding is they have a very large surplus of apples in America at the moment, and they're looking for a home to send them to."

Mr Griffith said the imports would have "a significant impact upon the very viability of all our orchards".

"Because we're a very good free-trading country, we're not allowed to consider the economic implications of this," Mr Griffith said.

"We can only look at biosecurity issues."

At the moment, nearly all apples consumed in Australia are grown locally, with less than 1 per cent imported from China and New Zealand.

"Having the US to come in would [be] a very direct threat, and it goes to the heart of our own food security," Mr Griffith said.

Ninety-nine per cent of apples consumed in Australia are locally grown. (ABC Rural: Justine Longmore)

A DAFF spokesperson confirmed the department was in "ongoing discussions with the US" about apple imports.

But the spokesperson did not say how long that process was likely to take.

"[DAFF] has not finalised the procedures the US will use to meet the recommended risk management measures," the spokesperson said.

"The department has engaged regularly with Australia's apple industry, through Apple and Pear Australia Ltd (APAL), on the import risk analysis for fresh apple fruit from Pacific Northwest USA."

Biosecurity nerves

The federal government's risk analysis report identified a host of biosecurity concerns.

Fire blight, a destructive bacterial disease, was of most concern to growers, but there were multiple other exotic diseases that also have them worried.

"Top of the list is fire blight, [but] you've got apple maggots, you've got leaf curling midges, you've got canker, lots of different types of rots and rusts," Mr Griffith said.

His biggest fear was that Australia's biosecurity system would not be strong enough to keep them out, citing the varroa mite incursion as an example.

"That's already having a profound impact upon all our bee colonies," he said.

Jeremy Griffith met with agriculture department officials for urgent talks in Canberra last week. (ABC Rural: Justine Longmore)

APAL rushed to Canberra last week to meet with DAFF officials.

"They're very, very conscious of the biosecurity risk," Mr Griffith said.

"We think there's enough red flags out there for the government to respond appropriately to ensure that proper protections are in place."

Fire blight would be 'catastrophic'

Half of Australia's apples are grown in Victoria's Goulburn and Murray Valleys.

The region sits within the federal seat of Nicholls, held by Nationals member and opposition agriculture spokesperson Sam Birrell.

"I'm very concerned because of the biosecurity risk," said Mr Birrell, who has a background in agricultural science and also worked in the fruit industry.

"The USA has fire blight, Australia does not, and we cannot allow fire blight to come in."

" It would be catastrophic for the apple and pear industry, an industry which is critical to Australia. "

Sam Birrell says fire blight would be devastating for the Australian apple and pear industry. (Supplied: Sam Birrell)

Australia allows apple imports from New Zealand, where fire blight has been present for more than a century.

But Mr Birrell said the "stringent biosecurity regulations" in place for the nation's trans-Tasman neighbour have meant "we haven't seen a lot of New Zealand apples here".

"Biosecurity needs to be number one," he said.

"I've seen what fire blight has done to apple orchards in the United States and I've seen what they have to do to deal with it."

Apples ready for processing at Montague Fresh, Victoria. (ABC News: Tim Lee)

GM apples

Five varieties of genetically modified (GM) apples are sold in the United States, but there are no GM varieties in Australia.

Mr Birrell said the move towards GM in the US shows what happens when diseases cause widespread problems.

"[It] explains what can happen when a new disease as catastrophic as fire blight gets into Australia," Mr Birrell said.

"We don't want to go down that path."

The ABC also contacted Agriculture Minister Julie Collins for comment.

World.title: 'Promised the world': Molly Ticehurst's friends say the system failed her
World.content:
As Molly Ticehurst's mother, Kate Shaw, and best friend, Meg Sladek, endured the devastating task of packing up her house after her murder, they made a shocking discovery.

"The postman arrived with a yellow document. We went to the mailbox to get it out and it was her AVO," Ms Sladek said.

"Kate's words were: 'Fat lot of good that was, wasn't it?'

" The rush of blood through your body in that moment. [The AVO] is meant to be protection and look where we are, look what we're doing. "

Molly Ticehurst's best friends, Gaby Shepherd, Meg Sladek and Aidan Clarke do not believe alleged offenders should be granted bail. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

The 28-year-old childcare worker was killed in her home at Forbes in central western New South Wales in April 2024 by her former partner, Daniel Billings, 31.

He has been sentenced to 28 years in jail after pleading guilty to murder in the NSW Supreme Court in November 2025.

Her family and friends have spoken exclusively to ABC's Australian Story about her experience, and how they believe she was failed by a system designed to protect women and children.

Ms Ticehurst endured several months of abuse from Billings before going to police because she was worried it would put her and her family in greater danger, her father, Tony Ticehurst, said.

Tony Ticehurst says his daughter was let down by the system designed to protect her and other women. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

"I believe that she didn't have faith in the system and it let her down in the end," Mr Ticehurst said.

" She was promised the world and given a street map. "

An apprehended violence order, or AVO, was served on Daniel Billings after he was charged with sexual assault and domestic violence offences on April 5, 2024.

A court transcript of his bail hearing at Dubbo Local Court on April 6 states one of the AVO's conditions was a 10-kilometre exclusion zone from Ms Ticehurst's home in Forbes.

Billings's bail conditions included "not to enter Forbes for any reason" and "not to contact or try to go near or contact Molly Ticehurst".

"We didn't build the Great Wall of China around Forbes and say 'don't come in'; we didn't build a moat," Ms Ticehurst's childhood friend, Aidan Clarke, said.

" An AVO is not worth the paper it's written on, I wouldn't even waste the ink. "

Two weeks after Billings was granted bail, he broke into her home late at night and killed her.

Prioritising women's safety

Ms Ticehurst's murder inspired bail reforms which make it harder for alleged perpetrators to get bail.

The changes reverse the presumption of the onus of bail, so offenders must demonstrate why they should be released, and electronic ankle monitoring is required for serious domestic violence offences.

Ms Ticehurst's friends are proud of this legislative reform but ultimately believe the only way to ensure women's safety is for offenders to remain in custody until their case is heard in court.

"They don't need to be out on the street. Let them have their day in court, but let's make these victims feel safe," Mr Clarke said.

"I believe Molly definitely did think that nothing was going to stop him," another of Ms Ticehurst's best friends, Gaby Shepherd, said.

"Nothing was going to stop him, whether that was an ankle [monitoring] bracelet or whatever means. I truly believe that."

Gaby Shepherd (right) believes the man who murdered her best friend, Molly Ticehurst (left), was determined to "get to her". (Supplied: Gaby Shepherd)

Their concerns are being echoed by Anne-Marie Mioche from CatholicCare Wilcannia-Forbes (CCWF), which delivers domestic violence support services in western New South Wales.

"Police don't have a crystal ball, so they can't tell whether the threat is going to be acted on and we don't either," Ms Mioche said.

" The onus has to be put on locking up the man, to keep the woman and the children safe. "

Figures from the NSW Coroners Court show that there have been 366 domestic violence homicides involving an "intimate partner" since 2000.

An apprehended domestic violence order (ADVO), which is specific to people who are or were in a domestic relationship, was in place in 88 of those murders.

The NSW independent member for Orange, Phil Donato, who was a police prosecutor before entering state politics, said AVOs and ADVOs were only effective if an alleged offender was willing to comply.

Anne-Marie Mioche says women will keep dying unless further legislative reform is made to domestic violence laws. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

"Ultimately if an offender … is determined to do what he did, an AVO or bail conditions is not going to deter him or stop him," he said.

Ms Mioche believes the legislation and enforcement tools, like AVOs, are still weighted towards perpetrators.

She said her organisation had instances where an alleged offender was allowed to stay with family near where their former partner lived.

"The laws need to change in favour of the victims of domestic violence and their rights, as opposed to the civil rights of the perpetrators," she said.

"There have been some great changes in recent years, but I actually think it needs to go further, otherwise women will keep dying.

"If [a man] wants to be free, he has to be a long, long way away. In another state, for example."

The NSW government did not answer the ABC's questions about the effectiveness of AVOs but said it had made "significant reforms to protect victim-survivors of domestic and family violence" since Ms Ticehurst's murder.

In a statement, a spokesperson said crime data showed that the legislative reforms were "working to help community safe with record remand numbers".

"We know domestic and family violence still occurs at unacceptable levels in the community and there is more work to do."

Phil Donato believes AVOs and bail conditions are not enough to deter certain offenders. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

24-hour policing lacking

A central plank of NSW's bail reforms is the use of electronic ankle monitoring for certain offenders.

Authorities are alerted if a perpetrator breaches an exclusion zone set out in their AVO.

Ms Ticehurst's home town of Forbes, like many in rural and regional Australia, does not have a police station that is open 24 hours a day.

At certain times of the night, the closest overnight station is 30 kilometres away at Parkes.

Phyllis Miller says women are not safe if towns do not have 24-hour police stations. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

"There's nothing that acts better as a deterrent than knowing that there's police in town that can respond quickly," Mr Donato said.

"Criminals who know they've got 20, 30 minutes before police arrive, even under lights and sirens, that gives them so much more confidence to commit crimes."

Ms Ticehurst's friends believe Daniel Billings knew that there were times of the day when Forbes Police Station was not staffed.

In the days before Ms Ticehurst laid charges, he told her:

" I will come in the middle of the night … The police won't stop me. I will get to you quicker than they will. "

Mayor Phyllis Miller said she was fighting to have 24-hour policing restored at Forbes.

"Women in rural and regional New South Wales or Australia are not safe," Cr Miller said.

"We do not have enough police."

Forbes Police Station has a phone the public can use to ring for assistance if the station is not staffed. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

NSW Police and the state's police minister, Yasmin Catley, declined an interview.

In a statement, a spokesperson for NSW Police said smaller stations had a "variety of operating hours supplemented by after hours/on-call arrangements".

"This, in effect ensures an appropriate police response is provided to regional communities 24/7.

"The safety and wellbeing of the community remains our priority and the community can be assured that all police vehicles serve as mobile police stations and can respond based on demand."

World.title: Man climbs into hospital ceiling in bid to escape police custody
World.content:
An alleged thief attempted to escape police guard at a Melbourne hospital by climbing through the ceiling.

Victoria Police said the 21-year-old man had been charged and remanded following an alleged theft in Preston.

He was taken to the Austin Hospital in Heidelberg yesterday after reporting a medical episode.

Police said the Carrum Downs man escaped custody at the hospital and climbed through a false ceiling about 10:30pm.

Victoria Police said the man was eventually taken back into custody. (ABC News)

Police negotiated with the man for about three hours before he climbed down and was taken back into custody.

In addition to the theft charges, police also charged him with escaping custody and criminal damage.

He was remanded to face Heidelberg Magistrates' Court today.

World.title: Whyalla steelworkers 'stubbornly determined' to keep plant going
World.content:
When speaking to residents and workers in Whyalla one word you'll often hear is "resilient".

But as the government made the announcement that the local steelworks' blast furnace is to close, a union official had another way to describe it.

"I just use the term 'stubbornly determined'," AWU organiser Shane Karger said.

"We've had a rough end of the stick for quite a few years now, you know just over 10 years and we've never given up. We're still not going to give up."

Shane Karger says steelworks employees are "stubbornly determined". (ABC News)

The blast furnace closure hasn't come as a surprise to locals — workers have been pushing against the odds to get the 60 year old plant back online since April.

Mayor Phill Stone said it was a sad day for Whyalla, but it would allow people to move forward.

"Our community, in some respects, will breathe a sigh of relief that this announcement has been made," he said.

"This is essential. There is no other way out other than to close the blast furnace and we as a council and the government and our community, I believe, will pull together to ensure the minimal impact on those that are going to suffer."

Phill Stone says the council, government and locals will "pull together". (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Australia's largest manufacturer of structural steel

The Whyalla steelworks is Australia's biggest manufacturer of structural steel, used for rail lines, bridges and industrial buildings.

In a 2025 press conference, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it accounted for 75 per cent of Australia's structural steel.

A vital part of the process is the now closed blast furnace — a coal fired oven, used to smelt iron ore, transforming it into pig iron that is ultimately used to make steel.

The loss of it is the latest blow to an industrial city that's become used to hard knocks.

Whyalla began as a mining settlement at the turn of the 20th century, when BHP began mining nearby iron deposits.

Whyalla began as a mining settlement, with the first blast furnace built in the late 1930s. (ABC News)

In the late 1930s, the first blast furnace was built, and as Australia went to war, BHP added a shipyard.

The shipyards saw Whyalla boom, and in 1976 it was South Australia's biggest regional city with a population of 33,000 and a plan to expand to 100,000.

But in 1978, the last ship was built in the city.

The closure of the shipyards resulted in a rapid population decline, with current numbers down to just over 21,000.

The blast furnace smelts iron ore, transforming it into pig iron that is ultimately used to make steel. (ABC News)

Whyalla steelworks city's largest employer

Despite the end of shipbuilding, the steelworks kept going, and is the city's largest employer.

But the steelworks has struggled through a decade of financial problems and uncertainty.

In 2016, owner Arrium collapsed into voluntary administration.

A saviour came in the form of British billionaire Sanjeev Gupta, who promised to keep local jobs and even add to them.

His pledge came with a projection of population growth to 80,000, as Mr Gupta said he would build a "next-gen mega steel plant" that would be one of the biggest in the world.

But Mr Gupta's global operations began to struggle following the collapse of his key lender Greensill capital.

Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance bought the steelworks after Arrium went into administration. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In 2025, the South Australian Government took the extraordinary step of forcing the steelworks into administration.

It was celebrated as a move to save the steelworks, with hopes it would turn the plant's fortunes around.

"Workers at the steelworks itself, they will now have their futures assured," Premier Peter Malinauskas said at the time.

"They're in a situation now where they're not going to wake up tomorrow and the administrator is making people redundant."

But the blast furnace closure will now reduce the workforce from 1,700 to 1,200.

Workers have been pushing against the odds to restart the aging blast furnace since April. (ABC News)

There are two bidders to take over the steelworks, and the state government says that process remains on track despite the blast furnace closure.

It's expected the winner of that bidding process will be announced by the end of the year.

Local businesses worried economy will suffer

While union organisers and the Mayor are talking about resilience, with this latest blow, some locals are losing confidence.

Whyalla cafe worker June Worsnop fears the job losses will hit the local economy. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Cafe worker June Worsnop said job losses would bring uncertainty to the local economy and residents.

"Everyone is going to stop spending money, they're going to be scared," she said.

"All this money they've put into the plant, what for?

"I know this could be the crunch and if so, what, we'll end up being a welfare town?"

Darryl Durdin owns a local scaffolding business and said he's now facing possible closure.

"Here I am on the outside, looking in, I'm watching it implode," he said.

Darryl Durdin says he will remain optimistic about the future of his business. (ABC News)

But Mr Durdin is holding on to some hope, and said it was "possible" his business could hang on until a new buyer had taken over the steelworks.

"If you lose hope, you've lost everything," he said.

"I'm shrewd with my money, I never waste my money, things like that. You've just gotta do what you've gotta do to hang in there."

World.title: Uni sector says campuses will shut under One Nation plan
World.content:
Australia's university lobby has accused One Nation of "joining the conga line" with the government and Coalition on populist jockeying, in a crackdown on international students that would leave the country poorer and less skilled.

One Nation has proposed cutting international student numbers by hundreds of thousands, with party leader Pauline Hanson calling universities "visa factories".

"One Nation are just joining the conga line in this furphy, which is blaming international students for all things to do with the migration debate. And it's just frankly wrong," Universities Australia CEO Luke Sheehy told ABC News.

The proposal would slash international student places from 590,000 to 350,000, and cut the number of graduates who wished to remain in Australia after their studies from 270,000 to 40,000.

"If numbers actually materialised as One Nation proposed … you would see university campuses shut down, Australian students unable to get a place at university and thousands of university workers have their jobs put at risk," Mr Sheehy said.

Universities have long relied on international students to cross-subsidise domestic student places. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

Phil Honeywood, a former state Liberal MP in Victoria, who runs the International Education Association of Australia and has clashed with Senator Hanson over decades, was also scathing of the proposal.

"For 30 years, Pauline Hanson has been attacking Asians, attacking Muslims, and now attacking young people that just want to come to Australia and get a world-class qualification," Mr Honeywood said.

Phil Honeywood has clashed with Pauline Hanson for decades. (Supplied)

He said the policy would, in addition to the financial hit on universities, limit Australia's future influence in the region.

"We'd rather have young Australians working with, studying with young people from our own region, who then go back to their home countries and become future leaders rather than another country," Mr Honeywood said.

Universities have long relied on international students to cross-subsidise domestic student places, especially since the introduction of a policy called Job Ready Graduates, introduced by the Coalition in 2020, which changed the amount universities were paid to teach.

The most recent data shows international student fees comprised about 27 per cent of all the income universities received. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"International students help subsidise the experience of the nearly one million Australian students right across the system. For many, many years, the federal treasury and the federal government have got a cut-price deal on how much they have to spend on universities," Mr Sheehy said.

"It's not just for medicine, it's for disciplines like engineering, science, health sciences, humanities, you name it."

Luke Sheehy says student fees were the bedrock for universities being able to carry out research. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The same is true for Australia's research effort, where universities often receive only a portion of the total cost of carrying out research.

"It is the bedrock of the way that we do so much of our research in our universities. The fees that students pay link directly to the amount of research Australian universities can do," Mr Sheehy said.

"Australian universities are doing the lion's share of research and development in Australia right now. So frankly, if you slash the number of international students, you're actually putting at risk Australia's overall R&D effort, which is economically reckless."

International students make up more than a quarter of revenue

Director at the University of Melbourne's Centre for the Study of Higher Education, Professor Chris Ziguras, said international student fees amounted to more than a quarter of the sector's total revenue.

"So, they are more than a quarter of all of our students, and they're also more than a quarter of the revenue of the system totally," Professor Ziguras said.

"The most recent data we've got from 2024 and the international student fees comprised about 27 per cent of all the income of the system as a whole."

Christopher Ziguras says there is "a lot of populist jockeying" jeopardising long-standing bipartisan policies. (Supplied)

International student numbers have reached record highs in recent years, rising after the pandemic.

That led to questions about universities' social licences, as some institutions approached 50 per cent of the student body being made up of international students.

Migration is more complicated than this one number It's one thing to set a net migration target, but working out how to achieve that is a conversation that political leaders have been less keen to have.

Professor Ziguras said there was "a lot of populist jockeying" going on, which was jeopardising long-standing bipartisan policies.

"Both temporary and permanent immigration to Australia is essential for all sorts of sectors, and it's part of how our society runs, and that's not a new thing," Professor Ziguras said.

"We've been teaching international students in Australia for many decades, just as farmers have been relying on backpackers and seasonal workers."

The government introduced caps on international student numbers two years ago, but the sector is braced for the government and Coalition to cut further.

The sector is bracing for more cuts, after caps on international student numbers were introduced two years ago. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Vicki Thomson, the CEO of Australia's Group of Eight, which represents Australia's research-intensive universities, also hit out at the One Nation announcement.

"You do not strengthen Australia's future by shrinking one of our largest exports, weakening our research engine and sending the world's best students to our competitors," Ms Thomson said.

"Countries that attract talent prosper. Countries that drive it away pay the price."

World.title: Prince Harry’s children move school after two days over security concerns
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Prince Harry’s children move school after two days over security concerns Michael Holden September 15, 2026 — 7:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: The children of Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, are to swap schools after just two days because of concerns over the security of transporting them, the couple’s spokesperson said. Harry, the younger son of King Charles, and his family relocated to Britain last month after six years of living in California, with Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, starting school in September. An image posted on Instagram by Meghan shows Harry being hugged by their children on Father’s Day. Instagram/meghan The location of their new home and details of the children’s school have been kept private. But on Monday (UK time), a spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex confirmed reports that Archie and Lilibet were changing schools after just two days. The distance between their home and the original school, along with heavy traffic in the area, had raised concerns for their security team.



“The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” the spokesperson said. Related Article Royal family Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, gives first glimpse of family life in Britain “The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family. This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.” According to HELLO! magazine, a friend of the couple said: “It’s a real shame because they absolutely adored the school, the kids and their parents. It was perfect for them in every way, and the children really enjoyed their time there. They really wanted to make it work, but they had to make a difficult decision based on the fact that the team couldn’t make the school run operationally secure.” Meghan and Harry stepped down from royal duties and moved to the US in 2020, leading to estrangement ​and awkward relations with the royal family as they delivered a series of barbed comments about the institution.



Their return came as a surprise, with even the monarch unaware of their plans until just days before it became public. They are not living in a royal residence and will remain non-working royals, as agreed with the late Queen Elizabeth before their move. Related Article Royal family Privacy concerns cloud Prince George’s first day at prestigious Eton College The duke and duchess’s status as private citizens was confirmed in a letter authorised by Charles and sent to senior ​British officials last week, a step which their spokesperson said had come as a surprise. The prince has also been critical of the government’s decision to strip him and his family of ​automatic police ⁠protection afforded to other senior royals, with a bespoke system put in place instead. US President Donald Trump said that he would be a sufficient guardrail against rogue artificial intelligence, claiming that any efforts to limit the technology was part of a “SICK conspiracy.”

Trump was pushing back against calls by tech leaders such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk to have greater government oversight of AI. Donald Trump wants to be the guardrail of AI. AP

World.title: ASX set to slip, tech stocks weigh on Wall Street; Trump lashes out over ‘SICK conspiracy’ against AI
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip, tech stocks weigh on Wall Street; Trump lashes out over ‘SICK conspiracy’ against AI Stan Choe Updated September 15, 2026 — 6:31am ,first published 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Artificial-intelligence stocks slid worldwide after leaders of the industry warned a slowdown is needed for the safety of humanity. Another jump in oil prices, meanwhile, briefly sent the yield of the 10-year Treasury to 5 per cent for the bond market’s latest pressure-raising milestone. Despite all the downers for Wall Street, gains for many stocks outside AI helped limit the market’s losses. So did a midday tempering of oil prices, and the S&P 500 fell a relatively modest 0.5 per cent. More stocks rose within the index than fell. Wall Street is in the red on Monday, with AI stocks tumbling. Bloomberg The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 152 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.6 per cent after clawing back most of an early loss of 1.3 per cent. The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures at 6.18am AEST pointing to a slide of 16 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.45¢.



Related Article Opinion

AI These three kings of AI have a plan. It could blow everything up Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist AI stocks have been under pressure a while because of worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around the technology. The concerns jumped to another level over the weekend after one of the industry’s leading voices, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, called for a deliberate and global slowdown in the development of AI. He cited safety issues, including the risk that AI becomes capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months. Nvidia, whose profits have soared because its chips are helping to train AI models, sank 3.4 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the market because of its massive size. SpaceX, which gets a chunk of its business from AI, fell 2 per cent after Elon Musk said over the weekend that he agrees with Amodei. Softbank Group, the Japanese giant that is a major investor of OpenAI, lost 10.7 per cent in Tokyo after OpenAI’s Sam Altman likewise supported the concept of a slowdown.



Altman also said in an interview with Fortune published Saturday that the company behind ChatGPT would likely wait until next year for a sale of its stock on Wall Street. That would delay a potential gusher of cash for Softbank and other early investors in OpenAI. In South Korea, the Kospi index dropped 3.3 per cent due to losses for its two most influential stocks, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. President Donald Trump played down the need for his administration to check the development of AI, saying he worried about ceding his country’s edge over China in a global competition and that winning would help address the risks from the advancing technology. Even with many voices inside and outside the AI industry calling for a slowdown to protect humanity, Trump said on his social media network Monday that the only guardrail it needs “is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Helping to limit Wall Street’s losses on Monday were several software companies that tumbled earlier on worries AI-powered competitors would undercut their businesses.



Intuit, the company behind TurboTax and QuickBooks, rose 5.5 per cent. Autodesk, whose software helps designers, climbed 7.8 per cent, and Adobe added 5.3 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 slipped 37.00 points to 7,619.98. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 152.09 to 54,421.20, and the Nasdaq composite fell 146.62 to 26,186.41. Oil prices, meanwhile, continued to climb as fighting in the Middle East keeps squeezing the global flow of crude. The price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 1 per cent to $US105.68 after getting near $US110 in the morning. An important Saudi oil pipeline will mostly be out of service for weeks following an attack last week, two regional officials told The Associated Press. The pipeline offered a way for Saudi Arabia to shift exports to the Red Sea and avoid the Persian Gulf’s Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks have stifled the movement of oil tankers. Brent has jumped from less than $US72 in early July as doubts rise that the United States and Iran can come to an agreement that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf through the strait again.



While the prospect of a de-escalation of war in Iran may have dimmed, ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary on Monday that the situation is still fluid and “sizable” volumes of oil have still been moving through the strait. So far, the jump in oil prices has sent the average cost of a gallon of regular gasoline across the country to nearly $US4.32 from $US4.08 a month ago and $US3.18 a year ago, according to AAA. Related Article Energy Fuel price blowout piles pressure on Albanese for second excise cut Such upward pressure on inflation has much of Wall Street expecting the Federal Reserve will hike its main interest rate on Wednesday at the end of its next meeting. Besides high inflation, worries about rising debt for the U.S. and other governments and other concerns have sent longer-term Treasury yields to their highest levels in years.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury briefly breached the 5.00 per cent level during the morning for the first time in nearly three years. That’s up from 4.96 per cent late Friday and just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began in February. But the 10-year yield later pulled back to 4.98 per cent after oil prices came off their highs for the day. The 10-year yield has not consistently remained above 5 per cent since the turn of the millennium, and its jump has already made it more expensive for U.S. households and companies to borrow. That includes the highest average long-term mortgage rate in more than 14 months. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Trump Jr’s Bahamas wedding weekend bankrolled by Russian oligarch, Putin ally
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDonald Trump Jr Trump Jr’s Bahamas wedding weekend bankrolled by Russian oligarch, Putin ally Michael Koziol September 15, 2026 — 6:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The wife of US President Donald Trump’s eldest son has insisted there was nothing sinister about a controversial Russian oligarch paying for their recent wedding celebrations, after it was revealed that an ally of Vladimir Putin partially bankrolled the luxurious Bahamas weekend. Umar Kremlev, president of the International Boxing Association, sponsored and attended the festivities that took place on two ultra-exclusive private islands in May when Donald Trump Jr married Bettina Anderson. Donald Trump Jr and his wife Bettina travelled with the president to Ireland on the weekend. Getty Images The gift was revealed by the US investigative journalism outlet ProPublica on Monday (US time) and confirmed by Anderson, now Bettina Trump, on social media. “Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding,” she wrote on Instagram. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.”



According to ProPublica, which cites records and three sources familiar with the event, Kremlev contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars to rent one of the private islands for a reception. He also funded a fireworks show, and his staff helped with event planning, ProPublica reported. Bettina Trump indicated Kremlev did not attend the wedding ceremony itself, which she said was for family only. The pair were married at a private ceremony in the Bahamas in May, followed by a lavish weekend of celebrations. Getty Images “The weekend that followed had actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds,” she wrote on Instagram. “It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift.”



Photos from the weekend show guests, including Eric and Lara Trump, Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner, the president’s fourth child, Tiffany, and her husband, Michael Boulos, enjoying dinner, drinks, and dancing by the beach. Umar Kremlev (right) with Vladimir Putin in 2022. Sputnik A funfetti cake served over the weekend was flown in from Palm Beach in Florida, according to an authorised account of the wedding published by HELLO! magazine. Celebrations also featured a Bahamian roasted pig, a rum bar, a Junkanoo band and an extravagant fireworks display. The president did not attend the wedding or the subsequent celebrations, saying it was “not good timing” for him as he was dealing with the Iran war. He cancelled a planned visit to his New Jersey golf club and spent the weekend at the White House instead. Forbes magazine recently estimated Trump Jr’s wealth at more than $US300 million ($419 million), up from $US50 million in 2024, largely thanks to investments in crypto.



ProPublica estimated the bill footed by Kremlev was in the hundreds of thousands of dollars. A spokesperson for Kremlev told the publication that the Russian billionaire and Trump Jr were friends who met “a couple of years ago”. Related Article Exclusive

Russia-Ukraine war Australia exposed to growing risk from deepening China-Russia-North Korea alliance Kremlev’s ties to the Kremlin appear substantial. In 2021, Putin reportedly appointed Kremlev’s company TsUPIS as the centralised owner and operator of sports betting in Russia. Two weeks ago, Kremlev became the owner of Russia’s largest car dealership, Rolf, which was seized by Putin at the end of 2023 and nationalised. Kremlev’s International Boxing Association was excommunicated by the International Olympic Committee in 2023 over concerns about governance, finance and refereeing integrity. The IBA is financially dependent on the Russian state-owned energy giant Gazprom. President Donald Trump’s closeness to Putin has been a recurring theme of his presidency. Despite once promising to end the war between Russia and Ukraine in a single day, Trump has been unable to do so – nor has he exerted significant pressure on Putin to stop fighting or curb his ambitions.



On Monday, he wrote on Truth Social that Ukraine had agreed to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure – a demand he made in previous days amid climbing diesel prices. “Russia has agreed to do so, likewise!” he said.
