World.title: Bob Mackie, fashion designer to the stars, dies aged 87
World.content:
LifestyleFashionVale Bob Mackie, fashion designer to the stars, dies aged 87 Mark Kennedy Updated September 15, 2026 — 5:31am ,first published 2:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bob Mackie, the fashion designer whose visually provocative Hollywood style defined glamour for the 1970s – including putting Carol Burnett in some of her kookiest outfits and Cher in her raciest ones – died on Monday (US time). He was 87. “He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” read a statement on his social media accounts. Mackie died in Palm Springs, California, from pneumonia, his publicist said. Bob Mackie at his home in Palm Springs in 2021. AP Dubbed the “Designer to the Stars”, Mackie won nine Emmy Awards, a Tony Award and was nominated for three Oscars, including one for Barbra Streisand’s Funny Lady, in which she wore a sheer batwing gown. He was inducted into the Academy of Television Arts & Sciences’ Hall of Fame in 2002. He designed gowns for Madonna, Streisand, Sharon Stone, Diana Ross and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and concert costumes for Pink. When Marilyn Monroe delivered a breathy, seductive take on Happy Birthday at a fundraiser for President John F. Kennedy and the Democratic National Committee, she did it in a sheer, beaded gown that Mackie dreamed up in a sketch.



His influence can be seen in the styles of Kendall Jenner and Bella Hadid. His archival pieces are worn today by the likes of Anya Taylor-Joy, Miley Cyrus and Zendaya, the latter who wore a Mackie gown to honour Cher at the 2024 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony. When Taylor Swift wanted to look like a showgirl on the cover of her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl, she turned to some Mackie originals. Sequins and embellishment were natural tools – other nicknames were the Sultan of Sequins, the Rajah of Rhinestones and the Guru of Glitter – but he had a simple motto: “You don’t try to change anybody, you just try to make them look better than ever,” he told The Associated Press in 2018. Tributes came from fellow designers and those lucky enough to wear his outfits. Actor Kristin Chenoweth called him a “legend” and designer Isaac Mizrahi wrote, simply, “heartbroken”. Actor Alyssa Milano called him “one of the best that ever was”. On Broadway, Mackie dressed the casts of On the Town in 1971 and Moon Over Buffalo in 1995. He also created costumes for Burnett in the revue Putting It Together, Debbie Reynolds in Debbie in 1976, Liza Minnelli in Minnelli on Minnelli in 1999 and, most recently, the cast of The Cher Show, winning his Tony Award.



Mackie was a Southern California native and embraced the idea of Hollywood movie glamour as a young child, inspired by Technicolour musicals. He would dream elaborate costumes for his mother and sister and sketch them, and he was active in costume and set design of his high school plays. He went to Pasadena City College to study advertising and illustration, and then costume design at LA’s Chouinard Art Institute. Host Whoopi Goldberg appears as Queen Elizabeth, in a Bob Mackie costume, during the 71st Annual Academy Awards in Los Angeles in 1999. AP He also grew up a fan of all the variety-show and pop stars of the 1950s and ’60s and especially their glitzy wardrobes. He went to work for costume designer Edith Head, then got the gig for The Carol Burnett Show. He and Burnett had a close friendship and collaborated on memorable characters such as Nora Desmond, Eunice and her take on Scarlett O’Hara in Gone With the Wind – called Starlet O’Hara – wearing her green curtain dress on its rods. “I love doing funny things,” Mackie said in a 1999 interview with the AP. “One week I’d have to make Carol an unattractive postal worker, and who knows what I’d have to do the next.” (Starlet’s dress is now part of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.) Mackie’s TV work continued on The Sonny and Cher Show, after Cher had guest-starred on Burnett’s show and took a liking to him. He had said that her Laverne character, with her leopard-print jumpsuit and dangling earrings, was one of his favourites.



He and Cher took a much sexier turn when she moved to movies and was invited to the Academy Awards. All those beaded, belly-baring numbers she’d wear on the stuffy red carpets came from Mackie. Cher and Bob Mackie at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures Gala in LA in 2021. AP Mackie attended the 1974 Met Gala with Cher on his arm dressed in what is perhaps one of the most famous so-called naked dresses of all time: a sheer beaded gown with white feathered sleeves and a white feathered skirt. She and the dress ended up on the cover of Time magazine. Looks such as the 1986 beaded spiderweb – worn with complementary Mohawk – and the barely there gown she wore for her best actress win in 1988 turned heads and set tongues wagging at the time. Cher wears a creation by designer Bob Mackie as she poses with actor Don Ameche after presenting him with the Oscar for best supporting actor in 1986. AP



“The outfits are sometimes mistaken for fashion, but they’re costumes like for a character in a play,” Mackie told the AP in 1999. “I want people to have fun. I want people to say ‘Wasn’t that interesting?’ or ‘Wasn’t that wild?’” Mackie had some retail success in the 1980s and ’90s, launching a ready-to-wear line in 1982 that would ultimately land on the runway at New York Fashion Week, and he was an early partner of QVC. Naked dresses only got more popular but Mackie later in life was unimpressed. “You watch awards shows and say, ‘Oh, cover up! Put it away! Honey, I don’t need to see all of that!’ It gets to be so vulgar, you don’t even want to look at it any more,” he told The Hollywood Reporter in 2024. “I was so bored watching The Met Ball – everyone exposing everything, the same look-alike dress – I shut it off. If you’ve seen one Kardashian, you’ve seen them all. And we have seen all of them.” Cher, wearing a Bob Mackie black-sequinned gown, poses with her Oscar for best actress for her role as the superstitious young widow of Moonstruck in 1988. AP Mackie also created dozens of different Barbie dolls for Mattel, with a wide variety of face sculpts, body types and storylines. He is credited as the first designer to create a complete doll. One was Lady Dracula Cher, with little baby fangs and her box resembling a coffin.



The documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion debuted in 2024. A Mackie dress Cher wore in 1975 was auctioned off in 2024 for $US101,600, 25 times its original estimate. Mackie was married to showgirl Lulu Porter from 1960 until 1963; their son, makeup artist Robert Gordon Mackie Jr., died from AIDS at age 35. Costume designer Ray Aghayan, his longtime partner, died in 2011. Related Article Emmys Full list of nominees for the 2026 Emmy Awards He had said practicality was never a driving force in his design: “It’s all about looking good and living your fantasies.” In 2017, a 71-year-old Cher once again turned heads, dressed in two Bob Mackie specials at the Billboard Music Awards. It was a blast from a different era, unlike the boring fashion world he saw.



“Nothing is very interesting any more,” he told Vogue in 2017. “You just keep seeing the same thing over and over again and there are no surprises. Unfortunately, you don’t see much fashion any more.” AP Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Why NFL-style entry to the MCG won’t happen for the footy any time soon
World.content:
The NFL’s extended perimeter around the MCG gave a glimpse into how Yarra Park could be used in the future, but also sparked renewed discussion about the privatisation of the key inner-city green space. Australia’s inaugural regular-season American football game attracted more than 100,000 people last Friday, but regular attendees to the stadium noticed a significant change to how fans entered the ground. The temporary perimeter around the MCG precinct being removed on Monday. Ruby Alexander Instead of scanning tickets at the purpose-built MCG turnstiles, a fenced perimeter was installed near the boundary of Yarra Park and acted as a ticket checkpoint. This meant only ticket holders were able to access the precinct and its many fan activation sites. The NFL’s approach was applauded by many attendees, who said it made entering the venue a smoother process – particularly because fans could enter through any gate.



But the decision has also resurfaced debate regarding the privatisation of Yarra Park. While the space is located within the City of Melbourne, the Melbourne Cricket Club is responsible for its day-to-day management. The MCC released an updated Yarra Park master plan in June, which announced the intention to scrap permits and install permanent infrastructure in the park. The document is awaiting a response from Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny. City of Melbourne councillor and East Melbourne resident Owen Guest told The Age it took NFL organisers two weeks to set up in the parkland and some residents’ cars were towed away without fair warning during the process. “The real issue, really, is a case of big business taking over the public asset by stealth,” Guest said. “There are no checks and balances there. No guardrails, no consequences should they fail to do what they say they’ll do.



“Do we want to lose Yarra Park to the interests of big corporations to make money from?” Related Article City life MCG plan for Yarra Park raises fears of stealth privatisation “Give an inch, they’ll take a mile. “Yarra Park is meant to be everybody’s park. It’s not the MCG’s. It’s not the residents’.” A spokesperson from the MCC said the extended perimeter was not currently being considered for future events, and this decision would primarily lie with a venue hirer such as the AFL or Cricket Australia.



At a Future Melbourne Committee meeting on Tuesday, councillor Rafael Camillo will move a motion reiterating the City of Melbourne’s desire for Yarra Park to remain as public parkland, and not to become “a source of revenue for select institutions”. “The MCG has a unique and important role in Melbourne, but that role must be balanced with the rights of the wider community to enjoy Yarra Park as public open space,” Camillo said. Fans queuing at the temporary entrance to the MCG precinct on Friday. Getty Images “The challenge is finding the right balance between activation and the park’s primary purpose as public open space. Yarra Park should not be treated as either an event-free zone or an unlimited event venue.” While the extended perimeter has been criticised by the councillors, the NFL’s set-up had support within the AFL community, who suggest it could function well for the league’s upcoming grand final.



Sports broadcaster Gerard Whateley expressed his support for the new entry protocols on the Sports Entertainment Network’s Crunch Time podcast on Saturday. “It actually opened the whole precinct up … that should be in place for Saturday’s preliminary final. It should certainly be in place for the grand final,” he said. But AFL spokesman Jay Allen said that complexities, such as the MCC and AFL reserve areas, meant that the traditional gate structure would be required for football matches. He added that the NFL’s extended perimeter approach meant that the precinct was restricted to those holding tickets, while the league would prefer to open the area to a wider crowd. “There will be no change on grand final day in terms of fan entry into the match and we encourage everyone to arrive early to soak up the atmosphere,” Allen said.

World.title: The NRL is bending the rules to anoint Peter V’landys. Strap yourselves in
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 The NRL is bending the rules to anoint Peter V’landys. Strap yourselves in Chris Barrett September 15, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Later this week, rugby league’s version of white smoke from the Sistine Chapel is expected to emerge from NRL headquarters as Peter V’landys is anointed executive chairman. In the midst of the NRL and NRLW finals series and on the eve of racing’s spring carnival, it would complete a long-anticipated permanent switch of sports for the bull-at-a-gate administrator. Peter V’landys. Steven Siewert/Michael Howard The newly created position stands to give him unprecedented power, making him effectively the NRL’s chief executive as well as chairman of the Australian Rugby League Commission. He has held the latter role since 2019. The dual functions of CEO and chairman are explicitly not allowed under the ARLC’s constitution, drawn up 15 years ago by the former Super League combatants News Limited and the ARL.



V’landys himself is on record as saying a removal of the separation between the board and management was not appropriate. “I’ve always believed in proper corporate governance, so it would be hypocritical to do anything other than that,” he told this masthead in 2020. Loading Six years later, however, the goalposts have moved. They have also shifted since May, when V’landys was asked again about becoming executive chairman as Andrew Abdo announced his departure as CEO and replied that a change to the constitution was required to facilitate it.



Since then, V’landys and his fellow commissioners have come across a workaround deep within the foundation document which, they have been advised, would allow him to become executive chairman without amending the constitution – something that would need the acquiescence of the clubs and state associations. It was one of the clubs that brought the clause to the Commission’s attention. Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V’landys at the NRLW finals launch on Monday. Oscar Colman With the code in rude financial health on the back of a record seven-year $5.3 billion broadcast rights deal, few, if any, will block his coronation. The clubs are mostly behind V’landys. Even those hesitant about handing such power to one person largely admit that it is better to have him on your side than not.



The NSWRL and the Queensland Rugby League, however, are yet to give their seal of approval, and have not even been approached. They and any wavering clubs are effectively being dared to take V’landys on. To do so, they would have to go to court. Loading Officially, the man himself is still to decide whether he will take the job. As he continues to weigh it up, he has been out and about. He was a guest in the suite of NFL commissioner Roger Goodell at the MCG last Friday before being spotted flying back to Sydney on Lachlan Murdoch’s private jet. He then attended NRL finals games over the weekend and the launch of the NRLW finals on Monday morning.



“I’ve been given a few more days, so I’ll take those days,” he said at the NRLW event. “And for me, at the moment, the focus is on the semi-finals, not on me.” As a hands-on chairman, the reality is that he has essentially already run the game for six years. V’landys’ supporters argue having him do it full-time is too good an opportunity to let go. It has also been said there is little alternative because of a lack of succession planning at the NRL. As for V’landys’ comments of six years ago, he believes the circumstances have changed. However, his amassing of even more authority raises a series of questions, not least about who will challenge him, whether the post will come with a term limit, who will set his salary, and what the clubs will do when they don’t get their way.



As for what kind of leader he will be, there is less mystery. V’landys’ modus operandi is well known. He runs a tight ship, wrests a dollar for his sport from wherever he can, thinks outside the square and pursues his goals aggressively. Related Article NRL 2026 PNG Chiefs in war over name as NZ Rugby threatens legal action It’s instructive, though, that his confrontational style and Racing NSW’s vast tentacles of control have worn thin in some quarters of the industry he has led for the past 22 years. V’landys once elicited reverence across racing in much the same way as his backers laud his achievements in the NRL. He delivered unprecedented rivers of gold from betting turnover and other deals and demonstrated the same kind of entrepreneurial zeal he has brought to league with innovations such as The Everest, the $20 million slot race that has drawn younger crowds to the track. Given his propensity for a fight, he was never going to keep everyone on side, but after more than two decades in charge, many believe his tenure has run its course.



His exit looms as an epochal moment for racing and rugby league. The NRL should at least know what it’s in for. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: National and Labour below 30% mark latest poll shows
World.content:
Both major parties are below the 30 percent mark with less than two months until the election, according to a new poll.

The latest The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll, funded by Infrastructure New Zealand, shows neither the current coalition bloc nor the opposition bloc would have the numbers to form a government, with both blocs on 60 seats.

Since the last of this poll in June, Labour has slumped by 7 points. It remains in the lead, but only just.

National has also fallen, by 2 points, while the Greens, New Zealand First, and ACT have all gone up.

For the first time in this poll, the Opportunity Party is above the 5 percent threshold, but its numbers are still not enough to help the left bloc into government.

Labour: 28 percent (down 7)

National: 27 percent (down 2)

Greens: 14 percent (up 4)

NZ First: 13 percent (up 1)

ACT: 9 percent (up 1)

Opportunity: 6 percent (previously included with 'other')

Te Pāti Māori: 2 percent (no change)

Other: 2 percent (down 1)

According to The Post's calculations, which assume that parties win electorate seats broadly in line with their share of the party vote, and retain at least one electorate seat each, the coalition bloc would have 60 seats, while the parliamentary opposition would have 53. Add in Opportunity's 7 and that leads to a hung Parliament.

Those numbers could change if there is an overhang, as Te Pāti Māori has been campaigning on.

In the preferred prime minister stakes, Chris Hipkins is on 45 percent, up 1 point from June's poll. Christopher Luxon is down 2 points to 35 percent. A further 16 percent of people chose neither, while 4 percent were unsure.

A majority of voters also still believe the country is heading in the wrong direction, with 56 percent saying so. Those feeling the country is heading in the right direction numbered 27 percent.

World.title: 'A lot' of pressure on any incoming government, Labour leader says
World.content:
Weekly interview with opposition leader, Chris Hipkins Morning Report Download MP3 9m

Labour leader Chris Hipkins says his party cannot bring back the government KiwiSaver contributions to what they were, but is blaming the government for making the cuts in the first place.

As part of Budget 2025, the government halved its KiwiSaver contribution from $521 to $260, and limited eligibility to those earning under $180,000.

Labour's KiwiSaver policy package, released on Sunday, did not include a commitment to returning the government contribution to what it was.

Appearing on Morning Report on Tuesday, Chris Hipkins criticised the government for cutting the contribution, but said Labour would not bring it back.

"The National Party have cut the government contribution not once but twice. We're not in a position where we can promise to reverse that cut at this stage in time," he said.

"If there's an opportunity to do that, that's something we could look at. But I'm only promising things that I know we can afford right now, and we can't afford to do that right at the moment."

Labour said the government had made "different choices" like tax cuts for landlords and tobacco companies, instead of keeping its contribution to KiwiSaver as it was.

Asked if Labour would get rid of the interest deductibility for landlords, Hipkins said Labour would set out its position "in due course," indicating that would come after the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update later this month.

"We need the government to open the books before we can finalise our plans, because they have done so much damage. We've got a health system that's descending further into crisis.

"We've got a cost-of-living crisis that's getting deeper for New Zealand families. There is a lot of pressure on any incoming government after the election, and I want New Zealanders to know that any promises that I make, I can afford, and I can deliver on them."

Asked whether Labour's policy to raise the employer KiwiSaver contributions to 6 percent would hurt businesses, Hipkins said that was the same as National's policy.

Where Labour's differed was that it would not make employees also put in 6 percent, instead allowing them to put in 4 percent and pause their contributions if they wished.

"It's about making sure that everybody gets access to a KiwiSaver nest egg in retirement, not just those who can afford to make the salary sacrifice right at the moment," he said.

World.title: 'Music is our language' - Auckland family trio win the Kiwi Cover Song Contest
World.content: "We try not to let the world see us struggling. We just live to prove that it can be done despite [those struggles] … If we get somewhere, it's not [because of] pity parties."

World.title: $500 compensation for man who may lose house after giving up job over vaccine rules
World.content:
When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

A man who left his job because of Covid-19 vaccine requirements, and later fell into significant arrears on his home loan, has been awarded $500 in compensation from the bank.

The man complained to the Banking Ombudsman, one of 283 disputes it investigated in its most recent financial year.

It said the man bought a house in 2022 with a bank loan, but left his job later that year because of a vaccine requirement. He survived on savings for a few months and then started a consultancy business.

But by the next year, he was struggling financially. He asked the bank to align his repayments with his monthly invoicing, which it did.

In April 2023, he stopped making payments and was in arrears.

He asked to be changed to interest-only payments, but the bank did not respond. He repeated the request in August and was asked to complete a statement of position, which he did not.

He contacted the bank in November 2024, but the bank did not respond. In January last year, he entered a repayment arrangement, but did not stick with it.

The bank said it would be willing to consolidate the arrears into his loan if he could make on-time repayments for three months, but by February he had not made any payments.

The man said the bank had not given him sufficient support. He did not want the bank to stop working on his complaint, but it said it was deadlocked and referred it to the ombudsman.

The ombudsman looked into the case and said, by the time he told the bank about his circumstances, he had been in default for more than two months so he was not able to apply for hardship support under the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act.

"Despite this, the bank still had an obligation to treat him in a reasonable and ethical manner when he failed to meet his loan repayments. We considered that it had mostly done so… however, elements of the bank's service were inadequate. [He] twice contacted the bank but received no response. The bank also omitted some of the personal information he requested. Even so, these failings had no tangible impact on his financial situation.:

It recommended $500 compensation for the communication failures.

The bank has issued a notice that it will sell the house if the arrears are not paid.

Banking Ombudsman Nicola Sladden said the number of complaints in the 2025/26 year was up 26 percent on the year before.

Lending disputes were up 59 percent, which she said reflected the financial pressure that many people were under.

Financial hardship was a factor in 20 percent of cases.

A spokesperson said the increase in lending cases reflected challenges customers had keeping up with loans they had had for some time, particularly when their circumstances had changed.

Sladden said people were increasingly using AI tools to understand their rights and prepare their complaints. "These tools are giving users the confidence to pursue their complaints as far as possible."

The scheme awarded $1.3 million in compensation in the year.

Big banks had the largest percentage of dispute cases. ASB had the most, at 18.8 percent of cases and 18 percent of the market. ANZ was next, at 18.3 percent but it had 28 percent of the market.

Of the disputes that were decided by the scheme, 29 were in the customer's favour, 146 in the bank's and 61 both parties.

Sladden said there had been a notable drop in fraud and scam complaints, down 40 percent year-on-year.

She said that was due to the efforts of banks and government agencies to raise awareness abotu how to avoid being duped by scammers.

She said the introduction of stronger fraud detection and prevention measures by banks in December was already having a bearing on the improved figures.

More than half of scam complaints involved unauthorised transactions, of which phishing and information harvesting scams remained the most common types.

Despite the rise in disputes, the scheme's overall caseload fell 13 per cent for the year, due to a 10 per cent decline in general inquiries and a 14 per cent drop in simple complaints. The report said loans, bank accounts and service were the most common complaint categories.

World.title: Retirement village law change taking far too long, association says
World.content:
Retirement resident advocacy group calls for better protections Morning Report Download MP3 7m

A group representing retirement village residents says it is taking far too long to get a law change that will ensure faster payouts for people who leave.

The government is proposing changes that would see residents and their families paid interest after six months of leaving a unit, and fully repaid no later than 12 months after a unit was vacated.

But Retirement Village Residents' Association national vice president and complaints coordinator Di Sinclair told Morning Report action seemed to have stalled with an amendment bill yet to be introduced to Parliament.

Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka told Morning Report Cabinet had made decisions about a substantial package of reforms, which would be announced shortly and progressed next term.

Sinclair said she was hearing many complaints from residents in retirement villages but the main one was the late return of the capital sum that they paid when they went into a village.

"Depending on the operator or the village they would expect to get that back, minus 25 or 30 percent, which is the fee that is charged which covers all their costs."

She said currently it was taking anything between nine months and two years to get that capital sum back if a resident left or if they had died then the family had to wait that long.

Residents were supposed to get the money back within six months or so, but it was dragging on and on, she said.

"In the case of a deceased resident the family needs the money back, basically to bury them and to get on and sort things out in the estate."

Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka said Cabinet had agreed on a package of reforms which would be announced shortly. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

For a resident who wanted to leave the village because they were moving, then it put them in limbo because they could not get their money back for some time, she said.

Sinclair said in the worst one she had ever dealt with it took three and a half years for the money to be returned, she said.

"You often see residents who don't know their rights, who don't understand what they're entitled to, and they just put up with it for a long time until they can't any longer."

The review of the sector took place over successive governments, the retirement commissioner pushed for the review and it happened, she said.

But she said it had stalled with this government and there was still no legislation in Parliament to address the issue, she said.

There was a huge power imbalance between the operators and the residents, she said.

"The old adage is, 'you know you signed the contract, you knew what you were going into', well even the government's people who are investigating this have said that the contracts are unfair, just because you sign a contract it doesn't make it fair.

"It's all about justice and consumer protection and you can't negotiate the contracts, you can't negotiate it."

The association wants people leaving retirement villages to get their money back in three months, but the government was wanting to mandate 12 months, she said.

The village operators are saying they cannot afford it, but no one had ever produced figures to indicate they could not afford it, she said.

"So we're at a bit of an impasse."

World.title: KiwiSaver: Would Labour or National make you better off?
World.content:
KiwiSaver is on the table as a major issue of this year's election.

But would you be better off under National's KiwiSaver plan, or Labour's?

National is promising to make participation compulsory, with a 6 percent employee plus 6 percent employer contribution required by 2032.

Labour would only make the employer contribution compulsory, rising to 6 percent, and would remove any minimum employee contribution so that people could pause or reduce their payments.

When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

National would automatically enrol babies at birth and give them $1500.

Both parties would require employer contributions for people who are over 65. National would provide a government contribution for people who are on paid parental leave and not contributing to KiwiSaver. Labour would require employer contributions to continue when someone was off on parental leave.

Labour would ban new total remuneration packages.

As a general comparison and not including the impact of income tax over a person's working life, a 25-year-old currently earning $60,000 a year and making contributions at the default rate could end up with $1.014 million in their account under Labour's plan and $1.241 million under National's.

The worker would have given up more of their own salary over their working life in the National scenario.

A 45-year-old earning $100,000 would end up with $340,000 under Labour's plan and $424,000 under National's.

A 25-year-old not contributing themselves could still end up with $561,000 under Labour's plan. National would require them to contribute.

The $1500 baby payment could grow to be worth about $8000 over 25 years.

Infometrics managing director Gareth Kiernan said it was hard to compare the two policies.

"We can effectively ignore the higher contributions being required of employers because they are set at 6 percent across both parties' policies.

"The question then essentially becomes, are workers better off if they are forced to save 6 percent of their income rather than 4 percent of their income? If people were rational and planned appropriately for the future, the answer would be no - because allowing people to choose what to do with their income would enable them to make the best choices for their individual circumstances. For example, people with a mortgage could decide that the best way to improve their long-term financial position is to prioritise paying off the mortgage first rather than investing, and then save and invest at a faster rate later.

"However, it's questionable whether many people act in this way. I won't say they are irrational; rather, that they have a high discount rate, which means they place little weighting on events a long way in the future when making decisions. Put simply, spending money now is a more attractive option than saving money to use in 40 years' time. Thus outcomes could be better from a broad societal point of view if the government legislates that people must save so that retired people are less of a drain on society in the future. The alternatives to legislating higher KiwiSaver rates now might be, in the future, higher tax rates or reduced levels of government superannuation - outcomes that might not be fiscally achievable or could provide insufficient support for future retirees."

He said there would also be questions about whether forcing people to save more would eventually result in less universal government superannuation in the future.

"If that is the case, then a 25-year-old saving 6 percent now achieves a larger KiwiSaver balance at retirement but it might be offset by less government support after they retire.

"Nevertheless, even this part of the argument becomes nuanced when one considers what an appropriate level of retirement income might be. It could be argued that even the current superannuation rate of $44,400 per annum per couple after tax is not enough for a comfortable lifestyle, let alone any possible future reductions in support as fiscal settings become more stretched. In that case, some level of forced private saving by the government to top up this amount would improve people's future wellbeing.

"Essentially, which policy makes people better off comes down to the trade-off between current personal spending and saving for retirement -and lower-income people are likely to have less room in their budget for saving, how bad people are at planning for the future, and whether they need to be protected from themselves and any differences in future government policy that might see higher-wealth people receive less government superannuation support."

Pathfinder Asset Management founder John Berry said it was disappointing that KiwiSaver had ended up being an election issue rather than a wider discussion about retirement settings and where NZ Super would fit in.

"The bigger question for people in their 30s and 40s at the moment is what is NZ Super going to mean for them in retirement? Are the settings going to be the same or less? That impacts how much they need to save in KiwiSaver."

But he said it was important that New Zealand moved towards matching Australia's contribution rate of 12 percent.

"We're not all saving enough for retirement. The Retirement Commission is saying 40 percent of people over 65 have virtually no other income besides NZ Super. That is quite astonishing. Forty percent of New Zealanders are relying on NZ Super for retirement. We need to fix that. The best way to do it and give people the sort of lifestyle they want from retirement is larger KiwiSaver balances, saving small amounts compounding over a very long time frame."

He said there needed to be cross-party support for a different approach. "People in their 20s are kind of in a difficult spot at the moment where they're saving for their own retirement and their taxes are paying super payments to retirees, but they may not or are unlikely to get the same benefit when they get to retirement."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said the difference between the two policies came down to National requiring people to save more, but that could mean people had less take-home pay.

"Under the Labour scenario you are going to save less but you have more flexibility. Those who can save more will save more."

He supported delinking employer and employee contributions. "If you are going through a hardship, it doesn't mean the employer should suddenly experience a lower cost of employing you. It doesn't make sense."

Read all of the election policies released so far in our full guide

World.title: Auckland and Wellington hit record property market lows
World.content:
When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

Auckland and Wellington both recorded the longest period it has ever taken a property to sell in August last month, and Wellington had its lowest-ever August sales count.

The Real Estate Institute has released its data for the month.

It shows Auckland recorded a median 54 days to sell compared to a 10-year average for August of 43.

Wellington's median was 60, compared to a 10-year average for August of 41.

Nationwide, sales numbers were down 13 percent compared to the same time a year earlier.

The 5430 properties that changed hands was the sixth-lowest number for any August in 35 years.

The house price index, which smooths out variation in median price data cause by the type of homes selling, was down 0.9 percent year-on-year.

Excluding Auckland, it was down 0.2 percent.

Nationally, house prices remain 17.1 percent below their peak. They are just under 25 percent below in Auckland, 30.3 percent below the peak in Wellington, but 0.8 percent below in Canterbury and 1.1 percent below in Otago and Southland.

Chief executive Lizzy Ryley said within the national figures, there was significant variation. The South Island's housing market was much stronger than the North Island's. Southland had a median price of $505,000 up 7.4 percent year-on-year. Tasman was up 5.6 percent, Northland up 3.6 percent, West Coast up 2.5 percent and Canterbury up 1.5 percent.

She said Auckland and Wellington buyers seemed to feel they could take their time because there was no need to hurry.

"Whereas if you look into the South Island, particularly down in Southland, the market seems to move itself towards that slight fear of missing out. At the moment in Auckland, there is no real fear of missing out. The market feels stable and so people make decisions when they are ready to make decisions."

She said household costs, job security, global uncertainty and the lead-up to the election were all shaping buyer and seller sentiment.

"Stock levels are playing an important role in how individual markets are moving," she said.

"Where buyers have a lot of options, they can take more time before deciding. In other areas with fewer new listings, competition is helping maintain momentum." The number of new listings in the month fell 5.1 percent year-on-year to 8326.

"Our members tell us they generally expect conditions to remain broadly steady over the coming months, with improving enquiry levels in some areas supporting cautious optimism," she said.

"Borrowing costs, job security, the lead-up to the general election and local stock levels will also influence activity. That makes guidance from local real estate professionals particularly valuable for people considering their next move."

Ryley said it was an "amazing" time to get into he market as a first-home buyer.

"I think it's a very, very stable market in which both buyers and sellers can feel relatively confident to do what they want to do when they need to do it. I don't believe we are going to see anything shift dramatically."

World.title: 'We all cried together': Families count blessings after Vanuatu ferry disaster
World.content:
Two siblings survive Vanuatu disaster swimming to Santo island Pacific Waves Download MP3 1m 53s

Families of the Vanuatu ferry survivors are counting their blessings as the search continues for people still missing at sea.

Two young siblings swam towards Santo Island after the ferry they were travelling on sank, according to their aunt, Violet Tari.

Arian and Talesa Tari were travelling from Santo to Ambae aboard the MV Matui on Friday morning, when large waves capsized the ferry.

Luganville MP Matai Seremaiah said the vessel sank at about 9:30am.

The number of death remains at two, and more than 30 people are still missing, while 14 have been rescued.

Speaking to Pacific Waves, Violet Tari said she is grateful that her niece and nephew are still alive. It is understood that while the siblings were swimming towards Santo, the superyacht Lunaris spotted them and were rescued between 10pm and 10:15pm on Saturday night.

"They only swim to find the islands, they came across as if they were on the sea and they were pulled by the tides, and they came across the islands and they came to Santo."

Arian and Talesa Tari are both recovering at the Northern Provincial Hospital in Luganville, Santo and their aunt said it was an emotional reunion when she visited them.

"They were only crying when they saw us, when they saw us in the hospital. We all cried together first. No talking, no anything but crying," Tari said.

"I feel happy because we received them."

Tari said the siblings have not spoken much about what happened but understands they are still in shock.

"We only encourage them not to worry about anything because now we already there, we will be as good. But maybe they will say things with their experience later."

While neither siblings have suffered major injuries, Tari said her niece appears to have rashes on her neck. She said they have been in contact with the police.

The family is now focused on supporting the pair as they receive medical care.

Mother of survivor feared the worst

Another survivor, Max Tari is also recovering in hospital after spending hours at sea.

His mother, Primerose Garae told Pacific Waves she feared he had died knowing how rough the sea was and prayed for him.

"When the boat drowned, I'm thinking that he already died," Garae said.

"I'm very sad that time ... I pray to Jehovah that Jehovah will be helping him."

However, her fears had been eased when she saw Max's name on a list of people who had been found.

Search and rescue ongoing

The Vanuatu government has said the sinking appears to have involved strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, with possible negligence including overloading of the vessel.

A full investigation is expected to examine what happened.

World.title: The Stinear effect: The stat changing Geelong in 2026
World.content:
The biggest coup of the off-season wasn't Anne Hatchard to Gold Coast, Taylor Smith to Sydney, or Eden Zanker to Fremantle.

It was premiership coach Mick Stinear's shift away from Melbourne to take the reins at Geelong.

He became the first coach to be poached by another club, leaving his position to take up another, and just the third coach to ply their trade at a second club.

The reasons behind Geelong's desperation to appoint Stinear have been immediately evident. Outside of a big round one loss to two-time reigning premier North Melbourne, the Cats have found their feet in a new style.

And although there have been early challenges on the injury front — the club has been forced to name top up players in its extended squad already this year — the system itself has proved sound.

Stinear's signature stat

Aishling Moloney has been a vital goal kicker for the Cats. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Josh Chadwick)

Teams coached by Stinear have one thing in common: Goal Assists are a priority. Sharing the ball neatly around the attacking arc to generate the highest percentage opportunity to score has always been fundamental to how his teams work, and that has already become a feature of Geelong in 2026.

Leading Melbourne for the first 10 seasons of its life in the AFLW, the Demons sat in the top two for goal assists in four of the five seasons from 2022 S6 onward. The one outlier was 2024, where the club was desperately stretched due to an onslaught of injury.

Melbourne's Goal Assists Avg. goal assists AFLW rank AFLW average 2025 5.3 2 3.6 2024 3.1 8 3.0 2023 6.3 1 3.4 2022 (S7) 4.2 1 2.6 2022 (S6) 3.9 2 2.5

This year the Cats average 7.8 goal assists — sitting second in the league behind only North Melbourne — and as a result, a host of other key scoring statistics have improved dramatically.

Aishling Moloney leads the way for the stat, with 1.6 per game, while having also kicked seven goals in the opening five games, but there are a total of seven Cats averaging 0.6 goal assists or more in that time.

Only two Geelong players averaged 0.6 or more goal assists across the 2025 AFLW season; Julia Crockett-Grills with 1.0, and Moloney with 0.6.

Julia Crockett-Grills averaged one goal assist per game in the 2025 AFLW season. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Elsby)

Because of this increased willingness to bring teammates in and create those deeper forward entries by way of looking for goal assist opportunities, Geelong is kicking more than four more goals per game in 2026, and goaling more regularly from the inside 50s it creates than in years gone past.

In five games the Cats have already kicked 50 goals. They kicked 69 across the whole of 2025.

They have made a marginal improvement on average inside 50s, but it is what they are doing once in the arc that has been the real difference.

Geelong's growing attack Avg. Points For Avg. Inside 50s Avg. Goal Efficiency (%) Avg. Goal Assists Avg. Goal Accuracy (%) Avg. Goal Kickers 2026 66.2 36.2 27.6 7.8 55.0 6.4 2025 41.7 32.6 17.7 3.4 36.3 4.1 2024 43.6 32.6 19.0 4.2 44.7 4.3 2023* 44.9 33.8 18.9 4.5 41.3 4.6

*Geelong reached the preliminary final

Getting it there

Obviously, to create these opportunities ahead of the ball, movement up the field needs to be more effective.

The Cats currently sit number one in the AFLW for disposal efficiency at an average of 69.8 per cent — this is something that the club has prided itself on in recent years.

The Cats move the ball via the hand a lot more under Mick Stinear. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Elsby)

The shift in disposal, however, has come via the method. A greater reliance on moving the ball by hand has been clear, with a league-low kick rate of 54.5 per cent, and a significant increase in uncontested possession indicates greater control outside the contest.

Issues of recent years are still present — ruck availability and strength is still a concern, clearance numbers have only marginally grown compared to 2025 — but the capacity to adapt on the outside has been the difference.

Outside ball Avg. uncontested possession Avg. contested possession rate (%) 2026 166.0 41.8 2025 136.4 45.8 2024 124.3 45.8 2023 131.5 46.0

Generating and scoring from turnover is a clear point of improvement, with the Cats averaging 24.0 points per game from the source in 2025 compared to its 42.6 points this year.

From turnover, they are effectively getting on the move, handballing to runners, and going quickly.

Becky Webster's work across the half back line, to intercept and drive the ball forward has been crucial in this respect, as has Mikayla Bowen's hard two-way running efforts while also carrying a heavy load through the midfield.

Not yet the complete package

Mick Stinear has moved to the Cats from Melbourne. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

While there are plenty of positive signs when it comes to Geelong's attacking game, there is still room for improvement in its defensive phase.

Conceding higher scores, more inside 50s, and more marks in the opposition's attacking zone, there is a vulnerability when sides can get the ball moving quickly against them.

There is an element of high risk, high reward in the game style the Cats have employed this year, and they are only five matches into the system, but protecting that defence more effectively is surely high on Stinear's priority list as they continue through the season.

Opposition attack Avg. Points Against Avg. Inside 50s Conceded Avg. Marks Inside 50s Conceded Avg. Shot Efficiency Conceded (%) 2026 53.8 38.4 9.6 50.0 2025 44.9 33.4 7.5 40.9 2024 39.7 30.7 6.3 44.4 2023 33.4 27.5 5.5 43.9

It is worth mentioning that after the Cats' round one loss to powerhouse North Melbourne, their average score conceded is in fact 42.3 points, indicating an improvement in that area.

But as the old adage goes; to be the best, you have to beat the best.

Come finals, this system needs to be able to stand up to what North Melbourne — or Stinear's old side Melbourne — has to offer.

There is every indication to suggest it can, but without a match against the Demons fixtured in the home and away season, and the Roos already in the rear view mirror, finals will be the chance to really test the system once more.

World.title: SA Health employee reprimanded for accessing Tony Modra's medical records
World.content:
One SA Health employee has been reprimanded for accessing AFL legend Tony Modra's private medical records after he was seriously injured in a truck crash, while two other employees remain under investigation, the health department says.

In a statement, SA Health said another six people were no longer being investigated.

"The number of employees under investigation for potentially accessing a patient's medical record inappropriately has been revised from nine individuals, to three," the statement said.

"Of these three, one individual has been reprimanded and two are still being investigated.

"Six individuals are no longer under investigation for this matter."

Any sanction imposed becomes part of an employee's permanent record.

Tony Modra spent time in hospital after the crash, and later shared a photo of himself in intensive care on Instagram. (Instagram: tonymodraofficial)

In July SA Health said nine staff were being either investigated for alleged inappropriate access to the records, or "assessed" to determine whether their access was "always appropriate".

At the time, the department also apologised to Modra's family for "any distress caused".

Modra underwent facial surgery and was in hospital for days after a truck crash at Back Valley, near Victor Harbor on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula, on June 18.

In July, the Crows legend posted an update of his progress on Instagram. In that post he said he was now able to get "out and about", and shared photos of himself in intensive care and recovering with his family.

In a statement earlier that month, he said he was "overwhelmed by the kindness and care" that he, and his family, had been shown.

Modra played a total of 165 AFL games for Adelaide and the Fremantle Dockers, after debuting for the Crows in 1992.

Police were called to the scene of the truck crash, near Victor Harbor, on June 18. (Supplied: SA Police)

The probe into staff accessing Modra's records is not the first time concerns have been raised about SA Health staff inappropriately accessing patient records in cases involving well-known people.

In 2016, 13 hospital staff were sanctioned after they were caught snooping on the medical records of Cy Walsh.

Cy Walsh had been charged with the stabbing murder of his father — Crows coach Phil Walsh — before being found not guilty by reason of mental incompetence.

In 2024, ABC News revealed a SA Health investigation had found 18 staff engaged in misconduct or inappropriately accessed the medical records of a patient understood to be Charlie Stevens, the late son of SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens.

The department has also previously said it regularly conducted audits "to ensure that staff are accessing appropriate information".

World.title: Star Hawk's season over after ACL injury
World.content:
Three-time All-Australian Emily Bates will miss the rest of the AFLW season with a knee injury in a huge blow to Hawthorn's chances of snaring a maiden premiership.

Scans have confirmed Bates tore the anterior cruciate ligament in her right knee when the leg twisted awkwardly in a tackle during the Hawks' win over the Western Bulldogs on Saturday.

The 30-year-old club captain also damaged the meniscus and will undergo surgery.

"This is clearly disappointing news for Emily," Hawks AFLW general manager Keegan Brooksby said.

"The playing group and wider club will support her through the recovery journey.

"We have no doubt she'll approach her rehab with the diligence and professionalism she's always been known for.

Emily Bates played her 100th game for the Hawks against Adelaide. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

"Although Emily won't return to the field in 2026, she will continue to play an important off-field role in our program, as our captain."

Hawthorn face a huge test against AFLW juggernaut North Melbourne in Cairns on Friday night without Bates and Laura Stone (concussion).

Fellow midfielder Daisy Flockhart also has to prove her fitness after suffering a knock to her chest against the Bulldogs.

"We've been playing different players through [the midfield] and trying to build some versatility in our side … we're confident in the players we'll have in there," Hawks coach Daniel Webster said post-match on Saturday.

"It'll be a good challenge next week with who we're playing.

"We'll probably have some sort of different look in there with different players and that's OK. We'll keep getting to work."

Hawthorn (3-2) sit eighth in their quest for another finals berth, while North Melbourne (5-0) are in familiar territory on top of the ladder.

AAP

World.title: 'Bittersweet' Swans captaincy call for Rampe
World.content:
Dane Rampe didn't think Sydney would still be here, let alone that he'd be tasked with leading the Swans to an unlikely AFL premiership again.

A heart-and-soul player, veteran defender Rampe will stand in for an injured Callum Mills and captain the club in Friday's preliminary final against Fremantle at the SCG.

Rampe had led the Swans to the eventual 2024 grand final loss when a luckless Mills suffered a hamstring strain before that year's preliminary final.

But the circumstances surrounding this year's premiership push wildly differ.

Mills's vice-captain Isaac Heeney is among five Swans players serving club-imposed bans after last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Many in the AFL world had written off Sydney in the lead-up to finals, with even club chairman Andrew Pridham believing their chances had been "torpedoed".

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

A gutsy 53-point qualifying final win over Brisbane went some way towards rebuilding respect for the club, especially after Mills suffered an ACL injury in the first quarter.

Sustained by the grit displayed against the back-to-back reigning premiers, Rampe was given the nod by Mills, coach Dean Cox and club leaders.

The former Swans co-captain is chasing his maiden premiership after playing in four grand final defeats (2014, 2016, 2022 and 2024).

"It's a thrill. It's a privilege. And yeah, it's a little bit bittersweet," Rampe said on Monday.

"The overwhelming emotion is probably just gratitude to be back here.

"Probably a month ago, we weren't sure what was going to happen with the team and with the club and with the players.

"To be here and challenging in a prelim is just something, particularly being at the back end of my career, I'm really grateful for."

Callum Mills may miss all of the 2027 season, or at least a sizable portion of it. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Rampe's return to captaincy comes after being re-drafted as a rookie by the Swans with fellow defender Jake Lloyd at the end of last year.

While Lloyd has signed on for a 15th season, neither Rampe nor the Swans have made a call on whether he will continue next year.

But the door is open, with defender Mills facing the possibility of missing the entire 2027 season.

"I haven't had a chance to think about that. I don't think it [being captain] does much," Rampe said.

"We'll wait and see. I'm just happy to be where I am at the moment and to have that little bit of hope and belief is, I feel, a real luxury."

Drafted at age 22 in 2013, Rampe was named co-captain with Josh Kennedy and Luke Parker for the 2019 season.

The trio handed the reins to Mills at the end of 2023, but their successor endured a tough 2024 season pockmarked by injury.

Mills was restricted to seven games, hurting his shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate before being ruled out of finals.

Cox's selection conundrum for Friday's clash is further complicated, with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) near full fitness.

Rampe said the Swans were playing the cards they were dealt.

"You've got one or two ways you can go in these circumstances," Rampe said.

"You can get the 'poor me' and feel sorry for yourself, or you can do something about it."

AAP

World.title: HYROX Beijing sparks backlash after Aussie athlete soils herself mid-race
World.content:
The organisers of a viral sporting event in Beijing have faced backlash and criticism after an Australian woman was allowed to continue competing after soiling herself.

Athlete Joanna Wietrzyk was participating in the global indoor fitness race HYROX in the Chinese capital at the weekend when she suffered a bout of faecal incontinence.

Wietrzyk was allowed to finish the course and won her event, with videos and photos posted online showing her continuing through demanding exercises and using communal equipment while visibly soiled.

The incident has gone viral on Chinese social media and sparked debate about HYROX's health and safety standards, as well as athlete responsibility.

"She's so selfish — she kept running the whole way even though she had diarrhoea," one user on Weibo questioned. "What about the runners behind her?"

Another wrote: "The host is ultimately unprofessional!"

On Weibo, the hashtag #Hyrox incontinence female competitor has not been punished# has more than 27 million views.

HYROX is a global fitness challenge in which participants race to complete often gruelling stations, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing.

An article on the Beijing incident was the most-viewed story on Chinese state media website the Global Times on Monday.

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) is an elite HYROX athlete who holds the Women's Solo Pro world record. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

In a statement, HYROX China said the area was decontaminated after the race had finished.

"After the incident, the organising committee immediately closed off and isolated the affected area and track, and completed comprehensive disinfection," organisers said.

"Relevant equipment was removed from the venue, and waste was disposed of in accordance with municipal waste-management standards."

The organisers also said they would replace flooring at the venue to protect future athlete health.

HYROX World also issued a statement addressing the incident.

"HYROX has clear bio-contaminant and medical procedures in place," the statement said.

"In this instance, an unforeseen situation arose in which protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood."

The incident went viral on Chinese social media at the weekend and triggered strong backlash to the organisers. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

But social media users and other athletes at the event have attacked the response and questioned why Wietrzyk was allowed to finish the race, potentially risking the health and safety of other competitors.

"For people who were exposed to that situation, there could be genuine physical and psychological consequences," one competitor named johopalooza posted on Instagram.

"I paid HYROX to provide a professionally organised and safe event. So while I understand the athlete perspective, ultimately my contract and expectation is with HYROX.

"Protecting athletes is important, but showing the wider community that HYROX takes responsibility when its own procedures fail is just as important."

Loading Instagram content

'Organisers should assess the risk'

HYROX has also been accused of double standards over its hygiene rules, which punish athletes with time penalties if they litter on the course, spit or clear their nose onto the floor.

HYROX has been contacted for comment.

Wietrzyk, who is a HYROX world record holder, was invited to compete at the Beijing event.

She has been contacted for comment.

Li Hongxin, an associate professor of sports management at China's Zhengzhou University of Light Industry, said the athlete should not be criticised or judged for experiencing a physiological problem.

"I think her determination and sportsmanship are very understandable," he said.

But he said the incident raised questions about the responsibility of event organisers.

"Organisers should assess whether such a situation could affect the health or wellbeing of other competitors," he said.

Dr Li said this was particularly important because HYROX was an indoor event.

"Take a marathon as an example. If a competitor is menstruating, organisers would generally respect their decision to continue because a marathon is an outdoor event," he said.

"They don't share equipment with other competitors, so it generally doesn't pose a public safety concern.

"But HYROX is an indoor event, where competitors share equipment. In that situation, I think the organisers should have staff step in and adjust the event, or take appropriate emergency measures."

World.title: Jordan Petaia returns to Wallabies squad after NFL stint
World.content:
Jordan Petaia has been selected in his first Wallabies squad since the 2023 Rugby World Cup as Les Kiss braces for the sternest test yet of his brief coaching reign.

A one-time teenage Test debutant, Petaia has been included in Australia's 34-man group for the upcoming showdown with back-to-back world champions South Africa in Perth.

The 26-year-old has been plying his trade in France and Japan since the end of the 2024 Super Rugby Pacific season, after seven seasons at the Queensland Reds.

He left the Reds in 2024 to pursue a career in the NFL, signing briefly for the Los Angeles Chargers in 2025, before being waived later that same year.

He then signed for Perpignan in the Top 14 before locking in a long-term spot at Urayasu D-Rocks.

Petaia made his Wallabies debut at just 19 at the 2019 World Cup in Japan, scoring a memorable try against Uruguay, and has since pulled on the gold jersey a total of 31 times.

With now just a year before Australia hosts the 2027 World Cup, Kiss says it's time to see if Petaia is ready to make a run at a third appearance at the global showpiece.

Jordan Petaia is set for a return to Wallaby gold. (Getty Images: PA Images/Bradley Collyer)

"Look, we've got a lot of good back-three players here in the country. We made sure we looked at all of them," Kiss said on Monday.

"It was just the ideal opportunity to see Jordan. He's been out of the system for a couple of years now. He has played in two World Cups. We just wanted to touch base with him, get him to come and work out with us, see how he's going.

"We haven't selected that team yet, but it was just a good opportunity to see Jordan back in the environment and him to have a good look at us with the new coaching structure and all those sort of things.

"From the team perspective, there was a lot of deep discussion about where we would go with that."

The classy utility back is one of three new faces in the squad that won back the Puma Trophy in an undefeated tour of Argentina earlier this month.

Another is Western Force recruit Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, who has been named in his first official Wallabies squad, replacing Carter Gordon who suffered a fractured calf bone in Mendoza.

Born in Toowoomba and raised in Gunnedah, the 22-year-old flyhalf was part of Australia's 2023 and 2024 World Rugby U20 Championships and has featured for the Reds on more than 35 occasions.

Queenslander Zane Nonggorr is back in the squad after completing a successful return to the field in Saturday's 2026 Super Rugby AUS opener having picked up a minor calf strain in Japan.

He replaces Wallaby number 1,000 Massimo De Lutiis, who is being managed after playing three straight Tests to kick off his international career.

Outside back Filipo Daugunu is also being managed due to a minor knee complaint.

"We've learned a bit more about ourselves as a group over the last four Tests and we know we still have a lot to work on to get to where we want to be," Kiss said of the Springboks challenge in Perth on September 27.

"South Africa have been the benchmark team in World Rugby for a long time and we're motivated by the challenge of meeting them in our own backyard in two weeks' time."

Wallabies Squad:

Forwards — Allan Alaalatoa, Angus Bell, Charlie Cale, Josh Canham, Tom Hooper, Isaac Kailea, Fraser McReight, Josh Nasser, Zane Nonggorr, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Billy Pollard, Aidan Ross, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Lachlan Shaw, Carlo Tizzano, Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Jeremy Williams, Harry Wilson (capt).

Backs: Jock Campbell, Ben Donaldson, Isaac Henry, Len Ikitau, Max Jorgensen, Ryan Lonergan, Tate McDermott, Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, Declan Meredith, Hunter Paisami, Jordan Petaia, Harry Potter, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Kalani Thomas, Tom Wright.

AAP

World.title: World Athletics firm on Russia ban, Coe acknowledges need for solution
World.content:
World Athletics president Sebastian Coe has said the governing body's position on the exclusion of Russian athletes has not changed ahead of an upcoming Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) case, while acknowledging the need for a resolution.

Russian Athletics last month filed a fresh appeal with CAS challenging sanctions imposed by World Athletics, which has barred Russian and Belarusian athletes from international competition since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Our position hasn't changed, and this isn't about politics or passports. It's about the integrity of competition," Coe told reporters on the final day of the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

Aussie athletics star shocked at massive pay packet for coming second Australia's Nicola Olyslagers finishes second in the high jump at the new Ultimate Championship competition.

"From the age of 18, I believe that every position I've taken … it's about integrity and it's about competition, and that matters to me."

Coe declined to discuss the federation's legal strategy ahead of the arbitration proceedings but said World Athletics would continue to defend its stance.

"So our position won't change," he said. "And look, yes, this does need to be resolved, and I'm acutely aware of that. (But) I don't think our legal teams would be particularly thankful if I laid out our approach on this."

The comments came a month after Russian Athletics confirmed a new CAS filing, following an initial filing in July, aimed at overturning sanctions it says prevent it from fully representing Russian athletes internationally and participating in World Athletics decision-making processes.

Despite reaffirming the federation's position, Coe said he recognised the importance of ultimately restoring full global participation in the sport.

"We want a full complement of people on a global level competing in our sport, and that has to be our overall objective. Of course, it does."

The Lausanne-based CAS serves as sport's highest arbitration body and is expected to hear Russian Athletics' challenge in the coming months.

World Athletics has maintained one of the toughest positions of any international federation since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, while some sports have gradually reintroduced Russian and Belarusian athletes under neutral status.

The International Skating Union has established a pathway for selected Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete as neutral competitors, although it confirmed earlier this week that Kamila Valieva and three other figure skaters had their neutral status revoked.

Russian state news agency TASS quoted Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev as saying that all the skaters affected by the ruling would appeal to CAS.

Reuters

World.title: Mas 'fulfils his destiny' to win historic Vuelta
World.content:
Enric Mas has finally delivered an expectant Spanish public an overall victory at the Vuelta a España, his win confirmed at the end of the final stage into Grenada on Sunday.

Mas finished safely in the peloton during the 21st and final stage of the race, won by Norway's Tobias Johannessen.

The 31-year-old from Mallorca held off four-time Vuelta champion Primož Roglič to become the first Spaniard to win the Vuelta since Alberto Contador in 2014.

Mas finished 2 minutes and 15 seconds ahead of Roglič overall, with Austria's Felix Gall finishing third at 2:44.

"It's just special," Mas told reporters after the race.

"It's been a day to remember, a special Vuelta, and it has been wonderful.

"There's always tension about what could happen, but you've seen it all went smoothly, so we're delighted and we enjoyed every kilometre today.

"It was a long wait and a long way to today. But to be honest, it was always special Vueltas, and this one I think is the special one."

Primož Roglič (left), has won four Vuelta's, while Enric Mas (centre) finally claimed his first aged 31. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Five-time Tour de France winner Tadej Pogačar had come into the race as the overwhelming favourite for victory, building an ominous lead of 3 minutes 50 seconds by the end of the seventh stage.

The freakish Slovenian star had won three of the six completed stages at that stage and looked set to claim a win of unparalleled dominance in the modern era.

However, the two-time reigning world champion badly crashed on the eighth stage of the race, breaking his collar bone and fracturing his neck, ending his season.

From that point though, Mas, who had tested Pogačar on the mountainous fourth stage in Andorra, dominated the race alongside his much-maligned Movistar team.

Mas had finished second at his home grand tour three times, in 2018, 2021 and 2022, and also finished third in 2024.

When he finished second to Simon Yates in 2018, triumphing on the queen stage at that year's race, there was an expectation that Mas would become the heir to seven-time grand tour winner Contador as Spanish cycling's next big thing.

Mas even spent his junior years racing with the Alberto Contador Academy, indicating just how high hopes were that he would excel.

And although Mas has achieved plenty, finishing in the top six overall at grand tours eight times over the course of his career, the expected Contador-like dominance never eventuated.

It is telling that long-time AS reporter Juan Gutiérrez entitled his post-Vuelta piece: "Enric Mas cumple su destino", "Enric Mas fulfils his destiny".

Movistar switched their usual blue jerseys for red ones to honour Enric Mas's achievement. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

Contador wrote in Spanish newspaper AS that he was "very happy and incredibly excited" to see Mas achieve his potential.

"I know how hard he's worked these past few years and how much criticism he's always faced," Contador said.

"Instead of letting it get him down, he turned it into motivation to demonstrate the talent he truly possesses.

"Every cyclist develops in their own way and, in Enric's case, it was fast because he finished second in the 2018 Vuelta a España.

"Then, when he didn't quite seal the deal, well, we all know how sports are — it seems like if you don't win, nothing has any merit.

"That's why cycling will be fair to Enric Mas for winning this Vuelta."

Contador acknowledged that Pogačar would likely had claimed victory had he remained in the race, but that Mas thoroughly deserved his victory.

" It's not a gift," Contador said. "It's thanks to his hard work and his form. He was the strongest. "

Santiago Buitrago of Colombia and Team Bahrain Victorious claimed the king of the mountains jersey, while British rider Oscar Onley won the white youth jersey.

Wout van Aert added some personal closure by claiming the green sprinter's jersey, and the super combative prize, after he crashed out while leading both the points and king of the mountains classifications in 2024.

"In a way this is finished business," van Aert said.

"After the near miss two years ago and the big injury I had afterwards, it was quite a disappointment.

"It makes it more special to be here, to come completely to the end, and to wear this beautiful jersey."

Tech.title: Trump throws out power plant climate pollution rules
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Environmental Protection Agency announced its plans today to kill any remaining standards on how much greenhouse gas pollution power plants are allowed to emit in the US. The move will only make electricity dirtier as AI, electric vehicles, and a revival of domestic manufacturing drive up power demand.

The EPA’s proposal today is a major escalation of President Donald Trump’s efforts to promote fossil fuels while making it easier to build out energy-hungry data centers. Environmental and consumer advocates, meanwhile, are fighting back — arguing that Trump’s deregulation spree comes with higher costs for the environment, public health, and Americans’ pocketbooks.

A major escalation of President Donald Trump’s efforts to promote fossil fuels while making it easier to build out energy-hungry data centers

“Failure to limit climate pollution means more children ending up in the emergency room with asthma attacks and heatstroke, more families struggling to rebuild homes after harrowing storms,” Moms Clean Air Force director and cofounder Dominique Browning said in an emailed statement. “It means higher health care bills, higher insurance costs, and more economic struggle at a time when Americans cannot afford it.”

There is scientific consensus that greenhouse gas pollution from fossil fuels causes climate change. But in its press release today, the EPA argues that greenhouse gas pollution is “out of its scope to regulate” because its impacts are “global in nature, and any potential public health harms are too uncertain, conjectural, remote, and convoluted to tie specifically to the U.S. power sector.” The US has produced more greenhouse gas pollution than any other country in history and is still a leading carbon emitter after China.

The agency today is finalizing its repeal of Biden-era greenhouse gas requirements for power plants, as well as proposing the elimination of any remaining limits to that climate pollution for the power sector. The EPA claims the finalized rule would save $310 billion while the additional proposed actions would shave off $370 million “in direct compliance costs.”

Related Trump is giving data centers a pass to pollute

The EPA’s proposed changes will be open for public comment for 45 days, and are likely to face a raft of legal challenges. “The Sierra Club will fight back against this reckless and dangerous proposal with everything we have in the courts, in Congress, and in communities across the country,” Sierra Club chief program officer Holly Bender said in an emailed press statement. “While wildfires rage, floods devastate communities, and families struggle to afford skyrocketing electricity bills and insurance premiums, the Trump administration is handing the fossil fuel industry a license to keep polluting.”

Tech.title: Jensen Huang puts Trump on speakerphone onstage to announce robots won’t take over the world
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a call from President Trump on Monday while onstage at the All-In Podcast’s All-In Summit. It’s not the first time Huang has taken a call from the president during work, but this time he put Trump on speakerphone before a big crowd.

During the call, the president launched into his take on recent fears about AI development, which he called a “hoax,” and told the crowd that “the robots will not be taking over.”

It’s already a frothy week for AI news. The call with the president followed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s long essay published this weekend titled “We Must Pace the Frontier” where he argued for slowing down AI development and coordination between governments. The essay sparked many responses from AI executives, who generally agreed. But Trump pushed back in Truth Social posts on Monday and repurposed some of what he said in those posts at the event. Heard onstage, Trump also commented on data centers, claiming there would be communities that would be “dying” without data centers but were now “really wealthy” (though without providing specifics).

Huang did not push back, saying instead that “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people.” Huang also appealed to Trump by telling him he was speaking to “thousands” of people.

Tech.title: Valve’s virtual reality plans hit actual reality
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Steam Frame headset is here, and it may not surprise you: it was supposed to cost less than $1,059. “We set out to come out with a device that would have been far more affordable, but the global RAM market, the global storage market have impacted us the same way they’ve impacted everybody,” Valve developer Jeremy Selan told the BBC. “We fought hard to get it even to this price.”

I haven’t yet seen Valve say whether it’s selling the Steam Frame at cost, like the company confirmed it was doing with the $1,049 Steam Machine living room PC. But Valve developer Pierre-Loup Griffais hinted maybe so in an interview with Tom’s Hardware: “there’s not really any sort of the kind of distortion compared to just the price of the parts in there.”

When IGN asked Griffais why Valve didn’t simply ship the Steam Frame with less RAM, he answered: “I think at this point, things were a little bit too far in development to fully rethink the product.”

When it first announced the Steam Frame, Valve said it was targeting a lower price than its previous Valve Index headset, which cost $999 at launch and required a direct plug into a PC. The Steam Frame is wireless, can stream from a PC over Wi-Fi or its included 6GHz USB wireless dongle, and it can also play not-so-demanding games on its own Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip and 16GB of RAM. Valve said that amount of RAM helped it get Half-Life: Alyx running natively on the headset.

While the price might be high, Valve says it’s “pretty comfortable” with it because other computing gear is getting more expensive at the same time.

“[I]f you look at the memory and anything that has a similar amount of memory, it’s kind of trending the same direction and Steam Machine is not really getting more expensive than a comparable PC,” Griffais told IGN. “They’re kind of evolving at the same spot in the same market, and I think the same will apply to the Frame as well.”

Tech.title: The best deals from Nintendo’s ‘customer appreciation’ sale
